nano-ros Book

Welcome

Explanation · Level 1: First contact

nano-ros runs ROS 2 nodes on microcontrollers and real-time operating systems, and those nodes talk to an ordinary ROS 2 system on your computer. In your first hour you install the nros command, scaffold a talker for an Arm Cortex-M3 board, run it in an emulator, and watch its messages arrive in ros2 topic echo. You need no board and you write no code to get there.

The talker you will run

The first Tutorial chapter scaffolds a workspace with one node package. Its code is a ROS 2 talker. This excerpt is the part that does the work:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
    let mut node = ctx.create_node(nros::NodeOptions::new("talker"))?;
    node.create_publisher_for_topic::<StringMsg>("/chatter")?;
    node.create_timer_for_callback_name("on_tick", TimerDuration::from_millis(1000))?;
    Ok(())
}

fn on_callback(state: &mut i32, callback: Callback<'_>, ctx: &mut CallbackCtx<'_>) {
    if callback.as_str() == "on_tick" {
        *state = state.wrapping_add(1);
        let mut msg = StringMsg::default();
        let _ = write!(msg.data, "Hello World: {}", *state);
        if ctx.publish_to_topic::<StringMsg, 64>("/chatter", &msg).is_ok() {
            log::info!("Publishing: '{}'", msg.data);
        }
    }
}
}

The node creates a publisher on /chatter and a one-second timer. Each tick publishes a std_msgs/String. You run it with nros run sensor_node, which builds the firmware, boots it in QEMU, and prints the board’s console:

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 3'

In a second terminal, the ROS 2 command line sees the same messages:

data: 'Hello World: 2'
---
data: 'Hello World: 3'
---

Nothing on the ROS 2 side knows that the talker is firmware on an emulated microcontroller. It is a ROS 2 node publishing a ROS 2 message type, and the ROS 2 tools you already use receive it. The same chapter also runs the talker as a process on your Linux host, for when you have no emulator set up.

Who nano-ros is for

nano-ros serves three kinds of work. Each has a budget that the book is written and tested against:

  • Education. Courses and labs on robotics and embedded systems. The install takes 15 minutes, a lab fits a two-hour session, and every seat gets the same result.
  • Field solutions. Engineers and technicians who build a system for each customer, often on a board they were handed. The target is 30 minutes from an unopened box to ros2 topic echo showing the board’s data.
  • Industrial. Teams who build products where safety and robustness matter. The same inputs give the same image, every fact about a board is on a page, and a build runs with no network.

Two more readers use the book: ROS 2 developers moving existing nodes onto a microcontroller, and porters who add a board or a platform. Choose your path gives each of the five a route through the book, in order, with its budget.

What you get

  • One node, any supported board. You write a node once. Moving it to another board is one line in the workspace’s configuration, the board’s name. The cross-compiler, linker flags, middleware and memory sizes follow from that line, so neither your code nor your build files change.
  • Your ROS 2 graph as it is. Your nodes join a stock ROS 2 system over Zenoh, through rmw_zenoh_cpp, or over DDS, through rmw_cyclonedds_cpp. Topics, services and actions work in both directions.
  • The middleware you choose, with the same code. Zenoh needs no agent. XRCE-DDS works with the micro-ROS agent. Cyclone DDS speaks plain RTPS. Switching between them is a one-line change and a rebuild.
  • A fit for a small microcontroller. The core runs with no operating system, and the heap is optional: whether an image needs one depends on the middleware you choose. Memory for nodes, topics and messages is sized when you build, in fixed pools.
  • Rust, C or C++. The core is Rust, with C and C++ APIs over it. The C API follows rclc conventions, and the C++ API uses rclcpp’s names. One workspace can mix all three.
  • Messages that match your peers. Message bindings are generated from the ROS 2 install you build against, so the types and their hashes are the ones your ROS 2 nodes use.
  • Claims you can check. Each board’s support level, where it runs, and how often it is tested come from one registry. The book prints them on generated pages, and nros board show <board> prints the same facts from the nros you installed.

Where nano-ros differs from ROS 2

nano-ros keeps ROS 2’s vocabulary (nodes, publishers, subscriptions, services, actions, timers, parameters, QoS) and its wire format. It is not a port of rclcpp, and some things you rely on in ROS 2 work differently:

  • Choices happen at build time. The middleware, the board and the memory sizes are fixed when you build. A running image cannot load a different middleware or create more topics than it was built for.
  • The executor comes first. An executor opens the middleware session and owns the nodes, instead of a global init followed by nodes.
  • A node is code you build into an image. On a microcontroller there is no process to start with ros2 run. The workspace says which board each image runs on, and nros run builds and boots it.
  • Parameters are smaller. Each node keeps its own parameter store, with no descriptors or change callbacks yet.
  • Some ROS 2 tools need the host. ros2 topic echo and ros2 node list run on your computer and see the board’s nodes. Runtime introspection on the board itself is limited.

How nano-ros differs from ROS 2 and micro-ROS gives each difference and its reason, and compares nano-ros with micro-ROS, the other ROS 2 stack for microcontrollers.

Does it run on my board?

Supported Boards lists every board the release knows, with its support level and where it runs: on your host, in an emulator, or on hardware. Board support levels says what each level means. These pages are generated from the board registry, so they always match the release.

Every board in this book has a way to run without its hardware: on your host, in an emulator, or in an emulated twin of the board. The first chapter uses QEMU’s model of the MPS2-AN385, an Arm Cortex-M3 board, because it boots in seconds and needs nothing but your computer. Boards with a hardware twin, such as the Nucleo-F767ZI, run the same firmware in an emulator first and then on the board.

A board that is not in the registry can still run nano-ros. You add it from your own tree, without changing nano-ros: Extending nano-ros shows how.

Choose your path

How-to · Level 1: First contact

Pick the card that matches your work and follow its route in order. Each step needs only the steps above it, so you never read a page that assumes one you skipped. Each card also states its budget: the time or the property the route is written and tested to meet.

Every route starts with Install. If you are not sure which card fits, start with Education: its first chapters are the common start of every other route.

Education

For: instructors and students in a course or lab on robotics or embedded systems.

Budget: a 15-minute install on each seat, labs that fit a two-hour session, and the same result on every seat.

Route:

  1. Install on each seat.
  2. Run a talker on an emulated board. The output it prints is the result to check on every seat.
  3. What you just built: the node package and the workspace around it.
  4. Add a second node, in Rust, C or C++.
  5. Pick and configure the RMW. Cyclone DDS needs no router, which keeps a lab machine simple.
  6. Your own message.
  7. Services and actions: the server, client and action templates in the C node chapter.
  8. Parameters and launch files.
  9. The lab’s board: its page under Get started on your board, such as Nucleo-F767ZI, or its entry in Supported Boards.

Field solutions

For: engineers and technicians who build a system for each customer, often on a board they were handed.

Budget: 30 minutes from an unopened box to ros2 topic echo showing the board’s data.

Route:

  1. Install.
  2. Your board’s page under Get started on your board. It runs the board’s emulated twin first, then the board itself: Nucleo-F767ZI. For any other board, find it in Supported Boards; its page names the chapter that runs it.
  3. Talk to ROS 2: the board’s topics in your ROS 2 graph, in both directions.

Industrial

For: teams who build products where safety and robustness matter.

Budget: reproducible, auditable and offline. The same inputs give the same image, every fact about a board is on a page, and the build runs with no network.

Route:

  1. Install.
  2. Background: the execution model, static memory and pools and safety.
  3. User guide: pin a release and work offline, build inside a vendor tree for air-gapped CI, and deploy to production.
  4. Reference: board support levels and the configuration keys. nros doctor --report prints the support level of every board your images name, as a report you can file with a review.

ROS 2 developer porting nodes

For: developers with existing rclcpp nodes who want them on a microcontroller.

Budget: Install’s 15 minutes, then the first chapter’s run. The port itself depends on your node, so this route sets no time for it.

Route:

  1. Install.
  2. Run a talker on an emulated board, to see the toolchain work before your own code is in it.
  3. How nano-ros differs from ROS 2.
  4. Port a C++ node.
  5. Move a ROS 2 project over.

Board porter

For: developers who bring nano-ros to a board, a platform or a transport it does not support yet.

Budget: Install’s 15 minutes, then the first chapter’s run. Porting is development work, so this route sets no time for it.

Route:

  1. Install.
  2. Run a talker on an emulated board and What you just built.
  3. How a build becomes an image.
  4. Extending nano-ros, then a custom board package. A board of yours lives in your own tree.
  5. nano-ros Internals, when the port needs a change inside nano-ros itself, such as a new platform.

If none of these fit

Read Welcome for what nano-ros is and what it is not, then follow the Education route as far as you need. Its first two chapters are the shortest way to see nano-ros run. If a step fails, Troubleshooting lists the problems readers meet in their first ten minutes.

The three purposes and their budgets are RFC-0116 D1. The five cards are RFC-0124 D10.

Install

How-to · Level 1: First contact

This page takes a Linux machine to one that builds nano-ros, in about 15 minutes. You install a few host packages, install the nros command, and let nros setup fetch the toolchains for your board. There is no nano-ros checkout and no system-wide install: everything lands under ~/.nros.

Before you start

  • A Linux host. The book’s steps are tested on Ubuntu 22.04, and the host packages below also cover Fedora and Arch. macOS is not supported.
  • ROS 2 Humble, with its Zenoh middleware. Install it from the ROS 2 documentation, then add ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp. nano-ros generates your project’s message bindings from this install, and the Tutorial watches your nodes with its ros2 command. You source it before your first build; the Tutorial shows where.
  • A network connection for this install. To install on a machine with no network, see Install options.

Steps

1. Install the host packages

The host needs git, curl, a C toolchain, CMake, Python 3, zstd, and the Python packages that ROS message generation uses. Run the line for your distribution.

Debian or Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y git curl ca-certificates build-essential \
    cmake pkg-config python3 python3-dev zstd \
    python3-catkin-pkg python3-empy python3-lark python3-yaml

Fedora:

sudo dnf install -y git curl ca-certificates gcc gcc-c++ make \
    cmake pkgconf-pkg-config python3 python3-devel python3-pip zstd
pip install --user catkin_pkg 'empy==3.3.4' lark PyYAML

Arch:

sudo pacman -S --needed git curl base-devel cmake python python-pip zstd
pip install --user --break-system-packages catkin_pkg 'empy==3.3.4' lark PyYAML

Fedora and Arch ship no packages for the Python side, so the last line installs it with pip, into your home directory. The command finishes with no error, and a package that is already installed is left as it is. Host packages says what each package is for, and how to use a virtual environment instead.

2. Install the nros command

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.nros/bin:$PATH"   # install.sh prints this line too

The installer downloads the newest release for your host, checks its checksum, and ends with lines like these:

nros-install: installed 0.6.0
nros-install:   /home/you/.nros/sdk/nros/0.6.0
nros-install:   /home/you/.nros/bin/nros -> /home/you/.nros/sdk/nros/0.6.0/bin/nros

nros-install: next →  nros setup <board>    (e.g. `nros setup linux`)

Add the export PATH=… line to your shell’s startup file, such as ~/.bashrc, so that nros is on your PATH in every new terminal.

3. Check the install

nros version

It prints the version of the command, of the code it generates, and of the libraries it was built with:

nros 0.6.0
codegen version 18
play_launch d9b79f2bf4505a04b5351c83e916aefaadaf805e
ros-launch-manifest v0.2.0

Your numbers are those of the release you installed.

4. Provision your board

nros setup fetches what a board needs: the cross-compiler, the emulator, the middleware’s host tools and the board’s sources, plus a Rust toolchain if the host has none. You do not install a cross-compiler yourself.

nros setup <board> --rmw <zenoh|xrce|cyclonedds>

Replace <board> and the middleware with the ones you run first:

  • For the first Tutorial chapter, the emulated Cortex-M3 board: mps2-an385-baremetal with zenoh. The chapter runs this step for you.
  • For a talker on this machine: linux with cyclonedds. Cyclone DDS runs inside your process, so it needs no router and no agent.
  • For any other board, its name from nros board list.

When the board is ready, the last line names it:

nros setup: linux ready; locked in /home/you/.nros/…

A board whose packages are already present prints nros setup: linux — all packages already present instead.

If it doesn’t work

  • nros: command not found. This shell does not have ~/.nros/bin on its PATH. Run the export PATH=… line from step 2, and add it to your shell’s startup file.
  • The installer stops with a checksum error. The download was cut short or changed. Run the curl line again. The installer never installs a release whose checksum it cannot check.
  • nros setup says it is building from source. The release has no prebuilt package for your host, so nros setup builds it. That is normal and takes several minutes. nros setup <board> --dry-run shows the plan before anything is fetched.
  • Something else. nros doctor checks the install: the command, the store under ~/.nros, and the version a project pins. It names what is wrong and the command that fixes it.

Troubleshooting covers what goes wrong in the first build and run, such as an unsourced ROS 2 shell.

Nucleo-F767ZI (Zephyr, Renode twin)

How-to · Level 1: First contact

Support level: nucleo-f767zi-zephyr. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

One talker on an ST Nucleo-F767ZI (STM32F767ZI, Cortex-M7) running Zephyr 3.7, talking to ROS 2 over the board’s USB serial port. You do not need the board: Renode emulates it on your machine, and its USART3, the UART the Nucleo’s ST-LINK carries to your USB port, is wired to your host the way the cable would be. No network is configured anywhere in this chapter; ethernet comes after it.

This chapter assumes a Linux x86_64 host (or the container the install page describes) with a C/C++ compiler, ROS 2 Humble with ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp, and the install done, so nros is on your PATH. It uses Zephyr’s own tools the way the Zephyr chapter does; read that one for what each piece is. WiFi is deferred to the Zephyr 4.4 line, where the Pico W’s WiFi driver exists, so no chapter here opens over WiFi yet.

Provision the board

Zephyr’s host tools first: west and the build tools Zephyr’s Getting Started lists (nros setup installs no system packages). On Debian/Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git cmake ninja-build gperf \
    device-tree-compiler python3-pip python3-venv xz-utils file wget
pip3 install --user west
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

Then the board:

nros setup nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --rmw zenoh
export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)"

That fetches what the board needs into a shared store under ~/.nros: the Zephyr SDK, the zenoh-pico sources, the Rust target, and Renode, the emulator the board runs in here. It installs no router: the router is ROS’s rmw_zenohd, from the ROS 2 install above.

A west workspace that pins Zephyr 3.7 and fetches only the modules this board builds with, hal_stm32 among them (import: true would fetch every vendor HAL):

mkdir -p nucleo_ws/manifest && cd nucleo_ws
cat > manifest/west.yml <<'WEST_YML'
manifest:
  remotes:
    - name: zephyrproject-rtos
      url-base: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos
  projects:
    - name: zephyr
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: v3.7.0
      import:
        name-allowlist: [cmsis, picolibc, mbedtls, tinycrypt, mcuboot, net-tools, hal_stm32]
    # Zephyr's Rust support. The board's setup patches it, so the workspace
    # needs it even for a C talker. Pinned to the revision nano-ros builds
    # with on the 3.7 line (it has no release tags).
    - name: zephyr-lang-rust
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: 404fcefdbab0f2711cd342a1fab9d2eda52a1ba9
      path: modules/lang/rust
  self:
    path: manifest
WEST_YML
west init -l manifest
west update --narrow -o=--depth=1
pip3 install --user -r zephyr/scripts/requirements-base.txt
export ZEPHYR_BASE="$PWD/zephyr"

Last, give the workspace the patches nano-ros carries for Zephyr 3.7:

nros setup board nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --zephyr-workspace "$PWD"

Scaffold the talker

nros new nucleo_ws --board nucleo-f767zi-zephyr --template talker --lang c
cd nucleo_ws

That wrote a workspace with two packages: src/nucleo_node/, the C talker, and src/nucleo_node_bringup/, whose system.toml ends in the [image.zephyr] block naming the board. The Zephyr application itself is generated under build/ when you build. The board reaches the zenoh router on your host through USART3, which Zephyr calls serial@40004800, at 115200 baud. Say so with one line at the end of the bringup’s system.toml:

echo 'locator = "serial/serial@40004800#baudrate=115200"' >> src/nucleo_node_bringup/system.toml

The line lands in the [image.zephyr] block, under the board = "nucleo-f767zi-zephyr" line the scaffold wrote. The board’s own configuration already turns Zephyr’s IP stack off and gives USART3 to zenoh; its console is USART6.

Run in the twin

Source ROS 2, then build and run. ROS 2 provides the router, and its message definitions are what the build generates the talker’s std_msgs code from. This first run records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later runs of it need no sourced shell:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run nucleo_node --expect 'Publishing:'

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after

nros run generates what the build reads (the message code and the board’s build settings, under build/), builds the firmware through west (the first build takes a few minutes; later ones take seconds), boots it in Renode’s nucleo_f767zi machine with USART3 on a terminal device of your host, starts rmw_zenohd on that device, and then lets the board run. What it prints is the board’s console, USART6: *** Booting Zephyr OS build v3.7.0 ***, then the talker’s Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' and on. With --expect it stops everything and exits 0 at the first console line containing that text, and exits 1 if the board stops first.

Without --expect it keeps running until you press Ctrl-C. Start it that way in one terminal:

nros run nucleo_node

Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

See it from ROS 2

In a second terminal, ask ROS 2 for the topic. The router nros run started also listens where a ROS 2 node on this machine looks for one, so nothing needs to be configured:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

data: 'Hello World:

The talker publishes best-effort, so the echo asks for best-effort too. Ctrl-C in the first terminal stops Renode and the router together.

Ethernet

The Nucleo’s on-chip ethernet MAC works in Renode: the talker reached a router over tcp/ with Zephyr’s eth_stm32_hal driver in an early spike. That run needed a host tap device bridged to Renode’s virtual switch, which takes CAP_NET_ADMIN (the spike made one inside a rootless network namespace), and nros run does not set one up yet. So this chapter stops at serial; the ethernet chapter comes with that support.

Flash a real board

On the bench, nros flash programs the same image through Zephyr’s own runner for the board, OpenOCD over the Nucleo’s ST-LINK:

nros flash

Not replayed. No probe runs this flash line (a CI runner has no board), so it is written from the board’s runner, not measured (tracking issue).

On the real board USART3 is the ST-LINK’s virtual COM port, so the zenoh link arrives on your host as a USB serial device (/dev/ttyACM0, say), and the router listens there instead of on Renode’s terminal device. The console, USART6, is on the board’s pins rather than on the USB cable.

If it didn’t work

  • nros run names what failed and the log it wrote. no runner package drives or the plan's tools name no renode: run the nros setup nucleo-f767zi-zephyr step again, which installs Renode.
  • A router that would not start usually means rmw_zenohd was not found (source your ROS 2 setup in that terminal) or another router already holds port 7447 on this machine.
  • A build that cannot find hal_stm32: the west workspace predates the hal_stm32 line in its allowlist; add it and run west update again.
  • Everything else: Troubleshooting - First 10 Minutes.

Where to go next

First Project

Tutorial · Level 1: First contact

Support level: mps2-an385-baremetal and the Linux host. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

In this chapter you scaffold a talker for an Arm Cortex-M3 board, run it in QEMU, and watch its messages arrive in ROS 2. You write no code and edit no configuration to get there.

What this assumes: a Linux host with ROS 2 Humble and its Zenoh middleware (ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp) installed, or the container from Installation Details, and the install done, so nros is on your PATH.

What it leaves for later: the board talks to your machine over its serial port, the way a real board’s first program does. The network comes in the board’s own chapter, Bare-metal Cortex-M3. WiFi is not covered yet: it arrives with the Zephyr 4.4 line.

Provision the board

nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal --rmw zenoh

This fetches the Arm cross-compiler, a QEMU that emulates the MPS2-AN385 board, and the Rust target. Nothing is installed system-wide.

Scaffold

nros new sensor_ws --board mps2-an385-baremetal --template talker
cd sensor_ws

That wrote two packages:

sensor_ws/
└── src/
    ├── sensor_node/            # your node: package.xml, Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs
    └── sensor_node_bringup/    # which board it runs on; you don't need to open it yet

sensor_node is the code: a talker that publishes std_msgs/String on /chatter once a second. sensor_node_bringup says what that code runs on. The scaffold filled it in, and this chapter never needs you to open it.

This is the shape of examples/mps2-an385-baremetal/rust/talker/ in the nano-ros repository, the example kept for reading beside this chapter: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own, because nros run generates it.

Run

Source ROS 2 first, then build and run. ROS 2 provides the router the board talks to, and its message definitions are what nros run generates the talker’s std_msgs bindings from. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so a later build of it needs no sourced shell (the router still does):

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run sensor_node --expect 'Publishing:'

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after

nros run does everything between your source and a running board: it builds the firmware (the first build compiles nano-ros for the Cortex-M3 and takes a few minutes; later builds take seconds), boots it in QEMU with the board’s serial port connected to a terminal device on your host, and starts the router on that device. The talker’s own output is the board’s console. With --expect, nros run stops everything and exits 0 the moment the console prints a line containing that text, and exits 1 if the board stops first, which makes it a one-line check that the whole path works.

Without --expect it keeps streaming until you press Ctrl-C, which stops QEMU and the router together. Start it that way in one terminal (source ROS 2 first if it is a new one, because the router comes from ROS 2):

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run sensor_node

Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

See it in ROS 2

Leave nros run going. In a second terminal:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

data: 'Hello World:

The talker publishes best-effort, and ros2 topic echo defaults to reliable, which receives nothing from it. That is why the command asks for best-effort.

Change it

Open src/sensor_node/src/lib.rs, change the "Hello World" text, and run nros run sensor_node again. It rebuilds what changed and boots the new image.

No QEMU, no router: run it on this machine

The same flow runs on your Linux host. Cyclone DDS needs no router, so nothing else has to be running. The build still generates the messages from ROS 2, so source it before the first run (later runs of host_ws need no sourced shell):

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds
nros new host_ws --board linux --template talker --lang cpp --rmw cyclonedds
cd host_ws
nros run host_node --expect 'Publishing:' --timeout 120

Only the board in the scaffold line changed. The node code is the same shape, and so is every command after it.

If nothing appears

  • nros run stops at once and names AMENT_PREFIX_PATH: this shell has not sourced ROS 2, and no earlier build of the workspace recorded it. Run source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash and run again.
  • nros run stops at once and names the router: it could not find the Zenoh router. Source ROS 2 in that shell (and install ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp if it is missing), or point NROS_RMW_ZENOHD at an rmw_zenohd binary.
  • No Publishing: line within a minute of boot: the router started but the board did not reach it. nros run names the router’s log when it stops.
  • nros run lists several names and refuses: you are in a workspace with more than one thing to run. Name one of the spellings it prints.
  • ros2 topic echo prints nothing: check the --qos-reliability best_effort flag and the RMW_IMPLEMENTATION line.

First 10 Minutes has the rest.

Design background

The chapter follows RFC-0116 D5 and D6 and RFC-0121 D4 and D5. Its pointer to the copy-out talker follows RFC-0122 (behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI) D3.

Anatomy of What You Just Built

Tutorial · Level 1: First contact

Two packages, two roles. Everything you add to this project later is another package with one of these roles, or a few more lines in the bringup. The shape never changes; it only gains packages.

If you come from ROS 2, each role is something you already know:

Your workspaceRoleIn ROS 2 terms
src/sensor_node/Node packagea composable node (rclcpp_components)
src/sensor_node_bringup/Bringup package<pkg>_bringup: configuration and launch, no code
(generated under build/)Entrythe composition container, the main()

The node package: the code

A node package is one node, as a library. It has no main() and names no board:

src/sensor_node/
├── Cargo.toml          # a library crate; dependencies only
├── package.xml         # ROS package manifest: std_msgs is declared here
└── src/lib.rs          # the Talker: a 1 s timer that publishes on /chatter

lib.rs declares what the node creates (a publisher, a timer) and what its callback does. Message types come from package.xml’s dependencies and are generated during the build; you never write them by hand.

The same node builds for any board. Nothing in this package says mps2-an385, zenoh or serial: those are the bringup’s.

The bringup package: what runs where

src/sensor_node_bringup/ holds no code, only package.xml and system.toml:

[system]
name = "sensor_node"
rmw = "zenoh"                        # which middleware
ros_edition = "humble"               # which ROS 2 your peers run
domain_id = 0

[[component]]                        # which nodes run
pkg = "sensor_node"
class = "sensor_node::Talker"
name = "sensor_node"

[image.baremetal]                    # one block per thing you deploy
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"

Every configuration choice lives here, never in a node package. Moving the talker to another board is a new [image.*] block; switching middleware is the rmw line. Neither touches src/sensor_node/.

The launch file: generated until you need one

ROS 2 projects describe what to start in a launch file. This bringup has no launch/ directory, so nros run generated one from the [[component]] rows, after the first build. To see it:

cat build/nros/launch/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.launch.xml

When you need what only a launch file can say (a parameter, a remap, a launch argument), add launch/system.launch.xml to the bringup and it replaces the generated one. The file is the ROS 2 launch XML schema, so a launch file from another ROS 2 project pastes in unchanged.

The entry: the binary, also generated

There is no entry package under src/. nros run (and nros build) reads each [image.*] block and generates the entry for it under build/: a main() that constructs each component, applies the launch file’s parameters, and runs them on one executor. Running the entry is launching the system; there is no separate ros2 launch step.

What is yours and what is generated

Everything under src/ is yours to edit and commit. build/ holds everything derived: generated message code, the launch file, the resolved system and the entry. Nothing in build/ is committed; if you can regenerate it, it does not belong in git.

  • Your own message package

  • First Node in C or C++: the same node package in another language.

Design background

RFC-0121 D1 to D3.

First Node — Rust (Linux)

Tutorial · Level 1: First contact

Build, run, and verify a single nano-ros publisher node on Linux in about ten minutes. Uses the canonical Zenoh backend. The zenoh router comes from ROS 2 (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd) — nano-ros no longer ships one. Rather not run a router? Use --rmw cyclonedds instead: it needs no router at all (see Choosing an RMW). Either way the build generates its messages from your ROS 2 install, so you need ROS 2 sourced for the first build.

Stuck? See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes for the common first-build errors.

Prereqs

The nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin), then provision the Linux host (installs the zenoh client stack into a shared store; the router itself comes from your ROS 2 install):

nros setup linux --rmw zenoh

Scaffold the talker

nros new talker_ws --board linux --template talker --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd talker_ws

That wrote a workspace with two packages:

talker_ws/
└── src/
    ├── talker_node/            # node package: the code
    │   ├── package.xml         # ROS manifest: <depend>std_msgs</depend>
    │   ├── Cargo.toml          # a library crate; names no board and no RMW
    │   └── src/lib.rs          # the Talker: a 1 s timer publishing /chatter
    └── talker_node_bringup/    # bringup package: what runs where
        ├── package.xml
        └── system.toml         # the board, the RMW, the node it runs

The node package

talker_node is a library. It has no main(), and nothing in it names a board, an RMW or a ROS edition. src/lib.rs declares what the node creates (a publisher on /chatter, a 1 s timer) and what the timer callback does, and its last line exports the node:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
nros::node!(Talker);
}

The program’s main() is generated by the build, from the bringup. That is what lets the same node package go into a Linux image today and a Cortex-M image later without a second copy. Growing your workspace walks through lib.rs line by line.

Cargo.toml holds Rust facts only: the [lib] target, the class the package registers, and its dependencies.

[lib]
path = "src/lib.rs"

[package.metadata.nros.node]
class = "talker_node::Talker"
name = "talker_node"

[dependencies]
nros = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = ["rmw-cffi", "macros"] }
std_msgs = { path = "../../generated/std_msgs", default-features = false }  # nros-managed

nano-ros crates are declared registry-style (version = "*"), but nothing of nano-ros is on crates.io: the build points them at the SDK the nros on PATH carries. The settings that takes (the [patch.crates-io] table, the target triple, linker flags) are generated under build/ from the bringup, never written by hand and never committed. No path in the package names where nano-ros lives, so the workspace copies anywhere.

Message packages are not listed by hand either: package.xml’s <depend>std_msgs</depend> is the one statement, and the build writes the matching # nros-managed row. To use another message package, add its <depend>; the next nros build adds the row.

The bringup package

talker_node_bringup/system.toml is the whole deployment statement:

[system]
name = "talker_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
ros_edition = "humble"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "talker_node"
class = "talker_node::Talker"
name = "talker_node"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

The [[component]] row says which node runs; [image.linux] says it runs on this machine. The --rmw you passed to nros new lives here and nowhere else, so switching RMW or ROS edition is editing rmw or ros_edition and building again.

Native (host) images read the locator and domain from environment variables (NROS_LOCATOR — the retired ZENOH_LOCATOR is refused at startup — and ROS_DOMAIN_ID). Embedded images bake theirs from the same [image.<id>] table (locator, and the address in net) — the shape shows up under the Embedded Starters section.

This is the same project as examples/linux/rust/talker/ on GitHub, the copy-out example for Rust on Linux: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own, since the build generates it. Its bringup goes further than the scaffold, with one image per RMW and ROS edition.

Configure

Three runtime knobs, each an env override on a built-in default:

KnobDefaultEnv override
Zenoh locatortcp/127.0.0.1:7447NROS_LOCATOR
ROS domain ID0ROS_DOMAIN_ID
Zenoh modeclientNROS_SESSION_MODE

On native these stay environment variables — [image.linux] declares no locator. An embedded image bakes them from its own [image.<id>] table instead; see the Configuration Guide.

Build

The build generates std_msgs from your ROS 2 install, so source it first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace; later builds and runs of talker_ws need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build            # builds the image `[image.linux]` declares

nros build prepares everything first: the message bindings package.xml declares, the generated main() for [image.linux], and the cargo settings derived from board = "linux", all under build/. Then it runs cargo. There is no step to run before it; when nothing changed, the preparation costs a comparison.

First build pulls dependencies (~3 minutes). Re-builds finish in seconds. When it finishes, nros build prints where the binary landed (under build/, never beside your sources) and how to run it.

Driving cargo yourself (an IDE, a CI step, --release) is supported: nros build --dry-run prints the exact cargo line, against the generated entry under build/. Before you open the workspace in an IDE, run the preparation on its own so rust-analyzer finds the generated crates:

nros configure

What it writes under build/ is regenerated on every build; never edit it, and never add a .cargo/config.toml of your own to carry board facts. Your own Rust-toolchain preferences go where cargo already looks for them — a parent directory or $CARGO_HOME.

Run

Two terminals (each command below blocks; keep them open):

# Terminal 1 — zenoh router (ROS 2's own). Blocks the shell until Ctrl-C.
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

# Terminal 2 — the talker. The talker logs via `log::info!`, so set
# RUST_LOG=info — without it `env_logger` only shows errors and the
# `Publishing:` lines stay hidden.
cd talker_ws
RUST_LOG=info nros run talker_node
# Expected output (on stderr):
#   [INFO  talker_node] Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
#   [INFO  talker_node] Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
#   …

nros run talker_node runs the bringup whose only node is talker_node, rebuilding first if anything changed. It keeps running until Ctrl-C.

That’s the nano-ros side fully working. Optional step: verify interop with stock ROS 2.

# Terminal 3 — stock ROS 2 with rmw_zenoh_cpp. It talks to the SAME
# router already running in terminal 1 (default tcp/127.0.0.1:7447).
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
# Talker publishes best-effort; stock `ros2 topic echo` defaults to
# RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing.
# Force best-effort to receive:
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

If ros2 topic echo shows no output despite the talker printing Publishing:, the routers aren’t peering — confirm both processes point at the same port (default tcp/127.0.0.1:7447).

Readiness signal. Within ~6 seconds of the program starting (session open + the first 1 s timer tick), the talker should print Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' — the count starts at 1, matching the official ROS 2 demo_nodes_cpp talker. If no Publishing: line in 30 seconds:

  1. Confirm RUST_LOG is set. Without RUST_LOG=info (or debug), env_logger filters out the Publishing: lines and the run looks silent even when it’s working.
  2. Confirm the router is running (terminal 1). Without it, the talker blocks on Executor::open indefinitely.
  3. Re-run with RUST_LOG=debug and look for “RMW session open failed” — usually a wrong locator or wrong port.
  4. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Retargeting

To run the same node on a board, add an image for it to src/talker_node_bringup/system.toml, named by that board’s id (Supported Boards), and provision it:

[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"

nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal --rmw zenoh
nros run talker_node_bringup:baremetal

Nothing in src/talker_node/ changes: the board’s descriptor supplies the target triple, the board crate and the memory budgets. With two images the short nros run talker_node no longer picks one, so name the image you mean; nros run lists the spellings when it refuses. The platform chapters scaffold with --board <board> from the start, which writes the image for you.

  • Generate bindings for custom .msg / .srv / .action files: Message Generation
  • Cross-compile for an RTOS: pick the right Embedded Starter from the next section (FreeRTOS / Zephyr / NuttX / ThreadX / ESP32 / Bare-metal Cortex-M3).

First Node — C (Linux)

Tutorial · Level 1: First contact

Build, run, and verify a single nano-ros publisher node on Linux from C. The node is a C library built with CMake; the program around it is generated. Uses the Zenoh backend.

Stuck? See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes for the common first-build errors.

Prereqs

The nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin), then provision the Linux host (installs the zenoh client stack into a shared store; the router itself comes from your ROS 2 install — ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd):

nros setup linux --rmw zenoh

Scaffold the talker

nros new c_talker_ws --board linux --template talker --lang c --rmw zenoh
cd c_talker_ws

That wrote a workspace with two packages:

c_talker_ws/
└── src/
    ├── c_talker_node/            # node package: the code
    │   ├── package.xml           # ROS manifest: <depend>std_msgs</depend>
    │   ├── CMakeLists.txt        # a library and its registration; no board facts
    │   └── src/Talker.c          # the talker: a 1 s timer publishing /chatter
    └── c_talker_node_bringup/    # bringup package: what runs where
        ├── package.xml
        └── system.toml           # the board, the RMW, the node it runs

This is the same project as examples/linux/c/talker/ on GitHub, the copy-out example for C on Linux: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own, since the build generates it.

The bringup package

c_talker_node_bringup/system.toml is the whole deployment statement, the same schema whatever language the node is written in:

[system]
name = "c_talker_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "c_talker_node"
class = "c_talker_node::Talker"
name = "c_talker_node"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

The [[component]] row says which node runs; [image.linux] says it runs on this machine. Nothing in the node package names a platform, a board or an RMW — and the package.xml <nano_ros deploy=… board=… rmw=…/> export that used to carry that tuple is retired and refused. Moving the talker to a board is another [image.<id>] block here, with no edit to src/c_talker_node/.

On native, locator + domain come from env vars (NROS_LOCATOR, ROS_DOMAIN_ID) with built-in defaults; an embedded image declares them in its own [image.<id>] table (locator, and its address in the board network file os_config names) and they are baked at build time (see Configuration).

The node package

A C node package is a library, not a program. The scaffolded CMakeLists.txt is (comments trimmed):

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(c_talker_node VERSION 0.1.0 LANGUAGES C)

set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 11)
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.c)

nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    PLUGIN c_talker_node::Talker
    EXECUTABLE c_talker_node
    SHAPE configure
    TYPED)

nano_ros_auto_add_library generates the C bindings the package declares and links nano-ros. nros_components_register_node registers the class the bringup’s [[component]] row names, the CMake spelling of ROS 2’s rclcpp_components_register_node.

There is no main(). The build generates one for each image, which opens the session and executor, creates the node, and hands both to your code. Your code is a state struct and a configure function, exported with RCLC_C_COMPONENT:

#include <stdio.h>
#include <rclc/rclc.h>
#include <std_msgs/msg/string.h>

typedef struct {
    rcl_publisher_t pub;
    rcl_timer_t timer;
    int32_t count;
    char text[32];
} talker_t;

static void on_tick(rcl_timer_t* timer, int64_t last_call_time) {
    talker_t* self = RCLC_CONTAINER_OF(timer, talker_t, timer);
    (void)last_call_time;
    self->count++;
    int n = snprintf(self->text, sizeof self->text, "Hello World: %d", (int)self->count);
    std_msgs__msg__String msg;
    msg.data.data = self->text;          // your buffer; nothing allocates
    msg.data.size = (size_t)n;
    msg.data.capacity = sizeof self->text;
    if (rcl_publish(&self->pub, &msg, NULL) == RCL_RET_OK) {
        printf("Publishing: '%s'\n", self->text);
    }
}

static rcl_ret_t talker_configure(rcl_node_t* node, rclc_executor_t* executor,
                                  talker_t* self) {
    self->count = 0;
    self->pub = rcl_get_zero_initialized_publisher();
    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_publisher_init_default(
        &self->pub, node, ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(std_msgs, msg, String), "/chatter");
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) return rc;
    self->timer = rcl_get_zero_initialized_timer();
    rc = rclc_timer_init_default(&self->timer, NULL, 1000000000ULL, on_tick);
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) return rc;
    return rclc_executor_add_timer(executor, &self->timer);
}

RCLC_C_COMPONENT(talker_t, talker_configure)

configure runs once at startup, on the generated entry’s own node and executor; after that the executor calls on_tick once a second. Because the entry owns startup, the same file runs on Linux and on a board whose C runtime never calls main (Zephyr, an RTOS startup task).

--template picks a different node: listener, server / client (AddTwoInts) or action-server / action-client (Fibonacci).

Generated messages take rosidl’s C names and member shape (std_msgs__msg__String in <std_msgs/msg/string.h>, msg.data.data / .size / .capacity). Their strings and sequences point at memory you own: wire them with the generated <Msg>__init_in(&msg, &storage) over a <Msg>__Storage, or point data at your own buffer as above and as micro-ROS code does. Nothing on this path allocates, so rosidl’s allocating <Msg>__init / __fini are not declared.

Configure

Three runtime knobs:

KnobDefaultEnv override
Zenoh locatortcp/127.0.0.1:7447NROS_LOCATOR
ROS domain ID0ROS_DOMAIN_ID
Node namec_talker_nodethe [[component]] row’s name (a launch file can remap it)

On an embedded image the same knobs are compile-baked from that image’s [image.<id>] table in system.toml (see Configuration).

Build

The build generates std_msgs from your ROS 2 install, so source it first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace; later builds and runs of c_talker_ws need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build

nros build prepares the build from the bringup (the generated main() for [image.linux] and a CMake root that adds your package), configures it with the SDK root and the toolchain file the board names, and builds it. The C message bindings are generated during that CMake configure, from the package’s declared dependencies. There is no step to run before it.

When it finishes, nros build prints what it built and how to run it:

nros build: next for `c_talker_node_bringup:linux`:
  artifact: /home/you/c_talker_ws/build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry
  run:
    nros run c_talker_node

Driving CMake yourself. The CMake root nros build configures is generated under build/, never at the workspace root, and nros build --dry-run prints the exact cmake lines it would run. To have that root in place without building (before opening the workspace in an IDE, or to run those lines by hand), prepare it on its own:

nros configure

For a CMake tree that is not a nano-ros workspace at all, see Build inside an existing CMake or vendor tree.

The first configure pulls and builds nano-ros’s Rust staticlibs (~3 minutes). Re-builds finish in seconds.

Run

Three terminals.

# 1. Start the zenoh router (ROS 2's own):
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

# 2. Run the talker:
cd c_talker_ws
nros run c_talker_node
# Expected output, once a second:
#   Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
#   Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
#   …

# 3. Verify from stock ROS 2:
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
# Talker publishes best-effort; stock `ros2 topic echo` defaults to
# RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing.
# Force best-effort to receive:
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

Readiness signal. Within ~6 seconds (session open + the first 1 s timer tick), the talker prints Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' on stdout — Rust + C + C++ all start the count at 1, matching the official ROS 2 demo talker. If it does not appear in 30 seconds:

  1. Confirm the router is running (terminal 1). Without it, the generated entry’s session open fails at once with -4 (RCLC_RET_NOT_FOUND — connection refused) and the program stops, naming the step.
  2. Wrong locator / unreachable host → same -4 signature in stderr. Reachable host but mismatched port → talker hangs on session-open handshake rather than returning a code.
  3. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

First Node — C++ (Linux)

Tutorial · Level 1: First contact

Build, run, and verify a single nano-ros publisher node on Linux from C++. The node is a C++ library built with CMake, in the ament shape; the program around it is generated. Uses the Zenoh backend.

Stuck? See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes for the common first-build errors.

Prereqs

The nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin), then provision the Linux host (installs the zenoh client stack into a shared store; the router itself comes from your ROS 2 install — ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd):

nros setup linux --rmw zenoh

Scaffold the talker

nros new cpp_talker_ws --board linux --template talker --lang cpp --rmw zenoh
cd cpp_talker_ws

That wrote a workspace with two packages:

cpp_talker_ws/
└── src/
    ├── cpp_talker_node/            # node package: the code
    │   ├── package.xml             # ROS manifest: <depend>std_msgs</depend>
    │   ├── CMakeLists.txt          # a library and its registration; no board facts
    │   ├── include/cpp_talker_node/Talker.hpp
    │   └── src/Talker.cpp          # the talker: a 1 s timer publishing /chatter
    └── cpp_talker_node_bringup/    # bringup package: what runs where
        ├── package.xml
        └── system.toml             # the board, the RMW, the node it runs

This is the same project as examples/linux/cpp/talker/ on GitHub, the copy-out example for C++ on Linux: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own, since the build generates it.

cpp_talker_node_bringup/system.toml is the whole deployment statement — [system] for the RMW and domain, one [[component]] row naming the node, and one [image.<id>] per target naming its board. No line of the node package names a platform, a board or an RMW, so moving the talker to a board is another [image.<id>] block in the bringup; First Node — C shows the file in full. The package.xml <nano_ros deploy=… board=… rmw=…/> export that used to carry that tuple is retired and refused.

The node package

The CMakeLists is the ament shape you already know — this is the scaffolded file, comments trimmed (the message-package Find-stubs make find_package(std_msgs) generate bindings on the fly):

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(cpp_talker_node VERSION 0.1.0 LANGUAGES C CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.cpp)

nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    PLUGIN cpp_talker_node::Talker
    EXECUTABLE cpp_talker_node
    SHAPE configure)

nros_components_register_node has rclcpp_components_register_node’s keywords: the class the bringup’s [[component]] row names, and its executable name.

LANGUAGES C CXX (not CXX alone): the per-target register stub is a C translation unit, so C must be enabled in this directory scope or the link fails. Backend selection is [system] rmw in the bringup, not CMake code and not a configure-line cache variable.

There is no main(). The node is a class with a configure(rclcpp::Node&) method, the shape of a composable node: the generated entry initialises nano-ros, creates the node, constructs your class in static storage and calls configure on it, then spins the executor.

// include/cpp_talker_node/Talker.hpp
#pragma once
#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>
#include "std_msgs.hpp"

namespace cpp_talker_node {

class Talker {
    ::rclcpp::Publisher<std_msgs::msg::String> pub_;
    ::rclcpp::Timer timer_;
    int count_ = 0;

    void on_tick();   // bound by &Talker::on_tick, not by a name

  public:
    ::rclcpp::Result configure(::rclcpp::Node& node);
};

}  // namespace cpp_talker_node

// src/Talker.cpp
#include "cpp_talker_node/Talker.hpp"
#include <cstdio>

namespace cpp_talker_node {

void Talker::on_tick() {
    char payload[64];
    std::snprintf(payload, sizeof payload, "Hello World: %d", ++count_);
    std_msgs::msg::String m;
    m.data = payload;
    if (pub_.publish(m).ok()) std::printf("Publishing: '%s'\n", m.data.c_str());
}

::rclcpp::Result Talker::configure(::rclcpp::Node& node) {
    ::rclcpp::Result r = node.create_publisher(pub_, "/chatter");
    if (!r.ok()) return r;
    return node.create_wall_timer<Talker, &Talker::on_tick>(timer_, 1000, this);
}

}  // namespace cpp_talker_node

The publisher and timer are typed wrappers over the C ABI, and every call returns a Result rather than throwing: every nano-ros build is -fno-exceptions. configure returns the first failure, and the generated entry halts naming the node that failed, so there is no unchecked construction to forget. Porting a ROS 2 C++ node covers the rclcpp-shaped constructors, shared_from_this() and rclcpp::TimerBase.

--template picks a different node: listener, server / client (AddTwoInts) or action-server / action-client (Fibonacci).

Configure

Three runtime knobs:

KnobDefaultOverride
Zenoh locatortcp/127.0.0.1:7447NROS_LOCATOR
ROS domain ID0ROS_DOMAIN_ID
Node namecpp_talker_nodethe [[component]] row’s name (a launch file can remap it)

On a hosted target the generated entry takes the locator and domain from the build, then from the environment variables. An embedded image declares its locator in its own [image.<id>] table and its address in the board network file os_config names, and bakes them at build time.

Build

The build generates std_msgs from your ROS 2 install, so source it first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace; later builds and runs of cpp_talker_ws need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build

nros build prepares the build from the bringup (the generated main() for [image.linux] and a CMake root that adds your package), configures it with the SDK root and the board’s toolchain file, and builds it. The C++ message bindings are generated during that CMake configure. There is no step to run before it.

When it finishes, nros build prints what it built and how to run it:

nros build: next for `cpp_talker_node_bringup:linux`:
  artifact: /home/you/cpp_talker_ws/build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry
  run:
    nros run cpp_talker_node

Driving CMake yourself. The CMake root is generated under build/, and nros build --dry-run prints the exact cmake lines it would run. To have that root in place without building (before opening the workspace in an IDE, or to run those lines by hand), prepare it on its own:

nros configure

For a CMake tree that is not a nano-ros workspace at all, see Build inside an existing CMake or vendor tree.

First configure builds nano-ros’s Rust staticlibs (~3 minutes). Re-builds finish in seconds.

Run

Three terminals.

# 1. zenoh router (ROS 2's own):
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

# 2. Run the talker:
cd cpp_talker_ws
nros run cpp_talker_node
# Expected output:
#   Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
#   Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
#   …

# 3. Verify from stock ROS 2:
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
# Talker publishes best-effort; stock `ros2 topic echo` defaults to
# RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing.
# Force best-effort to receive:
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

Readiness signal. Within ~6 seconds (session open + the first 1 s timer tick), the talker prints Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' — Rust + C

  • C++ all start the count at 1, matching the official ROS 2 demo talker. If it does not appear in 30 seconds:
  1. Confirm the router is running (terminal 1). Without it, the generated entry’s session open fails with -100 (TransportError) and the program stops, naming the step.
  2. -3 / -100 on stderr both mean the transport did not open: check NROS_LOCATOR and the router’s port.
  3. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Next

  • Add a subscriber: from the workspace root, nros new cpp_listener_node --lang cpp --template listener --to cpp_talker_node_bringup adds a second node package and its component row (Growing your workspace).
  • Services, actions and several C++ node packages in one workspace: the C++ language workspace, examples/workspaces/cpp/, where each paired example is an image row under its behaviour’s bringup (pubsub_bringup, service_bringup, action_bringup), and C / C++ multi-node workspaces.
  • Custom .msg / .srv / .action: Message Generation
  • Cross-compile for an RTOS: pick the right Embedded Starter from the next section.

Design background

  • RFC-0121: workspace-first project layout
  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The copy-out talker kept for each platform and language, and the language workspaces that hold the paired examples.

Choosing an RMW

Tutorial · Level 1: First contact

Every nano-ros binary picks its RMW (ROS Middleware) backend at build time. There are three: Cyclone DDS, Zenoh (zenoh-pico), and XRCE-DDS. This page helps you pick one and explains how each backend connects your device to a ROS 2 network. The mechanics of changing your pick are in Switch the RMW per image.

Start with Cyclone DDS

For getting started, use Cyclone DDS. It is the one backend that needs no daemon, router, or agent: a nano-ros node publishes with nothing else running, and a stock ROS 2 node using rmw_cyclonedds_cpp sees it directly — same RTPS wire protocol, same discovery, no translation layer in between.

The reason the other two are not the starting point: nano-ros ships no bridge process of its own. The zenoh router is ROS 2’s own rmw_zenohd, so the zenoh backend requires a ROS 2 installation just to start the router; the XRCE backend requires a running Micro-XRCE-DDS Agent. Cyclone DDS requires neither.

Current maturity: pub/sub and services interoperate with stock rmw_cyclonedds_cpp. Which status events and other features it wires is listed in the Per-RMW Feature Matrix; the remaining known limitations are in docs/reference/cyclonedds-known-limitations.md.

Zenoh — ROS 2 interop and small embedded targets

Choose the Zenoh backend (built on zenoh-pico) when:

  • You are integrating with a ROS 2 fleet running rmw_zenoh_cpp.
  • Your target is a small MCU: ~16 KB of heap and ~100 KB of flash are enough, versus ~32 KB+ RAM for Cyclone DDS.
  • Your network cannot do UDP multicast (RTPS discovery needs IGMP; zenoh-pico in client mode runs over plain TCP).

The zenoh backend needs a router, and the router comes from your ROS 2 installation — it is the same rmw_zenohd that ROS 2 zenoh nodes use:

ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

That invocation works on any host with rmw_zenoh_cpp installed, regardless of where ROS 2 lives — never hard-code an install path to the router binary. See ROS 2 Interop for the full three-terminal walkthrough.

XRCE-DDS — smallest footprint, serial transport

Choose the XRCE-DDS backend when:

  • RAM is the constraint: ~3 KB of client RAM, and the backend allocates only when a session or entity is created — never per message. (It is not heap-free: each allocation goes through nros_platform_alloc, and their number follows the entities you declare.)
  • You need a serial (UART) transport — the only backend that works on an MCU with no networking hardware. See Use a serial link.
  • You are joining an existing micro-ROS / DDS deployment: the agent bridges to any DDS-based RMW.

The MCU cannot participate without the Micro-XRCE-DDS Agent (MicroXRCEAgent) running on a host; if the agent stops, the device loses all connectivity.

What each backend supports

The Per-RMW Feature Matrix is the one capability table in this book. It is generated from the backend sources, so it is current: services, status events, graph introspection, zero-copy loans and the rest, per backend. In short, all three backends do publish/subscribe, service servers and clients, and status events; they differ in the less common features (for example, XRCE-DDS has no graph introspection, and only Zenoh has the zero-copy loan API). The version of each backend’s upstream library is listed on Support Status.

How each backend works

The three backends differ less in what they can do than in the shape of the network around your device: what else has to run, who handles discovery, and what happens when a process goes away.

Zenoh

The Zenoh backend uses zenoh-pico, a lightweight C client for the Zenoh protocol. The MCU takes part in the Zenoh network directly; there is no protocol translation layer.

  1. The MCU runs zenoh-pico in client mode and connects to a zenoh router (rmw_zenohd, ROS 2’s own) over TCP, UDP or TLS.
  2. zenoh-pico creates publishers and subscribers directly on the Zenoh network.
  3. ROS 2 nodes running rmw_zenoh_cpp connect to the same router. The router forwards messages without interpreting them; it is not a protocol translator.
  4. The device takes part in ROS 2 graph discovery through liveliness tokens, so ros2 topic list and ros2 node list see it.

Zenoh itself defines a peer mode in which two zenoh-pico devices talk directly with no router. nano-ros does not ship it: zenoh-pico is built without its multicast transport and scouting, because every nano-ros deployment reaches its peers through a router or an agent and those code paths cost flash on an MCU. Setting NROS_SESSION_MODE=peer is therefore refused at session open, with a message saying so.

If the router stops, the device loses routing but keeps running. Footprint: roughly 16 KB+ of RAM (heap required) and 100 KB+ of flash.

XRCE-DDS

The XRCE-DDS backend uses Micro-XRCE-DDS-Client, the same client library micro-ROS uses. It follows an agent-based model: a small client on the MCU delegates entity creation to an agent process.

  1. The MCU runs the XRCE-DDS client and connects to an Agent process over UDP or serial (UART, HDLC framing).
  2. The client asks the Agent to create entities (“a publisher on topic X with type Y”).
  3. The Agent creates full DDS entities on the client’s behalf and bridges data between the XRCE protocol and the DDS data space.
  4. ROS 2 nodes using any DDS-based RMW (Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS) communicate through the Agent.

The Agent is mandatory and handles discovery; the client does none of its own. If the Agent stops, the device loses all connectivity.

Heap use on the MCU is small and bounded: the backend allocates when a session or entity is created, never per message. Each XRCE_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS slot is heap, so size it to the subscriptions you declare. Footprint: roughly 3 KB of client RAM and 75 KB of flash. The upstream client also defines a CAN FD transport, but nano-ros builds do not enable it.

Cyclone DDS

The Cyclone DDS backend uses Eclipse Cyclone DDS, the same DDS implementation ROS 2 uses through rmw_cyclonedds_cpp. It is a C++ library that registers itself with the nano-ros runtime through the RMW C ABI.

  1. Selecting cyclonedds for the image links the backend and registers it before the executor opens; you do not call a register function yourself.
  2. The executor’s session, publisher, subscriber and service operations dispatch to Cyclone, which creates the DDS domain, participant, topics, writers and readers. Cyclone runs its own receive threads.
  3. ROS 2 nodes using stock rmw_cyclonedds_cpp interoperate directly: same wire protocol, same discovery, and no key rewriting (unlike rmw_zenoh’s <domain>/<topic>/<type>/… key expressions).

Discovery is SPDP / SEDP over UDP multicast, or a static unicast peer list. The domain is configured from a built-in configuration rather than an XML file, so no XML parser is linked. Cyclone allocates with malloc, so a heap is required: plan for roughly 32 KB+ of RAM and 150 KB+ of flash on an embedded link (the POSIX shared library, libddsc.so, is about 1.4 MB). When a peer goes offline, only its samples stop arriving; there is no central process whose loss takes the network down.

Getting the Cyclone library. Selecting cyclonedds for an image is all you have to do; the build provides Cyclone itself. It uses a prebuilt install if you point at one (-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<install> or -DCycloneDDS_DIR=); otherwise it builds Cyclone from source, by default from the pinned sources that ship with nano-ros, or from your own copy with -DCYCLONEDDS_SOURCE_DIR=<path>. A plain nros build therefore needs no separate Cyclone step. The idlc code generator is a host tool, found on PATH (for example from a ROS 2 install) or through -DIDLC_EXECUTABLE=.

Zephyr on Cortex-A / Cortex-R needs the aarch64-zephyr-elf toolchain in your Zephyr SDK install; toolchain setup for these targets is in docs/reference/zephyr-armv8r-setup.md.

The footprint figures in this section are order-of-magnitude planning numbers, not measurements; they vary with features, message set and optimisation level. Size your own image with arm-none-eabi-size; the RAM knobs are listed in the Static Pool Inventory.

Cyclone DDS network configuration per platform

Cyclone DDS speaks RTPS over UDP multicast and unicast. On every RTOS the network stack needs IGMP enabled, enough network buffers for the SPDP / SEDP discovery burst, and a way to join a multicast group. The settings per platform:

Zephyr

# IGMP for SPDP multicast discovery (239.255.0.1:7400+).
CONFIG_NET_IPV4_IGMP=y

# Multicast group slots — RTPS uses up to 4 builtin groups per
# participant (SPDP + SEDP pubs / subs / topics).
CONFIG_NET_IF_MCAST_IPV4_ADDR_COUNT=4

# Net-buffer pools — defaults of 14 / 36 are too small for the SEDP
# burst when more than two service / action entities exist on each
# participant. Symptom of undersizing: runtime starvation as the
# discovery exchange backs up.
CONFIG_NET_PKT_RX_COUNT=256
CONFIG_NET_PKT_TX_COUNT=128
CONFIG_NET_BUF_RX_COUNT=512
CONFIG_NET_BUF_TX_COUNT=256
CONFIG_NET_BUF_DATA_SIZE=512

# Heap — Cyclone DDS (malloc) + heapless mailboxes.
CONFIG_COMMON_LIBC_MALLOC_ARENA_SIZE=4194304
CONFIG_HEAP_MEM_POOL_SIZE=524288

On qemu_cortex_a9, also use a board overlay to enlarge the GEM driver’s RX / TX descriptor rings (default 32), so a brief pause in draining does not immediately drop frames:

&gem0 {
    promiscuous-mode;
    rx-buffer-descriptors = <128>;
    tx-buffer-descriptors = <64>;
};

On native_sim, Zephyr’s offloaded-sockets driver does not forward IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP to the host kernel, so multicast discovery does not work there. The native_sim configuration discovers peers by unicast to 127.0.0.1 instead (see Troubleshooting); use qemu_cortex_a9 to exercise multicast DDS on Zephyr.

FreeRTOS + lwIP

// FreeRTOSConfig.h / lwipopts.h
#define LWIP_IGMP            1   // SPDP multicast
#define LWIP_SO_RCVTIMEO     1   // Cyclone DDS recv timeouts
#define LWIP_BROADCAST       1
#define IP_REASSEMBLY        1   // RTPS DATA_FRAG fragments
#define MEMP_NUM_NETBUF      32  // discovery burst headroom

NuttX

CONFIG_NET_IGMP=y
CONFIG_NET_BROADCAST=y
CONFIG_NET_UDP_NRECVS=4
CONFIG_NET_RECV_TIMEO=y

ThreadX + NetX Duo

tx_user.h / nx_user.h:

#define NX_ENABLE_IGMPV2          // IGMP v2 for RTPS multicast
// NetX BSD layer init must call `bsd_initialize` early — required
// for `setsockopt(SO_RCVTIMEO)` support.

Bare-metal smoltcp

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Bridge config in the board crate.
let mut config = smoltcp::iface::Config::new(...);
config.multicast_groups = vec![Ipv4Address::new(239, 255, 0, 1)];
// MulticastConfig::Strict in smoltcp 0.x; the bridge must expose
// a `join_multicast_group` API.
}

POSIX

No configuration is needed: the kernel handles IGMP and setsockopt. Make sure the loopback interface is up (it is by default).

Decision summary

  • Default / getting started / DDS fleet → Cyclone DDS. Nothing to run beside your node; direct rmw_cyclonedds_cpp interop. Needs ~32 KB RAM and a network stack with IGMP.
  • rmw_zenoh_cpp fleet, small MCU, or TCP-only network → Zenoh. Needs the router from your ROS 2 install (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd).
  • Tiny MCU, serial link, or micro-ROS deployment → XRCE-DDS. Smallest footprint and no per-message allocation, but the agent is mandatory.

Any of the three handles standard publish/subscribe and services, integration with ROS 2 desktop nodes, and development under QEMU.

You do not have to pick exactly one per system: a single binary can link multiple backends and bridge between them, for example zenoh devices to a Cyclone DDS stack, or XRCE devices to a Zenoh network — see Bridge between backends.

Once you have picked, Switch the RMW per image shows the edits, and Configure zenoh, Use Cyclone DDS and Use XRCE-DDS show what each backend needs after that.

Design background

  • RFC-0031: RMW selection and lowering
  • RFC-0075: zenoh router provenance and the unstable seam

Your own message package

Tutorial · Level 2: Building real applications

You write a ROS 2 msg package once. The same src/my_msgs/ directory builds under both:

  • a nano-ros build — rosidl_generate_interfaces(...) is intercepted by nano-ros’s wrapper and routed through nano-ros codegen. No ROS 2 build tools run: even the rclcpp-shaped consumer below compiles against nano-ros’s own rclcpp CMake package. nros build still reads message definitions from your ROS 2 install, so source it for the first build (below).
  • colcon build — upstream rosidl_default_generators produces the upstream-ROS bindings (this half, and only this half, needs a ROS 2 install; it is the optional cross-build proof at the end).

Different build systems, identical source tree. No nano-ros-specific files in the msg package.

Where this fits. This chapter uses ROS 2 vocabulary (ament_cmake, rosidl, rclcpp) because its point is that stock ROS shapes work unchanged. If you came straight from First Project and none of that means anything yet, you can skim to “The Rust side” below or skip ahead to First Node — Rust and return later. The standalone tree here is for clarity — in your scaffolded my_robot workspace the same drop-in applies: put src/my_msgs/ next to your node packages.

The msg package — stock ROS shape

Drop a verbatim ROS msg pkg under src/ of your workspace:

src/my_msgs/
├── package.xml
├── CMakeLists.txt
└── msg/
    └── MyMsg.msg

src/my_msgs/package.xml:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<package format="3">
  <name>my_msgs</name>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
  <description>My ROS 2 msg package</description>
  <maintainer email="you@example.org">you</maintainer>
  <license>Apache-2.0</license>

  <buildtool_depend>ament_cmake</buildtool_depend>
  <depend>std_msgs</depend>
  <build_depend>rosidl_default_generators</build_depend>
  <exec_depend>rosidl_default_runtime</exec_depend>

  <member_of_group>rosidl_interface_packages</member_of_group>

  <export>
    <build_type>ament_cmake</build_type>
  </export>
</package>

src/my_msgs/CMakeLists.txt:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(my_msgs)

find_package(ament_cmake REQUIRED)
find_package(rosidl_default_generators REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

rosidl_generate_interfaces(${PROJECT_NAME}
    msg/MyMsg.msg
    DEPENDENCIES std_msgs
)

ament_export_dependencies(rosidl_default_runtime)
ament_package()

src/my_msgs/msg/MyMsg.msg:

std_msgs/Header header
string payload
int32 sequence

Zero nano-ros-specific lines. Run colcon build from this dir — upstream ROS produces a working msg package. Drop the same dir into a nano-ros build (below) — nano-ros codegen produces the equivalent bindings.

The consumer — stock ROS shape

// src/my_app/src/my_app.cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <memory>

#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>
#include "my_msgs/msg/my_msg.hpp"

using namespace std::chrono_literals;

class MyNode : public rclcpp::Node {
public:
    MyNode() : rclcpp::Node("my_node") {
        publisher_ = this->create_publisher<my_msgs::msg::MyMsg>("topic", 10);
        timer_ = this->create_wall_timer(500ms, [this]() {
            my_msgs::msg::MyMsg m;
            m.payload = "hello";
            publisher_->publish(m);
        });
    }
private:
    rclcpp::TimerBase::SharedPtr timer_;
    rclcpp::Publisher<my_msgs::msg::MyMsg>::SharedPtr publisher_;
};

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    rclcpp::init(argc, argv);
    rclcpp::spin(std::make_shared<MyNode>());
    rclcpp::shutdown();
    return 0;
}

src/my_app/CMakeLists.txt:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(my_app LANGUAGES CXX)

find_package(ament_cmake REQUIRED)
find_package(rclcpp REQUIRED)
find_package(my_msgs REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

add_executable(my_app src/my_app.cpp)
target_link_libraries(my_app
    rclcpp::rclcpp
    my_msgs::my_msgs
    std_msgs::std_msgs
)

ament_package()

Build it with nros build

There is no nano-ros-specific file to add: a workspace has no root build file. With no bringup, nros build builds it the way colcon build does — every package it finds by its package.xml, in <depend> order, each in its own build/<pkg>/. For my_app it generates the CMake root that used to be hand-written (nano-ros, NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH at ./src/, the rclcpp / ament surface); my_msgs is not built on its own — its bindings are generated into the package that uses it.

The first nros build of the workspace needs ROS 2 sourced: it generates the bindings against your ROS 2 install’s message definitions, and refuses without one. It records the prefix, so later builds need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build
./build/my_app/cmake/pkg/my_app/my_app

In a workspace that also has a bringup (what nros new <ws> --board <board> writes), the same nros build builds my_msgs into whichever image’s packages depend on it.

Escape hatch — a hand-written umbrella. For a CMake tree that is not a nano-ros workspace, one top-level CMakeLists.txt pulls nano-ros in as a subdirectory, naming the SDK root on the configure line (Build inside an existing CMake or vendor tree has the mechanism):

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(my_workspace LANGUAGES CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14)

# Pull nano-ros — the installed SDK root, passed as -DNANO_ROS_SDK=….
set(NROS_PLATFORM posix)
set(NROS_RMW "zenoh" CACHE STRING "Active RMW.")
set(NROS_RMW "${NROS_RMW}")
add_subdirectory("${NANO_ROS_SDK}" nano_ros)

# Point the message-package resolver at this workspace (must precede the
# ament-surface include so the workspace Find<pkg>.cmake auto-emit picks it up).
set(NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/src")

# nano-ros's ament / rclcpp surface (find_package(rclcpp), ament_* verbs).
include("${NANO_ROS_SDK}/cmake/NanoRosAmentSurface.cmake")

# Bulk-build every workspace msg pkg in topo order. One line, no
# add_subdirectory(src/<pkg>) per pkg.
nros_workspace_interfaces()

# Build the consumer app.
add_subdirectory(src/my_app)

cmake -B build -S . -DNANO_ROS_SDK="$(nros locate nano-ros)"
cmake --build build -j
./build/src/my_app/my_app

The Rust side

The same msg package feeds a Rust node with no CMake involved: declare it in your node package’s package.xml (<depend>my_msgs</depend>) and run nros build from the workspace root — that is the whole change. The package index finds src/my_msgs/ by its package.xml, generates the generated/my_msgs crate, and writes the manifest row itself (my_msgs = { path = "../../generated/my_msgs", default-features = false } # nros-managed). The shipped precedent is examples/workspaces/features/src/custom_msgs with its rust_reading_listener_pkg consumer. Full detail: Message Generation.

use my_msgs::msg::MyMsg;   // generated crate, same field names

Cross-build proof — same source under colcon (optional; needs ROS 2)

cd src && colcon build

src/my_msgs/ produces the upstream my_msgs bindings; src/my_app/ links against the upstream rclcpp + my_msgs::my_msgs. The nano-ros build above produces the same source linked against NanoRos::NanoRosCpp through the nano-ros codegen, with the smart Find-stub forwarding find_package(my_msgs) → my_msgs::my_msgs.

The interface-package search path

find_package(<pkg>) walks three layers, highest priority first:

LayerSourceNotes
1NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATHColon/semicolon-separated colcon-src/-style roots; immediate subdirs with package.xml are candidates.
2AMENT_PREFIX_PATHThe standard ROS install-prefix layout (<prefix>/share/<pkg>/{msg,srv,action}/).
3Bundled<nano-ros>/packages/cli/interfaces/<pkg>/ (in-tree bundled definitions).

Shadowing — a workspace my_msgs and an AMENT my_msgs resolve to the workspace one, with a message(STATUS ...) line noting the shadow.

Shadowing contract

When two layers carry the same package name (e.g. a workspace std_msgs and /opt/ros/<distro>/share/std_msgs/), the higher layer wins — silently and deterministically. Concretely:

  1. NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH > AMENT_PREFIX_PATH > bundled. The message-package resolver (cmake/find/_NrosFindRosMsgPackage.cmake) walks the three layers in order; the first hit wins. Lower layers are skipped entirely.

  2. The configure pass emits a message(STATUS ...) line noting the resolved path, e.g.

    -- nros: find_package(std_msgs) -> /path/to/workspace/src/std_msgs

    Grep your configure log for nros: find_package(<pkg>) to confirm which layer supplied each pkg.

  3. Intra-workspace shadowing — when two roots under NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH both ship the same pkg, the nros_workspace_interfaces() bulk orchestrator keeps the earlier-listed one and warns about the shadowed copy.

  4. No partial overrides. Shadowing is whole-package: a workspace pkg replaces ALL of an AMENT pkg’s interfaces, not a subset. If you only want to add MyExtraMsg.msg to std_msgs, ship a separate pkg (e.g. my_std_extra_msgs) — don’t shadow.

Compile-time fail-safe

Shadowing is observed at compile time: if your workspace std_msgs declares a Marker.msg and your consumer includes "std_msgs/msg/marker.hpp", the build only succeeds when the workspace copy is the one linked. AMENT’s std_msgs ships no Marker.msg, so a fall-through resolves to a missing header. The build outcome is the strongest evidence — nm on the linked binary is the symbol-level corroborator.

Reference fixture for shadowing

The canonical smoke proof for the Layer 1 > Layer 2 case ships at examples/templates/workspace-shadowing/ — a workspace std_msgs carrying a Marker.msg shadows the AMENT-installed std_msgs. The fixture’s README.md walks through the cmake + nm verification. A regression test (packages/testing/nros-tests/tests/workspace_shadowing.rs) re-runs the same proof in CI when AMENT is sourced.

Reference fixture

examples/templates/local-msg-package/ ships the exact pattern above end-to-end (two workspace msg pkgs with a dep between them, plus a consumer node). Use it as a copy-out template.
