Growing your workspace

Tutorial · Level 2: Building real applications

First Project left you with a workspace of two packages: a node and the bringup that says what it runs on. A project grows from there by one path, in four steps, and you take only the ones you need:

  1. add a node package;
  2. add its component row to the bringup;
  3. add launch/ when you need a launch argument, a remap or a parameter;
  4. add an image for another board.

Each step adds a package or a few lines to the bringup. The shape of the workspace never changes, so nothing you did in an earlier step has to be undone.

Where you start

sensor_ws/
└── src/
    ├── sensor_node/            # node package: package.xml, Cargo.toml (a library), src/lib.rs
    └── sensor_node_bringup/    # package.xml and system.toml; no launch/ yet

The two roles, and what each one never holds:

PackageHoldsNever holds
Node packageone node: publishers, subscriptions, timers, services, callback bodiesa board, an RMW, a main()
Bringup packagesystem.toml: which nodes run, on which boards, with which RMW; optionally launch/compiled code

There is no third package to write. For each [image.*] block in the bringup’s system.toml, nros build and nros run generate the program’s entry (its main()) under build/. A workspace has no root Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt either: like a colcon workspace, it is a directory of packages.

system.toml lives only in a bringup package. A system.toml beside a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt is refused, and the message says where to move it.

1. Add a node package

From the workspace root:

nros new monitor_node --template listener --to sensor_node_bringup

Inside a workspace, nros new adds a package under src/ instead of writing a new workspace. --to also adds the node’s component row to the bringup (step 2). Pass --lang c or --lang cpp for a C or C++ node; the rest of this page is the same in every language.

A node package is a library with three files:

src/monitor_node/
├── package.xml          # ROS 2 manifest: one <depend> per message package
├── Cargo.toml           # a [lib] crate and its dependencies, nothing else
└── src/lib.rs           # the node; its last line is nros::node!(Listener);

It has no fn main() and names no board, RMW or board crate. That is what lets one node package go into a Cortex-M image and a Linux image unchanged: the difference between them is an [image.*] block, not a second copy of the node.

The manifests

package.xml is a standard ROS 2 manifest. Each message package the node uses is one <depend>:

<depend>std_msgs</depend>

That line is all you write for a message package. The build turns each <depend> on a message package into a dependency row in Cargo.toml, tagged # nros-managed, pointing at the crate it generates under generated/. Removing the <depend> removes the row. A row without the tag is yours and is never touched, so to override a generated row, delete its tag.

Cargo.toml registers the node class the package exports:

[lib]
path = "src/lib.rs"

[package.metadata.nros.node]
class = "monitor_node::Listener"
name = "monitor_node"

[dependencies]
nros = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = [
    "alloc",
    "rmw-cffi", "macros"] }
std_msgs = { path = "../../generated/std_msgs", default-features = false }  # nros-managed

This registration is the Rust spelling of nros_components_register_node(... PLUGIN pkg::Class ...) in a C or C++ package’s CMakeLists.txt. A package registers its class once, however many bringups run it. Which bringup runs it is the component row’s business (step 2). nros is never fetched from a registry: the build points it at your installed nano-ros, so no path in the manifest names where nano-ros lives and the package copies anywhere.

src/lib.rs

A Rust node implements Component (what the node creates, declared once at startup) and ExecutableNode (what each callback does), then exports both with nros::node!. The essential shape, from examples/workspaces/rust/src/talker_pkg/src/lib.rs:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use nros::{
    CallbackCtx, ExecutableNode, Component, NodeContext, DeclarativeNode, NodeOptions, NodeResult,
    TimerDuration,
};

pub struct Talker;

impl Component for Talker {
    const NAME: &'static str = "talker";

    // Per-instance slots, in order: publishers, service servers,
    // service clients, action clients, action servers.
    const ENTITY_BOUNDS: nros::EntityBounds = nros::EntityBounds::exact(1, 0, 0, 0, 0);

    fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
        let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("talker"))?;
        let chatter = node.create_publisher_for_topic::<MyMsg>("/chatter")?;
        let _timer =
            node.create_timer_for_callback_name("on_tick", TimerDuration::from_millis(1000))?;
        node.callback_for_name("on_tick")
            .publishes_entity(&chatter)?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl ExecutableNode for Talker {
    type State = i32;

    fn init() -> Self::State { 0 }

    // See the full example for the callback body.
}

nros::node!(Talker);   // exports the node; this is the last line
}
  • register declares; it does not run. It is called once at startup to declare publishers, subscriptions, timers and which callback publishes what. No message flows here.
  • on_callback is the body. The image’s executor calls it each time a callback fires; state is the node’s own mutable storage.
  • The node is the same type everywhere. ctx.create_node(...) returns the nros::Node a standalone program gets, with rclrs’s methods (create_publisher, create_subscription, timers, logger(), the graph queries). use nros::DeclarativeNode; adds the constructors that bind a callback by name, which is what lets the board run callbacks from its own tasks and lets the build measure the node without running it.
  • ENTITY_BOUNDS is static RAM. nros::node! emits a static sized from it, and a publisher slot carries a loan arena. The default (8 of each kind) measured 50,824 bytes of .bss for a one-service node, against 568 bytes when the node declared what it creates. Count the five kinds in your register(); timers and subscriptions need no slot here. Declaring fewer than register() creates is an error at boot, never a silent drop, so the exact number is safe.
  • Timers. In a timer callback, ctx.timer_info() returns the activation’s expected_call_time and actual_call_time (lateness_ns() is their difference). create_timer_for_callback_name_with_autostart(name, period, clock, false) declares a stopped timer; any callback starts it with ctx.reset_timer(nros::EntityId::new("on_tick")) and stops it with ctx.cancel_timer(..). To control timers by id, add .with_timers(n) to ENTITY_BOUNDS (16 bytes a timer).

Calling a service from a node

A node cannot make a blocking service or action call from on_callback: the executor is mid-dispatch there, and the call would deadlock it. Client calls go in ExecutableNode::tick, which the executor runs once per spin between callbacks. Arm the call in the callback and make it in tick:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn on_callback(state: &mut State, cb: Callback<'_>, ctx: &mut CallbackCtx<'_>) {
    state.want_call = true;          // decide; do not call here
}

fn tick(state: &mut State, ctx: &mut TickCtx<'_>) {
    if state.want_call {
        state.want_call = false;
        let reply = ctx.call_for_name("add_two_ints", &request);  // blocking is safe here
    }
}
}

A service server needs no such split: requests arrive in on_callback like any other callback. In C++, rclcpp::bind_service<Svc, T, &T::method>(node, "/add_two_ints", this) binds a typed member that takes the generated Svc::Request and returns Svc::Response.

2. Add a component row

--to sensor_node_bringup added this to src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml, beside the row the scaffold wrote for sensor_node:

[[component]]
pkg = "monitor_node"
class = "monitor_node::Listener"
name = "monitor_node"
FieldMeaning
pkgthe node package (its <name> in package.xml)
classthe type the package registers
namethe node’s name at runtime; a launch file can remap it
dispatchoptional: the dispatch shape, when it is not the default

It also added <exec_depend>monitor_node</exec_depend> to the bringup’s package.xml. To add a row by hand (for a node package you copied in), write both.

Run the system. The workspace’s first build, in First Project, recorded your ROS 2 prefix, so a shell that has not sourced ROS 2 builds it too; a workspace you start fresh needs ROS 2 sourced for its first build, because the messages are generated from it:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash   # only needed for a fresh workspace's first build
nros run

With nothing named, nros run runs the workspace’s only image, which now now holds both nodes in one program. nros run sensor_node no longer works. That spelling means “the bringup whose only node is sensor_node”, and this bringup now has two, so it refuses and prints the spellings that would resolve, here sensor_node_bringup:baremetal.

The bringup still has no launch/, so the build generates its launch file from the two rows. After a build, it is at:

cat build/nros/launch/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.launch.xml

Before a build, two checks catch most mistakes in a bringup (a [[component]] row naming a package or class that does not exist, a stray build file in the bringup):

nros check --bringup src/sensor_node_bringup
nros check --workspace .

3. Add a launch file when you need one

The generated launch file starts every component with its default name and nothing else. When you need a launch argument, a remap, a namespace or a parameter, the bringup gets a launch/ directory. Start from the generated file, so that adding it changes nothing until you edit it:

mkdir -p src/sensor_node_bringup/launch
cp build/nros/launch/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.launch.xml \
   src/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.launch.xml

From then on launch/system.launch.xml is used instead of the generated one. Deleting launch/ goes back to generation.

Keep each <node>’s pkg and exec as the generated file wrote them; the examples below write exec="…" for that value.

The file is the ROS 2 launch XML schema, read with the same parser, so a launch file from another ROS 2 project pastes in. For example, a launch argument that moves both nodes to another topic:

<launch>
  <arg name="topic" default="/chatter"/>

  <node pkg="sensor_node" exec="…" name="sensor_node">
    <remap from="/chatter" to="$(var topic)"/>
  </node>
  <node pkg="monitor_node" exec="…" name="monitor_node">
    <remap from="/chatter" to="$(var topic)"/>
  </node>
</launch>
TagPurpose
<arg name="…" default="…"/>declare a launch argument
<node pkg="…" exec="…" name="…"/>start a node
<param name="…" value="…"/>set one parameter (inside <node>)
<param from="….yaml"/>load a ROS parameter file (inside <node>)
<remap from="…" to="…"/>remap a topic or service (inside <node>)
<group ns="…">put a group of nodes in a namespace
<include file="…"/>include another launch file

Substitutions: $(var <arg>) expands a launch argument, $(find <pkg>) a package’s path, $(env <name>) an environment variable.

There is no ros2 launch step. The launch file is resolved when the image is built, and its result is compiled into the program. An image binds launch arguments, and can name another launch file in the same bringup:

[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
args = { topic = "/sensor" }

[image.baremetal_sim]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
launch = "sim.launch.xml"

Parameters

<param from="…"/> takes a standard ROS parameter file, relative to the launch file:

# launch/sensor.param.yaml
/**:                      # every node
  ros__parameters:
    use_sim_time: false
sensor_node:              # this node only
  ros__parameters:
    rate_hz: 25
    limits:
      max_accel: 1.5      # reaches the node as `limits.max_accel`

<node pkg="sensor_node" exec="…" name="sensor_node">
  <param from="sensor.param.yaml"/>
  <param name="rate_hz" value="50"/>   <!-- wins over the file -->
</node>

Precedence is ROS’s: the /** block, then the node’s own block (keyed sensor_node, /ns/sensor_node or /**/sensor_node), then inline <param name= value=>. The values are baked into the program at build time, so an embedded board reads no file at run time; editing the YAML rebuilds. A from= naming a missing file is a build error.

Two capabilities in [system] features decide what the image does with them:

declaredparameter store (declare_parameter, launch values, --ros-args -p)ros2 param services
paramsyesnone
param_servicesyessix per node (get, set, list, describe, …)

params suits a small board whose nodes only read their configuration: each of the six services costs a queryable per node. What it gives up is ros2 param get|set|list|describe|dump and the use_sim_time switch.

4. Add an image

An image is one program: the bringup’s nodes, built for one board with one RMW. It is a block in system.toml, not a package. Your bringup has one, written by the scaffold:

[image.baremetal]
board   = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"

Running the same two nodes on your Linux machine is one more block:

[image.linux]
board = "linux"
rmw   = "cyclonedds"       # this image only; needs no router on a host

nros run linux

Nothing in either node package changes. The board’s descriptor supplies the target triple, linker flags, cross compiler and memory budgets, so retargeting is the board line and nothing else.

KeyMeaning
boardthe nano-ros board id; Supported Boards lists them
rmwthis image’s RMW, when it differs from [system] rmw
locator, netan embedded image’s network identity (where its router is, its own address)
launcha launch file in the bringup; default [system] default_launch
argslaunch arguments bound for this image
featurescapability axes added to [system] features
os_configRTOS configuration files, in order: Zephyr prj-*.conf and overlays, or a board network file
panicpanic policy: platform, halt or own
profilea cargo or CMake build profile
before_boota function to call before the board boots (below)

[image_defaults] holds what every image shares, so eight images do not repeat their RMW eight times. A specific block’s values replace it; args merge, and os_config and features add up:

[image_defaults]
rmw = "zenoh"

The RMW, like the board, is chosen at build time; embedded targets have no RMW_IMPLEMENTATION switch. On a Linux image, ROS_DOMAIN_ID and NROS_LOCATOR still work at run time; an embedded image bakes the values from its block. See Configuration.

Naming what to run

With two images, nros run alone refuses and lists them. The target argument of nros run, nros build and nros flash accepts, in this order:

You typeIt means
sensor_node_bringup:linuxthat bringup’s image; always works
linuxthe image named linux, when only one bringup declares it
sensor_nodethe bringup whose only node is sensor_node, with its only image
nothingthe workspace’s only image

Anything else refuses and lists the <bringup>:<image> spellings that would resolve; a shortcut never picks one of several. --why says which row resolved. To make a bare nros build build a chosen set, declare it:

[system]
default_images = ["linux"]

Zephyr images

A Zephyr image also carries Zephyr’s own configuration (prj.conf, overlays), which nothing can derive. It lives in the bringup, one directory per board, and the image names the fragments it adds:

src/sensor_node_bringup/boards/native_sim_native_64/
├── prj.conf
└── prj-zenoh.conf               # named by [image.<id>] os_config

nros build writes the Zephyr application itself under build/ and runs west build on it. The board id is still nano-ros’s (zephyr), never Zephyr’s spelling. Configuring an image has the rest. A Zephyr application that keeps its own CMakeLists.txt and prj.conf and is built with plain west build is not a workspace image; it has its own chapter.

What nros build generates

Everything generated lands under build/, and none of it is yours to edit or commit:

  • the generated launch file of each bringup without launch/;
  • the resolved system for each image (build/nros/models/);
  • the generated message crates;
  • each image’s entry and the build root that compiles it: a cargo package when every node is Rust, a CMake project when any node is C or C++, a Zephyr application for a Zephyr board.

nros build then runs that host tool, so compiler errors are the compiler’s. nros build --dry-run prints the command for an image, and running it yourself works too. Where each binary lands is What nros build Produces.

Customising an entry

The generated entry is one nros::main!(…) call, and the macro does a lot: it opens the executor at the size the image declares, registers every node in the launch file, and adds the lifecycle, parameter services and sched tasks the system asks for. Take the smallest step that does what you need:

You needUseEntry stays generated
another panic policy, build profile, Kconfig fragment or capabilityan [image.*] keyyes
one step before the runtime starts (open a device, check a calibration)before_bootyes
hardware setup every image on a board needs (clocks, DMA)the board’s init_hardware, in a board packageyes
startup none of the above can expressnros materializeno

before_boot names a function in one of the image’s node packages:

[image.linux]
board = "linux"
before_boot = "sensor_node::prepare"

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// src/sensor_node/src/lib.rs
pub fn prepare() -> Result<(), &'static str> {
    // open the device, check the calibration, wait for the peripheral
    Ok(())
}
}

The entry calls it first, before the board does anything, so nothing has booted when it runs: no executor, no session, and on bare metal no hardware setup yet. Returning Err("reason") stops the image with that reason. It works in Rust images only; a C or C++ image that sets it is refused, and so is a board whose framework owns the first statement. The worked example is image linux_rust_before_boot in examples/workspaces/features.

nros materialize is the last resort. It copies an image’s generated entry into src/<image>_entry/, and from then on nros build uses your copy and does not regenerate it:

$ nros build linux
$ nros materialize linux
wrote …/src/linux_entry

This entry is YOURS now — `nros build` will not regenerate it.

What you get is the same nros::main!(…) call inside its crate root. While you keep the macro, launch-file changes still reach the program; what you own is the shell around it. Replacing the macro with your own main means writing the boot, node registration, executor sizing and every capability yourself, and keeping them in step with the launch file by hand. Deleting src/<image>_entry/ returns the image to generation.

Coming from ROS 2

ROS 2nano-ros
ros2 pkg createnros new <pkg> inside the workspace; --to <bringup> adds its component row
colcon buildnros build (every default image) or nros build <image>
ros2 run <pkg> <exe>nros run <node>
ros2 launch <pkg> <file>nros run <bringup>:<image>; the launch file is compiled into the image

One image is one program, which runs its nodes in one process on one board. Several processes are several images.

Other languages

Nothing on this page is Rust-specific except the node’s source file. C and C++ node packages, and workspaces that mix languages, are C / C++ multi-node workspaces and Mixed-language workspaces. Role reference lists every field of the three roles.

  • RFC-0120: one resolver for every build road: why nros build prepares the build itself.

ROS 2 Interop

Tutorial · Level 2: Building real applications

nano-ros communicates with standard ROS 2 nodes using the rmw_zenoh_cpp middleware. Both sides connect to the same zenohd router and exchange CDR-encoded messages with compatible key expressions.

Prerequisites

  • ROS 2 installed. For the zenoh path use ROS 2 Jazzy: sudo apt install ros-jazzy-rmw-zenoh-cpp. Humble and Iron ship no rmw_zenoh_cpp apt package — on those, either build rmw_zenoh from source as a colcon overlay, or use the Cyclone DDS backend instead (direct rmw_cyclonedds_cpp interop, no router at all — see Choosing an RMW)
  • The zenoh router running: ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Quick Start

Open three terminals:

# Terminal 1: Start the zenoh router
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

# Terminal 2: Scaffold, build and run a nano-ros talker
nros new talker_ws --board linux --template talker --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd talker_ws
RUST_LOG=info nros run talker_node   # builds first, then runs it

# Terminal 3: Run a ROS 2 listener
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
export ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='mode="client";connect/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"]'
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

You should see the ROS 2 listener printing messages published by nano-ros:

data: 'Hello World: 1'
---
data: 'Hello World: 2'
---

The Other Direction

ROS 2 publishers also work with nano-ros subscribers:

Scaffold a listener node instead, the same node as listener_pkg in the Rust language workspace (nros run pubsub_bringup:linux_listener there runs it); it subscribes to std_msgs/String on /chatter, the demo talker’s topic:

# Terminal 2: a nano-ros listener
nros new listener_ws --board linux --template listener --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd listener_ws
RUST_LOG=info nros run listener_node

# Terminal 3: ROS 2 talker
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
export ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='mode="client";connect/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"]'
ros2 topic pub /chatter std_msgs/msg/String "{data: 'Hello from ROS 2'}" --qos-reliability best_effort

The listener logs each message ROS 2 publishes.

Discovery

nano-ros publishes ROS 2-compatible liveliness tokens, so standard ROS 2 tools work:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
export ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='mode="client";connect/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"]'

ros2 topic list        # Shows /chatter
ros2 topic info /chatter   # Shows publisher/subscriber count
ros2 node list         # Shows nano-ros nodes

Configuration

Domain ID

Both sides must use the same ROS domain ID. On the native (host) build nano-ros reads ROS_DOMAIN_ID from the environment (default: 0). On embedded targets the domain ID is fixed at compile time — system.toml [system] domain_id (or an image’s own — on Zephyr the module renders it into CONFIG_NROS_DOMAIN_ID), or a hand-written config.toml on a direct-mode app (see Add an image):

ROS_DOMAIN_ID=42 ./build/linux/target/debug/talker   # nano-ros side
ROS_DOMAIN_ID=42 ros2 topic echo /chatter ...  # ROS 2 side

QoS

nano-ros defaults to BEST_EFFORT reliability and VOLATILE durability. When using ROS 2 subscribers, match the QoS:

ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

Without --qos-reliability best_effort, ROS 2 defaults to RELIABLE, which won’t match the nano-ros publisher’s BEST_EFFORT QoS.

rmw_zenoh Client Mode

By default, rmw_zenoh_cpp uses peer mode and won’t connect to a zenohd router. Force client mode with:

export ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='mode="client";connect/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"]'

Set this before any ros2 command.

Protocol Details

nano-ros speaks the same wire format as rmw_zenoh_cpp: the same key expressions, liveliness tokens, CDR encoding and per-message attachment. You do not configure any of it. How each piece is encoded is described in Internals → Zenoh protocol.

ROS 2 Editions

Three editions are supported: humble (default; TypeHashNotSupported key expressions, XCDR1), iron, and jazzy (both RIHS01 type hashes). Pick the edition matching the ROS 2 install you interop with — a Humble-edition image against a Jazzy bus (or vice versa) discovers nothing, because the key expressions differ.

The edition is declared like the RMW, per image, in system.toml: [image.<id>] ros_edition = "jazzy" (over [image_defaults], then [system] ros_edition). nros build <id> generates the messages for that edition and builds the image; the ros-<edition> cargo features are what the build lowers it to, not something you pass. A workspace is scaffolded for one edition — nros new talker_ws --board linux --template talker --ros-edition jazzy — and a bringup that builds for several declares one image per edition, as the bringup of the copy-out talker, examples/linux/rust/talker/system.toml, does (linux_jazzy, linux_xrce_jazzy, …), then picks one:

nros build linux_jazzy

Troubleshooting

These are the interop-specific failures. For problems that are not about the ROS 2 side (build failures, sessions that never open, transport errors), see Troubleshooting; for a first run, see Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Topic not visible in ros2 topic list: Ensure both nano-ros and ROS 2 use the same domain ID and that rmw_zenoh_cpp is in client mode pointing to the same router. Also check that both sides use the same ROS 2 edition (see ROS 2 Editions).

Discovery works but no messages received: Check that the QoS matches. Use --qos-reliability best_effort on the ROS 2 side.

rmw_zenoh not connecting: Verify ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE is set. Without it, rmw_zenoh uses peer mode and won’t find the router.

Configure zenoh

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Pick and configure the RMW

Use this page when an image runs on the zenoh backend and you need to say where its router is: on this machine, on another host, or at the other end of a serial link.

A nano-ros zenoh image is a zenoh-pico client. It dials one router and reaches every other node, nano-ros or ROS 2, through it. The router is the one ROS 2 ships, rmw_zenohd from rmw_zenoh_cpp; nano-ros ships none of its own. The image’s locator is the address it dials, and it is the only thing a board needs to find the router.

Before you start

  • A workspace with a zenoh image, such as the one from Run a talker.
  • ROS 2 Humble with ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp, sourced in each terminal (source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash). It provides rmw_zenohd.

Steps

  1. See which locator the image dials. --dry-run prints the run plan without running anything:

    nros run sensor_node --dry-run

    The [link] table is the image’s locator. The scaffold’s first image reaches the router over the board’s serial port:

    [link]
kind = "serial"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"
rmw = "zenoh"

    A host image (board = "linux") that states no locator dials the zenoh default, tcp/127.0.0.1:7447.

  2. Point the image at a router over the network. Set locator in the image’s block of src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml. Inside QEMU’s user network, the host is 10.0.2.2:

    [image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7447"

    Run it. nros run sees that 10.0.2.2 is this host as the emulator reaches it, and starts rmw_zenohd on the matching local port first:

    nros run sensor_node --expect 'Publishing:'

    nros run: starting the zenoh router on tcp/127.0.0.1:7447
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after

  3. Use a router on another host instead. Name its address in the locator:

    [image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "tcp/192.168.50.1:7447"

    nros run starts no router for an address that is not this machine’s, and says so:

    nros run: starting no router (tcp/192.168.50.1:7447 is not an address of this host, so its router runs elsewhere)

    On the other host, start the router. It reads no command-line arguments; its default configuration listens on port 7447:

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

  4. Reuse a router that is already running on this machine. Pass its locator to --router, and nros run starts nothing:

    nros run sensor_node --router tcp/127.0.0.1:7447

    nros run: starting no router (the router at tcp/127.0.0.1:7447)

  5. On a host image, change the locator at run time. A host image reads NROS_LOCATOR when it starts, and the variable wins over the locator baked from system.toml. Its first log line says which one it used:

    NROS_LOCATOR=tcp/192.168.50.1:7447 nros run host_node

    boot config: domain 0 (baked), locator tcp/192.168.50.1:7447 (env), …

    An embedded image has no environment: its locator is fixed when it is built.

  6. For more than one endpoint, TLS, or a user name and password, write the session’s own configuration file instead of a locator. Create rmw/zenoh.json5 beside system.toml. It is the same document rmw_zenoh reads from ZENOH_SESSION_CONFIG_URI on a ROS 2 host:

    // src/sensor_node_bringup/rmw/zenoh.json5
{
  mode: "client",
  connect: { endpoints: ["tcp/192.168.50.1:7447", "tcp/192.168.50.2:7447"] },
}

    Then delete the image’s locator line: the file is now the session’s wiring, and nros build refuses an image that states both. It also refuses a key zenoh-pico cannot take, and names the key, rather than dropping it. Because the file names routers elsewhere, run with --router none.

Client, not peer

zenoh defines a peer mode in which two devices talk with no router. nano-ros does not build it: zenoh-pico is compiled without the multicast transport and scouting that peer mode needs, to save flash. A session asked for peer mode, by mode: "peer" in the file or NROS_SESSION_MODE=peer, refuses to open and logs:

peer mode unsupported: shim built without multicast transport/scouting

Two nano-ros boards therefore talk through a router, as two rmw_zenoh_cpp nodes do. This differs from the ROS 2 DDS backends, where nodes discover each other directly; for that, use Cyclone DDS.

Downsample at the router

When a subscriber’s contract declares an arrival curve, nros configure writes a router downsampling rule beside the resolved model. nros router config --model <model> prints it as the ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE entry rmw_zenohd reads (--format json5 prints the rule file itself):

ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE="$(nros router config --model build/nros/models/<bringup>/<stem>.yaml)" rmw_zenohd

It fails when there is no rule: no subscriber declares an arrival curve, no image links zenoh, or the model was never configured. nros router is a command package (nros_zenoh_tools), not a built-in verb, so nros help --all lists it and nros router config --help prints its flags.

Example

A talker in QEMU and a ROS 2 listener on the host, sharing one router that nros run starts. The whole bringup:

# src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "sensor_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
ros_edition = "humble"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "sensor_node"
class = "sensor_node::Talker"
name = "sensor_node"

[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7447"

In one terminal:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run sensor_node

In a second terminal:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

data: 'Hello World: 3'

If it doesn’t work

  • nros run stops with no zenoh router: rmw_zenoh_cpp/rmw_zenohd was not found. Source ROS 2 in that terminal, install ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp, or set NROS_RMW_ZENOHD to the rmw_zenohd binary.
  • the zenoh router exited on tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 … is the port taken? Another router already holds the port. Stop it, or reuse it with --router tcp/127.0.0.1:7447.
  • The board boots but nothing arrives. Check the locator with --dry-run. 10.0.2.2 means the host only from inside QEMU’s user network; a board on a real network needs the router host’s real address. Both sides must use the same domain_id, and ros2 topic echo needs --qos-reliability best_effort for a best-effort talker.
  • A host image stops at start-up naming NROS_LOCATOR. ZENOH_LOCATOR and ZENOH_MODE are retired names. Use NROS_LOCATOR and NROS_SESSION_MODE.

See also

  • Use a serial link: the serial/ locator and a router on a serial device.
  • Configure an image: the session file, per-image files and the keys it takes.
  • Environment variables: NROS_LOCATOR, NROS_SESSION_MODE and the TLS variables.
  • CLI reference: every nros run flag.
  • Tune throughput and latency: zenoh-pico’s transmit path and buffers.
  • How nano-ros differs from ROS 2.

Use Cyclone DDS

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Pick and configure the RMW

Use Cyclone DDS when an image should talk to ROS 2 nodes directly, with no router or agent running beside it.

The Cyclone DDS backend is Eclipse Cyclone DDS, the same DDS implementation ROS 2 uses through rmw_cyclonedds_cpp, pinned to the version ROS 2 ships. An image on it speaks RTPS and discovers its peers itself, so a stock rmw_cyclonedds_cpp node sees it with nothing in between.

Where it runs

Which boards build and run a Cyclone DDS image is generated from the board registry, not written here:

  • Supported boards: each board’s evidence page lists, under Breadth, the RMWs its tests run.
  • Per-RMW feature matrix: what the backend implements (services, status events, QoS policies) next to zenoh and XRCE-DDS.
  • Support status: the pinned Cyclone version and the ROS 2 release it pairs with.

Before you start

  • A workspace, such as the host one from Run a talker.
  • ROS 2 Humble with ros-humble-rmw-cyclonedds-cpp on the same network, to see the image from ROS 2.

Steps

  1. Provision the backend for your board. --rmw cyclonedds adds Cyclone’s sources and the message tools its type support needs; nros build then builds Cyclone itself, with no separate step:

    nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds

  2. Select it. Set rmw in the bringup’s system.toml, for every image:

    [system]
rmw = "cyclonedds"

    Check what the bringup resolved:

    nros config show

    [system]
rmw                = cyclonedds                   # system.toml [system]

    To change one image only, put rmw = "cyclonedds" in its [image.<id>] block instead; see Switch the RMW per image.

  3. Run it. No router starts, because Cyclone DDS needs none:

    nros run host_node --expect 'Publishing:' --timeout 120

    Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after

  4. See it from ROS 2, in a second terminal:

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

    data: 'Hello World: 4'

  5. Pick the DDS domain. The image runs on [system] domain_id, and Cyclone’s own domain follows it. A ROS 2 peer must use the same number:

    [system]
domain_id = 5

    ROS_DOMAIN_ID=5 ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

  6. Configure Cyclone itself, if the defaults do not fit your network: which interface to use, whether to multicast, tracing. Write Cyclone’s own XML, the document CYCLONEDDS_URI names on a ROS 2 host, as rmw/cyclonedds.xml beside system.toml:

    <CycloneDDS xmlns="https://cdds.io/config">
  <Domain id="any">
    <General>
      <Interfaces>
        <NetworkInterface autodetermine="true" priority="default" multicast="default" />
      </Interfaces>
      <AllowMulticast>default</AllowMulticast>
    </General>
  </Domain>
</CycloneDDS>

    The build copies the file into the image and hands it to Cyclone’s own parser, so it reaches a target that has no file system. Use <Domain id="any">, or the image’s domain_id: nros build refuses any other id. On a host image, CYCLONEDDS_URI still replaces the file at run time.

  7. On an RTOS image, give the network stack what RTPS discovery needs: multicast (IGMP), enough network buffers for the burst of discovery traffic, and a heap, since Cyclone allocates with malloc. On Zephyr, start from the fragment the shipped examples use and name it in the image:

    [image.zephyr_cyclonedds]
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "cyclonedds"
os_config = ["prj-cyclonedds.conf"]

    Copy examples/zephyr/rust/talker/prj-cyclonedds.conf beside system.toml. Its lines that matter for Cyclone are CONFIG_NET_IPV4_IGMP=y, the CONFIG_NET_PKT_* and CONFIG_NET_BUF_* counts, and CONFIG_HEAP_MEM_POOL_SIZE. The settings for the other platforms are listed in Pick and configure the RMW.

Example

A host talker on DDS domain 5 with its own Cyclone configuration. This is the bringup nros new host_ws --board linux --template talker --rmw cyclonedds writes, with domain_id changed:

# src/host_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "host_node"
rmw = "cyclonedds"
ros_edition = "humble"
domain_id = 5

[[component]]
pkg = "host_node"
class = "host_node::Talker"
name = "host_node"

[image.posix]
board = "linux"

with src/host_node_bringup/rmw/cyclonedds.xml as in step 6. Run the image and the listener:

nros run host_node

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp ROS_DOMAIN_ID=5
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

If it doesn’t work

  • The build stops on <Domain id>. The XML names a domain other than any or the image’s domain_id. Change it to any.
  • ros2 topic echo shows nothing. Check that both sides use the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID and that the ROS 2 side runs rmw_cyclonedds_cpp. On a network without multicast, list the peers in the XML instead.
  • Two Zephyr native_sim images never discover each other. Its offloaded sockets do not pass multicast to the host; see Troubleshoot.
  • An RTOS image stalls during discovery. The network buffer counts or the heap are too small for the discovery burst. Raise them in the image’s fragment.

See also

  • Configure an image: the middleware’s own file, and one file per image.
  • Configuration surface: where rmw and domain_id are set and what they become on Zephyr.
  • Bridge between backends: Cyclone DDS beside zenoh or XRCE-DDS in one image.
  • How nano-ros differs from ROS 2.

Use XRCE-DDS

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Pick and configure the RMW

Use XRCE-DDS when the image must be as small as possible, or must join an existing micro-ROS or DDS system through an agent.

The XRCE-DDS backend is the Micro-XRCE-DDS client, the one micro-ROS uses. The client does no discovery of its own: it asks a Micro-XRCE-DDS Agent on a host to create DDS entities for it, and the agent carries the data between the client and the DDS network. ROS 2 nodes on any DDS-based RMW see those entities. The agent is required: an image whose agent stops loses all connectivity until it comes back.

Before you start

  • A workspace, such as the host one from Run a talker.
  • ROS 2 Humble, to see the image from ROS 2.

Steps

  1. Provision the backend. --rmw xrce installs the client sources and the agent at the version nano-ros pins:

    nros setup linux --rmw xrce

  2. Add an XRCE-DDS image and tell it where the agent listens. XRCE-DDS has no configuration file; its whole wiring is the image’s locator. Port 2018 is the client’s default agent port:

    [image.posix_xrce]
board = "linux"
rmw = "xrce"
locator = "udp/127.0.0.1:2018"

  3. Run it. For a UDP locator on this machine, nros run starts the agent on that port first:

    nros run posix_xrce --expect 'Publishing:' --timeout 120

    nros run: starting the XRCE agent (udp4 -p 2018)
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after

  4. See it from ROS 2. The agent creates ordinary DDS entities, so the default ROS 2 RMW receives them:

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

    data: 'Hello World: 5'

    Run nros run posix_xrce without --expect in the first terminal so the talker keeps going.

  5. Run the agent yourself instead, for example on another host or with your own options. Start the pinned agent, and tell nros run to start nothing:

    "$(nros locate tool xrce-agent)/bin/MicroXRCEAgent" udp4 -p 2018

    nros run posix_xrce --router none

    For an agent on another host, put that host’s address in the locator.

  6. Use a serial link. With a serial/ locator, nros run waits for the runner to report the serial device and then starts the agent on it with the locator’s baud rate (serial --dev <device> -b 115200). For a board on your desk, start the agent on the board’s USB serial device yourself:

    "$(nros locate tool xrce-agent)/bin/MicroXRCEAgent" serial --dev /dev/ttyACM0 -b 115200

    How a bare-metal board carries XRCE-DDS over its UART is the board’s: the mps2-an385 example examples/mps2-an385-baremetal/rust/talker-xrce states locator = "custom://uart", and its build then leaves out the IP transports.

  7. Size the session for a small target. The client’s buffers and entity counts are build-time knobs, stated per image:

    [image.posix_xrce.knobs.xrce]
buffer_size = 256
stream_history = 4

    stream_history must be at least 4. A received sample larger than buffer_size is refused on take.

Example

The host scaffold with a zenoh image and an XRCE-DDS image side by side. The bringup:

# src/host_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "host_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
ros_edition = "humble"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "host_node"
class = "host_node::Talker"
name = "host_node"

[image.posix]
board = "linux"

[image.posix_xrce]
board = "linux"
rmw = "xrce"
locator = "udp/127.0.0.1:2018"

nros run posix_xrce

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

If it doesn’t work

  • no XRCE agent at …. The agent is not provisioned. Run nros setup linux --rmw xrce, or start an agent of your own and pass --router none.
  • the agent exited (…) … so the target cannot work. Another agent or program already holds the port. Stop it, or change the port in the locator.
  • Entity creation times out. The agent is not running or not reachable at the locator’s address, or stream_history is below 4.
  • ros2 topic echo shows nothing. Both sides must use the same domain_id; the agent joins the domain the client asks for.

  • Support status: the pinned client and agent versions.

Switch the RMW per image

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Pick and configure the RMW

Use this page to build one bringup on more than one RMW backend, or to move an image from one backend to another.

nano-ros picks the backend when it builds an image. There is no RMW_IMPLEMENTATION to change at run time, as there is in ROS 2: an image is built for one backend, and a second backend is a second image. The backend names are zenoh, cyclonedds and xrce, everywhere. A bringup that names none builds zenoh.

Before you start

  • A workspace whose bringup builds, such as the one from Run a talker.
  • Each backend you add provisioned for the board: nros setup <board> --rmw <backend>.

Steps

  1. Choose the backend every image gets by default, in the bringup’s system.toml:

    [system]
rmw = "zenoh"

  2. Add an image on another backend. An image’s own rmw wins over [system] rmw:

    [image.posix]
board = "linux"

[image.posix_cyclonedds]
board = "linux"
rmw = "cyclonedds"

  3. Build the image by name. Each image builds into a directory of its own, so nothing from the other backend’s build is reused:

    nros build posix_cyclonedds

  4. Run it. A host image logs the backend it was built for in its first line:

    nros run posix_cyclonedds --expect 'Publishing:' --timeout 120

    boot config: … rmw cyclonedds (baked)
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after

  5. To move every image instead, change [system] rmw and drop the per-image lines. Then provision the new backend and build again:

    nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds
nros build posix

Node packages need no edit for any of this. A Rust node package names no backend feature and calls no backend register(); the entry nros build generates for the image links the backend and registers it.

On an RTOS image

The same rmw line selects the backend on every platform; the build turns it into the platform’s own setting. On Zephyr it becomes exactly one of CONFIG_NROS_RMW_ZENOH, CONFIG_NROS_RMW_XRCE or CONFIG_NROS_RMW_CYCLONEDDS, which you do not write in a .conf file yourself. Give each backend’s image the Zephyr fragment that backend needs:

[image.zephyr_zenoh]
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "zenoh"
os_config = ["prj-zenoh.conf"]

[image.zephyr_cyclonedds]
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "cyclonedds"
os_config = ["prj-cyclonedds.conf"]

A Cyclone DDS image also needs multicast networking on the target; see Use Cyclone DDS.

In a CMake project that is not a workspace

A CMake project with no system.toml that uses nano-ros through find_package(nano_ros) or add_subdirectory picks its backend on the configure line with NROS_RMW. nros setup presets writes the project a CMakePresets.json that already carries the SDK root and the board’s toolchain:

nros setup presets
cmake --preset linux -DNROS_RMW=cyclonedds    # zenoh | xrce | cyclonedds
cmake --build build/linux

Clear the build directory, or use one per backend, when you switch back and forth.

Example

One bringup, three images on the Linux host, one per backend:

# src/host_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "host_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
ros_edition = "humble"
domain_id = 0
default_images = ["posix"]

[[component]]
pkg = "host_node"
class = "host_node::Talker"
name = "host_node"

[image.posix]
board = "linux"

[image.posix_cyclonedds]
board = "linux"
rmw = "cyclonedds"

[image.posix_xrce]
board = "linux"
rmw = "xrce"
locator = "udp/127.0.0.1:2018"

nros setup linux --rmw zenoh
nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds
nros setup linux --rmw xrce
nros build posix_cyclonedds
nros run posix_xrce --expect 'Publishing:' --timeout 120

A bare nros build builds the default_images; with several images and no default_images, it lists them and stops rather than guess.

If it doesn’t work

  • nros build lists the images and stops. The bringup has several images and no default_images. Name the image, or add default_images.
  • The build cannot find the backend’s sources. That backend is not provisioned for the board; run nros setup <board> --rmw <backend>.
  • The image still talks the old backend. You ran a different image than you built. nros run <image> --dry-run prints the plan; its image line names the image it runs.
