Use a serial link

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Run a talker

Use a serial link when a board has a UART but no network, or when a point-to-point cable to one host is all the network you want. It is the link the board starters use first, because it needs no IP stack, no address and no switch.

The image’s locator makes the link. A locator that starts with serial/ tells the build to leave the IP stack out, and tells zenoh-pico to send its frames over that UART. On the host, rmw_zenohd listens on the serial device and connects the board to every other node. For XRCE-DDS over a UART, see Use XRCE-DDS; WiFi is not covered yet.

Before you start

  • The board provisioned for zenoh, for example nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal --rmw zenoh.
  • ROS 2 Humble with ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp, sourced in each terminal. It provides the router.

Steps

  1. Scaffold a project. A board that brings a UART out to the host gets a serial image from nros new:

    nros new serial_ws --board mps2-an385-baremetal --template talker
cd serial_ws

    The image block in src/serial_node_bringup/system.toml names the board’s UART and its rate:

    [image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"

  2. Run it in the emulator. nros run boots QEMU with the UART on a terminal device of your host, then starts the router on that device:

    nros run serial_node --expect 'Publishing:'

    nros run: starting the zenoh router on serial//dev/pts/4#baudrate=115200
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after

    The device number differs from run to run. The router also listens on tcp/127.0.0.1:7447, so ROS 2 nodes on this host can reach the board.

  3. Hear it from ROS 2. Leave nros run serial_node running in one terminal, and in another:

    export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

    data: 'Hello World: 2'

  4. Change the rate, for a board on a real cable. Edit the baudrate in the locator; nros run gives the router the same options. QEMU ignores the rate, so it matters only on hardware:

    locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=921600"

    115200 works on any adapter. Many USB serial adapters take 460800, and 921600 is the top rate of many MCU UARTs. A long or noisy cable gives framing errors at high rates.

  5. Run the router yourself for a real board. Flash the board as its starter shows. Its UART then appears as a USB serial device, /dev/ttyACM0 for example. rmw_zenohd reads no command-line arguments, so give it the endpoints in ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE: the serial device for the board, and a TCP port for ROS 2 nodes on this host:

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["serial//dev/ttyACM0#baudrate=115200","tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"]' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

    The router listens and the board dials it. Reset the board, then run the ros2 topic echo of step 3.

  6. On a Zephyr board, set the main thread below the zenoh read task. With Zephyr’s default main priority, 0, the main thread outranks the read task while it creates entities, the UART receive ring overflows, and a board joining a busy domain misses the router’s replies. Put this in the image’s Zephyr fragment, the file its os_config names:

    CONFIG_MAIN_THREAD_PRIORITY=5

    nros build refuses a serial image whose main thread is not below the read task, and its message names the value to use. If joins into a busy domain still fail, raise CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_SERIAL_RX_RING_BYTES from its default of 1024; the ring is static RAM.

Example

The scaffold’s whole bringup, which runs as is in QEMU:

# src/serial_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "serial_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
ros_edition = "humble"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "serial_node"
class = "serial_node::Talker"
name = "serial_node"

[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run serial_node

If it doesn’t work

  • The session never opens, or times out. The router listens on a different device than the board’s UART, or the two use different rates. Check the device in the router’s endpoint and the baudrate on both sides.
  • The board runs but ROS 2 hears nothing. The router has no TCP endpoint for host nodes (add tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 as in step 5), the two sides use different domain_id values, or ros2 topic echo is missing --qos-reliability best_effort.
  • Nothing arrives on hardware, but QEMU works. The UART may also carry the board’s debug console. Give zenoh a UART of its own, or turn the console off.
  • nros run stops and names the router. It could not find rmw_zenohd. Source ROS 2, or set NROS_RMW_ZENOHD to the binary.

See also

  • Configure zenoh: network locators, a router on another host, and the session file.
  • Tune throughput and latency: the buffers a serial image gets and how to change them.
  • Environment variables: the locator forms NROS_LOCATOR takes.
  • Troubleshoot: failures that are not specific to serial.

Design background

  • RFC-0109: network config layers
  • RFC-0121: workspace-first project layout

Bridge between backends

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Configure zenoh, Use Cyclone DDS

Use a bridge when one image must forward topics from one RMW backend to another: a field gateway that takes zenoh traffic from sensor boards and republishes it on a DDS network, or a flight controller on XRCE-DDS whose telemetry a DDS ground station reads.

A bridge is declared, not written. In the bringup’s system.toml, each backend session is a [[domain]] row and each forwarding is a [[bridge]] row between two of them. The build resolves every topic name to its ROS type and generates the forwarder; you write no bridge code. Most images use one backend; a bridge image links two and drains both in each executor spin.

Before you start

  • A workspace with a Rust node package that publishes what you want to forward. The shipped examples/workspaces/bridge-cyclonedds is this page’s example.
  • Both backends provisioned for the board, for example nros setup linux --rmw zenoh and nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds.
  • ROS 2 Humble with rmw_zenoh_cpp and rmw_cyclonedds_cpp, sourced.

Steps

  1. Declare what the node publishes, in its Cargo.toml, so the build can resolve a topic name to its type before anything is compiled:

    # src/talker_pkg/Cargo.toml
[[package.metadata.nros.node.publishes]]
topic = "/chatter"
type = "std_msgs/msg/Int32"

  2. Declare the two sessions. name is yours, rmw is the backend and id the domain. The node runs on the image’s own backend, [system] rmw:

    # src/demo_bringup/system.toml
[[domain]]
name = "zen"
rmw = "zenoh"
id = 0

[[domain]]
name = "dds"
rmw = "cyclonedds"
id = 5

  3. Declare the bridge. from and to are <rmw>:<domain name>. Leave out topics to forward every declared topic, or list some; set bidirectional = true to forward both ways without echoing a sample back:

    [[bridge]]
name = "gw"
from = "zenoh:zen"
to = "cyclonedds:dds"
topics = ["/chatter"]

  4. Give a session its middleware file when it needs more than its defaults. A [[domain]] names it with config, in the backend’s own language:

    [[domain]]
name = "zen"
rmw = "zenoh"
id = 0
config = "rmw/zenoh-zen.json5"

    // src/demo_bringup/rmw/zenoh-zen.json5
{
  mode: "client",
  connect: { endpoints: ["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"] },
}

    A domain with a config states no locator: the file is its wiring.

  5. Build the image. The build writes the bridge’s configuration, nros-bridge.toml, beside the bringup and links both backends:

    nros build linux
ls src/demo_bringup/nros-bridge.toml

    src/demo_bringup/nros-bridge.toml

  6. Run it. The image’s own backend is zenoh, so nros run starts the router for it first:

    nros run linux

    nros run: starting the zenoh router on tcp/127.0.0.1:7447

  7. Read the forwarded topic on the Cyclone DDS side, on domain 5, in a second terminal:

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp ROS_DOMAIN_ID=5
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/Int32

    data: 7

  8. Forward to XRCE-DDS instead. An XRCE-DDS session has no configuration file, so its domain names the agent’s address as locator:

    [[domain]]
name = "agent"
rmw = "xrce"
id = 0
locator = "udp/127.0.0.1:8888"

[[bridge]]
name = "gw"
from = "zenoh:zen"
to = "xrce:agent"

    Start the agent on that port, as in Use XRCE-DDS; the shipped examples/workspaces/bridge-xrce is this form.

  9. Change a session’s endpoint at run time on a host image, without a rebuild. For each [[node]] in the generated nros-bridge.toml, NROS_BRIDGE_<NODE>_LOCATOR replaces its locator and NROS_BRIDGE_<NODE>_DOMAIN its domain, with <NODE> the node’s name in upper case.

Example

The bringup of examples/workspaces/bridge-cyclonedds, which forwards /chatter from zenoh to Cyclone DDS domain 5:

# src/demo_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "bridge_demo"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0
default_launch = "system.launch.xml"

[[component]]
pkg = "talker_pkg"
class = "talker_pkg::Talker"
name = "talker"

[[domain]]
name = "zen"
rmw = "zenoh"
id = 0
config = "rmw/zenoh-zen.json5"

[[domain]]
name = "dds"
rmw = "cyclonedds"
id = 5
config = "rmw/cyclonedds-dds.xml"

[[bridge]]
name = "gw"
from = "zenoh:zen"
to = "cyclonedds:dds"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

The two rmw/ files are in the example. Build and run it with steps 5 to 7.

A bridge you write yourself

When the forwarding needs logic of its own, open the second session in code instead. Register each backend before the executor opens, open the primary session with Executor::open_with_rmw, and give each node its backend with node_builder(name).rmw(backend). A node whose backend is the primary’s shares the primary session; any other opens a session of its own. Set NROS_RMW to the primary’s name when the image links several backends, so the primary does not depend on link order:

NROS_RMW=zenoh ./my_bridge

Each extra session adds its backend’s poll and dispatch time to every spin, because one executor drains the sessions in turn. For a bridge with a deadline, put the fast side’s node in a higher-priority sched task; see Pick a scheduling model.

If it doesn’t work

  • The build cannot resolve a topic. The node package does not declare it under [[package.metadata.nros.node.publishes]], or the topics list names a topic no node publishes.
  • The build refuses a domain’s config. A domain with a file also states a locator, or no [[bridge]] uses the domain. Drop the locator, or the unused domain.
  • Nothing arrives on the far side. The reader is on another domain than the egress [[domain]]’s id, or, for XRCE-DDS, the agent is not running at the domain’s locator.
  • A hand-written bridge fails to open its second session. Both nodes asked for the primary’s backend while the primary opened on another one. Set NROS_RMW to the primary’s backend.

See also

  • nros-bridge.toml reference: the generated file, its keys and its errors.
  • Configure an image: one middleware file per domain, and per-image overrides.
  • Use XRCE-DDS: the agent an XRCE-DDS egress needs.
  • The execution model: how one executor drains several sessions.

Design background

  • RFC-0108: executor preemption levels
  • RFC-0109: network config layers

Tune throughput and latency

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Configure zenoh

Use this page when a zenoh image publishes more than its transport sends, a latency-critical topic arrives late, or large messages and service replies do not arrive at all.

Every language front end, Rust, C and C++, publishes through the same zenoh-pico transmit path, so these settings apply to all three. They matter most on Zephyr, whose socket layer serializes sends and receives on one socket: the zenoh-pico read task holds the session socket for a whole receive window, 100 ms by default, so an untuned image sends about once per window, about 9 messages a second, however many publishers it has. All of these are build-time settings; an embedded image has no run-time configuration.

Before you start

  • A zenoh image that builds, and a measure of its publish rate and the latency each topic can take.
  • The platform’s defaults. Zephyr builds with batching and split locking on; every other platform builds with both off.

Steps

  1. Read the values your platform resolves, and the rung that set each one (builtin, platform, board or env):

    nros config explain --platform zephyr

    knob                     value      set by
----                     -----      ------
zenoh.tx.batch           true       platform
zenoh.tx.split_lock      true       platform
zenoh.tx.flush_ms        50         platform

  2. Turn on transmit batching for an image that publishes many small or medium messages and can wait one flush period. Publishes then collect in the transport’s write buffer and leave as one socket send per flush:

    [image.posix.knobs.zenoh.tx]
batch = true

    A flush thread sends the batch every flush_ms; ThreadX has no background tasks, so there the executor’s spin sends it. Service requests and replies never wait in the batch. Do not batch a timer-paced image that publishes less than once per flush period: there is nothing to combine, and the flushes make it slower.

  3. Add split locking if a tight-loop or bursty publisher is still limited by the transport. The flush then sends one batch while publishers fill the next, and a full batch no longer blocks the publishing thread. It needs batch:

    [image.posix.knobs.zenoh.tx]
batch = true
split_lock = true

    On Zephyr native_sim, 64-byte messages from a tight loop went from about 9 a second untuned to about 136 with batching and about 181 with both. Those are single runs on one development host; the ratios hold, the absolute numbers move with the host.

  4. Bound the latency batching adds. A non-express sample waits up to flush_ms; lower it toward 10 to 20 ms when your budget needs fresher samples, at the cost of more, smaller sends:

    [image.posix.knobs.zenoh.tx]
batch = true
flush_ms = 20

  5. Mark a low-rate, latency-critical publisher express, such as a control setpoint or an emergency stop. Its samples skip the batch and leave at once, while the rest of the image stays batched. Express is a transport hint, not a DDS QoS policy: subscriptions and backends that do not batch ignore it.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let pub_ = node.publisher("/cmd_vel").typed::<Twist>().tx_express(true).build()?;
}
rclc_qos_t qos = RCLC_QOS_DEFAULT;
qos.tx_express = 1;
rclc_publisher_init_with_qos(&pub, &node, type_info, "/cmd_vel", &qos);

auto pub = node.create_publisher<Twist>("/cmd_vel", rclcpp::QoS().tx_express(true));

Do not mark a stream express on Zephyr: each express sample waits for the socket window on its own.

Set the wire buffers

The wire buffers decide the largest message an image can send and receive. They depend on your network and your largest message, so the build does not derive them. Set them per image:

[image.posix.knobs.zenoh.wire]
frag_max_size = 1400
batch_unicast_size = 1024
get_reply_buf_size = 1024

or for one build, in its environment, where an exported value wins:

NROS_ZENOH_FRAG_MAX_SIZE=1400 NROS_ZENOH_BATCH_UNICAST_SIZE=1024 nros build

or in the board descriptor’s [knobs], when the budget belongs to the hardware. frag_max_size is the largest message the image can receive; a larger one is dropped. batch_unicast_size is the largest it sends without fragmenting. On a network with a 1500-byte MTU, or Zephyr’s default of about 1400, keep the batch sizes below the MTU. A serial image gets a 1500-byte unicast batch by default.

Example

A Linux host image that streams telemetry batched every 20 ms and sends its command topic express:

# src/host_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "host_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
ros_edition = "humble"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "host_node"
class = "host_node::Talker"
name = "host_node"

[image.posix]
board = "linux"

[image.posix.knobs.zenoh.tx]
batch = true
split_lock = true
flush_ms = 20

with the command publisher built tx_express(true) as in step 5. Build it with nros build posix.

If it doesn’t work

What you seeWhat to change
Large messages never arriveraise frag_max_size: the message exceeds the reassembly limit
A subscription receives truncated data, or a large-type subscription fails to createthe receive slot is too small; see Size an image from its contract
Service calls with large replies time outraise get_reply_buf_size
Several concurrent service calls failraise NROS_ZENOH_MAX_PENDING_GETS
An entity create fails at run timea pool is full; the Static pool inventory names the knob that sizes it
A benchmark listener counts far fewer messages than were sentits receive ring is too shallow for a batch arriving at once; build the listener with NROS_ZENOH_SUBSCRIBER_RING_DEPTH=1024
Batching made a timer-paced image slowerturn batch off: at one message per flush there is nothing to combine

Do not flush from your own timers or executor threads. Flushing from a sched-task thread stalls the timers that produce the samples, and measured slower than no batching.

See also

  • Environment variables: every transmit knob and its Zephyr, cargo and CMake spelling, and the buffer knobs of zenoh-pico, smoltcp and XRCE-DDS.
  • CLI reference: nros config explain.
  • Use XRCE-DDS: sizing an XRCE-DDS session.
  • Static memory and pools: why these buffers are fixed at build time.

Design background

  • RFC-0049: hierarchical platform and board config
  • RFC-0103: one owner per fact

Use QoS, status events and discovery

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Talk to ROS 2

Use status events when a node must react to what its middleware sees: a publisher it depends on going silent, a periodic topic missing its deadline, samples lost to a slow consumer, or the first subscriber appearing.

The events are the ones ROS 2 defines, with the QoS policies behind them. Two things differ in nano-ros. A callback you register runs from inside spin_once, on the executor thread, like a message callback; there is no waitset to poll. And an incompatible QoS pair is not an event: it fails at create_publisher or create_subscription with NROS_RMW_RET_INCOMPATIBLE_QOS, so you see it at start-up.

EventSideFires when
LivelinessChangedsubscriptiona matched publisher starts or stops asserting liveliness
RequestedDeadlineMissedsubscriptionno sample arrived within the deadline
MessageLostsubscriptionthe backend dropped samples
LivelinessLostpublisherthis publisher missed its own liveliness deadline
OfferedDeadlineMissedpublisherthis publisher fell behind its offered rate
PublicationMatched, SubscriptionMatchedeitheran endpoint on the other side appears or leaves
PublisherIncompatibleType, SubscriptionIncompatibleTypeeitherthe same topic name appears with another type

Before you start

  • A node package whose subscription or publisher you want to watch.
  • Its backend. Not every backend generates every event; the Per-RMW feature matrix lists which ones each backend implements.

Steps

  1. Ask the backend first, if the node must run on more than one. A registration the backend cannot serve answers Unsupported:

    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
if sub.supports_event(EventKind::RequestedDeadlineMissed) {
    sub.on_requested_deadline_missed(Duration::from_millis(15), on_late)?;
} else {
    // fall back to a timeout of your own
}
}

  2. Register a subscription callback. The callback runs from spin_once, counts as one callback against the executor’s per-spin limit, and never runs after the subscription is finalized.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let mut sub = node.create_polling_subscription::<SensorReading>("/sensor")?;
sub.on_liveliness_changed(|status| {
    if status.alive_count == 0 {
        log::warn!("sensor publisher went silent");
    }
})?;
sub.on_message_lost(|status| {
    log::warn!("dropped {} samples", status.total_count_change);
})?;
}
static void on_liveliness_changed(rcl_subscription_t *sub,
                                  rclc_liveliness_changed_status_t status,
                                  void *user_context) {
    if (status.alive_count == 0) {
        trigger_failover();
    }
}

/* After rclc_executor_add_subscription(): */
rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_subscription_set_liveliness_changed_callback(
    &sub, on_liveliness_changed, NULL);

The C setters return RCL_RET_OK, or RCL_RET_UNSUPPORTED when the backend does not generate the event.

static void on_liveliness_changed(void* storage,
                                  nros_cpp_liveliness_changed_status_t status,
                                  void* user_context) {
    if (status.alive_count == 0) trigger_failover();
}

// On an rclcpp::PollingSubscription:
sub.on_liveliness_changed(on_liveliness_changed, nullptr);
sub.on_requested_deadline_missed(15 /* ms */, on_deadline_missed, nullptr);

The C++ setters take a function pointer and a user_context, not a lambda, and the subscription setters exist on PollingSubscription only. ErrorCode::Unsupported means the backend does not generate the event.

  1. Start publishing once someone listens. A matched callback on the publisher reports the subscribers it matches; publisher-side events are noticed when the publisher publishes or asserts liveliness, so a publisher that is not publishing yet asserts liveliness while it waits:

    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub_.on_matched(|s| {
    if s.current_count > 0 { LISTENER_PRESENT.store(true, Ordering::Release); }
})?;
while !LISTENER_PRESENT.load(Ordering::Acquire) {
    let _ = pub_.assert_liveliness();
    executor.spin_once(Duration::from_millis(50));
}
}

    When the subscriber goes away, current_count_change is -1.

  2. Watch a periodic topic’s deadline. Set the deadline to the period plus the jitter you accept; for a 100 Hz topic, 15 ms:

    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let mut sub = node.create_polling_subscription::<SensorReading>("/imu")?;
sub.on_requested_deadline_missed(Duration::from_millis(15), |status| {
    if status.total_count_change > 0 {
        log::error!("IMU late: {} missed deadlines", status.total_count_change);
    }
})?;
}

    On zenoh the argument is the deadline unless the subscription’s QoS states one. On Cyclone DDS the deadline comes from the QoS profile and the argument is ignored.

What each backend generates

  • zenoh generates the five core events and both matched and incompatible-type pairs. Liveliness is per publisher (alive_count is 0 or 1), and there is no LivelinessChanged on bare metal. Matched counts come from the graph cache, as in rmw_zenoh_cpp.
  • Cyclone DDS generates the same set by polling: the runtime asks Cyclone on the entity’s own data path. A publisher that stops publishing stops being asked, so its events arrive with its next publish or assert_liveliness.
  • XRCE-DDS generates the two deadline events only, by a clock check on the client. The agent’s DDS entity keeps an infinite deadline, so a DDS peer matching on deadline sees none.

A subscription with any status callback is asked on every spin, not only when data arrives, so a publisher leaving is noticed at the next spin after the backend sees it. A subscription with no status callback costs an idle executor nothing.

Example

A subscription that fails over when its publisher goes silent and counts late samples, on any backend:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use core::time::Duration;

let mut sub = node.create_polling_subscription::<VehicleAttitude>("/vehicle_attitude")?;
sub.on_liveliness_changed(|status| {
    if status.alive_count == 0 {
        request_minimum_risk_manoeuvre();
    } else if status.alive_count_change > 0 {
        clear_failover();
    }
})?;
if sub.supports_event(EventKind::RequestedDeadlineMissed) {
    sub.on_requested_deadline_missed(Duration::from_millis(15), |status| {
        LATE.fetch_add(status.total_count_change as u32, Ordering::Relaxed);
    })?;
}
}

If it doesn’t work

  • A C subscription setter returns RCL_RET_NOT_INIT. The subscription is not in an executor yet. Register after rclc_executor_add_subscription.
  • A C or C++ setter returns RCLC_RET_FULL or ErrorCode::Full. The process-wide table holds 16 registrations across every C and C++ entity. One publisher with all four of its kinds and one subscription with all five take nine.
  • A registration answers Unsupported. The backend does not generate that event; see the list above. Use supports_event and a fallback.
  • A publisher-side event never fires. The publisher is not publishing. Call assert_liveliness from its loop.

See also

  • Per-RMW feature matrix: the generated list of events and QoS policies per backend.
  • Talk to ROS 2: QoS on the wire between nano-ros and ROS 2.
  • The execution model: the per-spin callback limit that event callbacks share.
  • How nano-ros differs from ROS 2.

Declare QoS in a contract

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: the contract walkthrough · Project layout

Declare an endpoint’s QoS in its contract when you want the image to reserve memory for the history it keeps, rather than for the backend’s default.

QoS itself is the ROS 2 idea you already know: see About Quality of Service settings. What differs in nano-ros is that every queue is static. The build sizes the receive rings, the executor arena and the transient-local retention from what the contract declares, before any of your code is compiled. A QoS you pass in code and never declare is a QoS the image did not reserve for.

Before you start

  • A bringup that builds and runs, with a contract beside its launch file (<bringup>/launch/<stem>.contract.yaml), or beside system.toml for a bringup with no launch/ directory (Contracts for a bringup with no launch file).
  • The endpoint is already declared under nodes: and wired under topics:.
  • The call site registers the endpoint on an absolute name ("/chatter", not "chatter"). A contract states resolved names, and the build will not match a relative one.

Steps

  1. Add a qos: block to the endpoint. Edit the endpoint’s row under nodes.<node>.pub or nodes.<node>.sub. The keys are those of the contract format’s qos section: reliability, durability, history, depth, lifespan, liveliness, deadline, lease_duration.

    nodes:
  qos_listener:
    sub:
      qos_chatter:
        qos:
          history: keep_last
          depth: 5
          durability: transient_local

    Use history: keep_last with the depth: you mean. keep_all has no static bound, so the build cannot size a buffer from it.

    A qos: block under topics.<name> sets the topic’s QoS for every endpoint on it; an endpoint’s own block overrides it.

  2. Make the call site state the same QoS. The contract says what the build reserved; the code says what the endpoint asks for. Each language holds the two together differently.

Pass the profile to the _with_qos registration. Rust checks at registration: where the code asks for a deeper queue than the contract reserved, it takes the contract’s depth and logs a warning; where the code asks for a shallower one, it refuses the registration. From rust_qos_talker_pkg/src/lib.rs:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn qos_profile() -> QoSProfile {
    QoSProfile::default().reliable().transient_local().depth(5)
}

let pub_chatter =
    node.create_publisher_for_topic_with_qos::<Int32>("/qos_chatter", qos_profile())?;
}

Build an rclc_qos_t and pass it to rclc_subscription_init_with_qos (or rclc_publisher_init_with_qos). At registration, a C subscription whose depth, reliability or durability differs from the contract is refused. From c_qos_listener_pkg/src/QosListener.c, whose contract row would state depth: 1:

static rclc_qos_t qos_profile(void) {
    rclc_qos_t q = RCLC_QOS_DEFAULT;
    q.reliability = RCLC_QOS_RELIABILITY_RELIABLE;
    q.durability = RCLC_QOS_DURABILITY_TRANSIENT_LOCAL;
    q.history = RCLC_QOS_HISTORY_KEEP_LAST;
    q.depth = 1;
    return q;
}

const rclc_qos_t qos = qos_profile();
self->sub = rcl_get_zero_initialized_subscription();
rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_subscription_init_with_qos(
    &self->sub, node, ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(std_msgs, msg, Int32), "/chatter", &qos);

Make the QoS a constexpr and assert it against the contract beside the call. A disagreement then fails to compile, naming the topic and both values. NROS_ASSERT_DECLARED_PUB_QOS does the same for a publisher. From examples/workspaces/cpp/src/listener_pkg/src/Listener.cpp, whose contract row is chatter: { qos: { depth: 1 } }:

constexpr ::rclcpp::QoS kChatterQos = ::rclcpp::QoS(1);
NROS_ASSERT_DECLARED_QOS(::std_msgs::msg::String::TYPE_NAME, "/chatter", kChatterQos,
                         "\"/chatter\"");
::rclcpp::Result r =
    ::rclcpp::bind_subscription<::std_msgs::msg::String, Listener, &Listener::on_msg>(
        node, "/chatter", this, kChatterQos);

  1. Rebuild the image.

    nros build linux_rust_qos

    Among the stage lines, the resolve line names the file the build sized the image from:

    nros build:   resolved → <workspace>/build/demo_bringup__linux_rust_qos/resolved.toml (max_cbs <n>, nodes <n>, digest <digest>)

    If it ends (entity counts not derived; configured defaults kept) instead, the contract did not describe the whole image: see Fix a contract refusal.

Example

The features workspace’s QoS pair, in examples/workspaces/features. A Rust talker publishes /qos_chatter as transient-local with KEEP_LAST(5), and the zenoh backend sizes its retention ring from the deepest transient-local depth the contract declares, so a late joiner receives the last five samples. This is src/demo_bringup/launch/rust_qos.contract.yaml, beside rust_qos.launch.xml:

version: 1

nodes:
  reliable_talker:
    paths:
      on_tick:
        trigger: { timer: { rate_hz: 1 } }
        output: [qos_chatter]
    pub:
      qos_chatter:
        qos:
          history: keep_last
          depth: 5
          durability: transient_local
          reliability: best_effort

  qos_listener:
    sub:
      qos_chatter:
        qos:
          history: keep_last
          depth: 5
          durability: transient_local
    pub:
      qos_ok:
        qos:
          history: keep_last
          depth: 10
          durability: volatile

topics:
  /qos_chatter:
    type: std_msgs/msg/Int32
    pub: [reliable_talker/qos_chatter]
    sub: [qos_listener/qos_chatter]
  /qos_ok:
    type: std_msgs/msg/Int32
    external: sub
    pub: [qos_listener/qos_ok]

The talker’s code asks for reliable; the publisher row says best_effort because the bringup’s system.toml overrides it with a qos_overrides./qos_chatter.publisher.reliability parameter, and the contract has to state the same fact as the override.

If it doesn’t work

  • The build refuses with “QoS statement(s) disagree between the launch contract and the qos_overrides.* parameters”. A launch or system.toml qos_overrides.* parameter and the contract state one policy two ways, or the parameter states one the contract omits. Make the contract state the same value; the message names the topic, the parameter and the contract row.
  • A C++ build fails with “nros: the QoS depth passed for topic … disagrees with the depth declared for that topic in the contract sidecar”. The call site and the row differ. The declared_depth_agrees<declared, passed> diagnostic beside it carries both numbers. Change whichever is wrong.
  • A Rust image logs declared depth: taking KEEP_LAST(…) at boot. The code asked for more than the contract reserved, and the registration took the contract’s depth. Raise the contract row to keep more.
  • A registration fails at boot and the log says the contract declares a deeper queue, or a stronger policy, than the code. Taking it would widen what the code narrowed. Lower the contract row or change the call site.

See also

  • Size an image from its contract: what the declared depths size, and how to see it.
  • Contract format reference: every qos key, generated from the grammar this release pins.
  • QoS, status events, and discovery: the QoS policies at run time.

Size an image from its contract

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: the contract walkthrough · Project layout

Write a contract that describes every node of an image when you want the build to size that image’s static pools from what it creates, instead of from the backend’s defaults.

Every pool in a nano-ros image is a fixed array: a slot costs its bytes whether an entity uses it or not. The build cannot count your entities from the code, because the crates that hold the pools compile before your components do. So it reads the count from the contract, once per image, before anything is compiled, and writes the answers where those crates read them. The steps are the same for Rust, C and C++ images.

Before you start

  • An image that builds and runs with no contract, so you have a baseline.
  • Every node the image launches, and every publisher, subscription, service, client, action and timer each one creates. A count over only some of them is refused, not guessed at (see step 3).

Steps

  1. Build without a contract and note the resolve line.

    nros build linux

    With nothing to count from, the build keeps the configured defaults:

    nros build:   resolved → <workspace>/build/<bringup>__linux/resolved.toml (entity counts not derived; configured defaults kept)

    If you can, measure this image’s static RAM now (Measure static memory), so you can show the saving afterwards.

  2. Write the contract. Put it beside the launch file, as <bringup>/launch/<stem>.contract.yaml for <stem>.launch.xml, or beside system.toml for a bringup with no launch/ (Contracts for a bringup with no launch file). Declare each node’s endpoints under nodes:, keyed by their local names; a timer is a paths: entry whose trigger is { timer: { rate_hz: N } }. Wire each endpoint to its absolute name under topics:, services: or actions:, with its type. To size the receive queues too, declare each endpoint’s depth (Declare QoS in a contract).

  3. Rebuild and read the resolve line.

    nros build linux

    nros build:   resolved → <workspace>/build/<bringup>__linux/resolved.toml (max_cbs <n>, nodes <n>, digest <digest>)

    max_cbs is the executor’s callback table. A publisher claims no callback slot, so it is smaller than the number of entities you declared; that is expected. If the line still says entity counts not derived, the contract does not describe some component: see Fix a contract refusal.

  4. Read what was derived. Open the resolved.toml the line names. [executor] holds the callback, node and action counts, [pools] the RMW session’s publisher, subscriber, queryable and liveliness counts, and [provenance] says where each number came from.

  5. Measure again. Rebuild with the memory report, as in step 1, and compare the two images symbol by symbol (Showing a saving).

Example

The Rust listener in examples/linux/rust/listener runs one subscription. Its system.contract.yaml declares that subscription with KEEP_LAST(1):

version: 1

nodes:
  listener:
    sub:
      chatter:
        qos:
          history: keep_last
          depth: 1

topics:
  /chatter:
    type: std_msgs/msg/String
    sub: [listener/chatter]

With it, the zenoh backend sizes the subscriber’s payload pools for the one sample the image keeps instead of the four its ring would hold by default. The image’s static RAM falls from 273,802 to 172,298 bytes on Linux.

Which knobs the build derives

The pools that dominate static RAM are derived per image from what the contract declares. The build writes the answers into its generated cargo [env] table (on Zephyr, into the Kconfig defaults). Stating one of them by hand is an override, not a requirement.

KnobDerived from
NROS_ZENOH_MAX_PUBLISHERS, NROS_ZENOH_MAX_SUBSCRIBERSthe declared entity inventory, floored at 1: each sizes a fixed C array, where zero is not a smaller pool
NROS_ZENOH_MAX_QUERYABLESthe declared service servers, plus the parameter and lifecycle services the image’s nodes register; with no readable declaration it stays at its undeclared budget (8 embedded, 32 hosted)
NROS_ZENOH_MAX_LIVELINESSone per node name plus the session’s own, one per publisher, subscriber, service server and client, and the parameter and lifecycle families’ entities
NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_CBS, NROS_EXECUTOR_ACTION_CLIENTS, NROS_RMW_SUBSCRIBER_SLOTSthe declared entity inventory
NROS_SUBSCRIBER_BUFFER_SIZEthe largest small-class message type the image subscribes to
NROS_ZENOH_SUBSCRIBER_LARGE_SIZEthe largest large-class type; stated only when the large count is non-zero
NROS_ZENOH_MAX_LARGE_SUBSCRIBERShow many subscribed types fall in the large class. Zero is an answer, not a floor: the pool becomes zero bytes
NROS_SUBSCRIPTION_BUFFER_SIZEthe executor’s take buffer, from the same message bounds
NROS_EXECUTOR_ARENA_SIZEthe same inventory, in the executor’s own build; the variable is the override

The transport’s wire buffers (NROS_ZENOH_FRAG_MAX_SIZE, the batch sizes, NROS_ZENOH_SERVICE_BUFFER_SIZE, NROS_ZENOH_GET_REPLY_BUF_SIZE, NROS_ZENOH_MAX_PENDING_GETS), the smoltcp socket pools and the parameter store limits are not derived: they are yours. They are covered in Tune throughput and latency.

Precedence. A value you state wins over a derived one: an exported environment variable first, then the image’s [image.<id>.knobs], then the board descriptor’s [knobs]. The derived value comes next, and the crate’s own default applies only when nothing is stated and nothing can be derived.

If it doesn’t work

  • The derived buffer size is larger than any message you send. The message-bound sizes (NROS_SUBSCRIBER_BUFFER_SIZE, the large class, NROS_SUBSCRIPTION_BUFFER_SIZE) come from every type in the interface closure the image links, not only the types it subscribes to, so they are an upper bound: never too small, sometimes larger than you need. The build names the type that set the size. When that type is not one of yours, state your own value or trim the package’s <depend> list.
  • Nothing message-bound is derived, and the build names an unbounded type. One unbounded type refuses the whole message-bound derivation, and the stated or default values stand. Bound the field in the .msg (string<=64) or cap it inline in nros-codegen.toml; one cap on a declaring type such as "std_msgs/Header.frame_id" reaches every message that nests it.
  • Entity creation fails at boot after you trimmed the contract. Each slot is exactly what the contract declares, with no headroom, so a contract that leaves out an endpoint the code creates makes a pool one short. On an image for a board other than the host, the census check catches this before the build: see Fix a contract refusal.

See also

  • Static pool inventory: every sizing knob, its default and what it costs at that default.
  • Measure static memory: what your image actually reserved.
  • Contract format reference: every contract key, generated from the grammar this release pins.
  • Static memory and pools: why nano-ros pools are fixed-size.

Contracts for a bringup with no launch file

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Project layout · the contract walkthrough

Write a contract for a bringup that has no launch/ directory when you want its image sized from what it creates, or its QoS declared, without adding a launch file.

A bringup with no launch/ runs the nodes its system.toml lists in [[component]] rows, and the build generates its launch file from those rows. A contract normally sits beside the launch file it describes, but a generated launch file lives under build/, where you cannot author anything. So you write the contract beside system.toml instead, as system.contract.yaml, and the build carries it to the generated launch file.

Before you start

  • A bringup with system.toml, at least one [[component]] row, and no launch/ directory, that builds. If the bringup has a launch/ directory, this page does not apply: write launch/<stem>.contract.yaml beside the launch file instead.
  • The name each node registers its endpoints on, written as an absolute name at the call site.

Steps

  1. Find each node’s name. In the generated launch file, a node’s name is its [[component]] row’s name, so that is the key you use under nodes:.
[[component]]
pkg = "native_listener"
class = "native_rs_listener::Listener"
name = "listener"

[[component]]
pkg = "native_c_listener"
class = "native_c_listener::Listener"
name = "listener"

[[component]]
pkg = "cpp_listener"
class = "cpp_listener::Listener"
name = "listener"

  1. Write system.contract.yaml beside system.toml. Key nodes: by the name from step 1 and each endpoint by its local name; wire it under topics: to the absolute name the code registers:

    version: 1

nodes:
  listener:
    sub:
      chatter:
        qos:
          history: keep_last
          depth: 1

topics:
  /chatter:
    type: std_msgs/msg/String
    sub: [listener/chatter]

    For a C or C++ node, state the depth its call site passes: a C or C++ registration whose depth differs from the contract’s is refused (Declare QoS in a contract).

  2. Build the image.

    nros build linux

    The build generates the launch file and copies your contract beside it. In a workspace, both are under build/nros/launch/<bringup>/launch/:

    ls build/nros/launch/<bringup>/launch/

    system.contract.yaml
system.launch.xml

    For a single package that holds its own system.toml, the directory is <package>/build/nros/launch/<package>/. The copy is rewritten only when your file changes, and deleted when you delete yours.

  3. Check the resolve line. It reports the counts the contract produced:

    nros build:   resolved → <workspace>/build/<bringup>__linux/resolved.toml (max_cbs <n>, nodes <n>, digest <digest>)

    (entity counts not derived; configured defaults kept) means some component is not described: see Fix a contract refusal.

Example

examples/linux/rust/listener is a single-package Rust listener with no launch/. Its system.toml holds the [[component]] row from the Rust tab above and an [image.linux], and its system.contract.yaml is the file from step 2. The code registers the subscription on /chatter, the absolute name the contract states:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
node.create_subscription_for_callback_name::<StringMsg>("on_chatter", "/chatter")?;
}

The contract’s one line of QoS takes the image’s static RAM on Linux from 273,802 to 172,298 bytes, because the zenoh backend then sizes its payload pools for one sample instead of four. The listener still receives every message a 1 Hz talker publishes.

If it doesn’t work

  • The build ignores system.contract.yaml. The bringup has a launch/ directory, so its own launch files are used and nothing is generated or carried. Move the contract to launch/<stem>.contract.yaml, beside the launch file it describes.

  • The build warns that the bringup has no launch/ directory and no [[component]] row. The warning reads:

    nros: warning: <bringup>/system.toml: this bringup has no `launch/` directory and no `[[component]]` row, so nothing says what it runs and no system model is resolved for it. Add a `[[component]]` row (pkg, class, name) to system.toml, or add `launch/system.launch.xml`.

    With no row, there is no launch file to carry the contract to. Add the row.

  • A node’s endpoints are refused, or never matched. The nodes: key is not the row’s name, or the code registers a relative name. Use the row’s name, and an absolute name at the call site. See Fix a contract refusal for the messages.

See also

  • Size an image from its contract: what the counts size, and how to measure the result.
  • Declare QoS in a contract.
  • Contract format reference: every contract key, generated from the grammar this release pins.

Fix a contract refusal

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: the contract walkthrough · Size an image from its contract

Use this page when nros build refuses a contract, or builds the image without sizing it from the contract, and you need to know which statement is wrong.

The contract is a statement about the code, made beside it. The build checks it at several points, and each check refuses rather than guesses, because a pool sized from a wrong statement fails at boot on a board that may have no console. Find the message you have below; each section names the fix. In the messages, angle brackets stand for your own names.

Before you start

  • The full output of the nros build <image> that failed.
  • The contract it read: <bringup>/launch/<stem>.contract.yaml, or <bringup>/system.contract.yaml for a bringup with no launch/.

Steps

  1. Rebuild the image and keep the output.

    nros build <image>

  2. Find the first refusal in the output and match it to a section below. Fix the contract or the code, then rebuild.

The contract does not parse

The contract grammar refuses any key it does not list:

at '<path>': unknown key in `qos` — did you mean `depth`? An unrecognised key used to be discarded in silence, which deleted whatever it was meant to declare

Correct the spelling; the contract format reference lists every key. An endpoint key holding a / is refused the same way:

endpoint key `/chatter` contains `/`: an endpoint key is a local name, and the node's FQN is prefixed to it (`/chatter` would become `<node>//chatter`). Use the endpoint's local name; remap the topic in the launch file or wire it under `topics:`

Key the endpoint by its local name (chatter) and put the absolute name under topics:. Once a contract has been refused, later commands refuse the model it left behind until a resolve succeeds:

SystemModel `<model>` was refused by its producer and cannot be trusted (marker `<marker>`):
  check: <check>
  input: <input>
  Fix the input and run `nros configure`; the next successful resolve removes the marker.

Fix the contract and run nros configure (or nros build) again.

The contract and a qos_overrides parameter disagree

<n> QoS statement(s) disagree between the launch contract and the `qos_overrides.*` parameters.

Each disagreement that follows names the topic, the parameter and its node, and the contract row, or says the row states no such policy. Make the contract state the value the parameter sets. The parameter configures the runtime and the contract sizes the buffers, so the two must agree.

The image was built with its configured defaults

The resolve line says the contract sized nothing:

nros build:   resolved → <workspace>/build/<bringup>__<image>/resolved.toml (entity counts not derived; configured defaults kept)

The reason is the refused line under [provenance] in that resolved.toml. The most common one:

<n> of <m> components in this image declare no entities:
    <pkg>::<component> (<class>)
Deriving over only the components that did would publish a slot count smaller than the image needs, and a short NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_CBS fails entity creation at boot.

Sizing is all or nothing per image. Declare every listed component under nodes:, keyed by its node name. If the reason begins the launch tree resolved, and it declares neither wiring nor parameters, the build found no contract at all: check its file name and where it sits.

An endpoint is not matched

On a Rust image the build prints one line per endpoint it could not match to the contract, for example:

nros build:   subscription `chatter`: this subscription registers on `chatter`, which is not an absolute name. A contract states RESOLVED names, and resolving `chatter` needs the node's namespace AND its remappings -- neither of which reaches this reader per endpoint. Write the name absolutely at the call site, or declare the endpoint the contract already names

Write the name absolutely at the call site ("/chatter"). A node the launch file remaps is refused too (the launch description applies name REMAPPINGS to node): drop the remap, or accept that the endpoint keeps its worst-case sizes. A line beginning no subscription in this image's contract carries type names what the contract does describe; correct the type or the topic.

The census check refuses a cross image

Before it builds an image for a board other than the host, nros build runs the host image generated from the same launch file once, records what every component creates, and compares that census with the contract, row by row:

error missing-in-contract <node> sub /chatter
    the code creates this subscription on `/chatter`; no `sub:` row of `nodes.<node>` is wired to it, so no `topics:` entry names it either
    in <contract>, add under `nodes.<node>.sub` (the alias is the author's; `chatter` is this name's last segment):
        chatter: { qos: { depth: <depth> } }
    and wire it under `topics`:
        /chatter:
          type: <package>/msg/<Name>
          sub: [<node>/chatter]
    not waivable: every pool derives one short; the first catch is ExecutorFull on a board with no console
census check: <n> confirmed, <n> error(s), <n> warning(s), <n> waived

Each row gives the edit. The verdicts:

VerdictMeansFix
missing-in-contractthe code creates it, the contract does not declare itadd the row the message prints
phantomthe contract declares and wires it, the code never creates itremove the row, or waive it
unwireddeclared under nodes: but named by no topics:, services: or actions: entrywire it or remove it
depth-mismatch, qos-mismatch, type-mismatchboth sides name it and disagreechange one side
period-mismatcha timer’s period differs from its path’s rate_hzchange one side
param-missing-in-contract, param-phantom, param-type-mismatchthe same, for a node’s params:as above

Only phantom and param-phantom rows are waivable, one row at a time, in the bringup’s system.toml. The message prints the key to copy:

[census.waive."<node>:sub:/chatter"]
reason = "..."

A refusal that begins census missing: or census stale: means the census is absent or older than the code. Run nros build <image> for the cross image, which takes the census first. If it reports that the bringup declares no HOST image resolved from the same launch and arguments, add one, such as [image.linux] board = "linux" with the same launch and args.

Example

The C++ workspace in examples/workspaces/cpp declares both its nodes in src/demo_bringup/launch/system.contract.yaml. Delete the listener from it:

version: 1

nodes:
  talker:
    paths:
      on_timer:
        trigger: { timer: { rate_hz: 1 } }
        output: [chatter]
    pub:
      chatter: { qos: { depth: 1 } }

topics:
  /chatter:
    type: std_msgs/msg/String
    pub: [talker/chatter]

The listener’s code still subscribes to /chatter, so building the freertos image (board mps2-an385-freertos) is refused by the census: one missing-in-contract row for listener sub /chatter, whose remedy is the listener: entry with chatter: { qos: { depth: 1 } } and the sub: [listener/chatter] wiring. Put them back and the census confirms every row.

If it doesn’t work

  • A configure stops with ENTITIES was retired. A CMakeLists.txt still passes ENTITIES to nano_ros_node_register. Delete the argument and state the component’s entities in the contract.
  • [census] on_missing = "warn" or on_stale = "warn" is set. The bringup has opted out of the refusal, and the build prints a census missing (WARNING line instead. Remove the key to make it a refusal again.

See also

  • Declare QoS in a contract: the compile-time and boot-time QoS checks for each language.
  • Contract format reference: every contract key, generated from the grammar this release pins.

Measure static memory

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Size an image from its contract

The Static Pool Inventory tells you which knobs exist and what each one costs: a byte figure at its default where the pool is a plain product of knobs, and otherwise where its bytes go — a named static, the executor’s storage, a heap — and why no figure can be stated without building. It cannot tell you what your image costs — your knobs differ, your backend differs, and several pools are sized by a sizeof that no comment can see.

For that, measure the image you built with the memory report, which reads the linked ELF. The report ships in the nano-ros source tree, not in a release; running it: see Internals → The memory report.

You get RAM broken down by symbol, by owner, by storage role and by pool, plus the section totals, so you can see how much is not attributable to any symbol:

RAM (writable allocated sections): 518,234 bytes
RAM attributed to symbols:         489,771 bytes
unattributed (padding, linker reservations, symbol-less data): 28,463 bytes (5.5%)

That last line matters. Alignment padding and linker-script reservations are real RAM that no symbol names, so a budget built only from a list of pools will come up short. “Writable allocated sections” means every section the linker marks allocated and writable, whatever it is called — on Zephyr that includes the per-file .noinit.* sections holding thread stacks and the kernel heap.

Who owns the bytes

The RAM by owner table puts every byte under the owner you would name:

       177,112   34.2%  [executor storage]
       206,358   39.8%  nros_rmw_zenoh
        88,280   17.0%  (C / asm / no path)
         8,064    1.6%  [component storage]
  • [executor storage] — the executor’s backing, whichever language placed it: the C/C++ entry’s __nros_executor_storage / __nros_sched_task_executor_storage, the C++ boot storage Node::GlobalStorageHolder<0>::storage, and the Rust EXECUTOR_BACKING / __NROS_SCHED_TASK_EXECUTOR_BACKING. In a sched-task image this is usually the largest single owner.
  • [component storage] — the generated per-component storage (__nros_comp_buf_N for C++, __NROS_COMPONENT_<pkg>_SLOT_STORE for Rust).
  • A Rust crate name, C++ <namespace>, or (C / asm / no path) otherwise. The language comes from the symbol’s mangling, so a C++ namespace that happens to share a Rust crate’s name is never filed under that crate.

For the C and C++ executor storage, the report also reads the build’s own sizes header and tells you how many executors’ worth the image reserved:

        95,904  executor storage   __nros_sched_task_executor_storage
                                   = 4 x 23,976 (NROS_CPP_EXECUTOR_STORAGE_SIZE = 23,976)

The header is found beside the image (the build’s nros-cpp-generated/ mirror); pass --sizes-header <path> if your build keeps it elsewhere. If the header is newer than the image, or two headers disagree, the report says so instead of pricing.

Finding what to cut

The per-symbol list is sorted, so the first few lines are usually the whole story:

## top 5 RAM symbols

       131,072   25.3%  nros_rmw_zenoh::shim::subscriber::LARGE_PAYLOADS
        88,560   17.1%  linux_entry::__nros_entry_run::__NROS_SCHED_TASK_EXECUTOR_BACKING
        88,552   17.1%  nros_node::executor::backing::EXECUTOR_BACKING
        87,072   16.8%  g_sessions
        33,536    6.5%  nros_rmw_zenoh::shim::service::USER_SERVICE_INBOX

The last two sections of the report join these symbols to their knobs for you: declared pools lists the pools that carry a formula (and whether the image agrees with it), and knob-sized pools lists every other static the inventory knows a knob for, with its exact measured size:

        87,072  g_sessions
                pool sized by NROS_ZENOH_MAX_SESSIONS, NROS_ZENOH_MAX_PUBLISHERS, ...

Be aware that today these pools are sized by which backend you link, not by what your node actually does: a publisher-only node still reserves the service and large-payload pools in full. If your image looks far larger than the entities you created would suggest, that is expected rather than a misconfiguration on your side. Turning the corresponding knobs down is the current remedy (see Which knobs the build derives).

The zenoh service inboxes (USER_SERVICE_INBOX, ACTION_INBOX, BUILTIN_INBOX) are one table per family, each sized for its own requests; how their slots are sized is in Static memory and pools.

Showing a saving

Take a baseline (the report’s --json output), change something, rebuild, and compare against it (--baseline; the commands are on the Internals page).

Every symbol row then carries an annotation: (+12,288) for a change, (=) for a symbol that matched and did not move, (new) for one the baseline does not have. A baseline join section lists what matched, what is new and what is gone, and the owner table shows each owner’s delta — so a pool that disappears entirely is reported, not silently absent.

Symbols are matched across builds by name with the compiler’s per-build decorations removed (.llvm.<hash>, .0, .constprop.0, Rust crate hashes), so a static the linker renamed between two builds still compares. A baseline written by an older version of the tool lists only its top symbols; the report marks it incomplete and will not call a symbol “new” on its evidence.

This is also how a change to nano-ros itself should report a memory saving: as a measured difference between two named images, not as an estimate.

Cross-compiled images

The tool prefers llvm-nm, which reads ELF files for any target; your host’s GNU nm is built for one target family and refuses a cross-built image with “File format not recognized”.

You probably already have llvm-nm without knowing it: rustup ships it as part of the llvm-tools component, under the toolchain’s own bin directory rather than on your PATH, and the tool looks there. If it reports that it found no usable nm, run:

rustup component add llvm-tools

llvm-cxxfilt (from a system LLVM) is used when present to demangle; without it the tool falls back to nm -C.

See also

  • Size an image from its contract: the pools the build sizes for you, and how to override one.
  • Static pool inventory: every sizing knob and its default.
  • Static memory and pools: why nano-ros reserves its memory statically.

C / C++ multi-node workspaces

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

This page now holds only the contract sections of the C and C++ workspace walkthrough. The workspace layout, the node and bringup packages, the image and the entry it generates moved to Organize a larger workspace and Mix languages.

The reference C++ workspace is examples/workspaces/cpp/.

Contracts for a C or C++ workspace

Telling the build what the component creates

NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_CBS, the subscriber slots and the arena are const sizes compiled into nros-node before a component TU is compiled, while a typed component wires itself in its CONSTRUCTOR, at runtime. Nothing the macros emit can supply those sizes — it exists only after linking. So somebody has to state what the image creates, ahead of the build.

That statement is a contract sidecar beside the launch file, not something in this CMakeLists. <stem>.contract.yaml next to <stem>.launch.xml in the bringup package:

# src/demo_bringup/launch/system.contract.yaml
version: 1

nodes:
  talker:
    paths:
      on_timer:                                  # a path with a timer trigger
        trigger: { timer: { rate_hz: 1 } }       # IS the periodic callback
        output: [chatter]
    pub:
      chatter: {}
  listener:
    sub:
      chatter: {}

topics:
  /chatter:
    type: std_msgs/msg/Int32
    pub: [talker/chatter]
    sub: [listener/chatter]

nodes: keys are LOCAL endpoint names — an absolute path there is concatenated onto the node’s FQN and matches no topic. topics:, services: and actions: wire those endpoints to absolute names and carry the type. paths: is where timers live: the model records a path with no input as the periodic callback.

The build folds it into the resolved SystemModel and sizes the image’s pools from it; nothing in the CMakeLists takes an argument for it. The tasks that build on this sidecar have their own pages, for every language:

  • Declare QoS in a contract
  • Size an image from its contract
  • Contracts for a bringup with no launch file
  • Fix a contract refusal

Design background

  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The paired examples as image rows of behaviour bringups in the language workspaces.

Organize a larger workspace

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Add a second node

Use this page when a workspace grows past one node and one board: several node packages, several images, and a bringup per behaviour.

A nano-ros workspace has two kinds of package you write, and one thing that is not a package:

  • A node package is a library that says what a node does: its publishers, subscriptions, timers and callbacks. It has no main(), no board and no deployment settings, so one node package runs on every board.
  • A bringup package says what runs and where. It holds a package.xml and a system.toml, and optionally launch/ and config/. It has no Cargo.toml, no CMakeLists.txt and no code. Name it <system>_bringup, as nav2 and Autoware do.
  • An image is one row, [image.<id>], in that system.toml: a board, a launch topology and a backend. nros build <id> generates the program’s entry under build/ and hands off to cargo, CMake or west.

The workspace root has no build file at all. Where ROS 2 has you write a launch file and a main() per process, nano-ros generates the entry from the image row, so adding a board is adding a row, never a package.

Before you start

  • nano-ros installed and the board provisioned, for example nros setup linux.
  • ROS 2 sourced for the first build, which generates message bindings from it.

Steps

  1. Start from a one-node workspace:

    nros new host_ws --board linux --template talker
cd host_ws

    ✓ Created the workspace host_ws
  src/host_node/   the node: a rust talker (library)
  src/host_node_bringup/   what it runs on: `linux`, image `linux`, zenoh

  2. Add a node package. Run nros new from the workspace root; --to adds its [[component]] row to the bringup, and --lang picks its language:

    nros new listener_pkg --lang cpp --template listener --to host_node_bringup

    nros new: added the node package src/listener_pkg/ (listener, cpp) to …/host_ws
  declared it in …/host_ws/src/host_node_bringup: a [[component]] row and an <exec_depend>

Each language states the node in its own build file, and none of them names a board:

# src/host_node/Cargo.toml: a library; `nros::node!(Talker);` ends src/lib.rs
[lib]
path = "src/lib.rs"

# src/talker_pkg/CMakeLists.txt
find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)
nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.cpp)
nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    PLUGIN talker_pkg::Talker
    EXECUTABLE talker
    SHAPE configure)

The class has a configure(::rclcpp::Node&) method that creates its entities and binds member callbacks by identity, with no callback name and no allocation; the generated entry constructs it and calls configure:

::rclcpp::Result Talker::configure(::rclcpp::Node& node) {
    ::rclcpp::Result r = node.create_publisher(pub_, "/chatter");
    if (!r.ok()) return r;
    // Member-fn-pointer-as-template-param → no-alloc trampoline; `this` is ctx.
    return node.create_wall_timer<Talker, &Talker::on_tick>(timer_, 1000, this);
}

The C shape, and packages of several languages in one image, are in Mix languages.

  1. Add an image for a second board:

    nros new --image freertos --board mps2-an385-freertos

    nros new: added [image.freertos] to …/src/host_node_bringup/system.toml
  build it with `nros build freertos`

  2. Build. With two images and no default, a bare nros build lists them and stops:

    nros build

    Error: this workspace declares 2 images and no default.

  host_node_bringup:freertos
  host_node_bringup:linux

  build one:   nros build freertos
  build all:   nros build --all
  or declare:  [system] default_images = ["freertos"]

    Name one image, build them all, or set [system] default_images in the bringup. nros build linux --dry-run prints the handoff and runs nothing:

    nros build: host_node_bringup:linux -> board linux (platform posix), driver cmake

    The driver is CMake here because the image now holds a C++ package.

  3. Run one image. Once a bringup has a second node, the node’s name no longer names one image, so name <bringup>:<image>:

    nros run host_node_bringup:linux

  4. Select a machine with launch arguments. Several images can share one launch file and differ only in its arguments, which is how one launch tree describes several hosts:

    [image.linux_robot1]
board = "linux"
launch = "multihost.launch.xml"
args = { host = "robot1" }

[image.linux_robot2]
board = "linux"
launch = "multihost.launch.xml"
args = { host = "robot2" }

    [image.<id>] says what is built. [host.<name>] says which machine a node runs on, with launch and nodes keys. An image needs no host, and a host needs no image.

  5. Give each behaviour its own bringup when one workspace holds several programs. The language workspaces in the examples keep pubsub_bringup, service_bringup and action_bringup side by side, with one image row per platform and role:

    nros run pubsub_bringup:linux_listener

    A variant with different code is its own node package with its own image row. A variant that only changes a setting, such as a serial link, is an image row over the same packages.

  6. Check what the workspace holds. nros list prints each package and its kind, and nros graph prints the dependency order:

    nros graph

    host_node
listener_pkg
host_node_bringup  <- host_node, listener_pkg

Example

The bringup after the steps above:

# src/host_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "host_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
ros_edition = "humble"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "host_node"
class = "host_node::Talker"
name = "host_node"

[[component]]
pkg = "listener_pkg"
class = "listener_pkg::Listener"
name = "listener_pkg"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

[image.freertos]
board = "mps2-an385-freertos"

nros build --all
nros run host_node_bringup:linux

The bringup has no launch/, so its launch file is generated from the [[component]] rows. Add launch/system.launch.xml when you need a launch argument, a remap or a parameter, as in Parameters and launch files. The workspaces under examples/workspaces/ (rust, c, cpp and mixed) have this shape, Zephyr images included.

When the generated entry is not enough

Reach for these in order, smallest first:

  1. An image key: panic, profile, os_config or features.
  2. before_boot = "<pkg>::<fn>" on the image, for one step before the runtime starts. Rust images only.
  3. The board’s own hardware setup, for what every image on that board needs.
  4. nros materialize <bringup>:<image>, which copies the generated entry to src/<image>_entry/ as a package you own. nros build then leaves it alone; delete the directory to go back to a generated one.

If it doesn’t work

  • nros build refuses a system.toml. It sits beside a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt. A system.toml lives only in a bringup package; the message says where to move it.
  • nros run <node> lists images instead of running. The bringup has more than one node or image. Name <bringup>:<image>.
  • An edit to the image row changes nothing. A hand-written src/<image>_entry/ with a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt takes precedence. Move its settings to the [image.*] row and delete it.

See also

  • system.toml keys: every [image.<id>] key and how blocks fold over [image_defaults].
  • Build outputs: what nros build generates under build/, and where each artifact lands.
  • Build inside an existing CMake or vendor tree: projects that own their build and have no system.toml.
  • How a build becomes an image: the model behind the generated entry.
