  • RFC-0121: workspace-first project layout
  • RFC-0065: colcon-like workspace builder (images, hosts, generated entries)
  • RFC-0057: ament-parity component registration
  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI

Mix languages

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Organize a larger workspace

Mix languages when one image should run node packages written in C, C++ and Rust: C code you want to keep in C, beside new C++ or Rust nodes.

Languages mix per package, not per file. A bringup’s [[component]] row names a package and a class whatever language implements it, and each node package registers itself through a C ABI the generated entry calls. The workspace shape does not change with the language, and neither does system.toml.

Before you start

  • A workspace with a bringup, as in Organize a larger workspace.
  • ROS 2 sourced for the first build. It generates the message bindings for every language.

Steps

  1. Add a node package per language. From the workspace root, --lang picks the language and --to adds the package’s row to the bringup:

    nros new c_talker_pkg --lang c --template talker --to host_node_bringup
nros new listener_pkg --lang cpp --template listener --to host_node_bringup

    nros new: added the node package src/c_talker_pkg/ (talker, c) to …/host_ws
  declared it in …/host_ws/src/host_node_bringup: a [[component]] row and an <exec_depend>

  2. Write the C node as a typed component. It has no main(): it defines a state struct and a configure function, and exports them with RCLC_C_COMPONENT. configure receives the entry’s own node and executor, so a C and a C++ component in one image share both:

    #include <stdint.h>
#include <rclc/rclc.h>
#include <std_msgs/msg/int32.h>

typedef struct {
    rcl_publisher_t pub;
    rcl_timer_t timer;
    int32_t count;
} c_talker_pkg_t;

static void on_tick(rcl_timer_t* timer, int64_t last_call_time) {
    c_talker_pkg_t* self = RCLC_CONTAINER_OF(timer, c_talker_pkg_t, timer);
    (void)last_call_time;
    std_msgs__msg__Int32 msg = {.data = self->count};
    (void)rcl_publish(&self->pub, &msg, NULL);
    self->count++;
}

static rcl_ret_t talker_configure(rcl_node_t* node, rclc_executor_t* executor,
                                  c_talker_pkg_t* self) {
    self->count = 0;
    self->pub = rcl_get_zero_initialized_publisher();
    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_publisher_init_default(
        &self->pub, node, ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(std_msgs, msg, Int32), "/chatter");
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) return rc;
    self->timer = rcl_get_zero_initialized_timer();
    rc = rclc_timer_init_default(&self->timer, NULL, 1000000000ULL, on_tick);
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) return rc;
    return rclc_executor_add_timer(executor, &self->timer);
}

RCLC_C_COMPONENT(c_talker_pkg_t, talker_configure)

    Its CMakeLists.txt registers the component the same way a C++ package does, with TYPED:

    find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)   # declared as <depend>std_msgs</depend> in package.xml
nano_ros_auto_add_library(talker_lib STATIC src/Talker.c)
nros_components_register_node(talker_lib
    PLUGIN c_talker_pkg::Talker
    EXECUTABLE talker
    SHAPE configure
    TYPED)

  3. Name the packages in the launch file, if the bringup has one. Without launch/, the build generates the launch file from the [[component]] rows. Either way, nothing names a language. The mixed example workspace’s launch file:

    <launch>
  <node pkg="c_talker_pkg" exec="talker" name="talker"/>
  <node pkg="cpp_listener_pkg" exec="listener" name="listener"/>
  <node pkg="rust_heartbeat_pkg" exec="heartbeat" name="heartbeat"/>
</launch>

  4. Build. Once the image holds a C or C++ package, the build runs CMake, and the Rust packages build inside it through Corrosion. --dry-run shows the handoff:

    nros build linux --dry-run

    nros build: host_node_bringup:linux -> board linux (platform posix), driver cmake
cmake -S build/posix-zenoh-linux -B build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake …
cmake --build build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake

    The generated build/posix-zenoh-linux/CMakeLists.txt is the CMake root. You do not write it, and the workspace has no root build file.

  5. Run it:

    nros run host_node_bringup:linux

Example

examples/workspaces/mixed/ runs a C talker, a C++ listener and a Rust heartbeat in one image, with C and C++ service and action pairs beside them. Its bringup states the image the same way a one-language workspace does:

# src/demo_bringup/system.toml (excerpt)
[system]
name = "mixed_demo"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0
default_launch = "system.launch.xml"

[[component]]
pkg = "c_talker_pkg"
class = "c_talker_pkg::Talker"
name = "talker"

[[component]]
pkg = "cpp_listener_pkg"
class = "cpp_listener_pkg::Listener"
name = "listener"

[image_defaults]
rmw = "zenoh"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

[image.freertos]
board = "mps2-an385-freertos"

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build linux
nros run demo_bringup:linux

The first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later shells need not source ROS 2.

Per-language notes

  • Rust. A node package is a library crate ending in nros::node!(YourNode). Its message crates and cargo settings are generated under build/. In a mixed image its compiler errors are still cargo’s.
  • C. Its message bindings are generated during the CMake configure.
  • C++. The component has a configure(::rclcpp::Node&) method, as in Organize a larger workspace.
  • The RMW is stated once, whatever the languages: [system] rmw, or rmw = on one image block. See Switch the RMW per image.

If it doesn’t work

  • A node is missing at run time. Its [[component]] row or launch <node> names a package or class that does not match the package’s own registration (PLUGIN in CMake, the class in nros::node!).
  • The first build stops on AMENT_PREFIX_PATH. ROS 2 was not sourced and the workspace has no recorded prefix yet. Source ROS 2 and build again.

See also

  • Build outputs: where a CMake-driven image lands.
  • C API and C++ API.

Design background

  • RFC-0121: workspace-first project layout

Configure an image

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Organize a larger workspace

Configure an image when it needs more than a board: an address on a network, a router to dial, a per-image build knob, a flash or console override, or a smaller binary for a constrained board.

Everything here goes in the image’s row of the bringup’s system.toml, or in a file that row names. The toolchain bakes it in at build time: an embedded image has no configuration file on the device and parses nothing at run time. Cargo.toml and CMakeLists.txt carry language facts only, and nothing a board implies is written anywhere: the build derives it from the board’s descriptor.

Building and configuring

nros build prepares everything the build needs (generated messages, the resolved system, the image’s build settings) and then runs the host build tool. A project that stays in west, CMake, NuttX make or an IDE runs the preparation step, nros configure, from that tool’s own configure step instead.

Before you start

  • A workspace with a bringup and at least one image, as in Organize a larger workspace.

Steps

See what the image resolves to

nros config show prints the resolved configuration of the bringup, with the file and table each value came from:

nros config show

# Resolved config for system 'host_node' (bringup pkg: host_node_bringup)
# source: …/src/host_node_bringup/system.toml

[system]
rmw                = zenoh                        # system.toml [system]
domain_id          = 0                            # system.toml [system]

Resolution is a fixed ladder, not a merge: a command-line or build flag, then [image.<id>], then [system], then the board descriptor’s [knobs], then the built-in default. nros config explain prints the build-time knob ladder for a platform.

Retarget the image

board is the one key that has to change. The image’s id is the name you pass to nros build:

[image.mps2-an385-baremetal]
board   = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7447"

locator is the router or agent the image dials. Without it, the image dials [system] locator, then the board’s default.

Give the image an address

On a board where nano-ros owns the network (the reference FreeRTOS, ThreadX and bare-metal boards), the address is in a board network file the image names with os_config. On Linux, Zephyr and NuttX the operating system owns the network, and you set the address in its own configuration.

  1. Name the file on the image:

    [image.talker]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
os_config = ["board-net.toml"]

  2. Write one table per interface, beside system.toml. On QEMU’s built-in network, host is enough:

    # board-net.toml
[eth0]
network = "qemu"
host = 10                      # 10.0.2.10

  3. For a network of your own, define it in the same file and state the router on the image:

    # board-net-sensor.toml
[eth0]
network = "lab"
address = "192.168.50.20"

[network.lab]
subnet  = "192.168.50.0/24"
gateway = "192.168.50.1"

    [image.sensor]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
os_config = ["board-net-sensor.toml"]
locator = "tcp/192.168.50.1:7447"

    Two images on one network each define it, and the definitions must agree. A mistake fails the build and names the image: an address outside the subnet, two images with one address, or a network no file defines.

  4. To run that image under QEMU on a host bridge, say how it joins:

    [image.sensor.run]
nic = { bridge = "qemu-br" }

    nros run passes the -nic value to QEMU. An image on a network other than qemu with no nic is physical only.

The middleware’s own file

How a session finds its peers is the middleware’s own configuration, in its own language: rmw/zenoh.json5 or rmw/cyclonedds.xml beside system.toml, the same documents ROS 2 reads. To ship a different file for one image, name it:

[image.qemu]
board = "mps2-an385-freertos"
rmw_config = "rmw/zenoh-qemu.json5"

Configure zenoh and Use Cyclone DDS show the files themselves.

Per-image build knobs

A build knob one image needs, and its board does not state, goes in [image.<id>.knobs.<group>]:

[image.linux.knobs.log]
max_level = "warn"           # NROS_LOG_MAX_LEVEL

[image.linux.knobs.executor]
max_cbs = 16                 # NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_CBS

An unknown key, a wrong type or an out-of-range value stops nros build, naming the key. An application’s own build variable, one the knob registry does not hold, goes in env = { NAME = "value" } instead.

Override how a board is flashed and watched

A board’s descriptor states its flasher and console. An image overrides any key of them:

[image.lab.flash]
command = "pyocd flash -t stm32f767zi {hex}"
prepare = [{ say = "Set BOOT0 to 1, then press RESET", wait_for = "usb:0483:df11" }]

[image.lab.console]
baud = 921600

Both tables are checked when system.toml is read, and nros flash and nros monitor use them.

Shrink the image for a small board

  1. Build with the size profile. Name it on the image, and nros build passes it to whichever tool it drives:

    [image.mps2-an385-baremetal]
board   = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
profile = "nros-minsizerel"

  2. Drop what a brokered client does not need. These are ordinary build environment variables, and a value you export wins over the generated one:

    NROS_LINK_IP=0 ZPICO_NO_SMOLTCP=1 \
NROS_SMOLTCP_MAX_SOCKETS=1 NROS_SMOLTCP_MAX_UDP_SOCKETS=1 \
    nros build mps2-an385-baremetal

    NROS_LINK_IP=0 drops zenoh-pico’s TCP and UDP links on a serial-only image, and ZPICO_NO_SMOLTCP=1 skips the smoltcp glue on bare metal. A knob you always want for a board belongs in that board’s descriptor [knobs], not on every command line.

  3. Keep the heap at the board default for a nros::main! image. Its executor backing is one large allocation; shrink NROS_HEAP_SIZE only on a hand-written direct-mode image whose peak you measured.

Moving from ethernet to a serial link is the largest saving. The measured sizes are in Build outputs.

Example

A bare-metal image on a lab network, with its own router and a log ceiling:

# src/sensor_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "sensor"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "sensor_node"
class = "sensor_node::Sensor"
name = "sensor"

[image.sensor]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
os_config = ["board-net-sensor.toml"]
locator = "tcp/192.168.50.1:7447"

[image.sensor.run]
nic = { bridge = "qemu-br" }

[image.sensor.knobs.log]
max_level = "info"

nros build sensor

A hand-written no_std app

An app that writes its own main() instead of using nros::main!() keeps its network settings in a config.toml beside it, compiled in with include_str!. It has the board network file’s tables, plus a [node] table for the session:

# config.toml
[node]
domain_id = 0
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7447"

[eth0]
network = "qemu"
host = 10

use nros_board_mps2_an385::{Config, run};

fn main() -> ! {
    run(Config::from_toml(include_str!("../config.toml")), |config| {
        let exec = ExecutorConfig::new(config.zenoh_locator)
            .domain_id(config.domain_id);
        // ...
    })
}

If it doesn’t work

  • The build names a retired key. ip, gateway, netmask, transport and [image.<id>.net.<if>] moved to the board network file and the locator. The message names the new spelling.
  • A board network file is refused. The board’s network belongs to the host OS (linux, freertos-posix, threadx-linux), or the board declares no interfaces. Zephyr boards take their address from Kconfig.
  • An image with a zenoh file is refused. It also states a locator. With a file, the file is the wiring; remove one of the two.

See also

  • system.toml keys: every image key, the network file, the run, flash and console tables.
  • Environment variables: the build-time and runtime variables, and the buffer knobs.
  • Configuration surface: the Kconfig symbols and where each decision is made.
  • Retired configuration files.

Build profiles

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Configure an image

Choose a build profile when an image must be smaller, faster or easier to debug, and profile the build when it takes too long.

nano-ros builds C, C++ and Rust code on your behalf. You choose the optimization level once, on the image, and the build passes it to every crate and library it builds: the cargo profile on the cargo driver, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE on the CMake one.

Before you start

  • A workspace with an image, or a CMake project that adds nano-ros as in Build inside an existing CMake or vendor tree.

Steps

Set the profile on the image

  1. Name it in the bringup’s system.toml, on one image or on [image_defaults] for all of them:

    [image_defaults]
profile = "nros-relwithdebinfo"   # the base every image folds over

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

[image.mps2]
board   = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
profile = "nros-minsizerel"       # this one goes on a board

  2. Build. You do not repeat the profile on the command line, and you do not define the nros-* profiles anywhere: the build writes them into the image’s generated cargo settings under build/.

    nros build mps2

The nros-* profiles and the CMake build types they come from:

CMAKE_BUILD_TYPEcargo profileMeaning
Debugdevdebuggable, minimal optimization
RelWithDebInfonros-relwithdebinfoopt-level 2, debug info, no LTO; the default
MinSizeRelnros-minsizerelopt-level s, fat LTO; smallest images
Releasereleaseopt-level 3, fat LTO; fastest code
(unset)nros-relwithdebinfothe development default

Set it from CMake

When you drive CMake yourself, set CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE as in any CMake project, and nano-ros derives the cargo profile for the Rust it builds underneath:

cmake --preset linux -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel
cmake --build build/linux

The configure prints the profile it chose and the target/ directory it builds into:

-- nano-ros: cargo profile `nros-minsizerel` (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel) → target/nros-minsizerel

Set NROS_CARGO_PROFILE when the two halves should differ, for example a small C++ image with debuggable Rust:

cmake --preset linux \
    -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel -DNROS_CARGO_PROFILE=nros-relwithdebinfo

An unrecognized build type is an error, never a guess.

Use a profile of your own

Name any profile. When the name is not one of the nros-* profiles, you own its definition, and nano-ros passes the name through and injects nothing:

[profile.prod]
inherits = "release"
opt-level = 3
lto = "fat"

Put it where cargo already looks: the package’s Cargo.toml for a one-package project, or a .cargo/config.toml in a directory above the project. A nano-ros workspace has no root Cargo.toml, and the generated entry under build/ is rewritten on every build. An undefined name fails as cargo always does: error: profile 'prod' is not defined.

Find where the build time goes

nros-build-profile reads the timing files the build already wrote and reports where the time went: code generation, compile and link, which unit dominated, and which crate was built more than once. It never builds anything. The release installs it beside nros; release 0.6.0-nros4 and older do not carry it.

  1. For per-crate detail on the cargo driver, build with cargo’s timings. ninja, which the CMake and west drivers use, always writes its log, so those need nothing.

    cargo build --timings --manifest-path build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/Cargo.toml \
    --config build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/nros-cargo.toml

  2. Point it at the directory that holds build*/ or target*/:

    nros-build-profile build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry --deep

    It prints a stage table, the slowest units with --deep, and hints. Without cargo’s timings you still get the stage table, and a note on how to get the drill-down.

  3. For CI, write it as JSON and compare runs:

    nros-build-profile build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry --json

    The hints flag a large C unit built with no compiler cache, a crate compiled more than once, and a job count too high for the RAM. Silence them with --no-hints.

Example

One workspace, a debuggable host image and a small board image:

# src/demo_bringup/system.toml (images)
[image_defaults]
profile = "nros-relwithdebinfo"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

[image.mps2]
board   = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
profile = "nros-minsizerel"

nros build --all

If it doesn’t work

  • A board image is larger than expected. It built at the default, nros-relwithdebinfo, which trades size for build speed. Use nros-minsizerel for a constrained board.
  • The profile you chose is not the one used. Two platforms pin their own and say so: NuttX Rust images, and FreeRTOS images under QEMU, which miss zenoh-pico’s handshake window at low optimization.
  • error: profile '<name>' is not defined. A profile of your own needs a definition where cargo looks for one; see above.

See also

  • Configure an image: the size knobs beside the profile.
  • Build outputs: where the target/ directory of each profile lands, and the measured sizes per profile.

Build inside an existing CMake or vendor tree

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Install options, pinning, working offline

Use this page when nano-ros has to live inside a build you already own: a C or C++ CMake tree with its own layout, or a company tree (a BSP, a forked RTOS, a CI system) that drives cargo or CMake itself.

If your project is a nano-ros workspace, you do not need this page. You state the board once in the bringup’s system.toml, and nros build sets everything below for you. Start at Organize a larger workspace instead.

nano-ros is distributed as a release: the nros CLI and the library source it builds against, the SDK root. Nothing is on crates.io and there is no prebuilt library or install prefix, so “vendoring” nano-ros means pinning and mirroring a release, not copying its repository into your tree.

Before you start

  • A release installed and pinned, as in Install options, pinning, working offline.
  • The board provisioned with nros setup <board>. For every board with a CMake build, that also installs Corrosion, which a C or C++ configure needs and never downloads.

Steps

Add nano-ros to a CMake tree

  1. Ask for the SDK root. It is the installed release’s share/nano-ros, for the version the project is pinned to:

    nros locate nano-ros

  2. Pick the platform and the backend before you add nano-ros, then link it. The variables must be set before add_subdirectory, because nano-ros reads them when it is included:

    cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(my_app C)

set(NROS_PLATFORM posix)   # posix | freertos | nuttx | threadx
set(NROS_RMW     zenoh)    # zenoh | xrce | cyclonedds

add_subdirectory("${NANO_ROS_SDK}" nano_ros)

add_executable(my_app main.c)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE NanoRos::NanoRos)
if(COMMAND nros_platform_link_app)   # defined by the zephyr and threadx platforms
    nros_platform_link_app(my_app)
endif()

    The variables and their values are listed in CMake cache variables. Zephyr and bare metal do not enter this way: Zephyr has its own module, and bare metal builds through cargo.

  3. Generate the message bindings your sources include:

    nano_ros_generate_interfaces(std_msgs LANGUAGE C
    DEPENDENCIES builtin_interfaces)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE std_msgs__nano_ros_c)

  4. Configure with the SDK root and build:

    cmake -B build -DNANO_ROS_SDK="$(nros locate nano-ros)"
cmake --build build

    CMake’s target propagation brings in the nano-ros libraries, the platform’s own system libraries and the per-build configuration header.

The higher-level form is find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED), located with -Dnano_ros_ROOT=<sdk-root>. The CMake presets nros setup presets writes pass it for you, so cmake --preset <board> works.

Drive cargo or CMake yourself from CI

In a nano-ros workspace, a CI job that runs cargo or CMake itself prepares the generated inputs first, without building, and then runs the line nros build prints:

nros configure
nros build linux --dry-run

nros build: host_node_bringup:linux -> board linux (platform posix), driver cargo
cargo update --workspace --manifest-path build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/Cargo.toml --config build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/nros-cargo.toml
cargo build --manifest-path build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/Cargo.toml --config build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/nros-cargo.toml

A run of nros configure with nothing changed does nothing, and its stamp under build/nros/configured/<image>/ holds a digest of every input the image read, which makes a CI cache key.

Everything the build reads is generated under build/, never beside your packages: the message crates, the target triple, the runner, the link flags, the resolved [env] and the [patch.crates-io] rows that point registry-style names such as nros = { version = "*" } at the SDK root. So a tree moves freely. After you relocate it, or install another release, the next build rewrites what is under build/ and touches nothing you track.

Keep your own boards in your tree

Point NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATH (an environment variable, or a CMake cache variable for nano_ros_use_board()) at a directory of board crates in your tree, laid out like the SDK’s packages/boards/. Board keys stay global: one name under two roots is an error. A new platform, an RTOS port of your own, is the one extension that edits nano-ros itself; see Add a platform.

Example

A complete C project with no system.toml, my_app/CMakeLists.txt:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(my_app C)

set(NROS_PLATFORM posix)
set(NROS_RMW     zenoh)
add_subdirectory("${NANO_ROS_SDK}" nano_ros)

add_executable(my_app main.c)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE NanoRos::NanoRos)

nano_ros_generate_interfaces(std_msgs LANGUAGE C
    DEPENDENCIES builtin_interfaces)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE std_msgs__nano_ros_c)

cmake -B build -DNANO_ROS_SDK="$(nros locate nano-ros)"
cmake --build build

If it doesn’t work

  • The configure stops and names nros setup --tool corrosion. Corrosion is not in the SDK store. Run that command, or the nros setup <board> you already use.
  • A setting in your CMakeLists has no effect. It was set after add_subdirectory. Move every NROS_* variable above it.
  • A message crate resolves from crates.io. A Rust package named it by registry name (std_msgs = "*"). Let nros build write the # nros-managed path row from package.xml instead.
  • You set NROS_PLATFORM in a nano-ros workspace. The generated root already derives it from the image’s board. Remove it: two answers to one question.

See also

  • Install options, pinning, working offline: pin the release, mirror it, and build with no network.
  • Build outputs: where each target family’s artifact lands.
  • How a build becomes an image.
  • Vendor Overlay Board Crate and STM32F4 Out of Tree: board code that lives in your tree.

Design background

  • RFC-0098: generated leaf build config
  • RFC-0103: one owner per fact

Install options, pinning, working offline

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Install

Install is the short path. Use this page to install a specific release, provision a whole workspace, pin a project to a release, or build on a machine with no network.

A release carries everything a project needs: the nros CLI, and the library as source in its SDK root, which nros build compiles into your project. There is no prebuilt library, no system-wide install and no nano-ros clone. Its nros-sdk-index.toml pins every toolchain and SDK version nros setup provisions, so pinning nano-ros is pinning a release.

Before you start

  • Linux. The host board is linux; macOS is not supported.
  • The host packages Install lists. Each tool’s absence produces an error that names it.

Host packages

cmake builds the C and C++ quick start and every generated workspace root. zstd unpacks the release and the prebuilt assets nros setup fetches. python3-dev is used only by a from-source build of the launch resolver, which a release ships prebuilt. The Python packages feed rosidl_adapter, the message-to-IDL step the Cyclone DDS backend uses; empy must stay 3.x.

Fedora and Arch ship no packages for the rosidl Python side, so Install has them installed with pip install --user; Arch’s externally managed Python also needs --break-system-packages. To keep them out of your user site, create a virtual environment (python -m venv ~/.venvs/nros), activate it, run the same pip install without --user, and activate it in every shell you build from.

Install a specific release

install.sh installs into ~/.nros/sdk/nros/<version>/ and points ~/.nros/bin/nros at the newest version installed. It refuses an asset whose checksum it cannot verify.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh \
    | sh -s -- --version 0.6.0-nros4     # a specific release instead of the newest
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh \
    | sh -s -- --dry-run                 # print what would happen, change nothing

NROS_HOME moves the install root away from ~/.nros. nros version then prints the CLI, codegen and library versions, and nros doctor, run outside a workspace, checks the install itself.

Provisioning with nros setup

  1. See what a board needs before fetching anything:

    nros setup linux --dry-run

    nros setup: linux (rmw zenoh) needs 3 package(s):
  rust                   already present (rustup, default stable-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)
  rust target            no cross target for this board
  …
(--dry-run: nothing installed)

  2. Provision the board and the RMW’s host tools. --rmw defaults to zenoh:

    nros setup <board> --rmw <zenoh|xrce|cyclonedds>

    Packages are prebuilt where the index has a binary for your host and built from source otherwise; nros setup announces a source build before it starts. For every board with a CMake build it also installs Corrosion. If the host has no Rust, it installs rustup into ~/.cargo with the stable toolchain.

Provision a whole workspace

In a workspace, provision every image at once: run nros setup with no board at the workspace root, or pass --workspace <dir>. For a Linux and a FreeRTOS image:

nros new two_ws --board linux --template talker --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd two_ws
nros new --image freertos --board mps2-an385-freertos   # adds [image.freertos]

nros setup

It reads every system.toml, provisions each image’s board and RMW in one plan, and lists the OS packages the workspace names, with the install command (--sudo runs it, --check only reports). Every <depend> must resolve first; one that does not stops it and names its package.xml.

Then build every image. The first build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install, so source it in that shell:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build --all

Other selections: nros setup --list lists every package in the index, --tool <name> and --source <name> fetch one package, --licenses lists the license-gated ones, and nros setup --system prints the OS packages a board needs for your package manager.

ROS 2 and the zenoh router

nros build, nros run and nros configure generate the message bindings from the ROS 2 install you sourced, so the layouts and type hashes match your ROS 2 peers. The first configure of a project records the prefix (AMENT_PREFIX_PATH), and later shells, IDEs and CI steps reuse it. A project with no message dependency configures without ROS 2.

Running two zenoh nodes needs a router, and nano-ros uses the one ROS 2 ships, rmw_zenohd from ros-<distro>-rmw-zenoh-cpp. Cyclone DDS needs no router, and the XRCE agent comes from nros setup … --rmw xrce. Start the router with ROS 2 sourced:

ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

rmw_zenohd reads no arguments, only ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE. It installs into <prefix>/lib/rmw_zenoh_cpp/, so command -v rmw_zenohd printing nothing is normal. nano-ros finds it through NROS_RMW_ZENOHD, then the prefixes you sourced, then $ROS_DISTRO, and never searches PATH or globs /opt/ros/*: a zenohd elsewhere is usually a different zenoh. On a distro with no ROS 2 packages, install ROS 2 from source or a container and source its setup.bash the same way.

Pinning a version

The pin is a file, nros-toolchain.toml, beside your project. Commit it. Every nros you run in that directory or below it is then the pinned release: the nros on PATH hands the command to it, fetching it with that release’s own install.sh the first time.

Write the pin, for a project pinned to an older release than the one you installed (nros pin <version> writes the same file):

mkdir pinned_app && cd pinned_app
printf '[toolchain]\nversion = "0.6.0-nros4"\n' > nros-toolchain.toml

Ask for the pin. The release that answers is the pinned one, fetched on first use, and it names its own manifest:

nros pin

sdk/nros/0.6.0-nros4/share/nros/manifest.toml

With no pin, nros pin says so:

pinned: NOTHING — no nros-toolchain.toml at or above …/empty.
    This project floats: `nros build` will write a pin, and until it does, firmware built here is reproducible only by accident.

Build with it. The pinned release is older than this page, so it takes the scaffold spelling it shipped with, --workspace:

nros new pinned_ws --workspace
cd pinned_ws
nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds
nros build

Move the pin forward only. nros pin <newer> reports the codegen delta between the two releases before it writes anything (--dry-run writes nothing), and the next nros build regenerates the bindings. Then run nros setup <board> again to bring the SDK store up to the new index:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh \
    | sh -s -- --version <newer>
nros pin <newer>
nros setup <board>
nros build

Take the toolchain versions the release pinned: its cross compilers, the Cyclone DDS ROS ships and its zenoh-pico are chosen together.

Working offline

  1. Mirror the release asset. install.sh takes NROS_INSTALL_URL=<url>: a mirror, an air-gapped copy or a test server. The asset’s .sha256 must sit beside it.
  2. Pin the SDK index. nros setup --index <path> uses a copy you have; NROS_INDEX_URL=<url> fetches one from a mirror. The index names every asset’s upstream, so a full mirror rehosts those URLs in your copy.
  3. Stage Corrosion with nros setup --tool corrosion, or the nros setup <board> you already run.
  4. Prepare each workspace while online. nros configure fetches the crates its images need into cargo’s cache and writes everything generated.
  5. Carry the stores. ~/.nros (or NROS_HOME) holds the CLI, the SDK root and every package nros setup fetched. The Rust toolchain lives in ~/.rustup and ~/.cargo, with cargo’s registry cache; carry those too, or nros setup tries to download rustup again.
  6. Build with NROS_OFFLINE=1. nros then fetches nothing, and runs every cargo it starts with CARGO_NET_OFFLINE=true. A build that needs something missing stops and names it.

If it doesn’t work

  • The first configure stops on AMENT_PREFIX_PATH. Source ROS 2 once (source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash) and configure again; see the troubleshooting index.
  • A C++ image is refused for an old compiler. With no pinned arm-none-eabi-gcc in the store, the configure uses one from PATH, and below GCC 11 a C++ image is refused (Ubuntu 22.04’s apt package is 10.3). Run nros setup --tool arm-none-eabi-gcc.
  • A zenoh example hangs at start with no output. No router is running, or it listens on another endpoint. nros setup reports where it found rmw_zenohd, or the apt packages that provide it.
  • nros doctor reports a retired store entry. Remove it with the command it prints.

See also

  • Build inside an existing CMake or vendor tree: nano-ros in a tree you already build.
  • Supported boards and the nros CLI.
  • Migrating from install-local, for a project that used nano-ros from a checkout.

Design background

  • RFC-0075: zenoh router provenance
  • RFC-0116: adoption purposes and budgets

Native (Host) Build

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Use the host (linux) board for first experiments, CI smoke tests, and ROS 2 interoperability checks on Linux. It uses OS sockets, the host process environment, and the same project layout as the embedded targets.

The host board is named linux ([image.<id>] board = "linux") because that is all it supports: the platform layer (nros-platform-posix) is POSIX, but the host board crate’s apply_sched_task_affinity calls sched_setaffinity with cpu_set_t, which libc does not define for macOS, Windows or FreeBSD. Only Linux is supported. Neither native (every general-purpose host) nor posix (the platform) names a board: board = "…", nros setup, and nros new --board refuse both with a hint naming linux.

When to Use It

  • You want the shortest path to a working nano-ros publisher or subscriber.
  • You are validating message generation, CMake integration, or ROS 2 interop before moving to an RTOS.
  • Your deployment target is Linux or an embedded Linux system.

Setup

Install the nros CLI (Installation), then provision the native host. For a host build there is no cross-toolchain to fetch — nros setup linux installs the client stack (and for xrce the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent) into a shared store. The zenoh router is NOT installed: it comes from a ROS 2 install (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd). Rather not run a router? Use --rmw cyclonedds — it needs no daemon. Either way the first build generates the messages from your ROS 2 install, so it needs ROS 2 sourced.

With the nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin):

# Provision the Linux host (zenoh RMW is the default):
nros setup linux --rmw zenoh        # or: --rmw xrce / --rmw cyclonedds

linux is this board’s one name; posix names the platform layer underneath it, and native names no board at all (Retired names).

For a colcon consumer workspace that already has nano-ros under src/:

colcon build && source install/setup.bash

Workspace Layout

A host project is a workspace, like every other board’s:

nros new host_ws --board linux --template talker --lang rust   # or --lang c / cpp
cd host_ws

host_ws/
└── src/
    ├── host_node/              # node package: package.xml + Cargo.toml (or CMakeLists.txt), the node
    └── host_node_bringup/      # package.xml and system.toml: board, rmw, domain, components

The node package is a library with no main(); the bringup’s [image.linux] block (board = "linux") is what makes it a host program. The examples on GitHub are copy-out ready: nothing in one names a path into the SDK. nros finds its own SDK; --nano-ros-path names another.

Code Example

A Rust node package’s src/lib.rs declares what the node creates and what its callbacks do, and exports the node; the entry that opens the executor and spins it is generated:

pub struct Talker;

impl Component for Talker {
    const NAME: &'static str = "talker";
    const ENTITY_BOUNDS: nros::EntityBounds = nros::EntityBounds::exact(1, 0, 0, 0, 0);

    fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
        let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("talker"))?;
        let chatter = node.create_publisher_for_topic::<StringMsg>("/chatter")?;
        let _timer =
            node.create_timer_for_callback_name("on_tick", TimerDuration::from_millis(1000))?;
        node.callback_for_name("on_tick").publishes_entity(&chatter)?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

// impl ExecutableNode for Talker { … the timer callback publishes "Hello World: N" … }

nros::node!(Talker);

Use the full First Node — Rust walkthrough for generated messages and runnable commands, and Growing your workspace for each line of lib.rs.

Build and Run

Start the RMW host daemon (the router comes from ROS 2). For zenoh:

ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Then build and run the node from the workspace root, in a shell that has sourced ROS 2. The first build generates the messages from it and records the prefix, so later runs need no sourced shell:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run host_node

nros run builds first if anything changed. nros build alone prints the binary’s path under build/, which runs directly too. For a workspace that lives in a colcon consumer workspace, colcon build && source install/setup.bash && ros2 run … works as well.

Configuration

Native examples can read runtime settings from the shell:

export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=0
export NROS_LOCATOR=tcp/127.0.0.1:7447

The same fields are compiled into embedded targets through their platform-specific configuration files. See Configuration for the full layering.

Deployment

Host deployment is normal process deployment: install the workspace, source install/setup.bash, set environment, and run the binary. For ROS 2 interop, run ROS 2 Interoperability and set the ROS side to rmw_zenoh_cpp.

Design background

  • RFC-0075: zenoh router provenance

Bare-metal Cortex-M3 (QEMU)

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Support level: mps2-an385-baremetal. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

Single-node starter on bare-metal Cortex-M3 (QEMU MPS2-AN385) — no RTOS, no kernel scheduler. Pure cooperative spin via zpico_spin_once. Rust only. nros-c / nros-cpp are not supported on bare-metal targets (they assume a hosted RTOS for startup / heap / libc); see the examples coverage matrix for the policy.

When to use this path: ultra-constrained Cortex-M0+ / M3 / M4 targets with no OS scheduler, no pthread. If you have FreeRTOS or any RTOS, use the FreeRTOS starter instead — it’s more ergonomic and produces smaller code overall.

Prereqs. Install the nros CLI once per machine (scripts/install.sh, see Installation), then provision this board. nros setup fetches a prebuilt bare-metal toolchain (arm-none-eabi-gcc, qemu-system-arm) plus the Rust thumbv7m-none-eabi target into a shared store — no manual cross-compiler install. It provides no zenoh router: that is ROS’s rmw_zenohd (see the RMW design), so running a zenoh image needs it from a ROS 2 install.

# Provision the bare-metal Cortex-M3 board (zenoh RMW is the default):
nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal --rmw zenoh

One key, not two: qemu-arm-baremetal is a retired spelling of the same entry. A board name states the reach of its build, and this build is true for one silicon part. Nothing extra is provisioned for physical hardware — no probe/flash tooling. For a real STM32F4 see the out-of-tree worked example.

Project layout

Scaffold a workspace for the board:

nros new bm_ws --board mps2-an385-baremetal --template talker --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd bm_ws

bm_ws/
└── src/
    ├── bm_node/                 # node package: package.xml, Cargo.toml (a library), src/lib.rs
    └── bm_node_bringup/         # package.xml and system.toml: the board, the RMW, the node

bm_node is the talker, a library with no main() that names no board. The bringup’s system.toml holds one image, [image.baremetal]. There is no .cargo/ to edit: the target triple, the linker script, the --gc-sections flag, the QEMU runner and the [patch.crates-io] rows that resolve nano-ros’s crates all come from the board, and nros build writes them under build/ together with the generated entry it compiles.

The board crate is nros-board-mps2-an385 (note: no -freertos suffix — this is the bare-metal variant) which provides:

  • Cortex-M3 startup + linker script
  • LAN9118 driver for smoltcp
  • BoardIdle::wfi() for cooperative wait

The entry shape

The image’s board line names the board, and the generated entry depends on the board crate with the feature that shape needs. Pick it there — never a different board crate, and never an edit to the node package:

Entry shape[image.<id>] board =board crate feature the entry enables
direct-exec (inline spin loop)"mps2-an385-baremetal"board-entry

Which network the defaults describe is stated by the board: its nros-board.toml says [board.net] network = "qemu", so Config::default() sits on QEMU’s own user-mode network (10.0.2.15/24, gateway and router 10.0.2.2) — the network every QEMU board shares. Config::qemu_slirp() is the same network at a second address (10.0.2.10, router port 7450). Either way, an image that sets its locator in its [image.<id>] and its address in a board network file ([eth0] network = "qemu", host = N) table overrides the default — which every in-tree example does, and which you should too. The address goes in the image’s board network file, named by os_config (below).

Configure

The whole deployment statement is the bringup’s system.toml. It is baked at compile time: the generated entry folds the image’s network identity into a DeployOverlay the board’s boot Config applies. With a locator and an address added, src/bm_node_bringup/system.toml reads:

[system]
name = "bm_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "bm_node"
class = "bm_node::Talker"
name = "bm_node"
dispatch = "deferred"

[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:10500"
os_config = ["board-net.toml"]

and the image’s address sits in the board network file it names, board-net.toml beside system.toml in the bringup (the board package owns the device, so its address lives in the board’s own file):

[eth0]
network = "qemu"
host = 10

board picks the silicon and everything that follows from it; rmw picks the backend. Everything the board implies — triple, linker script, runner, cross compiler, [patch.crates-io], the board crate and its features — follows the board = line on the next nros build, so no linker flag and no triple ever moves by hand. The node package’s Cargo.toml names no board crate, RMW backend or panic handler: those are the generated entry’s dependencies. So changing board = to "mps2-an385-freertos" and building again builds the FreeRTOS image with no other edit.

QEMU Slirp networking: no host TAP, bridge or sudo. The guest reaches the host as 10.0.2.2, so nros run starts the router on the host’s port 10500 (the locator above) when it boots the image. Change the port in the locator; nothing else moves.

Build

The build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install, so source it in this shell first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later builds and runs of it need no sourced shell.

In the workspace root (where the scaffold step left you):

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build           # builds the image `[image.baremetal]` declares

nros build prepares the build first (message bindings, the generated entry for [image.baremetal], the cargo settings the board implies), then runs cargo. There is no step to run before it.

First build (~5 min) cross-compiles all of nano-ros’s Rust deps for thumbv7m-none-eabi. Re-builds finish in seconds. The ELF lands under build/, never beside your sources; nros build prints its path and a run: line when it finishes.

Driving cargo yourself (an IDE, a CI step, --release) is supported: nros build --dry-run prints the exact cargo line, against the generated entry under build/. To write that entry and its settings without building, before you open the workspace in an IDE, run:

nros configure

What it writes is regenerated on every build; never edit it, and never add a .cargo/config.toml of your own to carry board facts. Your own Rust-toolchain preferences go where cargo already looks for them — a parent directory or $CARGO_HOME. See When nros build drives the build.

Run on QEMU

Two terminals: the board, and a stock ROS 2 peer.

1. The board, from the workspace root. Source ROS 2 first: the router nros run starts is ROS’s rmw_zenohd.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run bm_node

nros run rebuilds if anything changed, then boots the talker in QEMU with the board’s runner: the patched qemu-system-arm that nros setup mps2-an385-baremetal provisioned into the SDK store, with -icount shift=auto, which keeps the board’s timer in step with the host. The scaffold’s image names no locator, so it talks to the router over the board’s serial port: nros run connects that port to a terminal device on the host and starts the router on it. It streams the semihosting console until you press Ctrl-C, which stops QEMU and the router together.

Expected serial-over-semihosting output:

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
...

With the tcp/10.0.2.2:10500 locator of Configure, nros run starts the router on the host’s port 10500 instead, so don’t start one of your own: a second router on the same port stops the first run. To use a router you already have, pass --router <its locator>.

2. A stock ROS 2 peer. The talker publishes best-effort; stock ros2 topic echo defaults to RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing. Force best-effort to receive:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

data: 'Hello World:

Ctrl-C stops nros run and QEMU with it.

Readiness signal. Within ~15 seconds of QEMU boot (no RTOS init delay, but smoltcp + zenoh handshake still takes a few seconds), expect Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' on semihosting stdout — the count starts at 1, matching the official ROS 2 demo talker. If no Publishing: line:

  1. The router did not start — nros run says so and names its log under build/nros/run/. A router you started yourself on the same port is the usual cause.
  2. No network on the guest — if you boot the ELF with your own QEMU line, an explicit -nic/-netdev that does not reach the LAN9118 (or -nic none, -nodefaults) leaves it unwired. The board’s runner passes -nic user,model=lan9118.
  3. Cooperative spin starvation — if you added a long-running callback, the entire executor stalls; bare-metal has no preemption.
  4. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Flash a real board

Nothing in-tree is flashed: mps2-an385 is a QEMU machine, and nros setup provisions no probe or flash tooling for it. A real Cortex-M board is a board crate of your own — Worked Example — STM32F4 Out of Tree takes one through the whole ladder — and its ELF goes to the board with the probe tool its vendor supports. Add an image for it to the bringup ([image.stm32f4] board = "<your board id>"); once that board package declares its flash runner, nros flash names the image:

nros flash bm_node_bringup:stm32f4
# or by hand, on the ELF path `nros build` printed:
#   probe-rs run --chip STM32F407VGTx <elf>
#   openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -f target/stm32f4x.cfg \
#       -c "program <elf> verify reset exit"

Not replayed. No probe runs this flash line (a CI runner has no board), so it is written from the board’s runner, not measured (tracking issue).

The chip, interface and triple above are the STM32F4-Discovery’s; yours come from your board.

GitHub source

  • Bare-metal talker, the copy-out example for this board and the same project as the one this page builds: examples/mps2-an385-baremetal/rust/talker/
  • Board crate: packages/boards/nros-board-mps2-an385/

Constraints to be aware of

  • No alloc by default. Pure no_std + heapless for bounded collections. If you need alloc, opt in via the alloc feature on your board crate and supply a #[global_allocator].
  • No wake primitive. Cooperative single-thread spin only; the executor’s nros_platform_wake_* slots return Unsupported.
  • No preemption. A long-running user callback blocks every other dispatchable handle until it returns.
  • nros-c / nros-cpp NOT supported. These wrappers assume hosted-RTOS libc + heap. Pure-Rust API only on this target.

For Cortex-M3 with an RTOS, switch to the FreeRTOS starter.

Next

  • Subscriber / service / action: the bare-metal image rows of the Rust language workspace, examples/workspaces/rust, under pubsub_bringup, service_bringup and action_bringup. The serial talker and listener are image rows there too, stating transport = "serial" over the same packages.
  • Wake-callback opt-in: the wake-callback (latency-probe) bench under packages/testing/nros-bench/wake-latency-cortex-m3/ shows how to feed a backend’s transport-notify into the cooperative spin loop on bare-metal.
  • Real hardware: the same code runs on an STM32F4-Discovery with a board crate of your own and a different linker script — see Worked Example — STM32F4 Out of Tree, which takes that board through the customization ladder end to end.

Design background

  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The copy-out talker per platform and language, and the paired examples, variants and configurations as image rows of behaviour bringups.

FreeRTOS (QEMU MPS2-AN385)

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Support level: mps2-an385-freertos, freertos-posix, s32z270-freertos, mps3-an536-freertos. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

Single-node starter on FreeRTOS + lwIP, cross-compiled for Cortex-M3 and booted in QEMU MPS2-AN385. Slirp networking; no host TAP / bridge / sudo. Rust, C, and C++ talkers are on GitHub as reading material; this page scaffolds your own.

Prereqs. nros setup mps2-an385-freertos is the single command that prepares your machine for this board. It fetches a prebuilt toolchain set into the shared store at ~/.nros/sdk — the arm-none-eabi-gcc cross-compiler, the patched qemu-system-arm emulator, and the FreeRTOS kernel + lwIP sources. You do not hand-install a cross-toolchain. The zenoh path DOES need a ROS 2 install for the router (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd); the xrce path needs only the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent, which nros setup installs.

Setup

With the nros CLI on PATH (Installation — install.sh puts it in ~/.nros/bin), provision the board (--rmw defaults to zenoh; pick xrce or cyclonedds to match the example you intend to run):

nros setup mps2-an385-freertos --rmw zenoh

This fetches the cross-compiler, the patched qemu-system-arm, and the FreeRTOS + lwIP sources into ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/sdk (plus the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent when you pick --rmw xrce). The zenoh router is NOT installed — it comes from your ROS 2 install.

Project layout

nros new scaffolds a workspace for the board, in any of the three languages:

nros new fr_ws --board mps2-an385-freertos --template talker --lang c      # or --lang cpp
cd fr_ws

nros new fr_ws --board mps2-an385-freertos --template talker --lang rust
cd fr_ws

fr_ws/
└── src/
    ├── fr_node/                 # node package: package.xml + CMakeLists.txt (or Cargo.toml), the talker
    └── fr_node_bringup/         # package.xml and system.toml: the board, the RMW, the node

fr_node is a library: no main(), no board, no RMW. The bringup’s system.toml holds one image, [image.freertos], with board = "mps2-an385-freertos". The program’s entry, the FreeRTOS startup task that runs your node, is generated from that image at build time.

Nothing else states the deployment. The Rust side has no .cargo/ to edit — the thumbv7m-none-eabi triple, the -Tmps2_an385.ld --nmagic --gc-sections link group, the QEMU runner and the [patch.crates-io] rows all come from the board and are written by nros build under build/. A C or C++ node package has no <nano_ros deploy=… board=… rmw=…/> tuple in its package.xml and names no board in its CMakeLists.txt.

The board crate (nros-board-mps2-an385-freertos) wraps the kernel + lwIP + LAN9118 driver build; the generated entry depends on it, so nothing you write names it.

Configure

Board, RMW, domain and network identity are declared in the bringup’s system.toml and baked at compile time — there is no config file on the device. With a locator and an address added, src/fr_node_bringup/system.toml reads:

[system]
name = "fr_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "fr_node"
class = "fr_node::Talker"
name = "fr_node"

[image.freertos]
board = "mps2-an385-freertos"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7800"
os_config = ["board-net.toml"]    # [eth0] network = "qemu", host = 15

locator is where the router is (the QEMU guest reaches the host’s router through the Slirp gateway 10.0.2.2); os_config names the board network file, board-net.toml beside system.toml in the bringup. The file is the same whatever language the node is written in. Nothing about the deployment lives in Cargo.toml, in CMakeLists.txt, or in the package.xml <export> block.

Switching board is editing [image.<id>] board and rebuilding: nros build picks the cross-toolchain file the board names, and the generated entry brings the board crate, its RMW and nros-platform’s FreeRTOS feature.

Task stacks / priorities come from the board crate’s defaults (Cargo features), not a config file — see the Configuration Guide.

The 10.0.2.0/24 subnet is QEMU Slirp’s default; 10.0.2.2 is the Slirp gateway that forwards to host loopback. No TAP, no sudo.

Ports: read your image’s own locator. The image above dials host port 7800; with no locator, as scaffolded, an image dials the board’s default (tcp/10.0.2.2:7447).

Changing this in the tree: see Internals → per-platform lanes.

Build

The build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install, so source it in this shell first. This first build records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later builds and runs of it need no sourced shell.

In the workspace root (fr_ws/, where nros new left you), whatever the language:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build

nros build prepares the build first (message bindings, the resolved launch model, the generated entry for [image.freertos]), then hands off to cargo or CMake with the board’s cross-toolchain file and the SDK root. There is no step to run before it.

The first build cross-compiles nano-ros’s dependencies and the FreeRTOS kernel

  • lwIP (~3 min for C / C++, ~5 min for Rust). The ELF lands under build/. nros build --dry-run prints the native commands without building.

After a successful build nros build prints what it built and the command that runs it — a block like

nros build: next for `fr_node_bringup:freertos`:
  artifact: /home/you/fr_ws/build/…/freertos_entry
  run:
    nros run fr_node

Driving the native tool yourself is the escape hatch, not the path. nros build --dry-run prints the exact cargo build … or cmake lines, run against the generated entry under build/. To write that entry without building (an IDE, a CI cache step), run:

nros configure

For a CMake tree that is not a nano-ros workspace at all, see Build inside an existing CMake or vendor tree.

See When nros build drives the build for which tool builds each image.

Run on QEMU

Three terminals: the router, the board, and a stock ROS 2 peer.

1. The router — ROS’s rmw_zenohd, on the port your image’s locator names (7447 when it names none, as a scaffolded image; 7800 in the example shown above). It must listen on 0.0.0.0 for the Slirp gateway: Slirp forwards the guest’s 10.0.2.2:<p> to the host’s <p>.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Started Zenoh router with id

2. The board — from the workspace root:

nros run fr_node

nros run rebuilds if anything changed, then boots the image in QEMU with the board’s runner: the store’s patched qemu-system-arm (nros setup mps2-an385-freertos installed it), the LAN9118 on Slirp, and -icount shift=auto, which keeps the board’s timer in step with Slirp’s I/O. It streams the semihosting console until you press Ctrl-C.

The scaffolded talker publishes std_msgs/String once a second, in every language:

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

3. A stock ROS 2 peer. The talker publishes best-effort; stock ros2 topic echo defaults to RELIABLE, so the QoS-mismatched echo silently delivers nothing. Force best-effort to receive:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

It prints a data: line per message:

data:

Ctrl-C stops nros run and QEMU with it.

Readiness signal. Within ~20 seconds of QEMU boot, the image prints Publishing: 'Hello World: 1' on its semihosting stdout — a std_msgs/String counted from 1, like the official ROS 2 demo talker. QEMU cold-boot through FreeRTOS init + lwIP DHCP + zenoh session open typically takes 10–15 s. If no Publishing: line in 30 seconds:

  1. Confirm the router is running on the host on the port the image dials — the locator in its system.toml (Slirp forwards 10.0.2.2:<p> → host:

    ). Without it the talker makes one connection attempt and stops with Failed to open session; a board that should wait for a late router sets [knobs.zenoh.limits] connect_forever = true (or connect_timeout_ms for a bounded wait).

  2. Check the talker’s early log for lwIP DHCP timeout or Failed to open session.
  3. Bridge tip: ros2 topic echo /chatter from a stock ROS 2 install (with RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp) confirms end-to-end interop.
  4. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

Run on the POSIX simulator

The freertos-posix board runs the FreeRTOS kernel as an ordinary Linux process (FreeRTOS’s POSIX port) — no QEMU, host networking. It is a C / C++ board (it has no Rust entry shape). Provision it, point the image of a C or C++ workspace at it, and run:

nros setup freertos-posix --rmw zenoh
# in src/fr_node_bringup/system.toml:  [image.freertos] board = "freertos-posix"
nros run fr_node

The image dials the router on the host directly (no Slirp gateway), so start rmw_zenohd on the port its locator names, as in Run on QEMU step 1.

Flash a real board

No in-tree FreeRTOS board is flashed by a documented flow, and none is claimed: the MPS2-AN385 boards above are QEMU machines.

  • NXP S32Z270 (s32z270-freertos; its status is on its board page). No emulator models its Cortex-R52 RTU, so nothing here boots it. It builds like the other boards — the licensed pieces (NXP’s GCC/ARM_CR52_GIC FreeRTOS port, the RTD NETC Ethernet driver, the S32 Config Tools PBcfg) are yours to supply, as its descriptor explains — and the ELF is flashed with your own S32 tooling (S32 Design Studio, a Lauterbach/PEmicro probe); nano-ros adds no flash step:

    nros setup s32z270-freertos --rmw zenoh
# in src/fr_node_bringup/system.toml, a second image:
#   [image.s32z] board = "s32z270-freertos"
nros build s32z
# → nros build prints the ELF path; flash it with your S32 tooling

  • Your own FreeRTOS board is a board package of your own — see Adding a FreeRTOS Board — and is flashed with whatever that board’s vendor uses (probe-rs, OpenOCD, a vendor IDE).

Neither flash path is run by any probe (a CI runner has no board): both stand unverified until run against a named board. How often the QEMU line above runs is on each board’s page under Supported Boards.

GitHub source

The copy-out talkers for this board, one per language. Each is the same project this page scaffolds: one node package and a bringup with no launch file of its own.

  • Rust: examples/mps2-an385-freertos/rust/talker/
  • C: examples/mps2-an385-freertos/c/talker/
  • C++: examples/mps2-an385-freertos/cpp/talker/

Next

  • Subscriber, services and actions: the freertos_* image rows of the language workspaces, examples/workspaces/{rust,c,cpp}, one bringup per behaviour (pubsub_bringup, service_bringup, action_bringup). nros run pubsub_bringup:freertos_listener runs the listener; freertos_listener_xrce is the same role over XRCE.
  • No RTOS: the Bare-metal Cortex-M3 page is the same board without FreeRTOS.
  • Your own board / RTOS: the Board Integration matrix maps each user profile (Cargo-first, vendor-IDE, Zephyr, NuttX, ESP32-C3, niche fork) to the shortest bring-up path.
  • RTOS-specific debugging: FreeRTOS LAN9118 Debugging.

Design background

  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The copy-out talker per platform and language, and the paired examples as image rows of behaviour bringups.

Zephyr (west module)

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Support level: native_sim, mps2_an385, the S32K344 safety island. Each page states what nano-ros can show for the board (where it runs, how often, and its breadth), generated from the board support registry; Board Support Levels explains the words.

Single-node starter on Zephyr via the in-tree zephyr/ west module. nano-ros ships as a Zephyr module — west discovers it from your workspace’s west.yml, drops in a prj.conf Kconfig surface, and the standard west build / west flash flow takes care of the rest.

Changing this in the tree: see Internals → in-tree examples.

Just want a working starter? Clone the nano-ros-zephyr-example repo (west init -m …) — a manifest + zenoh talker app pinned to a tested Zephyr, with the same quickstart as below baked in. The steps here explain what it does so you can adapt it to your own workspace.

Prereqs. Run nros setup zephyr --rmw <rmw> once (see Prerequisites below) — it provisions the Zephyr west workspace + Zephyr SDK bits, the emulator, and your RMW’s host daemon into the shared store. No hand-installed Zephyr SDK, west, or cross-toolchain. nros build generates the messages from your ROS 2 install, so its first build of a workspace needs ROS 2 sourced. Python: 3.10+ on Zephyr 3.7 LTS, but ≥ 3.12 on Zephyr 4.x (4.x’s find_package(Python3) requires 3.12 — see the version matrix below). nano-ros’s imported west fragment zephyr/west.yml is a manifest-only file — it does NOT pull Zephyr itself; that has to be in your parent manifest (zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr).

Which Zephyr? — 3.7 LTS and 4.x both supported

nano-ros consumes as a module on both the 3.7 LTS line (supported to Jan 2027; the safety-island default) and the current 4.x rolling line. You build against whatever Zephyr your workspace already pins — nano-ros adapts. The two lines differ only in how you select an RMW and apply nano-ros’s Zephyr patches:

CapabilityZephyr 3.7 LTSZephyr 4.x
Min Python3.103.12 (find_package(Python3))
RMW selectionthe image’s rmw in system.tomlthe image’s rmw in system.toml (an app with no system.toml: the -S nros-<rmw> snippet)
nano-ros patchesapplied during nros setup zephyr provisioningapplied during nros setup zephyr provisioning
Examples as samples / Twister—samples: + Twister (sample.nano-ros.*)
zenoh (native_sim)✅ build + e2e✅ build + e2e
cyclonedds (native_sim)✅ build + e2e✅ build · publish · receive · multicast-join (stable 2-node run pending a tracked k_mutex fix)
xrce✅build path WIP

native_sim networking uses NSOS (host loopback) on both lines — no TAP/bridge/root. The copy-out, snippet, patch-apply, and dual-line build flows are exercised in CI; the lanes are in Internals → Zephyr in-tree examples.

Project layout

A nano-ros project on Zephyr is a workspace like on every other platform, beside the west workspace that holds Zephyr. Your code is node packages; the bringup’s system.toml names the board. The Zephyr application is generated: nros build writes it under build/ and runs west build on it.

my_zephyr_ws/                          # the west workspace: Zephyr and its modules
├── .west/
├── manifest/west.yml
├── zephyr/                            # cloned by `west update`
└── modules/
c_ws/                                  # the nano-ros workspace
├── src/
│   ├── c_node/                        # your node package
│   └── c_node_bringup/
│       ├── package.xml
│       └── system.toml                # [image.zephyr] board = "zephyr"
└── build/                             # generated, the Zephyr application among it

Quick start builds exactly this. An application that owns its west build and has no bringup (its own CMakeLists.txt and prj.conf, with nano-ros added as one more module) is the subject of its own chapter, A Zephyr App You Build with West.

Prerequisites

nros setup zephyr provisions what the index declares for the board — the Zephyr SDK ([board.zephyr] packages = ["zephyr-sdk"]) and the RMW transport sources (zenoh-pico + mbedtls for zenoh, the cyclonedds fork) — from a pinned index into ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/sdk. The Zephyr sources and modules themselves are a west workspace, which you keep the standard Zephyr way. It provides no zenoh router: that is ROS’s rmw_zenohd (see the RMW design); Cyclone DDS needs no daemon at all.

  1. Get the nros CLI — install a release with scripts/install.sh (Installation); it lands in ~/.nros/bin.
  2. Provision the board + RMW: 
    nros setup zephyr --rmw zenoh       # Zephyr SDK + zenoh-pico + mbedtls
nros setup --source px4-rs          # workspace cargo-load dep
  3. Point Zephyr at the SDK if your shell does not already find it — export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)", which prints where nros setup installed it (or register it via the SDK’s setup.sh -c).
  4. Source ROS 2 for the first build. nros build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install’s definitions, std_msgs included, so the types match your ROS 2 peers: source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash before the first nros build, nros run or nros configure of a workspace. That configure records the prefix, so later shells need not source ROS.

The zenoh router must be running before an example connects (ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd); for xrce, the Micro-XRCE-DDS agent nros setup … --rmw xrce installed; for cyclonedds, nothing.

Quick start: a talker on native_sim, from nothing

The sections after this one explain each piece; this is the whole path in order, for a C talker on native_sim (a host executable, so no emulator). Zephyr’s own host tools come first — west and the build tools Zephyr’s Getting Started lists; nros setup installs no system packages. On Debian/Ubuntu:

sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git cmake ninja-build gperf \
    device-tree-compiler python3-pip python3-venv xz-utils file wget
pip3 install --user west
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

Provision the board and RMW (the Zephyr SDK, zenoh-pico, mbedtls):

nros setup zephyr --rmw zenoh
export ZEPHYR_SDK_INSTALL_DIR="$(nros locate tool zephyr-sdk)"

A west workspace that pins Zephyr 3.7 and fetches only the modules nano-ros’s boards build with (nros setup zephyr lists them; import: true would fetch every vendor HAL, ~2.5 GB more):

mkdir -p my_zephyr_ws/manifest && cd my_zephyr_ws
cat > manifest/west.yml <<'WEST_YML'
manifest:
  remotes:
    - name: zephyrproject-rtos
      url-base: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos
  projects:
    - name: zephyr
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: v3.7.0
      import:
        name-allowlist: [cmsis, picolibc, mbedtls, tinycrypt, mcuboot, net-tools]
    # Rust support: only a Rust app builds with it. Pinned to the revision
    # nano-ros's own west.yml pins for the 3.7 line (it has no release tags).
    - name: zephyr-lang-rust
      remote: zephyrproject-rtos
      revision: 404fcefdbab0f2711cd342a1fab9d2eda52a1ba9
      path: modules/lang/rust
  self:
    path: manifest
WEST_YML
west init -l manifest
west update --narrow -o=--depth=1
pip3 install --user -r zephyr/scripts/requirements-base.txt
export ZEPHYR_BASE="$PWD/zephyr"

Scaffold a workspace beside the west workspace: a C talker node package and its bringup, whose image runs on board zephyr (Zephyr’s native_sim/native/64). nros build writes the Zephyr application for that image under build/ and runs west build on it, from the west workspace NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE names. You write no CMakeLists.txt and no prj.conf.

The board package also applies nano-ros’s nros-nsos snippet, which routes the image’s sockets to the host’s (Zephyr’s NSOS) instead of a TAP interface. Without it native_sim tries to create one (eth_posix: Cannot create zeth), which needs privileges a container or an ordinary user does not have, and the image never reaches the router.

The first build generates the message bindings from your ROS 2 install, so source it in this shell first. It records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later builds and runs of it need no sourced shell.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE="$PWD"
cd ..
nros new c_ws --board zephyr --template talker --lang c --rmw zenoh
cd c_ws
nros build

That wrote two packages, the same shape every platform’s scaffold has:

c_ws/
└── src/
    ├── c_node/            # the talker: package.xml, CMakeLists.txt, its C source
    └── c_node_bringup/    # package.xml, and system.toml: [image.zephyr] board = "zephyr"

Run it against a router on the host’s loopback — native_sim uses the host’s sockets, and the image dials tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 unless the bringup’s system.toml states a locator:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Started Zenoh router with id

With the router running, run the talker:

nros run c_node

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

An application you already build with west. A Zephyr application that keeps its own CMakeLists.txt and prj.conf and has no bringup is not a workspace image: it adds the nano-ros module to a plain west build, as A Zephyr App You Build with West shows.

The same talker in Rust. The scaffold is the same with --lang rust, and so is everything nros build does with it. Make it beside the west workspace above.

zephyr-lang-rust needs three things the C app does not: the Rust target the Zephyr board implies (x86_64-unknown-none for native_sim/64 on an x86_64 host), rustup’s clippy (it lints every Rust app as part of the build), and clang and libclang, for the bindings it generates from Zephyr’s headers. nros setup in the workspace installs the target and clippy, and with --sudo the two packages (without it, it prints the install command). nros build refuses a Rust Zephyr image that lacks any of them, naming the command.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
. "$HOME/.cargo/env"     # the cargo `nros setup` installed (Installation)
export NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE="$PWD"
cd ..
nros new rs_ws --board zephyr --template talker --lang rust --rmw zenoh
cd rs_ws
nros setup --sudo
nros build

With the router above running, run it:

nros run rs_node

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'

Configure

nano-ros’s Zephyr module ships in the installed SDK — the SDK root (the release’s share/nano-ros; nros locate nano-ros prints it) holds its zephyr/module.yml. You do not add nano-ros to your west.yml: nros build names the module on the west build line it runs (-DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES=<sdk root>), and a west build you run yourself passes the same:

west build -b native_sim/native/64 apps/my_app -- \
    -DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES="$(nros locate nano-ros)"

Your west.yml pins Zephyr itself (and whatever modules your application uses) the standard Zephyr way:

manifest:
  remotes:
    - name: zephyr
      url-base: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos
  projects:
    - name: zephyr
      remote: zephyr
      revision: v3.7.0          # or your chosen 3.7 LTS / 4.x SHA
      path: zephyr
      import: true               # pulls Zephyr's own modules

The transport sources the module compiles (zenoh-pico, mbedtls, the Cyclone DDS fork) come from nros setup zephyr --rmw <rmw>, not from west.

Then nano-ros’s half of the configuration goes in the bringup’s system.toml, and Zephyr’s own half in prj.conf fragments (in a workspace, under the bringup’s boards/<board>/, as Growing your workspace shows):

# src/c_node_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "c_node_bringup"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0

[image.zephyr]
board = "zephyr"            # the concrete board is west's `-b`
rmw = "zenoh"               # zenoh | xrce | cyclonedds
# locator = "tcp/192.0.2.10:7447"
# [image.zephyr.knobs.zenoh]
# max_publishers = 4

# prj.conf — Zephyr settings only; never a CONFIG_NROS_* knob here
CONFIG_NROS=y               # enables the module; everything else is the image's
CONFIG_NETWORKING=y
CONFIG_NET_IPV4=y
CONFIG_NET_TCP=y

The module renders the image into a Kconfig fragment merged after prj.conf: the RMW from rmw, the language API from your app, the endpoint from locator, the domain from domain_id, and every env knob (any symbol in the Kconfig reference, spelled without CONFIG_). A CONFIG_NROS_* line in prj.conf would be overridden by it, so it is at best dead. Several images in one file — one per RMW — are picked with west build … -- -DNROS_IMAGE=<id>; see Configuring an image. An app with NO system.toml gets no rendering and is configured in its own prj.conf (A Zephyr App You Build with West).

CONFIG_NROS=y activates the shell, which maps Kconfig values to NROS_* CMake cache vars and add_subdirectory()s the root nano-ros CMake. NanoRos::NanoRos is linked into your app library transparently.

Configuring an image: system.toml, not prj.conf

An image’s nano-ros configuration lives in ONE place, the bringup’s system.toml. The nano-ros Zephyr module renders the selected image into a Kconfig fragment and merges it last, after every conf file. So the prj*.conf files hold Zephyr’s own settings only (networking, POSIX, stacks, heaps) and never a CONFIG_NROS_* line: one there is either dead (the image overrides it) or a second source that can disagree with the first. A gate (check-leaf-conf-nros-knobs) refuses one in the tree.

What the module renders, and from where:

You write in system.tomlThe build gets
[image.<id>] rmw = "xrce"CONFIG_NROS_RMW_XRCE=y
(nothing — the package’s language)CONFIG_NROS_{C,CPP,RUST}_API=y
locator = "tcp/…" (zenoh)CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATOR
locator = "udp/<host>:<port>" (XRCE)CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_AGENT_ADDR + _PORT
domain_id = 7 (image, [defaults] or [system])CONFIG_NROS_DOMAIN_ID
[image.<id>.knobs.zenoh] max_queryables = 12CONFIG_NROS_MAX_QUERYABLES=12 — a registry knob, spelled as a board’s [knobs] is (see Configuration)
[image.<id>.knobs.xrce] max_subscribers = 0CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS=0 — likewise
env = { NROS_ZEPHYR_TASK_STACK_SIZE = "16384" }CONFIG_NROS_ZEPHYR_TASK_STACK_SIZE=16384 — any other option in the reference below, spelled without CONFIG_
os_config = ["prj-xrce.conf"]that Zephyr-native fragment, added ahead of your own EXTRA_CONF_FILE

An env row with no Kconfig symbol is not lost: it reaches the image’s cargo builds as an [env] row instead. A row whose type does not fit its symbol, or that only exists under another RMW, is refused at configure time, naming the system.toml line.

One image per RMW

A bringup built for several backends states one image per RMW, and picks one at build time. From examples/zephyr/c/talker/system.toml:

[system]
name = "nros_zephyr_talker_c"
rmw = "zenoh"
domain_id = 0
default_images = ["zephyr_zenoh"]

[image.zephyr_zenoh]
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "zenoh"
os_config = ["prj-zenoh.conf"]

[image.zephyr_xrce]
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "xrce"
os_config = ["prj-xrce.conf"]
locator = "udp/127.0.0.1:2018"

[image.zephyr_xrce.knobs.xrce]
max_subscribers = 0
max_service_servers = 0
max_service_clients = 0

[image.zephyr_cyclonedds]
board = "zephyr"
rmw = "cyclonedds"
os_config = ["prj-cyclonedds.conf"]

nros build                    # the default_images: zephyr_zenoh
nros build zephyr_xrce        # another image — its own west build dir

Each image builds into its own directory, build/<platform>-<rmw>/<package>__<image>_west, so switching images never reuses another image’s cache.

To run west yourself on one image, nros build zephyr_xrce --dry-run prints the west build line for that image’s generated application and its own build directory.

Precedence, last wins: the conf files, then a 4.x -S nros-<rmw> snippet, then the image’s rendering, then any -DCONFIG_… on the command line (how a test harness passes a per-run port). A snippet naming a DIFFERENT RMW than the image is refused rather than silently overridden; one that agrees is redundant. An application with no system.toml gets no rendering, so for it the snippets and Kconfig defaults still choose.

What each RMW’s Zephyr-native fragment needs

The image’s os_config file carries what the backend needs from Zephyr itself:

  • Zenoh (the Kconfig default): TCP and POSIX threads for zenoh-pico — CONFIG_NET_TCP=y, CONFIG_POSIX_API=y, and pthread pools big enough for it (examples/zephyr/rust/talker/prj-zenoh.conf uses CONFIG_MAX_PTHREAD_MUTEX_COUNT=64, CONFIG_MAX_PTHREAD_COND_COUNT=16).
  • XRCE-DDS: CONFIG_NET_TCP=y, on top of the BSD sockets (CONFIG_NET_SOCKETS=y) every image’s shared prj.conf enables. The agent endpoint is the image’s locator.
  • Cyclone DDS: brokerless RTPS, wire-compatible with stock ROS 2 (rmw_cyclonedds_cpp). Its source is C++, so CONFIG_CPP=y even for Rust callers; it needs a large stack (CONFIG_MAIN_STACK_SIZE=524288), pthread pools, and CONFIG_NET_IPV4_IGMP=y for SPDP multicast. The bool prerequisites (thread-local storage, dynamic threads, NET_TCP, …) are selected by CONFIG_NROS_RMW_CYCLONEDDS. Its ddsrt_malloc draws on the nano-ros platform heap, 1 MiB by default under Cyclone — raise it with [image.<id>.knobs.zephyr] heap_size = … on the image, not in the conf.

On native_sim, add the NSOS host-socket offload (CONFIG_NET_SOCKETS_OFFLOAD=y + CONFIG_NET_NATIVE_OFFLOADED_SOCKETS=y) so discovery uses host BSD sockets instead of zeth/TAP. See examples/zephyr/rust/talker/prj-cyclonedds.conf for the full fragment.

Build
