// application's entry point around the component.
nros::force_link_backend!(nros_rmw_zenoh);
nros::zephyr_component_main!(crate::Talker);
EOF

Write prj.conf and package.xml as for the C application (Configure, Messages), then change two lines of prj.conf: a Rust application selects CONFIG_NROS_RUST_API (which needs CONFIG_RUST, Zephyr’s switch for zephyr-lang-rust) instead of CONFIG_NROS_CPP_API, and needs no C++ standard:

sed -i -e '/^CONFIG_NROS_CPP_API=y$/d' -e '/^CONFIG_STD_CPP17=y$/d' apps/my_app/prj.conf
cat >> apps/my_app/prj.conf <<'EOF'
CONFIG_RUST=y
CONFIG_NROS_RUST_API=y
EOF
``` The other settings stay as they are. `build.rs` hands the Kconfig
values to the crate, among them the locator and the domain, so they are still
set in `prj.conf` alone.

The crate names the nano-ros crates and `std_msgs` but does not say where they
come from. `nros configure`, run in the application directory, generates the
Rust types for the message packages `package.xml` lists, under `generated/`,
and writes `.cargo/config.toml`, which points the nano-ros crates at your
nano-ros install and the message crates at `generated/`. Run it before the
first `west build`, and again when `package.xml` changes. It generates the
types from your ROS 2 install, so source it first; the configure records the
prefix, and a later `nros configure` of the application needs no sourced
shell:

```bash probe=49 track=installed variant=west-app-rust
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
cd apps/my_app && nros configure && cd ../..

From there the application builds and runs as the C one does: the same west build line, and the same run on native_sim. The log line reads <inf> nros: rustapp: Published: 1, from Zephyr’s logger.

If it doesn’t work

Could not find a package configuration file provided by "nano_ros". The module is not in the build. Check that nros locate nano-ros prints a directory, and that the build line passes it as -DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES after the --.

attempt to assign the value ... to the undefined symbol NROS_.... The symbol is misspelled or does not exist. Search for it in west build -t menuconfig (/ searches). CONFIG_NROS_ROS_EDITION is a common one: it does not exist.

No Published: line within 30 seconds.

  1. Check that the router is running and listening on the port in CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATOR.
  2. On native_sim, check that the build line has -S nros-nsos. A line eth_posix: Cannot create zeth in the output means it did not.
  3. Check CONFIG_NETWORKING=y, CONFIG_NET_IPV4=y and CONFIG_NET_TCP=y in prj.conf. Zephyr’s networking is opt-in.

A message with an unbounded string or sequence field fails to generate, asking for a bound. nano-ros sizes its buffers at build time, so a field with no stated maximum needs one. Put it in an nros-codegen.toml beside package.xml:

[fields]
"std_msgs/String.data" = 256

The Zephyr 4.x line says Could NOT find Python3 ... required is at least "3.12". Zephyr 4.x needs Python 3.12 or newer for west and its build scripts.

For anything else, Troubleshooting: First 10 Minutes walks through the common failures.

Design background

A nano-ros project is normally a workspace, and its bringup’s system.toml says what runs where. An application that owns its own build stays outside that model on purpose (RFC-0121 D6): nano-ros joins the build the way any library would, and asks the build for nothing back. For Zephyr, that application is a guest (RFC-0085 D14): it loads nano-ros as a module, states the middleware, locator and domain in Kconfig, and builds with west alone. With no system.toml beside it, the module gives every nano-ros setting its Kconfig prompt, so prj.conf, menuconfig and -DCONFIG_* are the one source of its configuration.

  • RFC-0121: workspace-first project layout
  • RFC-0085: Zephyr workspace and west handoff

PX4 Autopilot (external module)

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Single-node starter on PX4 Autopilot via the external-module copy-out template. PX4’s EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION pattern lets downstream firmware drop in nano-ros without forking PX4 itself. C++ only — PX4’s uORB binding is C++-only (Rust + C not in the coverage matrix).

Prereqs. A PX4-Autopilot ≥ v1.16 clone, the matching cross toolchain (e.g. gcc-arm-none-eabi for Pixhawk targets), and python3 with the PX4 development requirements installed (bash ./Tools/setup/ubuntu.sh once).

Project layout

PX4 external modules live outside the PX4 source tree and are hooked in at configure time. The template — shipped in the SDK root at integrations/px4/module-template/ (the SDK root is the installed release’s share/nano-ros, nros locate nano-ros prints it) — has the PX4-required src/modules/<name>/ shape:

my_drone_firmware/
├── PX4-Autopilot/                          # PX4 source tree (submodule)
└── px4-modules/                            # passed via EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION
    └── nano-ros/                           # copy-out from integrations/px4/module-template/
        └── src/
            ├── CMakeLists.txt              # populates config_module_list_external
            └── modules/
                └── nano_ros_app/
                    ├── CMakeLists.txt      # px4_add_module(... MAIN nano_ros_app)
                    └── nano_ros_app.cpp    # the user-editable app

Prereq. PX4 is your own checkout — the firmware tree you already build. Clone it (or use the one you have) and initialize its submodules; nano-ros is tested against PX4 v1.17.0.

git clone --branch v1.17.0 https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot.git
git -C PX4-Autopilot submodule update --init \
    --depth 1 --recommend-shallow --recursive

PX4’s own Python dependencies come from its Tools/setup scripts (e.g. PX4-Autopilot/Tools/setup/ubuntu.sh) — run those per PX4’s documentation if the firmware build complains about missing Python modules.

Copy the template into your firmware repo; PX4 is pointed at the copy at build time:

mkdir -p px4-modules
sdk="$(nros locate nano-ros)"   # this project's nano-ros SDK root
cp -r "$sdk/integrations/px4/module-template" px4-modules/nano-ros

(Releases after 0.6.0-nros4 ship the template; with an older one, copy it from GitHub.)

PX4 enforces the src/modules/<name>/ layout exactly. To make the module your own, rename nano_ros_app in all three places at once: the directory, the module list in src/CMakeLists.txt, and the MAIN name in the module’s own CMakeLists.txt. PX4 has no central module registry, so copying the template into your tree is how it is distributed.

PX4’s own make <target> is the build verb, and it configures and builds ONE tree, PX4-Autopilot/build/<target>/. The module joins it through EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION, passed on that same make line — PX4’s Makefile forwards it to its CMake configure — and pointing at the dir that contains the template’s src/ (that’s px4-modules/nano-ros, not its parent: PX4’s root CMakeLists.txt does add_subdirectory("${EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION}/src" …)).

The template finds nano-ros itself: an explicit -Dnano_ros_ROOT=<path> cache variable wins, otherwise it asks the nros on PATH, which answers with the SDK that binary belongs to. No environment variable is read. To name the root anyway, pass it through PX4’s CMAKE_ARGS:

make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_sitl_default \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros" \
    CMAKE_ARGS="-Dnano_ros_ROOT=$sdk"    # optional

Not replayed. No probe track runs the PX4 SITL build yet, so this line is unmeasured on the installed track (tracking issue).

Inside the module, the canonical pattern bridges uORB → nano-ros. The module is a PX4Module subclass that runs in its own work queue, opens an nros executor, and forwards uORB messages onto a zenoh / DDS topic (or vice versa). Edit nano_ros_app.cpp to add your topic bindings.

Generate px4_msgs

nros px4 msgs generates CDR-serializable px4_msgs::msg::* bindings from a PX4-Autopilot .msg tree (--px4 <dir>, default $PX4_AUTOPILOT_DIR) into --output. --lang rust (the default) writes a px4_msgs crate for an XRCE companion; --lang cpp writes headers and FFI glue for an in-firmware PX4 module. --topics keeps only the messages a bridge carries (by message name or uORB topic name), pulling in nested types:

nros px4 msgs --output generated/px4_msgs --topics vehicle_status

nros px4 is a command package (nros_px4_tools), not a built-in: nros runs its executable with the arguments unchanged, and nros px4 msgs --help prints its flags.

Configure

The template does not ship a Kconfig overlay (no Kconfig.projbuild files). Module enablement is implicit once EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION points at the template. Which RMW backends the module registers is the BACKENDS list of nros_px4_add_module(...) in src/modules/nano_ros_app/CMakeLists.txt — the template ships BACKENDS uorb — not a cache variable. (Adding a Kconfig overlay so the module appears under menuconfig → External modules is a follow-up task; for now the template is always enabled.)

Build

One make, one tree. For the SITL simulator (POSIX target — easier to develop against), or for a Pixhawk (px4_fmu-v5_default here; use your board’s PX4 target):

make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_sitl_default \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros"
make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_fmu-v5_default \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros"

The firmware lands in PX4’s own tree, PX4-Autopilot/build/<target>/ (px4_fmu-v5_default.px4 for the Pixhawk). The first build cross-compiles nano-ros’s Rust staticlibs alongside PX4’s NuttX kernel + apps (~10 min on a fresh checkout). Note that the module links prebuilt nano-ros archives (nros_px4_add_module resolves them at configure time and, when one is missing, stops naming the command that builds it).

Run on the SITL simulator

PX4’s SITL runs the autopilot as a host process against a simulator. With Gazebo (Harmonic) installed per PX4’s documentation:

make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_sitl_default gz_x500 \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros"
# In the PX4 console:
pxh> nano_ros_app start

# Verify from stock ROS 2 on the same network (only after you have
# added uORB → nano-ros forwarders to nano_ros_app.cpp — the shipped
# template forwards nothing on its own):
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /vehicle_local_position px4_msgs/msg/VehicleLocalPosition

Flash a real board

PX4’s own upload target flashes over the bootloader USB, with the same EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION as the build (it rebuilds if anything changed):

make -C PX4-Autopilot px4_fmu-v5_default upload \
    EXTERNAL_MODULES_LOCATION="$PWD/px4-modules/nano-ros"

Not replayed. No probe runs this flash line (a CI runner has no board), so it is written from the board’s runner, not measured (tracking issue).

QGroundControl can flash the same build/px4_fmu-v5_default/px4_fmu-v5_default.px4 instead. Start the module from the NSH console (nano_ros_app start) or the board’s startup script.

No probe runs the upload line (a CI runner has no board): it stands unverified until run against a named board. PX4 SITL is the replay that can run in CI, and it is not yet run there either.

Readiness signal. After nano_ros_app start in the PX4 console, the shipped template logs nano-ros uORB backend registered and returns immediately — it doesn’t start a publisher loop or print a “bridge started” line on its own. You’re expected to edit nano_ros_app.cpp to wire your uORB → nano-ros forwards. If nano_ros_app reports register failed, check:

  1. Module didn’t register — the template logs nros_rmw_uorb_register() -> <rc> on startup (search the PX4 boot log for nros_rmw_uorb_register). A non-zero <rc> usually means a NuttX kernel-config / feature-gate mismatch.
  2. Once you’ve added forwarders, zenohd must be reachable from the autopilot’s network (Pixhawk: configured via QGroundControl or param set).
  3. uORB topic not advertised yet — start the upstream PX4 module that publishes it (commander start etc.) first.
  4. See Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes.

GitHub source

  • PX4 external-module template: integrations/px4/module-template/
  • Worked PX4 example, the source of truth for the register-check shape (including the weak nros-rmw-cffi register stub on the Rust side): packages/testing/nros-px4-register-check/
  • PX4 integration roadmap notes: integrations/px4/README.md

Constraints to be aware of

  • uORB binding is C++-only. The PX4 example collapses uORB registration to a C++ port; Rust / C variants exist for non-PX4 RTOSes but not for PX4.
  • PX4’s NuttX kernel. Underneath, PX4 runs NuttX; if you need to debug at the kernel layer, the NuttX starter page applies too.
  • uORB throughput vs zenoh hops. uORB is in-process pub/sub at ~µs latency; zenoh adds network-RTT. Plan accordingly when bridging high-rate streams.

Next

  • Add your own uORB topics to the bridge: see the nano_ros_app.cpp template’s topic-table section.
  • Multi-vehicle: PX4-XRCE-Agent → nano-ros XRCE backend gives you the standard PX4-ROS bridge with nano-ros on the autopilot side.
  • For pure-NuttX (no PX4) firmware: see the NuttX starter.

Pick a scheduling model

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Organize a larger workspace

Pick a scheduling model when one image runs callbacks of different urgency: a 10 ms control loop beside a 100 ms telemetry publisher, for example, where the control loop must not wait behind the telemetry.

In nano-ros, the unit of scheduling is a sched task: one executor running on one RTOS thread, with its own priority and spin period, all of them sharing one middleware session. You name callback groups in code, map each group to a sched task in system.toml, and give each sched task its priority per RTOS. The build turns that into the threads each platform has. Where ROS 2 reaches for a MultiThreadedExecutor and callback groups, nano-ros gives you sched tasks: an executor dispatches on one thread, and parallelism is a sched task, not a callback group.

The scheduling theory behind the choice (fixed-priority preemption, rate-monotonic assignment, EDF, priority inversion) belongs to The execution model.

Before you start

  • A workspace whose image runs on an RTOS or on Linux.
  • The capabilities your platform delivers, from the generated Scheduling wiring matrix: kernel EDF on Zephyr, the sporadic server on NuttX, preemption threshold on ThreadX, core affinity on most.

Steps

  1. Name a callback group for each urgency, in the node’s code.

    In Rust, call node.callback_group("ctrl")? before creating the timer or subscription that belongs to it. In C++, use the named form, create_callback_group("ctrl"); an unnamed group runs on the node’s default sched task.

  2. Map each group to a sched task, on the node’s [[component]] row:

    [[component]]
pkg = "ctrl_pkg"
class = "ctrl_pkg::Control"
name = "control_node"
group_tasks = { ctrl = "high" }

[[component]]
pkg = "telem_pkg"
class = "telem_pkg::Telem"
name = "telem_node"
group_tasks = { telem = "low" }

  3. Declare the sched tasks. A key on [tasks.<name>] applies on every platform; a key on [tasks.<name>.<rtos>] applies only there:

    [tasks.high]
class = "real_time"
spin_period = "1000us"

[tasks.high.posix]
priority = 80
core = 0

[tasks.high.freertos]
priority = 3

[tasks.low]
spin_period = "10000us"

[tasks.low.posix]
priority = 10

[tasks.low.freertos]
priority = 2

    class is real_time (the default for a priority sched task), best_effort or time_triggered. Priorities are the RTOS’s own numbers, so their direction differs: on FreeRTOS, NuttX and Linux a bigger number is more urgent, and on ThreadX and Zephyr a smaller one is. The table of levels and directions per platform is in the Scheduling wiring matrix.

  4. Add the platform’s own mechanism where it has one. Scope it to that platform, so it lowers to nothing elsewhere:

    [tasks.high.zephyr]
priority = 9
deadline = "10000us"        # kernel EDF, Zephyr only

[tasks.high.nuttx]
priority = 99
budget = "5000us"           # SCHED_SPORADIC, NuttX only
period = "10000us"

[tasks.low.threadx]
priority = 16
preempt_threshold = 10      # ThreadX only
time_slice = "5000us"

    A budget on [tasks.high] itself would switch every platform’s executor to cooperative sporadic gating, which is why these keys go in the platform tables.

  5. Keep sched tasks below the transport. Each board reserves a priority band for the middleware’s own read and lease threads, and a sched task that outranks them cannot be served by them. The build allocates sched-task priorities from the board’s application pool and refuses a priority that lands on the reserved band. A sched task that really must run above it says so with above = "transport".

  6. Choose what a periodic timer does after a stall. When a sched task is preempted past several periods, the timer fires once and counts the missed periods (TimerOverrunPolicy::Skip, the default, as in rclcpp and Zephyr’s k_timer). Phase is kept, so activations stay on the declared cadence. Replay every missed period instead, for a counter or an accumulator, with executor.set_timer_overrun_policy(id, TimerOverrunPolicy::CatchUp). Do not replay a control loop: the replayed activations compute with stale inputs and send a burst of commands. Watch executor.timer_overruns(id), or the timer-overrun-runtime violation, rather than the publish rate, which looks nominal under CatchUp during exactly the stall it should catch. Timer periods are microseconds throughout, including across the C ABI.

  7. Build. The configure runs the host image once to take its census, and each node logs the sched task it registered on:

    nros configure

    [INFO] Telem::register on a sched task admitting group `telem`

Example

examples/workspaces/realtime-rust/ runs a 10 ms control node on high and a 100 ms telemetry node on low, with sched-task tables for Linux, FreeRTOS, NuttX, ThreadX and Zephyr in one system.toml. Its realtime-c and realtime-cpp siblings do the same in C and C++.

# src/demo_bringup/system.toml (excerpt)
[[component]]
pkg = "ctrl_pkg"
class = "ctrl_pkg::Control"
name = "control_node"
group_tasks = { ctrl = "high" }

[[component]]
pkg = "telem_pkg"
class = "telem_pkg::Telem"
name = "telem_node"
group_tasks = { telem = "low" }

[tasks.high]
class = "real_time"
spin_period = "1000us"
[tasks.high.posix]
priority = 80
core = 0
[tasks.high.freertos]
priority = 3

[tasks.low]
spin_period = "10000us"
[tasks.low.posix]
priority = 10
[tasks.low.freertos]
priority = 2

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

[image.freertos_realtime]
board = "freertos"
panic = "own"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7891"

nros run demo_bringup:linux

If it doesn’t work

  • The build refuses a priority. It lands on the board’s reserved transport band, or outranks it. Pick one from the application pool the message names, or state above = "transport".
  • A core pin falls back with a warning on Zephyr. The pin is on the boot sched task, which Zephyr started before nano-ros ran and cannot pin any more. Put core on a sched task nano-ros spawns.
  • MultiThreadedExecutor does not compile. It has no nano-ros form. Move the callbacks that need their own thread to a sched task of their own.

See also

  • Analyze timing: check the callbacks a sched task runs for unbounded work.
  • Scheduling wiring matrix: what each platform delivers.
  • The execution model: how executors, sched tasks, levels and dispatch fit together.

Design background

  • RFC-0015: RTOS orchestration
  • RFC-0053: ThreadX multi-tier execution
  • RFC-0079: priority is allocated, not authored
  • RFC-0002: RT execution model (timer overrun policy)

Analyze timing

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Pick a scheduling model

Analyze timing before you trust a sched task’s period: check the callbacks it runs for the code that breaks a time bound. This page covers the static checks for Rust node packages, the ones a CI job can run on every push.

A callback’s worst case is what matters, not its average. These patterns make it unbounded:

PatternProblemCheck
an unbounded loopno upper bound on execution timeClippy
recursionunbounded stack depthClippy, cargo-call-stack
heap allocationnon-deterministic time, fragmentationno allocator, disallowed-methods
blocking I/O, a missing timeoutan unbounded waitreview
a large stack framestack overflowcargo-call-stack

Before you start

  • A Rust node package that builds with nros build.
  • rustup with a nightly toolchain, for the stack analysis.

Steps

  1. Run Clippy with the loop and recursion lints as errors, from the node package’s directory:

    cargo clippy --all-targets -- \
    -D warnings \
    -D clippy::infinite_iter \
    -D clippy::while_immutable_condition \
    -D clippy::never_loop \
    -D clippy::empty_loop \
    -D unconditional_recursion \
    -W clippy::large_stack_arrays \
    -W clippy::large_types_passed_by_value

    infinite_iter finds iterator chains that never end, while_immutable_condition a loop condition nothing changes, and empty_loop a loop {} with no body (write loop { core::hint::spin_loop() }).

  2. Set the size thresholds in a clippy.toml beside the package’s Cargo.toml:

    array-size-threshold = 512         # bytes of stack array
trivial-copy-size-limit = 16       # bytes passed by value
cognitive-complexity-threshold = 15

  3. Keep the heap out of the real-time path. A no_std package with no #[global_allocator] cannot call Box, Vec or String at all; use heapless collections with a fixed capacity:

    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let v: heapless::Vec<u8, 256> = heapless::Vec::new();
}

    A package that needs alloc elsewhere can refuse it in one module with #![deny(clippy::disallowed_methods)] and a list in clippy.toml:

    disallowed-methods = [
    { path = "alloc::vec::Vec::push", reason = "Use heapless::Vec in RT code" },
    { path = "alloc::boxed::Box::new", reason = "No heap in RT code" },
    { path = "alloc::string::String::new", reason = "Use heapless::String" },
]

  4. Measure the stack. cargo-call-stack needs nightly and fat LTO (lto = "fat" in the profile), and works best on a no_std binary:

    cargo +nightly install cargo-call-stack
RUSTFLAGS="-Z emit-stack-sizes" cargo +nightly build --release
cargo +nightly call-stack --release > call_graph.dot

    The graph gives each function’s frame size and the deepest path. Calls through function pointers or trait objects may be missing from it.

  5. Look for recursion in the same graph. A cycle is recursion:

    cargo +nightly call-stack --release 2>&1 | grep -i cycle

    Replace it with a loop over a bounded stack, such as a heapless::Vec<&Node, 32>, and handle the full case.

  6. Review what Clippy cannot prove. It cannot show that a loop ends or that a call has a timeout. Check that every loop has a reachable break or return, that a loop in a callback has an iteration limit or a deadline, and that every blocking call states a bound:

    • nano-ros: spin_once(timeout); in C++, wait_for_service(10000) and wait_for_action_server(10000). The budget is required; there is no wait-forever form.
    • std on a host: connect_timeout, a socket read timeout, recv_timeout.
    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
// Bounded: stop after a deadline, not when the queue happens to empty.
let deadline = Instant::now() + Duration::from_millis(10);
while Instant::now() < deadline {
    match queue.pop() {
        Some(msg) => process(msg),
        None => break,
    }
}
}

  7. Run it in CI. The job below runs the lints, the stack analysis and Miri, for a project with its firmware in firmware/ and two host-testable crates, my_core and my_msgs:

    name: Real-time static analysis
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  clippy-realtime:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: clippy
      - run: |
          cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings \
            -D clippy::infinite_iter -D clippy::while_immutable_condition \
            -D unconditional_recursion -W clippy::large_stack_arrays

  stack-analysis:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: firmware
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@nightly
      - run: cargo +nightly install cargo-call-stack
      - run: |
          RUSTFLAGS="-Z emit-stack-sizes" cargo +nightly build --release
          cargo +nightly call-stack --release > stack_analysis.txt
          if grep -q cycle stack_analysis.txt; then
            echo "recursion in the call graph"; exit 1
          fi

  miri:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@nightly
        with:
          components: miri
      - run: cargo +nightly miri test -p my_core -p my_msgs

    Miri runs host tests, so point it at the crates whose logic does not depend on the target: serialization, state machines, protocol code.

Example

The one command to paste for a strict local check:

cargo clippy -- \
    -D warnings -D clippy::all \
    -D clippy::infinite_iter -D clippy::while_immutable_condition \
    -D clippy::never_loop -D clippy::empty_loop \
    -D unconditional_recursion \
    -W clippy::large_stack_arrays -W clippy::large_types_passed_by_value \
    -W clippy::cognitive_complexity

If it doesn’t work

  • cargo-call-stack reports nothing useful. The build was not fat-LTO, or the package links std. Analyze the no_std firmware crate.
  • Timing measured in QEMU is meaningless. QEMU’s Cortex-M3 does not implement the DWT cycle counter, so every read is zero, and wall-clock percentiles track the host’s load. Measure execution times on the real board.
  • A lint you need does not exist. Clippy cannot see a blocking call in a callback or an allocation in an interrupt handler. A Dylint library of your own can; see the Dylint documentation below.

See also

  • Pick a scheduling model: the periods these checks protect.
  • Deploy to production: what to measure on your silicon before shipping.
  • Clippy lints, cargo-call-stack, Dylint, heapless.

Deploy to production

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Configure an image

Use this page to take an image from a workspace to the machine or board it runs on, verify it from ROS 2, and check it is ready to ship.

The order is the same on every target: build the image, put it where it runs, then verify ROS 2 communication. On a host or an emulator nros run does the last two; on hardware nros flash --monitor does.

Before you start

  • A workspace whose images build, and the boards provisioned (nros setup at the workspace root).
  • For a zenoh image, ROS 2’s router; see ROS 2 and the zenoh router.

Steps

  1. Build every image the workspace declares:

    nros build --all

    After each image, nros build prints the artifact and the board’s own next command. Where each target family’s artifact lands is in Build outputs.

  2. Check how the image will run. --dry-run --why prints the run plan, and where each fact came from, without running anything:

    nros run host_node_bringup:linux --dry-run --why

    image = "host_node_bringup:linux"
verb = "run"

[runner]
package = "nros_runner_native"
name = "native"

[console]
kind = "stdio"

[link]
kind = "tcp"
locator = "tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"
rmw = "zenoh"

  3. Run a host or emulator image, with a smoke test. nros run builds it if it is stale, starts the router its link needs, streams the console, and with --expect exits successfully when the line appears:

    nros run host_node_bringup:linux --expect 'Publishing:'

  4. Flash a real board, and watch its console on the same port:

    nros flash <bringup>:<image> --monitor --expect 'Publishing:'

    nros flash runs the board’s human steps (a jumper, a reset), flashes through the board’s flash method, and watches the console. nros monitor attaches to a board that is already running. A board with no flash method stays on the vendor’s own tools.

  5. Verify from ROS 2. With the router running and ROS 2 sourced:

    export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic list
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

    If discovery works but samples do not arrive, check the domain ID, the router endpoint, QoS reliability and the board’s network.

  6. Check readiness for production, below, on your own board.

Check readiness for production

The in-tree tests run reference boards, mostly under emulation, where cycle counters read zero and wall-clock percentiles track the host’s load. What you ship has to be measured on your silicon, at its clock and load. Count the boxes per group; a group missing two or more is not ready.

Timing, measured on the board

  • End-to-end P99 latency, publisher to callback, within your budget.
  • Worst-case stack depth per sched task (Analyze timing), and the platform’s stack-overflow detection on (FreeRTOS configCHECK_FOR_STACK_OVERFLOW, Zephyr stack sentinels, NuttX CONFIG_DEBUG_STACK).
  • Timer overruns under sustained load (timer overrun policy).
  • Heap use over 24 hours at nominal load, and no allocation on a hot path.

Platform and network

  • Multicast discovery fires on your RTOS and driver, if you use Cyclone DDS.
  • The platform clock extends a narrow hardware counter to a monotonic 64-bit value (a 32-bit millisecond count wraps at 49.7 days).
  • The image recovers from 5% packet loss, a 30-second partition, and a restart of the router or agent.
  • Critical sections are short.

Middleware and interop

  • The release pinned with nros pin, so the backend versions are the tested ones (nros setup --list prints them).
  • Every QoS policy you use is supported by your backend; an unsupported one is reported at entity creation.
  • A stock ROS 2 node receives what the image publishes, with each custom message, and QoS profiles match.
  • Every nano-ros RTOS in your fleet sees every other.

Safety and operations

  • A timeout on every blocking call; nano-ros has no wait-forever form.
  • The E2E CRC attached, if you use the safety-e2e feature (Safety).
  • A hardware watchdog wired; the executor reports overruns but pets none.
  • A log sink chosen (Log and observe a board), time synchronization, and a bootloader and update strategy, none of which nano-ros ships.
  • The licenses accepted: nano-ros is MIT OR Apache-2.0; zenoh-pico, Cyclone DDS and Micro-XRCE-DDS-Client carry their own. nano-ros has no commercial support entity, so plan for in-house expertise.

Example

A workspace with a host image and a board image, built, smoke-tested, then flashed:

nros build --all
nros run host_node_bringup:linux --expect 'Publishing:'
nros flash <bringup>:<image> --monitor --expect 'Publishing:'

The target model

This section collects the target-model pages that were folded in here. The platform pages and “Flash a real board” will take them over.

Every place an image can run is described the same way: a launcher or a flasher (a host process, an emulator, or a tool that programs a board), a console (where the image’s output appears), and a link (how its middleware reaches the rest of the system). nros reads these from the board’s descriptor, so the same commands work on every board.

  • nros run launches an image on the host or in an emulator.
  • nros flash programs a real board, and nros monitor attaches to its console.
  • nros bench records which board on your machine is on which port.

See the nros CLI reference for each verb.

Running an image: nros run

nros run builds the image if it is stale, starts what its link needs, and streams the console, for host images and emulators. --expect '<line>' exits successfully when that line appears. On a real board it refuses and names the flashing step instead.

Run plans

Before it runs anything, nros run resolves a run plan: which launcher or flasher, which console and which link, and where each fact came from. The facts come from five levels, highest first: the command line, the image, your machine’s bench file, the board’s descriptor, and the runner’s defaults. --dry-run --why prints the plan without running it, as in step 2.

Flashing and monitoring a board

nros flash programs a real board with a built image, and nros monitor attaches to its console. Both read how to do it from the board’s descriptor, and an image overrides any key in its [image.<id>.flash] and [image.<id>.console] tables. Until those verbs work for your board, flash with the vendor’s own tools.

Your bench: nros bench

nros bench scan records which attached USB device is which board, in $NROS_HOME/bench.toml, so nros flash and nros monitor find the port and probe without being told. nros bench list prints the file and what is attached now.

If it doesn’t work

  • nros run refuses and names a flashing step. The image’s board is hardware. Use nros flash --monitor.
  • The image starts but never prints. A zenoh image blocks opening its session until it reaches the router. Check the router runs, on the endpoint in the run plan’s [link].
  • nros flash cannot find the board. Run nros bench scan with the board attached, or pass --port.

See also

  • Troubleshoot: failures by symptom.
  • Build outputs: artifacts and the vendor commands that take them.
  • nros CLI: every flag of run, flash, monitor and bench.

Design background

  • RFC-0003: RTOS integration pattern
  • RFC-0065: colcon-like workspace builder
  • RFC-0075: zenoh router provenance
  • RFC-0118: target execution model

Log and observe a board

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Run a talker

Use this page to log from a node, choose which records are kept, publish them on /rosout, and find out what happened on a board that has no console.

nano-ros logs through nros-log, which has the Logger and severity surface of rclcpp::Logger and rcutils_logging. Every record goes to one sink per platform: stderr on Linux, Zephyr’s log subsystem, NuttX’s syslog, a UART on FreeRTOS and ThreadX. The table is in Platform differences.

Before you start

  • A node package in a workspace that runs, for example the talker of Run a talker.

Log from a node

use nros_log::{Logger, Severity};
use nros_log::{log_info, log_warn};

static LOGGER: Logger = Logger::new("my_node");

fn main() {
    nros_log::register_logger(&LOGGER);
    nros_log::init(nros_log::sinks::default());

    log_info!(&LOGGER, "started; domain = {}", 42);
    log_warn!(&LOGGER, "queue depth {} exceeds soft limit", 5);
}

Inside a node, prefer the Node::logger() accessor — it resolves to the same intern’d entry when the name matches:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let mut node = executor.create_node("my_node")?;
log_info!(node.logger(), "subscribed to {}", topic);
}

rclrs’s modifiers chain off the logger, and each applies per call site:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use nros_log::ToLogParams;

log_info!(node.logger().once(), "link up");
log_warn!(node.logger().skip_first(), "late sample {}", seq);
log_debug!(node.logger().only_if(verbose), "state {:?}", state);
// needs the platform clock; a clockless image refuses it at compile time
log_warn!(node.logger().throttle(Duration::from_millis(500)), "lag {} ms", lag);
}
#include <rclc/rclc.h> /* also brings the RCLC_LOG_* macros */

int main(void) {
    rclc_support_t support = rclc_support_get_zero_initialized();
    rcl_allocator_t allocator = rcl_get_default_allocator();
    rclc_support_init(&support, 0, NULL, &allocator); /* locator: build, then NROS_LOCATOR */

    rcl_node_t node = rcl_get_zero_initialized_node();
    rclc_node_init_default(&node, "my_node", "/", &support);

    rclc_logger_t logger = rclc_node_get_logger(&node);
    RCLC_LOG_INFO(logger, "started; domain=%u", 42);
    RCLC_LOG_WARN(logger, "queue depth %u exceeds soft limit", 5);

    rcl_node_fini(&node);
    rclc_support_fini(&support);
    return 0;
}

#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>

int main() {
    rclcpp::init_in("tcp/127.0.0.1:7447", 0);

    rclcpp::Node node;
    rclcpp::create_node(node, "my_node");

    auto logger = node.get_logger();
    RCLC_LOG_INFO(logger, "started; domain=%u", 42);
    RCLC_LOG_WARN(logger, "queue depth %u exceeds soft limit", 5);

    rclcpp::shutdown_in();
    return 0;
}

The first log call in C or C++ installs the platform sink, so those call sites need no init step.

Set the level

  1. Set the compile-time ceiling. Records below it are compiled out: a Rust call becomes a constant-false branch, and a C or C++ record is refused by the same check. State it per image, or per board in its descriptor:

    # system.toml: this image only
[image.linux.knobs.log]
max_level = "info"

    The value is trace (the default), debug, info, warn, error, fatal or off, or 0–6 as Zephyr’s CONFIG_NROS_LOG_MAX_LEVEL states it. nros config explain prints which rung decided it.

  2. Move a logger’s level at run time, above the ceiling:

    #![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let logger = nros_log::get_logger("my_node");
logger.set_level(nros_log::Severity::Warn);   // silences Trace, Debug, Info
logger.unset_level();                         // follows the default again
nros_log::Logger::set_default_level(nros_log::Severity::Debug);
}

    A logger with no level of its own follows its nearest dotted ancestor (my_node.planner follows my_node), then the process default, Info. In C the same verbs are rclc_logger_set_level, rclc_log_set_default_level and rclc_logger_set_level(logger, RCLC_LOG_SEVERITY_UNSET).

  3. Make a child logger with upstream’s spelling: node.logger().create_child("planner")? in Rust, node->get_logger().get_child("planner") in C++, and rclc_logger_get_child(node_log, "planner") in C. Names are capped at 48 bytes and runtime loggers come from a bounded arena: when a child cannot be made, Rust returns an error, C returns NULL, and C++ logs through the parent and refuses set_level on the child.

Publish records on /rosout

  1. Declare the capability, [system] features = ["rosout"] in system.toml (or set(NROS_FEATURES "rosout") in a bare CMake project).

  2. Create the publisher and pump the queue from your spin loop:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use nros_rcl_interfaces::msg::Log;

let rosout = executor
    .create_node("my_node")?
    .create_publisher_with_qos::<Log>(nros::rosout::TOPIC, nros::rosout::qos_bounded())?;
nros::rosout::enable();
loop {
    executor.spin_once(budget);
    let _ = nros::rosout::pump(&rosout);
}
}
rcl_publisher_t rosout = rcl_get_zero_initialized_publisher();
rclc_rosout_publisher_init(&rosout, &node, NULL);   /* NULL = bounded QoS */
rclc_rosout_enable();
for (;;) {
    rclc_executor_spin_some(&executor, 10000000);
    rclc_rosout_pump(&rosout, NULL);
}

rclcpp::rosout::Publisher rosout;
RCLCPP_TRY(rosout.create(node));
RCLCPP_TRY(rclcpp::rosout::enable());
for (;;) {
    rclcpp::spin_once(10);
    rosout.pump();
}
  1. Read them from ROS 2: ros2 topic echo /rosout, or rqt_console.

Where this differs from ROS 2:

  • It is not automatic. The publisher is an entity, so you create it, and it counts in the image’s pools like any other.
  • The default QoS is bounded. qos_bounded() is volatile at the queue depth. Upstream’s profile (nros::rosout::qos(), keep-last 1000, transient-local) is expensive on a board; with the bounded one a late subscriber misses the boot records.
  • Which loggers publish follows the ROS release. On Humble only a node’s logger reaches /rosout, not a child or a free get_logger("x"); Iron and Jazzy also publish a node’s children.
  • The stamp is the platform’s monotonic clock, so rqt_console shows uptime as a time of day.
  • It costs .bss: 5,760 bytes at the defaults, from 16 queued records. An image without the feature pays nothing.

The sink never publishes from inside a log call: it copies the record into a ring, and pump() publishes on your spin thread. Records lost to a full ring or logged during a publish are counted (nros::rosout::dropped(), suppressed()) and reported on /rosout itself. The buffer sizes are knobs: see Logging.

Observe a board with no console

Some boards have no console you can read, for example one whose only wired UART carries the zenoh serial link, where a log line would corrupt the transport’s framing. Reach for these in order. A debug probe is not a passive instrument there: reading memory halts the core, and a serial zenoh session misses its keepalives and does not come back until the router restarts.

  1. Read the boot record. With CONFIG_NROS_BOOT_REPORT=y, the image keeps one fixed-size record in RAM, the NROS_BOOT_REPORT symbol, as it boots. It survives the failures that stop a log from ever printing. It holds the knobs the image was compiled with, the last boot stage it reached, the allocation that did not fit and which allocator refused it, the heap’s peak and capacity, samples dropped as too large, the domain and the rung that decided it, and a count of ERROR and FATAL records with the first one’s file and line. After the run, halt the core and save it, with the address and size from the image’s own symbol table:

    read ADDR LEN <<< "$(arm-none-eabi-nm -S build/zephyr/zephyr.elf \
    | awk '$4=="NROS_BOOT_REPORT"{print "0x"$1, "0x"$2}')"
pyocd commander -t <target> -c halt -c "savemem $ADDR $LEN report.bin"

    The nros CLI has no command that decodes the bytes yet. The record is off by default, and an image without it is byte-identical to one built before the feature existed.

  2. Read the fault record. CONFIG_NROS_FAULT_LOG=y replaces Zephyr’s fatal-error handler with one that writes the reason, the faulting PC, LR and PSR, and the thread name into a .noinit record that survives a functional reset. Set CONFIG_THREAD_NAME=y too, or the thread reads ?. CONFIG_NROS_FAULT_LOG_FLASH=y also copies it to the storage partition at the next boot. A power-on or pin reset may zero that RAM.

  3. Read a live log over RTT, last. Move the console to an unwired UART in a devicetree overlay, and read SEGGER RTT over the SWD link:

    script -qec "pyocd rtt -t <target> -a $(arm-none-eabi-nm build/zephyr/zephyr.elf \
    | awk '$3==\"_SEGGER_RTT\"{print \"0x\"$1}')" /dev/null

    It needs the zephyrproject-rtos/segger module in the workspace, passed with -DZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES=<path>; a TTY, which script provides; and the control block’s address, -a. Set CONFIG_SEGGER_RTT_BUFFER_SIZE_UP=16384, or the default 1 KiB buffer wraps before a late reader sees anything. Check anything found this way again with the probe detached, using the two records above.

Example

A Rust node that logs once at start and throttles a warning, in an image whose ceiling is info:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use nros_log::{log_info, log_warn, ToLogParams};

log_info!(node.logger().once(), "link up");
log_warn!(node.logger().throttle(Duration::from_millis(500)), "lag {} ms", lag);
}
[image.linux.knobs.log]
max_level = "info"

The logging demos, one node package per language, are in examples/workspaces/features.

If it doesn’t work

  • A debug! record never appears. The compile-time ceiling is above it, or the logger’s level is. Lower max_level, then the logger’s level.
  • Nothing reaches /rosout. The rosout feature is not declared, the queue is never pumped, or the record came from a child or free logger on Humble.
  • A throttled call does not compile. throttle needs the platform clock; a clockless image refuses it.

See also

  • Environment variables: logging: the ceiling and the buffer knobs.
  • Platform differences: logging: where records go, and the severity numbers.
  • Use a serial link: the two settings a Zephyr board joining over a UART needs.

Design background

  • RFC-0102: logger hierarchy

Use simulated time

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Parameters and launch files

Use simulated time when a node runs against a simulator or a replayed bag, and its timers should follow the simulation’s clock instead of the wall.

nano-ros implements ROS 2’s mechanism: rosgraph_msgs/msg/Clock on /clock, the use_sim_time parameter, and timers that state which clock advances them. As in rclcpp, the method name carries the choice:

You writeIt advances withFollows /clock
create_wall_timer(period, cb)the platform’s monotonic clockno
create_timer(clock, period, cb)the clock you passyes, for a ROS-time clock

Keep a wall timer for a watchdog or a keep-alive, anything whose job is to notice that real time passed; a paused simulator must not pause it. Older nano-ros code used create_timer for the wall timer. It no longer means that, and there is no alias.

Before you start

  • A node package whose timers should follow the simulation.
  • A /clock source: a simulator, or ros2 bag play --clock.

Steps

  1. Enable the feature in a Rust node package. The /clock subscription costs an entity slot and a receive buffer, so it is opt-in:

    nros = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = [
    "alloc", "rmw-cffi", "macros", "sim-time",
] }

  2. Turn it on with the parameter, as in ROS 2: from a launch file, a parameters file, or at run time. The runtime acts on use_sim_time itself; nothing in your code reads it:

    talker:
  ros__parameters:
    use_sim_time: true

    An image built with parameter services declares use_sim_time = false for every node, as rclcpp does, so this works on a node whose author never mentioned simulated time:

    ros2 param set /talker use_sim_time true

    A declaration of your own still wins. To attach the source in code instead, call node.install_ros_time_source()?, or node.install_ros_time_source_on("/sim/clock")? for a remapped clock.

  3. Write the timers that should follow it on the ROS clock:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
executor.register_timer_on_clock(
    TimerDuration::from_millis(100),
    TimerClockSource::Ros,
    || { /* … */ },
)?;
}

TimerClockSource::Steady is the default and costs nothing extra: it uses the spin delta the executor already measured. Ros and System read their clock on every poll, a platform call on a board, which is why they have their own entry point.

rclcpp::Timer t;
RCLCPP_TRY(node.create_timer(t, *node.get_clock(), 100, on_tick));

  1. Read the time. A node’s clock is ROS time, and with no /clock source it reads system time, as rclcpp::Clock does, so the node still runs standalone:

    rclcpp::Time now = node.get_clock()->now();
node.get_clock()->ros_time_is_active();  // is a /clock source driving it?
node.get_clock()->started();             // has a first sample arrived?

  2. Start the source and run the node:

    ros2 bag play my_bag --clock

Example

A talker that publishes every 100 ms of simulated time, switched on from its parameters file:

# config/talker.param.yaml
talker:
  ros__parameters:
    use_sim_time: true

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
executor.register_timer_on_clock(
    TimerDuration::from_millis(100),
    TimerClockSource::Ros,
    || { /* publish */ },
)?;
}
ros2 bag play my_bag --clock

What happens at the edges

  • Paused: the delta is zero, so a ROS-time timer does not fire. Wall timers on the same executor keep their cadence.
  • Replayed at 0.5× or 2×: the timer tracks the rate, because it advances by the clock’s own delta.
  • A jump backwards (a bag looping, a simulator reset) restarts the period.
  • A jump forwards lands as a backlog, and the timer overrun policy decides: Skip (the default) fires once, CatchUp replays every period.
  • Unsubscribing keeps the last simulated time rather than snapping back to the wall. Clear it on purpose with Clock::clear_ros_time_override().

Where nano-ros differs from rclcpp

  • One simulated clock per image. The override is process-wide; two nodes in one image cannot be on different simulated times.
  • No jump callbacks. create_jump_callback and rcl_jump_threshold_t have no counterpart.
  • No wait_until_started or sleep_until. Poll started() from your spin loop.
  • Timers only. Message delivery, QoS deadlines and transport leases stay on the monotonic clock, so a link stays up while the simulation is paused.

If it doesn’t work

  • ROS-time timers never fire. A never-connected /clock looks exactly like a paused one. Five seconds after the source attaches with no sample, the image logs one warning:

    use_sim_time is true but no /clock sample has arrived in 5s: ROS-time timers are
running on SYSTEM time meanwhile. Publish rosgraph_msgs/msg/Clock (ros2 bag play
--clock), or set use_sim_time false.

    Publish /clock, or turn use_sim_time off. The warning comes once; Executor::sim_time_silence_warnings() answers the same question in code.

  • Message ages are enormous. The max-age-runtime rule compares header.stamp with the epoch clock, not ROS time. Stamp from the epoch clock, or leave that rule off for the topic under simulation.

See also

  • Pick a scheduling model: the timer overrun policy.
  • ROS 2 clock and time: the upstream design.

Design background

  • RFC-0021: blocking API rules
  • RFC-0052: system model and RTOS mapper (runtime monitors)

Troubleshoot

How-to · Level 2: Building real applications

Needs first: Run a talker

Use this page when a build or a running image fails in a way the page you were following does not cover. Find the symptom, then apply its fix.

Some topics keep their own failures:

  • First build and first run: the troubleshooting index.
  • ROS 2 sees nothing (domain ID, QoS, client mode, edition): Talk to ROS 2.
  • Serial links: Use a serial link.
  • Several backends in one binary: Bridge between backends.

Before you start

Run the doctor in the workspace. It checks the SDK paths, toolchains and environment, and names what is missing:

nros doctor

Outside a workspace it checks the install instead, and reports store entries you can remove, with the command to remove them.

Steps

  1. Run nros doctor and fix what it names.
  2. Run the failing step again with --dry-run where it has one (nros build, nros run, nros flash), to see the plan and the exact command.
  3. Find the symptom in the sections below.

zenoh-pico multiple client issues

Symptom: the first of several zenoh clients on one router starts, and the next fails to open its session (-102, _Z_ERR_TRANSPORT_OPEN_FAILED) or to declare a publisher or subscriber (-78, _Z_ERR_SYSTEM_OUT_OF_MEMORY, or -128, _Z_ERR_GENERIC).

Fix: -102 means the client could not reach the router: check its locator and that the router listens there. -78 is an allocation that did not fit. Raise the image’s heap, or the zenoh pool that filled, which the image names at start-up; the knobs are in Environment variables.

zenoh-pico version compatibility

Symptom: publishing fails at once with -100 (_Z_ERR_TRANSPORT_TX_FAILED), then -73 (_Z_ERR_SESSION_CLOSED).

Fix: compare the zenoh on both sides. nano-ros does not pin the router, because the router is the one ROS ships:

grep 'define ZENOH_C ' /opt/ros/$ROS_DISTRO/opt/zenoh_cpp_vendor/include/zenoh_configure.h
nros setup --list | grep zenoh-pico

Read the header, not dpkg -l: the package version is a wrapper version. Under zenoh’s 1.x wire guarantee the two need not match, so a mismatch is evidence rather than a diagnosis.

Multiple Zephyr native_sim instances

Ephemeral port conflict

Symptom: two native_sim instances (a talker and a listener) both fail to open their sessions, or one fails with -100.

Cause: native_sim’s test entropy source gives every instance the same random sequence, so both pick the same ephemeral port.

Fix: give each instance its own seed:

./build-listener/zephyr/zephyr.exe --seed=12345
./build-talker/zephyr/zephyr.exe --seed=67890

Cyclone DDS: two native_sim nodes never discover each other

Symptom: with Cyclone DDS, the publisher prints Publishing: 'Hello World: N' and the subscriber never prints I heard:, with no error.

Cause: the same fixed entropy gives both participants the same DDSI GUID prefix, and a node drops discovery from a peer that shares its own GUID.

Fix: distinct seeds, as above. On native_sim, Cyclone discovery is unicast to 127.0.0.1. Real hardware has real entropy and multicast, and needs neither workaround.

Network configuration issues

  • QEMU cannot reach the network. An image on QEMU’s built-in qemu network uses user-mode networking and needs nothing on the host. An image on a network of your own needs [image.<id>.run] nic naming a host bridge or TAP device; see Configure an image.
  • Zephyr native_sim. Sockets are forwarded to host system calls, so there is no bridge to configure. Point each image at a router on host loopback, tcp/127.0.0.1:7447.

Message too large or truncated

Symptom: TransportError::MessageTooLarge, payloads that arrive corrupted, or large messages (images, point clouds) that disappear.

Cause: a message passes several static buffers on its way, and must fit each: zenoh’s defragmentation and batch sizes, XRCE’s transport MTU, and the entity’s own receive buffer.

Fix: raise the transport limit for the image, for example NROS_ZENOH_FRAG_MAX_SIZE or XRCE_TRANSPORT_MTU, from the buffer tuning tables, and size the entity’s buffer in code:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
let sub = node.create_subscription_sized::<MyMsg, 4096>(/* … */)?;
}

Build issues

  • The zenoh-pico source is not found. Let provisioning fetch it: nros setup <board> --rmw zenoh, or nros setup --source zenoh-pico.
  • A changed knob has no effect. An old CMake cache holds the previous value. Remove the image’s directory under build/ and build again.

Rust and C FFI issues

Subscriber callback crashes

Symptom: a callback registered from Rust through C crashes, or reads garbage fields, such as sub->callback=0x60.

Cause: the C side kept a pointer to a struct the Rust code then moved, for example by returning it from a function.

Fix: give the struct a stable address before you hand it to C: a static (with MaybeUninit), a Box, or Pin. Or have the C side keep an index instead of a pointer.

Function pointer ABI mismatch

Symptom: a callback passed between Rust and C receives garbage arguments.

Fix: declare it extern "C" fn, not a plain fn.

Example

The usual first pass on a failing image:

nros doctor
nros build <image> --dry-run
nros run <bringup>:<image> --dry-run --why

If it doesn’t work

  • Look the error up in the troubleshooting index, which also lists the zenoh-pico error codes.
  • File an issue with the doctor’s output and the dry-run plan.

See also

  • Log and observe a board: what to read when a board has no console.
  • Deploy to production: the run plan and the verify step.

Port a C++ node

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Move a ROS 2 project over

Port a C++ node when you have one that builds with colcon build against ROS 2 Humble and you want it on nano-ros, with as few source edits as possible.

nano-ros declares the rclcpp:: names in its own C++ headers, and its SDK root carries the CMake side: the ament_* verbs, Find<pkg>.cmake modules for the most-cited ROS 2 packages, and diagnostic_updater. So a port is mostly build glue. What the source still needs is what the compiler names: nano-ros has no exceptions, and a few handles observe rather than own.

Before you start

  • nano-ros installed, the host provisioned with nros setup linux, and ROS 2 sourced for the first configure.
  • The package’s message dependencies reachable through AMENT_PREFIX_PATH. For a project with its own message packages, source the project’s install too (source <project>/install/setup.bash); nano-ros generates its own bindings from those .msg files.

Steps

  1. Keep the package’s CMakeLists.txt as it is. It needs no nano-ros line:

    cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(my_node LANGUAGES CXX)

find_package(ament_cmake REQUIRED)
find_package(rclcpp REQUIRED)
find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)

add_executable(my_node src/my_node.cpp)
ament_target_dependencies(my_node rclcpp std_msgs)

ament_package()

    find_package(rclcpp) resolves to nano-ros’s find module, which wins over an installed ROS 2 even when ROS 2 is sourced, because CMake tries modules first. Every target an ament verb creates, or that links rclcpp::rclcpp, is built with NROS_CPP_STD, the std::shared_ptr-shaped API ported code expects.

  2. Add one root CMakeLists.txt beside src/. It is the only file that names nano-ros:

    cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.22)
project(my_workspace LANGUAGES CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14)

set(NROS_PLATFORM posix)
set(NROS_RMW zenoh)
add_subdirectory("${NANO_ROS_SDK}" nano_ros)

set(NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/src")
include("${NANO_ROS_SDK}/cmake/NanoRosAmentSurface.cmake")
nros_workspace_interfaces()     # every message package in src/, in order

add_subdirectory(src/my_node)

    Add each package before the packages that find_package it; the configure refuses an out-of-order find by name.

  3. Configure and build:

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
cmake -B build -DNANO_ROS_SDK="$(nros locate nano-ros)"
cmake --build build

  4. Fix what the compiler names. Most stock nodes need no edit. These are the two most common, from the stock ros2/examples ports:

    A global Node::SharedPtr assigned from a temporary does not compile, because nano-ros’s SharedPtr observes the node rather than owning it. Keep the node in a local first:

    // Before
g_node = rclcpp::Node::make_shared("minimal_service");
// After
auto node = rclcpp::Node::make_shared("minimal_service");
g_node = node;

    A try/catch does not compile, because nano-ros is built -fno-exceptions. A failed call reports a result instead:

    // Before
try {
  publisher->publish(message);
  rclcpp::spin_some(node);
} catch (const rclcpp::exceptions::RCLError & e) {
  RCLCPP_ERROR(node->get_logger(), "unexpectedly failed with %s", e.what());
}
// After
publisher->publish(message);
rclcpp::spin_some(node);

    A node you construct by hand, outside a generated entry, cannot throw either: check node.ok() after constructing it. The other spellings and what each maps to are in rclcpp compatibility.

  5. Run it against the router your ROS 2 peers use:

    NROS_LOCATOR=tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 ./build/src/my_node/my_node

  6. Size the pools for a large node. A package built this way declares no entity counts, so each pool starts at its embedded default and start-up stops at the first one that fills, naming its knob. In a nano-ros workspace, let the census count them: state entities = "census" on the component row, and the configure runs the program once on the host and sizes the pools from what it created:

    [[component]]
pkg = "my_pkg"
class = "my_pkg::MyNode"
name = "my_node"
entities = "census"

    Otherwise set the knobs in the configure’s environment. Autoware’s autoware_external_cmd_selector (12 subscriptions, 7 publishers, a service) needed:

    export NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_CBS=40 NROS_ZENOH_MAX_LIVELINESS=128 \
       NROS_ZENOH_MAX_PUBLISHERS=32 NROS_ZENOH_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS=32 \
       NROS_ZENOH_MAX_QUERYABLES=32

  7. To run it on a board, add a per-platform directory beside the source with a system.toml naming the board, and build it with nros build:

    find_package(nano_ros REQUIRED)
nano_ros_add_executable(minimal_publisher ../src/minimal_publisher.cpp ROS2_MAIN)

    No C runtime calls main on a board, so the build renames your main and calls it from the platform’s entry, with argc == 0. ROS2_MAIN gives the package the C++ standard library (on Zephyr, also set CONFIG_REQUIRES_FULL_LIBCPP=y and CONFIG_GLIBCXX_LIBCPP=y in prj.conf) and the NROS_CPP_STD API. A board has no command line, so state the launch file’s parameters on the image:

    [image.<id>]
params_files = ["config/x.param.yaml"]
ros_args = ["--ros-args", "-p", "update_rate:=10.0"]

    Zephyr’s native_sim cannot run a ported node; use a Cortex-M board such as mps2-an385 in QEMU.

Example

examples/templates/cpp-port-minimal-publisher/ vendors the ROS 2 tutorial’s minimal_publisher.cpp unmodified and builds it through the steps above, on Linux and, from its mps2-an385-freertos/ and zephyr/ directories, on two boards. Its package CMakeLists.txt is the stock ament_cmake_auto shape:

find_package(ament_cmake_auto REQUIRED)
find_package(rclcpp REQUIRED)
ament_auto_find_build_dependencies()

ament_auto_add_executable(minimal_publisher src/minimal_publisher.cpp)
ament_target_dependencies(minimal_publisher rclcpp)

ament_auto_package()

What still needs an edit

  • Exceptions. Guard a throw with #if defined(__cpp_exceptions) and abort in the other arm.

  • MultiThreadedExecutor. A compile error naming the alternative: parallelism is a sched task (Pick a scheduling model), not a callback group. Linux scheduling calls such as sched_setscheduler become no-ops on a board, where the sched task’s priority applies.

  • A thread per action goal. Run the goal from the accepted callback; a goal handle used from a thread you start races the executor.

  • Unbounded strings and sequences in a message you subscribe to stop the compile. Bound them in a nros-codegen.toml at the workspace root:

    [fields]
"std_msgs/String.data" = 256

  • Message strings are rclcpp::FixedString<N>, not std::string: assign with message.data = s.c_str().

  • Out of scope: tf2, image_transport, pluginlib, class_loader and dlopen composition, and generic publishers by type name alone (pass the type hash: create_generic_publisher(topic, type, type_hash, qos)). Parameters are not persisted across boots.

If it doesn’t work

  • find_package(<pkg>) is refused, naming an installed file. nano-ros does not ship that upstream library (bondcpp, tf2_ros). Remove the dependency, or port the library into your workspace as a package.
  • A node’s publishers silently do nothing. It failed to construct, and without exceptions nothing said so. Check node.ok() after a hand-written construction.
  • A stored timer or subscription keeps running after you drop it. Its SharedPtr is a handle, not an owner. Call timer_.reset() to release it; timer_->reset() restarts it, as upstream.
  • ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR} points at the wrong directory. Every package configures in one CMake run, so it is the workspace root. Use ${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR}.

See also

  • rclcpp compatibility: every upstream spelling and what it maps to, and the measured ports.
  • How nano-ros differs from ROS 2.
  • Message generation: the CMake spellings for message bindings.

Design background

  • RFC-0089: ROS 2 API adoption, and the compile-or-conform rule
  • RFC-0018: C++ API design
  • RFC-0033: message field capacity

Move a ROS 2 project over

How-to · Level 3: Production and tuning

Needs first: Organize a larger workspace

Use this page to move an existing ROS 2 workspace (a src/ of packages built with colcon, run with ros2 launch) to nano-ros, before you port the nodes one by one.

nano-ros keeps the workspace and package vocabulary: a src/ of packages with package.xml manifests, launch files in the ROS 2 schema, and the ROS-shaped names of nodes, topics, services, actions and QoS. It changes the setup boundary, because it targets embedded builds that have no shared libraries and no runtime plugin loading:

You have (ROS 2)You get (nano-ros)
a distro install, then rosdep installthe nros CLI, then nros setup <board> --rmw <rmw>
colcon buildnros build <image>, which drives cmake, cargo or west
ros2 launch pkg file, ros2 runnros run <bringup>:<image>: the launch topology is compiled in
RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=… at start-up[system] rmw = "…" in the bringup’s system.toml, at build time
package.xmlkept as it is
.launch.xml, .launch.pykept, in the bringup package; resolved at build time
message packages from the ament indexbindings generated under build/ by nros build
find_package(rclcpp), ament_target_dependencieskept: nano-ros’s own find modules and ament verbs

The full account of the differences is in How nano-ros differs from ROS 2.

Before you start

  • A ROS 2 Humble workspace that builds with colcon build.
  • ROS 2 Humble installed. nano-ros generates its message bindings from it, and its zenoh router is ROS 2’s rmw_zenohd.

Steps

  1. Install the CLI and provision the host, in place of the distro install and rosdep:

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.nros/bin:$PATH"
nros setup linux --rmw zenoh

    For a board, name it: nros setup mps2-an385-freertos --rmw zenoh fetches its cross compiler, emulator and SDK sources into ~/.nros/sdk. Nothing is installed system-wide.

  2. Add a bringup package. It replaces the ros2 launch command line: a package.xml, a system.toml, and your launch files under launch/:

    cd src
nros new system my_robot_bringup --components talker_pkg,listener_pkg

    nros new system: scaffolded bringup pkg my_robot_bringup at …/src/my_robot_bringup (2 component(s))

    It writes a [[component]] row per package with class = "<pkg>::TODO"; set each to the node’s class. Move the launch files you run into my_robot_bringup/launch/, replacing the generated system.launch.xml. Stock XML launch files work as they are; .launch.py files are resolved at build time too.

  3. State the backend and the target once, in the bringup’s system.toml. These two lines replace RMW_IMPLEMENTATION and any cross-compile recipe:

    [system]
name = "my_robot"
rmw  = "zenoh"                 # zenoh | cyclonedds | xrce

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

[image.freertos]
board = "mps2-an385-freertos"  # the platform follows from the board

    On Linux, ROS_DOMAIN_ID and NROS_LOCATOR still work at run time. On a board the same values come from the image row, because a board has no environment to read them from.

  4. Port the nodes. A C++ node keeps its source and its CMakeLists.txt; see Port a C++ node. For a Rust or C node, the Tutorial shows the node package shapes.

  5. Build and run one image:

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros build linux
nros run my_robot_bringup:linux

    The first build records the ROS 2 prefix, so later shells need not source ROS 2. A POSIX C++ workspace can still be built with colcon build for its existing consumers.

  6. Check it from stock ROS 2:

    export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

Example

The whole move for a two-node project that ran as ros2 launch my_robot system.launch.xml with Cyclone DDS:

my_robot_ws/
└── src/
    ├── talker_pkg/             # unchanged
    ├── listener_pkg/           # unchanged
    └── my_robot_bringup/
        ├── package.xml
        ├── system.toml
        └── launch/system.launch.xml   # moved here, unchanged

# src/my_robot_bringup/system.toml
[system]
name = "my_robot"
rmw  = "cyclonedds"
default_launch = "system.launch.xml"

[[component]]
pkg = "talker_pkg"
class = "talker_pkg::Talker"
name = "talker"

[[component]]
pkg = "listener_pkg"
class = "listener_pkg::Listener"
name = "listener"

[image.linux]
board = "linux"

nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds
nros build linux
nros run my_robot_bringup:linux

Cyclone DDS needs no router, so this interoperates with rmw_cyclonedds_cpp nodes directly.

If it doesn’t work

  • Changing RMW_IMPLEMENTATION changes nothing. The backend is compiled in. Edit [system] rmw and build again.
  • A stock ROS 2 node does not hear the image. The two use different domain IDs or QoS reliability, the ROS 2 side is on a different RMW, or no zenoh router runs. See Talk to ROS 2.
  • A <depend> stops nros setup. It names something that is neither a workspace package, a message package, a system key nor a package your ROS install provides. Remove it or add the package.
  • The store keeps growing. Provisioning never overwrites. nros toolchain list shows each entry and when it was last read, and nros toolchain gc --older-than 90d proposes what to remove; it removes nothing without --delete, and never an entry a pin names.

See also

  • Port a C++ node.
  • How nano-ros differs from ROS 2 and micro-ROS.
  • Switch the RMW per image and Bridge between backends.
