  • RFC-0075: zenoh router provenance
  • RFC-0098: generated leaf build config

How a build becomes an image

Explanation · Level 3: Production and tuning

Ask nros build what it would do for a host image, and it prints the handoff without running it:

nros build: host_node_bringup:linux -> board linux (platform posix), driver cargo
cargo update --workspace --manifest-path build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/Cargo.toml --config build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/nros-cargo.toml
cargo build --manifest-path build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/Cargo.toml --config build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/nros-cargo.toml

Three things in those lines are the subject of this page. The image is named by its bringup and its id, host_node_bringup:linux, and it resolves to one board. The build is done by an ordinary tool, here cargo, on a project you did not write: linux_entry lives under build/, generated. And every setting the compiler sees comes from a generated file beside it, nros-cargo.toml, never from your shell or a .cargo/config.toml of your own.

The rest of this page explains why a nano-ros image is built this way: what ends up in the binary, what nros build generates, which tool it hands off to, and how nano-ros fits into a project whose build you already own.

The layers in an image

An image is your nodes and the layers under them, linked into one binary:

Application       your Rust, C or C++ node packages
Board package     hardware and network bring-up, the entry point
Core runtime      executor, nodes, publishers, services, actions,
                  parameters, CDR serialization
RMW backend       zenoh, XRCE-DDS, Cyclone DDS, or your own
Platform          clock, memory, threads, sleep, random, sockets

Each layer owns one job. The core runtime is middleware-agnostic: it owns the executor, the entities and serialization. Your message types are generated Rust, C or C++ types with CDR serialization, and the RMW backend receives serialized bytes only. Publishing runs one way through the stack and receiving runs back:

your message -> CDR serializer -> RMW publish (bytes) -> transport
transport -> RMW receive (bytes) -> CDR deserializer -> your callback

That boundary keeps a backend small, and it lets one message type work the same from all three languages.

The platform layer supplies what a desktop ROS 2 gets from its operating system: a monotonic clock, memory, threads, sockets. On bare metal it can also expose a network poll hook, so the runtime advances the network stack while it waits. The board package joins a platform to real hardware: it brings up the clock, the network interface and its drivers, and it provides the entry point that starts the scheduler or the main loop.

Every layer is chosen when you build. The RMW backend is the image’s rmw, the platform follows from its board, and nothing is loaded at run time. A binary may link more than one backend and bridge between them (Bridge between backends).

When nros build drives the build

In a nano-ros workspace you write node packages and a bringup, and no build file for the image. nros build makes one. It is one pipeline for every board:

  1. Discover. It walks the package.xml files of the workspace and puts the packages in dependency order.
  2. Resolve. It picks the image: the one you named, else the bringup’s [system] default_images. With several images and no default it lists them and stops, rather than guess.
  3. Preflight. It checks that the toolchains, SDKs and sources the board needs are present.
  4. Generate. It writes the message bindings, the resolved system, the image’s entry and a root build file under build/.
  5. Hand off. It runs the native tool on what it generated, and passes the tool’s output through untouched.

The tool is chosen by the board, not by the languages in the image:

The imageThe driver
a Zephyr boardwest, on a generated Zephyr application
any C or C++ package, any other boardCMake; Rust packages join through Corrosion
only Rust packages, any other boardcargo, on the generated entry package

CMake wins when the languages mix because Corrosion lets CMake consume a cargo crate, and nothing lets cargo consume a CMake project. A Zephyr image gets no generated root at all: a Zephyr application already is a complete CMake project, and its Kconfig files are yours.

Because the last stage is the native tool, a compiler error is the compiler’s, unchanged. --dry-run prints the exact commands, and running them yourself gives the same artifact. No command line carries a --target: the board’s triple, its link flags and its emulator runner are in the settings generated for the image. What the tool leaves behind, and where, is listed in What nros build produces.

The entry is the system

The generated entry is the main() of the image. It constructs each component the bringup names, applies the launch file’s parameters, and runs them on the executor. Running the entry is launching the system.

So system.toml and the launch file are inputs on your host, and they never reach the device. The build resolves them and bakes the result into code the compiler sees: which nodes exist, their names and remappings, the parameter values, the pool sizes the contract asked for. A launch condition is decided at build time, and changing the system means building and flashing again. A value meant to change at run time is a parameter.

The same rule decides where a configuration fact belongs. A fact true of every copy of a board (its name, platform, target triple, how it boots) is in the board’s package, beside its nros-board.toml. A fact true of your machine or your application (where your SDK lives, which serial port, which config headers) is in the bringup’s system.toml, in the image’s [image.<id>] block or the [board_config.<board>] block beside it. If a fact would survive publishing the board, it is a board fact. If it names a path on your disk, it is yours. The keys are in system.toml keys, and the task is Configure an image.

When your build drives the build

An RTOS project you already have keeps its own build: a vendored Zephyr or NuttX tree, an STM32Cube or MCUXpresso project, a PX4 firmware. Here nano-ros is a library your project imports, and your build tool stays in charge. It never compiles your kernel, never owns your linker script, and never replaces your build system.

What nano-ros adds to such a build is small and fixed: the client runtime as a static library behind a C ABI, the generated code for your messages and your system, and a thin C shim that your build compiles. The shim is source, not a prebuilt, so it compiles against your own FreeRTOSConfig.h, lwipopts.h or sdkconfig. A mismatch between your kernel’s configuration header and a prebuilt binary would be an ABI break nothing reports.

Each host build system gets a small shell that makes nano-ros look native to it:

Your buildHow nano-ros joins itThe shell in the release
Zephyr (west)a west modulezephyr/
NuttX (make and Kconfig)an apps/external/ applicationintegrations/nuttx/
FreeRTOS or ThreadX, CMake projectadd_subdirectory(nano-ros)cmake/platform/
PX4 (make px4_…)a module directory, generated ahead of PX4integrations/px4/
PlatformIOa library with a pre-build codegen scriptlibrary.json, integrations/platformio/

In every row the split is the same: your build owns compiling and linking, and nano-ros owns the shell and the code it generates on your host. PX4 and PlatformIO have no configure hook that could run nano-ros’s generator from inside, so the generator runs before them and leaves a tree they build natively. The steps are in Build inside an existing CMake or vendor tree, Zephyr, NuttX and PX4.

FreeRTOS has one exception. For the QEMU reference board, nano-ros can build the FreeRTOS kernel and lwIP for you from a kernel checkout, so the demo works with no SDK. With a kernel your SDK vendors, do not use that path: your SDK builds the kernel, picks its port and owns FreeRTOSConfig.h, and nano-ros compiles against your include directories like every other row above.

Why it has this shape

Three choices shape almost everything else in the stack.

The RMW layer is nano-ros’s own. ROS 2’s rmw.h assumes a heap, an OS scheduler with preemptive threads, a dynamic loader and middleware that dispatches in its own background threads. None of that holds on a Cortex-M3 with 64 KB of RAM. The nano-ros RMW leaves the I/O buffers to the caller, replaces wait sets with an explicit call that drives I/O, and binds the backend when the image links, through a C ABI table. A backend can be written in C or C++ as well as Rust. RMW API design has the full argument.

One future type, and no hidden spin. rclcpp owns the spin loop, and rclc has no future type at all; neither suits a single-threaded MCU. nano-ros has one Promise<T> that you poll, block on with a timeout, or .await, and the library never runs a spin loop you did not ask for: every blocking helper takes the executor and drives it. The client library explains it.

Platform capabilities are separate. zenoh-pico needs a heap, threads, sockets and a clock. XRCE-DDS needs a clock and four C functions. Bare metal has no scheduler. So each capability is its own trait, which a platform may stub when it lacks it, and each method states whether it blocks, whether it can fail and what an unsupported call does. Platform API design lists them.

Where nano-ros differs from ROS 2

  • nros build takes the place of colcon build. It reads the same package.xml files, but it generates the image’s build itself and has no install space: what the native tool writes in its build tree is the deliverable.
  • The RMW is chosen when you build, not when you run. There is no RMW_IMPLEMENTATION plugin loader, because many targets have no dynamic loader.
  • No ros2 launch on the device. The launch file is read at build time, and the entry is the launched system.
  • The board is part of the build. An image names a board, and the board decides the toolchain, the build tool and how the image runs.

How nano-ros differs from ROS 2 and micro-ROS covers the API side.

Design background

  • RFC-0003: your build owns compiling and linking; nano-ros owns the shell and the host-time code generation; the bringup never reaches the device.
  • RFC-0065: the five stages, and the driver chosen by the board.
  • RFC-0054: C headers as the one source of the ABI.
  • RFC-0121: the workspace layout and the generated entry.
  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups and the copy-out examples.

The execution model

Explanation · Level 3: Production and tuning

The real-time example workspace runs a 10 ms control node and a 100 ms telemetry node in one image, each on a sched task of its own:

[[component]]
pkg = "ctrl_pkg"
class = "ctrl_pkg::Control"
name = "control_node"
group_tasks = { ctrl = "high" }

[[component]]
pkg = "telem_pkg"
class = "telem_pkg::Telem"
name = "telem_node"
group_tasks = { telem = "low" }

When the configure takes the image’s census, each node logs where it landed:

[INFO] Telem::register on a sched task admitting group `telem`

Why two sched tasks, and not one executor that runs both nodes? This page answers that question: how an executor runs callbacks, how the two ways of receiving data differ, where preemption comes from, and how the RTOS underneath schedules the threads nano-ros creates. The task itself is Pick a scheduling model.

A callback runs to completion

An executor runs one callback at a time, to completion. Within one thread nothing interrupts your code mid-callback, so a callback that becomes ready while another runs waits for it to return. Its worst case is its own execution time plus the longest other callback that can be running when it wakes:

response time  >=  own execution time  +  longest other callback on the thread

Put the 1 ms control loop and a 5 ms telemetry callback on one thread, and the loop misses its deadline every time the two meet, whatever priority or class either has. Priorities and classes decide which ready callback runs next. They cannot stop one that is already running. Preemption needs a second thread, which is what a sched task is.

Two ways to receive

Every entity (a subscription, a service, a client, an action server or client, a timer) can be used through one of two layers, with separate verbs, so the choice is visible in the source:

You pollThe executor dispatches
Rust verbsNode::create_polling_subscription, create_polling_service, create_client, create_publisherExecutor::register_subscription, register_service, register_timer, register_action_server; or rclrs’s Node::create_subscription(topic, callback)
You getan owned handle you take() from, or a Promise<T>a callback that runs when data, a request or a timer is ready
Who schedulesyour loop or your RTOS taskspin_once

The polled constructors are named create_polling_* because rclrs’s create_subscription takes a callback, and a polled form under the same name would compile a ported line into a different contract.

Poll when your code already owns its schedule (a bare-metal loop, one FreeRTOS task per entity) or when the flow is request and response: a service client’s call returns a Promise<Reply>, and an action client’s send_goal leads to get_result. Typed service and action clients have only the polling form. Dispatch when the code is callback-shaped, the way rclcpp code is: one closure per entity, all routed by one spin_once. A dispatched callback and its captures are stored in the executor’s arena, whose size the build sets; a polled handle needs no arena entry.

Both layers share one session and mix freely in one node. C and C++ split them by type: rclc_polling_subscription_t and the rclcpp::Poll* templates are the polling forms, beside the dispatched rcl_subscription_t and rclcpp::Subscription. A polled handle can also take a wake callback, so an RTOS task sleeps until data lands instead of polling; a backend that cannot wake falls back to polling. The signatures are in the Rust, C and C++ API references.

What one spin does

spin_once(timeout) waits for I/O, up to the timeout, in the platform’s own wait primitive, so the thread sleeps rather than spins. When I/O is ready it drains all of it, runs the ready callbacks, and then the expired timers and guard conditions. The backend may report its own next internal event (a lease keep-alive, a heartbeat), and the wait is capped at that.

Draining everything is the right default for one task doing all the ROS work: it gives the most throughput. Its cost is that a timer can wait behind every subscription callback that was ready before it. SpinOptions bounds a blocking spin:

OptionEffect
max_callbacks(n)return after n callbacks, so a loop re-checks timers between them
timeout(d)return after d, for a cyclic frame that gives ROS a fixed slot
spin_once()one round of work, then return
poll_interval(d)how long one pass may wait on the transport (default 10 ms)

With max_callbacks(1) a timer waits behind one callback, not all of them. With timeout(d) the work left over resumes next frame; a single callback longer than the slot still overruns it. Neither option bounds a callback itself, so a hard deadline still needs its own thread.

Sched tasks and levels: preemption from the kernel

A sched task is one executor on one RTOS thread, with its own priority and spin period. All of an image’s sched tasks share one middleware session. A more urgent task’s thread has a higher kernel priority, so when it wakes the kernel preempts a less urgent one mid-callback. That is the second thread the bound above asks for.

You don’t have to write sched tasks yourself. The build derives levels from the contract: each node’s rank comes from its trigger rate (rate monotonic: a faster timer is more urgent), and each distinct rank is one level, up to a cap that depends on the platform. When the ranks outnumber the cap, adjacent levels merge, and the build reports each node that lost its own rank. A sched task you declare in [tasks.<name>], bound to a callback group with group_tasks, is a pin: its members share one level at its stated priority, and derivation places only the nodes no task binds.

Three more rules shape what you see:

  • Priorities are allocated. A level takes its priority from the board’s application band, below the threads the transport runs for itself. A priority that would land in that band is refused, unless the task says above = "transport".
  • The boot level is the least urgent. It runs on main() and owns the session; the build spawns the others.
  • On a multi-core host, levels run in parallel. Preemption shows only when they compete for one CPU.

On Linux, the 1 kHz-loop-beside-5 ms-telemetry case is measured: on its own level, the loop misses no deadline in 60 s on a PREEMPT_RT kernel, and on one level it does.

Inside a level: scheduling classes

Within a level, a callback’s scheduling class orders the ready work:

ClassOrders ready work byUse it for
Fifo (default)registration order within a priority bucketmost callbacks
Edfabsolute deadlineperiodic work with stated deadlines on one level
SporadicFifo, plus a budget per replenishment perioda callback whose CPU share must be capped
BestEffortlast, after every other bucketlogging, telemetry

A sched task’s class (real_time, best_effort or time_triggered) is the deployment-side spelling.

Who enforces a budget

A level whose sched task states a budget and a period has exactly one enforcer. The kernel takes it where it can; otherwise the executor enforces the same numbers at callback boundaries. The image prints which:

nros: level budget sched_task=`capped` 2000us/10000us enforced by the KERNEL

On Linux the kernel enforces it with SCHED_DEADLINE, for a spawned real_time level, when the process holds CAP_SYS_NICE. On NuttX it is SCHED_SPORADIC. Zephyr, FreeRTOS and ThreadX have no kernel budget, so the executor enforces it. Without CAP_SYS_NICE, a Linux image keeps running: it prints the refusal once, with the setcap command that fixes it, and every level runs at the default policy. That image has levels but no preemption between them.

The RTOS underneath

Each level is an ordinary RTOS thread, and the RTOS schedules it. All of the supported kernels schedule by fixed-priority preemption: the highest-priority ready thread runs, and a more urgent thread that becomes ready preempts it at once. Rate-monotonic assignment, which the level derivation uses, gives shorter periods higher priority, and it is optimal among fixed-priority assignments for independent periodic tasks. A task’s worst-case response time under it is:

R_i = C_i + Σ_j ⌈R_i / T_j⌉ × C_j      (over every higher-priority task j)

where C is a worst-case execution time and T a period. The task meets its deadline when R_i ≤ D_i.

Earliest deadline first (EDF) runs the task with the nearest deadline. It can schedule any task set up to 100% utilization, where rate-monotonic assignment is guaranteed only to about 69% in general, but it is harder to analyze and less predictable in overload. nano-ros has EDF as the executor’s Edf class on every platform, and Zephyr also has it in the kernel.

Round-robin shares the CPU in time slices among threads of the same priority. It prevents starvation, at the price of jitter. FreeRTOS slices equal priorities by default, so two levels at one priority there would buy no preemption, only memory, and the build merges them.

Each kernel has its own mechanism beyond this, which you reach through a per-RTOS table of a sched task:

  • ThreadX preemption threshold: a thread may be preempted only by threads above its threshold, which makes a non-preemptible region without masking interrupts.
  • NuttX SCHED_SPORADIC: a sporadic server that caps an aperiodic task’s CPU share by a budget per period.
  • Zephyr: cooperative threads (preempted only by interrupts), preemptive threads, and kernel EDF among threads of one priority.

Priority numbers run in opposite directions: on FreeRTOS, NuttX and Linux a bigger number is more urgent, and on ThreadX and Zephyr a smaller one is. What each platform delivers is generated in the Scheduling wiring matrix.

Priority inversion

A high-priority task that waits on a lock held by a low-priority one can be held up indefinitely by a medium-priority task that preempts the holder. The usual cures are priority inheritance (the holder runs at the waiter’s priority), which every supported kernel offers on its mutexes, and priority ceilings (the holder runs at the lock’s fixed ceiling), which NuttX offers. The cheaper cure is to share nothing between levels: give each level its own data, and pass values between them as messages.

Deferred dispatch

By default a callback runs inline: from the executor’s spin, on the thread that drives the transport. A node declares otherwise through Node::DISPATCH, a DispatchStrategy:

  • Inline (the default) is served on every platform.
  • Deferred queues the callback for a dispatch task, which decouples its latency from network polling. The entries generated for the supported boards have no dispatch task, since each sched task’s loop is already the only task that runs its callbacks, so a Deferred node runs inline there. It still builds unchanged for an entry that does drain the queue.
  • FromIsr is reserved and refused by nros check: no generated entry dispatches from an interrupt handler.

The strategy is per node, not per callback, so a node is wholly one or the other. A deferred callback runs on a different task from the one that registered it, so its state cannot live in a closure’s captures without a heap. A Deferred node therefore registers with the _static forms (create_subscription_static) and gets a tag, a &'static str identifier. Its state lives in the node’s State, and its on_callback matches the tag against the event. An inline closure’s captures live on the spin task’s stack frame, no heap, no boxing, so closures stay on the inline path; the macro refuses a closure on a Deferred node.

The queue under Deferred is the executor’s own, and you can use it without the macros: set_deferred marks a callback, set_defer_notifier says which one is queued, and run_deferred or run_deferred_handle runs it from a task whose priority nano-ros owns. The queue is one bit per callback slot, so it allocates nothing, and a timer cannot be deferred.

What nano-ros does not run on

Every shape on this page keeps one promise: nano-ros decides which callback runs and at what priority. A loop owned by a foreign async runtime or event loop (tokio, Embassy, Qt, GLib) would decide that instead, so no real-time bound could be stated, and nano-ros does not support one. The same holds for a hand-written drain loop on a thread nano-ros did not create.

Timing evidence

nano-ros states no measured worst-case execution times. The analysis it supports is static: you check the callbacks a sched task runs for unbounded loops, recursion and missing timeouts with Clippy and a call-stack tool (Analyze timing), and the level derivation uses execution times where a callback record carries one. Certification evidence (ISO 26262, DO-178C) needs a static WCET tool on the final binary: aiT from AbsInt is the commercial standard, and Platin is an open-source option that works on LLVM output.

Where nano-ros differs from ROS 2

  • No MultiThreadedExecutor, and callback groups do not make threads. An executor dispatches on one thread. Parallelism is a sched task, and a callback group only names which sched task its callbacks run on.
  • Threads and priorities are generated. The build creates the RTOS threads, allocates their priorities from the board’s band and spawns them from the generated entry. You state rates and tasks, not thread code.
  • The spin is a poll loop. There is no wait set: spin_once drives I/O, and its wait is bounded by poll_interval.
  • Polled entities are first-class. ROS 2 receives through callbacks; nano-ros also has create_polling_*, under a different name.

The ROS 2 executor documentation describes the model nano-ros departs from.

  • RFC-0108: preemption levels, how they are derived and the budget enforcer.
  • RFC-0079: priority is allocated, not authored.
  • RFC-0113: every supported way to run nano-ros keeps the real-time promise; the dispatch strategies.
  • RFC-0053: ThreadX multi-tier execution.

Static memory and pools

Explanation · Level 3: Production and tuning

The memory report of a hosted zenoh image lists its largest RAM symbols first:

## top 5 RAM symbols

       131,072   25.3%  nros_rmw_zenoh::shim::subscriber::LARGE_PAYLOADS
        88,560   17.1%  linux_entry::__nros_entry_run::__NROS_SCHED_TASK_EXECUTOR_BACKING
        88,552   17.1%  nros_node::executor::backing::EXECUTOR_BACKING
        87,072   16.8%  g_sessions
        33,536    6.5%  nros_rmw_zenoh::shim::service::USER_SERVICE_INBOX

None of these is a heap. Each is a static array, sized when the image was built: a ring of large-message slots, the executor’s storage, the transport’s session table, a ring of service requests. Together they are most of the image’s RAM, and they are the same size whether the node creates one publisher or twenty. This page explains why nano-ros keeps its memory this way, where each size comes from, and what still allocates. The task of reading your own image is Measure static memory.

Why static

A microcontroller with 64 KB of RAM has no room for a heap that fragments, and a malloc that can fail at run time is a failure a review has to account for. So the nano-ros core is #![no_std]: the executor, nodes, publishers, subscriptions, services, actions, timers, parameters and CDR serialization all work with no allocator. Their storage is fixed-size pools, carved at build time.

A pool is an array of slots. Every slot costs its bytes whether an entity uses it or not. So an over-provisioned pool is wasted RAM, and an under-provisioned one is a create call that fails at run time, when the pool is full. Neither failure shows up at the compiler. The design answer is to size each pool from what the image declares, rather than from a guess.

Where a pool’s size comes from

The pools that dominate static RAM are derived per image from what the image’s components declare: the entity inventory of the contract (how many publishers, subscribers, services, clients and nodes), the message types they use and the parameters they declare. The build writes the answers into the image’s generated settings, so you state nothing for them:

  • The entity counts size the transport’s publisher, subscriber and queryable tables, the liveliness tokens and the executor’s callback slots.
  • The message types size the receive buffers: the largest small-class type the image subscribes to sets the small slot, and the large class gets its own pool, which is zero bytes when no subscribed type is large.
  • The executor’s arena, which holds the dispatched callbacks and their captures, is sized from the same inventory.

The transport’s wire buffers, the network stack’s socket pools and the parameter store limits are not derived: they depend on your traffic, not on your entities, so they are yours to set (Tune throughput and latency).

A value you state always wins over a derived one. The order is: an exported environment variable, then the image’s [image.<id>.knobs], then the board descriptor’s [knobs], then the derived value, and the crate’s default only when nothing is stated and nothing can be derived. nros config explain shows which of these answered for each knob.

Two properties of the message-derived sizes follow from how they are found:

  • They are upper bounds. The bounds come from every type in the interface closure the image links, not only the types it subscribes to, so a size is never too small but can be larger than you need. The build names the type that set it.
  • One unbounded type stops the derivation. A string or a sequence with no bound has no largest size. The build then derives nothing, keeps the stated or default values, and names every unbounded type and the member that makes it so. Bounding the field in the .msg (string<=64), or capping it in nros-codegen.toml, restores it.

Today some pools are sized by the backend you link rather than by what your node does: a publisher-only node still reserves the service pools. An image that looks larger than its entities suggest is expected, and turning those knobs down is the remedy. The Static pool inventory lists every knob and what it sizes.

The three service inboxes (zenoh)

The zenoh backend shows how a pool is split so that each part is sized for its own traffic. Every service server is a zenoh queryable, and each queryable owns an inbox ring: requests wait there between the transport’s read task and the executor’s spin. The rings sit in three tables, one per family, so a family is sized for its own requests rather than for the largest request any service could send:

SymbolHoldsOne ring isKnobs
USER_SERVICE_INBOXyour servicesdepth × (slot + 12 B)NROS_SERVICE_INBOX_BYTES, NROS_SERVICE_INBOX_DEPTH
ACTION_INBOXthe four queryables of each action serverdepth × (slot + 12 B)NROS_ACTION_INBOX_BYTES, NROS_ACTION_INBOX_DEPTH
BUILTIN_INBOXthe runtime’s own parameter and lifecycle servicesdepth × (slot + 12 B)NROS_PARAM_SERVICE_INBOX_BYTES, NROS_PARAM_SERVICE_INBOX_DEPTH

The 12 B is a ring entry’s length, sequence and overflow flag. Each table holds one ring per queryable of its family, for every session, and the image’s queryable pool is partitioned among the three.

A slot’s size comes from, in order: a value you state; otherwise the largest request type the image declares a server for (for user and action services), or the largest set_parameters request the declared parameters can produce (for the builtin family). With nothing declared, the user and action slots keep 1,024 B and the builtin table is empty. A bringup that declares params instead of param_services builds the parameter store but registers no service, so the builtin family claims no queryable at all.

On one safety-island image on an S32K344, BUILTIN_INBOX measured 24 parameter queryables × 1 × (1,016 + 12) = 24,672 B, and USER_SERVICE_INBOX fell from 3,744 B to 288 B when those 24 queryables left it. Read your own figures off the memory report, not off the formula: the compiler sizes the table, so the report is exact.

The executor’s storage

The executor’s own backing is usually the largest single owner in an image with several sched tasks: each sched task has an executor, and each executor has its storage. The C and C++ entries reserve it as one static sized by a generated header (NROS_CPP_EXECUTOR_STORAGE_SIZE for C++), the Rust entry as EXECUTOR_BACKING, and each component’s state has a generated slot of its own. The executor carves more than callbacks from its backing: when the image builds a parameter store, the store, the parameter services’ state, their request and reply buffers and the slot a remote set decodes into are carved there too. A Promise is allocation-free: it borrows its client’s reply slot rather than owning a buffer, so a pending service call costs no extra storage.

What alloc adds

alloc is an opt-in feature. It adds what needs a heap:

With allocWhy
Serialize and Deserialize for String and Vec<T>heap containers
boxed timer callbacks (Box<dyn FnMut()>)a closure stored by the timer
handle_request_boxed, a service reply in a Boxa reply too large for the stack
the blocking Executor::spin, spin_period and halt_flaga shared halt flag (Arc<AtomicBool>)
the heap fallback for parameter services, and -p / --params-file overridesstorage the backing did not carve, and owned override strings

The core ParameterServer API works without alloc, and so do parameter services whenever the build knows the image builds a store: without alloc, a build that carves no store is refused at compile time, naming NROS_PARAM_STORE. There is no std feature. A hosted program has std itself; the env feature reads the process environment, and log routes nano-ros’s diagnostics to the log logger you install.

The transport still allocates

Turning off alloc removes the Rust side’s heap use (Box, Vec, String). It does not remove allocation in the C libraries the RMW backends link. They keep their own session state, stream buffers and protocol metadata, through the platform’s allocator:

BackendAllocates through
zenohmalloc on POSIX, k_malloc on Zephyr, pvPortMalloc on FreeRTOS, a bump allocator on bare metal
XRCE-DDSmalloc on POSIX and NuttX, k_malloc on Zephyr, pvPortMalloc on FreeRTOS; only when an entity is set up
Cyclone DDSper message

So an image with a transport is not free of allocation, and a feature list is evidence that an image is heap-free and not proof of it: a vendored C dependency or a weak-symbol fallback can link an allocator without any Cargo feature changing. The proof is the linked image’s symbol table. nano-ros’s own executor path is heap-free in that checked sense: its CI links an image of the executor, component install and spin, with no transport, and fails on any allocation symbol in it. The shipped examples all enable alloc.

Where nano-ros differs from ROS 2

  • The core needs no allocator, and entities fit the pools. ROS 2 creates entities on the heap whenever you ask. A nano-ros image creates them in slots sized at build time, and a create past the pool’s size fails.
  • Message fields have a fixed capacity. A ROS 2 string or sequence grows on the heap. A nano-ros field is a fixed-capacity type: its bound, or a default capacity when the .msg states none. A field with no bound also stops the size derivation, so a bounded field is the norm.
  • Memory is a build output. The sizes come from the contract, and the memory report reads them off the linked image.

Design background

  • RFC-0100: the sizing model: pool sizes derived from what an image declares.
  • RFC-0034: the platform layer split, and the platform’s allocator.
  • RFC-0113: why no async runtime drives the executor.

The client library

Explanation · Level 3: Production and tuning

A nano-ros service client, from the Linux examples, sends one request and then keeps the loop in its own hands:

let mut executor = Executor::open(&config)?;
let mut node = executor.create_node("add_two_ints_client")?;
let mut client = node.create_client::<AddTwoInts>("/add_two_ints")?;

let mut promise = client.call(&AddTwoIntsRequest { a: 2, b: 3 })?;
loop {
    executor.spin_once(core::time::Duration::from_millis(0));
    if let Ok(Some(reply)) = promise.take() {
        log_info!(&LOGGER, "Result of add_two_ints: {}", reply.sum);
        break;
    }
}

Three things here differ from rclcpp. The node comes from the executor, not the other way round. The call returns a Promise, not a std::shared_future. And the loop that drives I/O is the application’s, not the library’s. This page explains why the nano-ros client library, the API above the RMW layer in Rust, C and C++, has this shape. The signatures are in the Rust, C and C++ API references.

Why a fourth client library

ROS 2 ships rclcpp for C++, rclc for C on microcontrollers, and rclrs for Rust. Each assumes something an RTOS target may lack. rclcpp blocks a thread inside rclcpp::spin(node) and waits on std::shared_future, which needs std::thread and a condition variable. rclc runs on a microcontroller, but it has no future type, so a request and its reply become an explicit state machine of callbacks. rclrs targets hosted Rust with std.

nano-ros needs one library that runs on a Cortex-M3 with no threads and on a Linux workstation, from the same node code. Its core is no_std Rust, and the C and C++ APIs are thin layers over it, spelled like rclc and rclcpp so ported code reads familiar.

The executor owns the session

In rclcpp the executor is a separate object you add nodes to (exec.add_node(node)), there are several executor classes, and each node holds its own RMW context. In nano-ros the executor is the session’s owner:

let mut executor = Executor::open(&config)?;           // opens the transport
let mut node = executor.create_node("my_node")?;      // borrows the session
let publisher = node.create_publisher::<Int32>("/topic")?;

There is one executor type, no separate context object, and no add or remove node lifecycle. The handles a node creates are owned, so they outlive the node; the usual pattern scopes the node to the creation calls. The entry that nros build generates goes further: it opens the session once and runs each sched task’s executor over it, and an executor can also hold several sessions at once, for a bridge between backends (Bridge between backends).

No hidden spin

rclcpp::spin(node) blocks the calling thread inside the library and owns the dispatch loop. That cannot work on bare metal: there is no thread to give up, and the application’s loop has to stay in user code, to service interrupts, poll the network stack and manage power.

nano-ros never runs a loop you did not ask for. The building block is spin_once(timeout), one pass of I/O and callbacks, and every other verb is a loop over it that you could write yourself:

VerbShapeNeeds alloc
spin_once(timeout)one passno
spin_some(max)rclcpp’s drain: run what is ready, then returnno
spin_forever(options)never returns; the body of an RTOS taskno
spin(options)rclrs’s name and shape: until cancelled, a timeout, or a callback countyes
spin_period(period)fixed rate, drift-compensatedyes

So the verbs that reach a no_std no-alloc target are spin_once, spin_some and spin_forever. In a generated entry you rarely call any of them: each sched task’s loop is generated, and your code is callbacks and handles.

One promise, two ways to wait

A service call or an action goal returns a Promise<T>. The same value serves two patterns:

  • Poll it. Keep running other work, spin, and call promise.take(), which returns None until the reply has arrived. The example at the top of this page does this.
  • Block on it. promise.wait(&mut executor, timeout) spins the executor in a loop until the reply arrives or the timeout passes.

A Promise borrows its client’s reply slot and a sequence number. It needs no allocation, and it is not a Future: there is deliberately no third pattern of .await on a foreign runtime. A Future completes only while something else spins the executor, and then that runtime’s scheduler, not nano-ros, decides when the reply is handled (see What nano-ros does not run on).

Why every blocking call takes the executor

Promise::wait, a subscription’s wait_next, the C++ Future::wait and C’s rclc_client_call all take the executor, or a handle to it, although the executor created the thing they wait on. There are two reasons.

The first is that no other thread drives I/O. If wait did not have the executor, it could not spin, the network would stand still, and the wait would always time out. Passing the executor makes that dependency explicit at the call site, where it cannot be forgotten.

The second is borrowing. A promise borrows the session through its client, and the executor owns the session, so the promise cannot also hold the executor. Passing &mut executor at the call, while the promise is a separate object, is how a wait gets a mutable executor while a request is in flight.

The same model in C and C++

C++ wraps the promise as rclcpp::Future<T>, and its wait takes the executor’s handle for the same reason the Rust API takes &mut executor:

auto fut = client.send_request(req);
ResponseType resp;
RCLCPP_TRY(fut.wait(executor.handle(), 5000, resp));

The handle comes from executor.handle(), or rclcpp::global_handle() for the free functions. There is no hidden global executor.

C has no generics, so it has no promise type, but the pattern is the same: a blocking call that drives the executor for you, beside an asynchronous send whose result arrives by callback while you keep spinning:

/* Blocking: spins the attached executor until the reply or the timeout. */
size_t reply_len = 0;
rclc_client_call(&client, req_buf, req_len, reply_buf, sizeof(reply_buf), &reply_len);

/* Asynchronous: returns at once; the result comes to a callback. */
rclc_action_send_goal_async(client, &goal, sizeof(goal));
rclc_action_client_set_result_callback(client, on_result);
/* keep calling rclc_executor_spin_some() */

Where nano-ros differs from ROS 2

  • Nodes come from the executor. There is no rclcpp::Node::make_shared with a context of its own, and no add_node.
  • No rclcpp::spin(node) that owns a thread. The loop is yours, or the generated entry’s.
  • A Promise, not a std::shared_future or a Rust Future. You poll it or block on it with the executor.
  • One executor type. No MultiThreadedExecutor or StaticSingleThreadedExecutor; parallelism is a sched task (The execution model).

For the rest of the C++ surface (what rclcpp names exist, and how they behave), see How nano-ros differs from ROS 2 and micro-ROS and the rclcpp documentation.

Design background

  • RFC-0113: one wait serves every platform and RMW; why there is no Future path.

Safety

Explanation · Level 3: Production and tuning

The safety example workspace turns on end-to-end message integrity with one line in its bringup:

# src/demo_bringup/system.toml
[system]
features = ["safety"]

Its talker is a plain talker. Its listener declares a validated subscription and reads a verdict with every message:

if let Some(status) = ctx.integrity() {
    if status.is_valid() {
        // CRC matched, no sequence gap, not a duplicate
    } else {
        state.integrity_faults += 1;
    }
}

Where does that verdict come from, what does it protect against, and what does it not? This page explains the end-to-end (E2E) safety protocol: a CRC-32 and a sequence check on every sample, added by the runtime, with no code in the node that publishes.

The transport is a black channel

A ROS 2 transport is trusted: a message is serialized, sent and deserialized with no check that it arrived intact, in order and once. A safety-related deployment cannot assume that. EN 50159, the railway standard for communication over an untrusted channel, treats the transport as a black channel: whatever is in between may corrupt, repeat, drop, insert, reorder or delay a message, or pretend to be another sender. The defence lives at the two ends, not in the channel.

nano-ros already sends most of what the ends need. Every zenoh sample carries a 33-byte attachment, for interoperability with rmw_zenoh_cpp:

BytesFieldPurpose
0–7sequence number (i64)increases by one per publisher
8–15timestamp (i64, ns)publication time
16length prefix (always 16)
17–32rmw_gidrandom per-publisher identifier

Without the feature, the subscriber parses this into the message info and checks nothing. With it, the publisher adds one field and the subscriber validates.

What the feature adds

features = ["safety"] turns on the safety-e2e feature of the runtime, and NROS_SAFETY_E2E for a C or C++ build. Then:

  • The publisher computes a CRC-32 over the serialized CDR payload and appends it to the attachment, which grows to 37 bytes. The payload format does not change. The CRC travels in the attachment, out of band from the payload it covers, so it is checked over a different data path.
  • The subscriber recomputes the CRC over the payload it received and compares, and tracks the sequence number it expects next. Each message gets an IntegrityStatus:
FieldMeaning
gaphow many messages were lost before this one (0 is normal)
duplicatethe sequence number is below the expected one
crc_validSome(true) matched, Some(false) corrupted, None no CRC sent

is_valid() is true when there is no gap, no duplicate, and the CRC is correct or absent. The first message a subscriber sees sets the expected sequence, so joining late is not a gap.

The CRC is CRC-32/ISO-HDLC, the Ethernet polynomial, through a lookup table generated at compile time. Its execution time does not depend on the data, only on its length, which suits timing analysis. The cost is a 1 KB table in read-only memory, four more attachment bytes per subscriber buffer, and a 16-byte validator per subscriber.

The plain take() path is unchanged. Only a subscription declared with safety (create_subscription_for_callback_name_with_safety for a declarative node, take_validated for a polled one, and the matching C and C++ forms) returns a verdict.

What it protects against, and what it does not

Threat (EN 50159)DefenceIn nano-ros
CorruptionCRCyes: crc_valid
Repetitionsequence numberyes: duplicate
Deletionsequence numberyes: gap
Resequencingsequence numberyes: a late message reads as a duplicate
Insertionsequence and sourcepartly: an unexpected sequence number shows as a gap or a duplicate
Delaytimestamp and timeoutno: the timestamp is sent but not checked
Masqueradesource authenticationno: the GID is sent but not checked

Freshness needs a clock both ends agree on, and source authentication needs the subscriber to know which publishers to expect. Neither is built. The protocol also has no state machine across messages: each message is valid or not on its own, and what the application does after a run of faults is the application’s decision. A watchdog that supervises liveness and deadlines is separate from this protocol.

Interoperability

The protocol never breaks a peer that lacks it. rmw_zenoh_cpp and a nano-ros image without the feature read the first 33 bytes of the attachment and ignore the rest.

SenderReceiverCRCSequenceResult
nano-ros with safetynano-ros with safetycheckedtrackedfull protection
nano-ros with safetynano-ros without, or ROS 2ignorednot trackedworks, no protection
nano-ros without, or ROS 2nano-ros with safetyNonetrackedsequence only

So mixing protected and unprotected nodes degrades protection; it never stops traffic. A safety argument has to check that every link it relies on is protected at both ends, because nothing on the wire will refuse an unprotected one.

The CRC path lives in the zenoh backend, which is why the safety workspace also states rmw = "zenoh": the protocol is zenoh-only.

Compared with AUTOSAR E2E

AUTOSAR E2E profiles 1 and 2nano-ros
CRC8-bit32-bit
Counter4-bit64-bit, no rollover in practice
Data ID16-bit128-bit GID, sent but not checked
Timeoutconfigurablenot built
State machineyesno: a verdict per message

The CRC and the counter are wider than those AUTOSAR profiles. The timeout and the state machine are missing.

How it is checked

The CRC and the validator have Verus proofs: the CRC is deterministic and detects a single flipped bit, the expected sequence advances on a normal message, a gap is reported as exactly the number of missing messages, and is_valid holds exactly when there is no gap, no duplicate and no known-bad CRC. The proofs run against a model of the validator’s state, which the production tests tie to the real type.

Where nano-ros differs from ROS 2

ROS 2’s client libraries and rmw_zenoh do not check a message end to end; a ROS 2 subscriber gets the message and its info, and nothing else. nano-ros adds the check below the client API, so it is a system feature you declare in the bringup, not code in a node. A ROS 2 peer still talks to a protected nano-ros node, but its messages carry no CRC, and a protected nano-ros publisher’s CRC is invisible to it.

Design background

  • RFC-0028: the E2E safety protocol, the threat model and the future extensions (freshness, source authentication, watchdog supervision).

How nano-ros differs from ROS 2 and micro-ROS

Explanation · Level 3: Production and tuning

A ported rclcpp node compiles against nano-ros with the same includes and the same names. One line it needs that upstream does not:

rclcpp::Node node("talker");
if (!node.ok()) return 1;        // replaces upstream's try/catch

Upstream’s rclcpp::Node constructor throws when the node cannot be created. nano-ros is built with -fno-exceptions, so the constructor records the failure instead, and the node answers false to ok(). The vocabulary is the same; the reason underneath is not.

That is the pattern of this page. nano-ros keeps ROS 2’s vocabulary and wire format so existing nodes port and talk to ROS 2 peers. Where it differs, the reason is almost always the same: it runs on a microcontroller with little RAM to spare, no dynamic loader and often no threads. This page states each difference plainly, then compares nano-ros with micro-ROS, its closest peer. The tasks are Port a C++ node and Move a ROS 2 project over.

What stays the same

  • The entity model. A node owns publishers, subscriptions, services, clients, action servers, action clients, timers and parameters, with ROS 2’s names (see the ROS 2 concepts).
  • Names and types. Topic, service and action names follow ROS 2’s conventions, message types are rosidl-shaped (std_msgs/msg/Int32), and CDR is the encoding on the wire.
  • Packages. A workspace is a src/ of packages with package.xml manifests.
  • The wire. The zenoh backend is compatible with upstream rmw_zenoh: a nano-ros publisher and an rclcpp subscriber on the same router exchange messages with no bridge (Talk to ROS 2).
  • The C and C++ spellings. The C API uses rclc’s names, argument order and arity; the C++ API uses rclcpp’s.

What changes in the workflow

  • One release, no package registry. The nros CLI is a GitHub release, and the library ships as source inside it, compiled into your build. Nothing comes from crates.io or a ROS 2 apt repository.
  • Per-board provisioning, no rosdep. nros setup <board> fetches the toolchains and SDKs for exactly that board and RMW into the user’s store, with no system-wide install. The zenoh router is not provisioned: it comes from a ROS 2 install.
  • nros build, not colcon build. It reads the same package.xml files and drives cargo, CMake or west, with no install space (How a build becomes an image).
  • Message code lands in your build. There is no installed _msgs library. The message definitions still come from your ROS 2 install, through AMENT_PREFIX_PATH, so the layouts and type hashes match your ROS 2 peers (Message generation).
  • No ros2 launch on the device. The launch file is read at build time, and the generated entry is the launched system.
  • Configuration is build-time on embedded. On a host, ROS_DOMAIN_ID and the other environment variables work. An embedded image bakes the same values from system.toml.

What changes in the API

The executor is the entry point

ROS 2 starts with a global init (rclcpp::init, rclc_support_init), then nodes, then optionally an executor. nano-ros inverts it: an Executor opens the session, and every node, entity and timer is created from it, in storage sized at build time. On a target with tens of kilobytes of RAM, a global allocator behind every create_publisher is a cost the image cannot carry, so the sizing moves to the build. The client library explains the model.

Polling and callbacks are both first-class

rclcpp is callback-only: every subscription has a callback the executor dispatches. nano-ros also has polled entities, under a different name (create_polling_subscription), so you choose per entity. A real-time loop often wants the predictability of an explicit poll; an event-driven service wants a callback (The execution model).

No async runtime and no multi-threaded executor

rclrs has an async spin and rclcpp has a MultiThreadedExecutor. nano-ros has neither, on purpose. A future polled by tokio or Embassy runs when that scheduler decides, so nano-ros could not state when a callback runs or at what priority. Parallelism is a sched task instead: an executor on an RTOS thread at a priority the build derives.

The heap is optional

ROS 2 assumes std and a heap. The nano-ros core is no_std with fixed-size pools, and alloc is opt-in (Static memory and pools). The C transport libraries still allocate through the platform’s allocator.

The backend is chosen when you build

ROS 2 reads RMW_IMPLEMENTATION at process start and loads a shared library. nano-ros links the backend when it builds the image, from the bringup’s rmw. Most embedded targets have no dlopen; linking only the chosen backend keeps its C client out of an image that does not use it; and the build knows what to link. The cost is that changing backends means rebuilding. One binary can still link several backends and bridge between them (Bridge between backends).

No introspection on the device

ros2 topic list, ros2 node info and the rmw_get_* graph queries run on a host. A nano-ros image answers what its backend’s discovery exposes, and you introspect it from a ROS 2 host over the interop path. Every byte of introspection is a byte a microcontroller pays for, when a ROS 2 host is one router hop away.

QoS: the full profile, with support stated per backend

The QoS profile has the full DDS field set, and the standard profiles (_DEFAULT, _SENSOR_DATA, _SERVICES_DEFAULT, _PARAMETERS, _SYSTEM_DEFAULT) match upstream field for field. What differs is enforcement. Each backend advertises which policies it can enforce (Session::supported_qos_policies()), and creating an entity with a policy the backend cannot honour fails at once with IncompatibleQos. A requested policy is never dropped silently. Upstream reports a mismatch later, as a run-time event; most mismatches are configuration errors visible at start-up.

Manual liveliness is the sharpest case. assert_liveliness() exists in every language, but only Cyclone DDS puts it on the wire. zenoh-pico’s liveliness is a session keep-alive with no per-topic lease, so under a manual kind zenoh, XRCE-DDS and uORB answer UNSUPPORTED rather than an Ok that would mean nothing was sent. The run-time side is Use QoS, status events and discovery, and per-backend coverage is the Per-RMW feature matrix.

Parameters: one store, a smaller surface

nano-ros keeps the vocabulary (declare_parameter<T>, get_parameter<T>, set_parameter<T>, has_parameter) and the remote services, so ros2 param list and ros2 param set reach a node with parameter services on. Underneath there is one store, owned by the executor and keyed by node, with a slot count fixed at build time; it is also the store the services read, so what you declare is what ros2 param get returns. A node does not own its parameters, because a store per node is a fixed arena per node on a target that has one.

What is smaller than rclcpp, and why:

rclcppnano-rosWhy
ParameterDescriptor (ranges, read-only, description)not exposedmetadata is a host concern; the type is enforced at declare time
three set callbacks (pre_set, on_set, post_set)one validation callback per C servereach callback is an indirection slot per node; one covers range checks
set_parameter returns SetParametersResult with a reasona return codea reason string needs a heap or a fixed buffer
set_parameters_atomicallynot exposedneeds a transaction log
declare_parameters with a std::mapC++ on a hosted build only, returning Resultthe map needs an allocator
overrides from the command line, launch file or YAMLthe launch file at build time; ~/set_parameters over the wire; -p and --params-file on a hosted buildan embedded image has no command line

An array value is rclcpp::Seq<T, N>, an array parameter, with no heap: the store copies the elements into its own slot. When you need the full upstream surface, run it on a host ROS 2 node and keep the embedded node a leaf. The calls and /parameter_events are in the rclcpp compatibility reference.

Where C++ code behaves differently

Most of the rclcpp surface either works or fails to compile. Three things compile and behave differently, each for a reason:

  • Node::ok(). With no exceptions, a failed constructor cannot throw, so you ask. A generated entry checks it and halts naming the node; a hand-written main must check, or a failed node goes on to create publishers that do nothing.
  • Node::SharedPtr observes; it does not own. It is a copyable handle, not a std::shared_ptr, on every target, embedded included. A node is constructed by the entry and outlives everything it is handed to, so no ownership needs counting. shared_from_this() returns the handle and never throws bad_weak_ptr. nano-ros cannot derive from std::enable_shared_from_this, because its std::weak_ptr member exists only where <memory> does, and two translation units of one image could then disagree about the node’s layout. Assigning a temporary make_shared result to a Node::SharedPtr is a compile error, since the handle would dangle; write auto.
  • rclcpp::TimerBase is a name, not a hierarchy. It is an alias of the one flat rclcpp::Timer, with no vtable: the executor dispatches through a plain function pointer, so a polymorphic base would cost bytes with no caller. The clock is a run-time field and a second verb, rclcpp::create_timer, not a type parameter, so WallTimer and GenericTimer do not exist. A SharedPtr to a timer, subscription, service or client is a small handle too: dropping it leaves the entity running, and reset() on the handle releases it.

Compared with micro-ROS

micro-ROS is the closest peer: a ROS 2 client stack for microcontrollers. The two differ mostly in what they assume about the network and the language.

nano-rosmicro-ROS
Application APIsRust, C (rclc’s names), C++ (rclcpp’s names)C (rclc)
RMWzenoh, XRCE-DDS, Cyclone DDS, chosen per imageXRCE-DDS
Network modelthrough a zenoh router, brokerless with Cyclone DDS, or agent-based with XRCE-DDSagent-based
Process beside the devicea zenoh router, none, or an XRCE-DDS agent, by backendalways the Micro XRCE-DDS Agent
Coreno_std, fixed-size poolsC with a static memory configuration
Schedulingsched tasks and derived levels, EDF and sporadic classes, budgets (The execution model)the rclc executor
Several backends in one binaryyes, with bridgesno
End-to-end integrityCRC and sequence check (Safety)none built in
Formal checksKani harnesses and Verus proofs over serialization, scheduling and protocol logicnone published
Buildnros build driving cargo, CMake or west; or nano-ros inside your CMake, Zephyr or NuttX buildcolcon and per-RTOS firmware scripts
LicenseMIT or Apache-2.0Apache-2.0

The boards nano-ros supports, and at what level, are generated in Supported boards.

Choose nano-ros when you want Rust as a first-class API, a zenoh router or brokerless DDS instead of an agent, several backends in one image, or scheduling beyond priorities. Choose micro-ROS when you already have rclc code and an agent deployment, when your toolchain must stay C-only, or when you need its ecosystem’s commercial support.

Moving from micro-ROS is mostly a rename, and in C often not even that: the C API keeps rclc’s spellings, so rclc_publisher_init_default, rclc_node_init_default (in rclc’s argument order) and rclc_executor_t are nano-ros’s names too. An existing XRCE agent serves nano-ros’s XRCE-DDS backend unchanged. A custom transport is a platform-level transport rather than rmw_uros_set_custom_transport (Add a transport).

Design background

  • RFC-0113: why there is no async executor.
  • RFC-0089: adopting the ROS 2 API, and the compile-or-conform rule: a ported line either behaves as upstream’s or does not compile.

Contract format reference

Reference · Level 3: Production and tuning

Every key a contract file (<stem>.contract.yaml beside a launch file, or system.contract.yaml in a bringup with no launch/) accepts. The contract format is ros-launch-manifest’s, and this page is its format reference at v0.3.12, the release the nros CLI is built against (commit d2e2290a327d). The CLI reads a contract with that release’s parser, so a key this page does not list is a parse error.

To write a contract for your own nodes, see Contracts for a C or C++ workspace.

Every key below is accepted in the context that heads its section, and a key that is not listed is a parse error. Contexts whose keys are chosen by the author — nodes:, topics:, services:, actions:, includes:, paths:, args:, external_topics:, the endpoint maps under pub:/sub:/srv:/cli:, and the parameter names under a node’s params: — have no section here, because no allowlist applies to them.

This is the core grammar. A contract that use:s an extension may also write the keys that extension declares, in hazards.<name> and safe_state.settle: those are listed per extension in extension-reference.md (the bundled vehicle.braking and the reference extensions), and extension-guide.md says how to write one.

The kind column is the rule of contract-primitives.md as data: a fact is what the code does, a requirement is what it must achieve, meta is structure, and a consequence is computable from the facts — a second copy the graph already knows, kept only where the graph has no answer (an external source). scripts/derivation_census.py counts how often each consequence agrees.

manifest

keykindstatusmeaning
versionmetaManifest format version. Absent means 1.
usemetaThe extensions this contract uses, a map of name -> version requirement (use: { vehicle.braking: "^1" }; ^, ~, = or >=). With it, hazards.<name> and safe_state.settle may carry the keys those extensions declare; without it an unknown key is an error.
rlmmetasince v0.1.49The grammar release this file needs, v<major>.<minor>.<patch> (or >= that). Checked before any other key: a checker whose grammar is older refuses the file naming both releases, instead of refusing the first key it does not know as if it were a typo. A checker before v0.1.49 refuses the key itself as unknown. Optional; beside version, which is the file format and stays 1.
argsmetaArguments this manifest requires, supplied by the launch scope.
exclude_patternsremovedRemoved — it was parsed and read by nothing, so it excluded nothing. Mark an expected-absent side with external:.
nodesmetaNode declarations, keyed by bare node name.
topicsmetaTopic declarations, keyed by topic name.
servicesmetaService declarations, keyed by service name.
actionsmetaAction declarations, keyed by action name.
includesmetaChild scopes, each an inline manifest (the file-reference form was removed in v0.1.59).
pathsmetaEvent chains: end-to-end requirements naming two topics and a budget.
hazardsmetaHazards: what is watched, how long the system has, and which path reaches the safe state.
functionsmetaNamed guard groups: what a set of topics together provides. A mode requires functions; a hazard may guard one by name.
modesmetaOperational modes: what each requires, and the fallback sequence (the ordered degradation levels) to fall to when it is lost.
severity_levelsremovedRenamed integrity_levels: in v0.3.3: an ASIL, SIL or DAL is an integrity level, and ISO 26262’s severity is the S0-S3 class it is derived from. play_launch migrate <contract> --write rewrites it.
integrity_levelsmetasince v0.3.3The integrity scale hazards draw from, ascending; the first entry derives no criticality. Default: QM, ASIL_A..ASIL_D (ISO 26262), so writing that scale out changes nothing and is only for the reader. A contract that uses a profile takes the profile’s scale and may not also write this.
external_topicsdeprecated — use topics.<name>.externalDeprecated in v0.1.59: the second place for the fact topics.<name>.external states. Move each entry under topics: as <name>: { external: <side>, type, qos }; play_launch migrate does it. Removed in the next grammar release.
chainsremovedRemoved — state the requirement as an event chain and let the route be derived.
ifmetaOnly on an INLINE includes: entry, whose value is a nested manifest: include this child only when the condition holds. Refused at the root of a standalone manifest.
unlessmetaOnly on an INLINE includes: entry: include this child unless the condition holds. Refused at the root of a standalone manifest.
policymetasince v0.1.61Project policy for the consumer’s rules: { unsupervised_measured: warn | error }. Absent: the defaults.
linksfactsince v0.3.4Named links: <name>: { max_transport, clock, monitor }, one transport stated once, with its source. A subscriber names the link its hop crosses (sub.<ep>.link). Visible to this manifest and its inline includes.
supervisionfactsince v0.1.61The platform terms of a supervised budget’s detection delay, stated once: { tick, switch }. Read by the consumer’s overrun case (supervised-fit); required once any budget states supervise:.
acknowledgedmetasince v0.2.3Findings the author has read and keeps: a list of { rule, at, reason }, at the contract’s root only. The consumer reports a warning or info whose rule id and path match an entry as acknowledged, with the reason, and counts it apart from the warnings; an entry matching an error is itself an error (errors cannot be acknowledged), and one matching nothing is a warning, so an acknowledgement cannot outlive its finding.
letmetasince v0.2.4Names for values, stated once and read as $(let <name>): a mapping of name to value, in order, at the contract’s root. An entry may read earlier entries (and $(param), $(var)); a forward reference or a cycle is an error. Separate from launch configurations: $(var) never reads it.

nodes.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
ifmetaInclude this node only when the condition holds.
unlessmetaInclude this node unless the condition holds.
lifecyclefactTrue for a ROS 2 managed node; runtime monitors skip checks until it is Active.
pubmetaPublisher endpoints, keyed by endpoint name. A key is a LOCAL name: the node’s FQN is prefixed to it, so a / in a key is refused; connect the topic with a launch remap or a topics: entry.
submetaSubscriber endpoints, keyed by endpoint name. A key is a LOCAL name: the node’s FQN is prefixed to it, so a / in a key is refused; connect the topic with a launch remap or a topics: entry.
srvmetaService server endpoints, keyed by LOCAL endpoint name. Not neutral when omitted: a consumer sizes the image’s pools from this list (an embedded realizer derives its service counts from it), so a server the code creates and the contract leaves out is found at boot, not here.
climetaService client endpoints, keyed by LOCAL endpoint name. Not neutral when omitted, for the same reason as srv:: pools are sized from the list. A reaction route crosses a client -> server edge as a message (the resolver’s reaction walk); a server with no path its request triggers latches the request for its own timer, and the walk charges that timer’s period as a sampling hop.
pathsmetaThis node’s internal paths, keyed by path name.
criticalityconsequenceScheduling criticality: high
concurrencyfactWhich of this node’s paths may NOT run concurrently. Absent means all of them serialize: every path of the node waits for any other that is running (a single-threaded executor), and the checker charges that wait (path-exclusion). Declare exclusive groups to say which may in fact overlap.
paramsfactParameters this node declares, keyed by name, each { type: <ROS 2 type> }. Names and types only: a string or array capacity is a board fact, not a contract one. params: {} means the node declares no parameters; a missing params: means not stated. The two stay distinct in the model: {} becomes an empty contracts.node_params entry, a missing key none.

pub/sub/cli.<endpoint>

keykindstatusmeaning
min_rate_hzfact (pub) / requirement (sub)Lower bound on this endpoint’s rate. A REQUIREMENT, not a mechanism: nothing fires when a period passes. A fault is detected only by a mechanism that does – a QoS lease_duration or deadline, or a max_age someone evaluates (on_violation.mechanism) – so min_rate_hz never counts as a hazard’s detector. A publisher that promises no rate states aperiodic: true instead of leaving this out.
max_rate_hzfact (pub) / requirement (sub)Upper bound on this endpoint’s rate.
max_agerequirementSubscriber: maximum data age at receive (now - header.stamp).
max_age_msremovedRemoved — write max_age: <n>ms (or ns/us/s). The unit in a NAME is what lets a value be 1000x wrong and still parse.
statefactSubscriber: read-latest rather than causal. The node caches the message and a timer path reads it, so a reaction arriving here waits for that timer: the walk charges one period (the timer’s jitter too, when stated) as a sampling hop, shown as (+Nms sampling) in a route.
requiredfactSubscriber: this endpoint must be connected.
qosfactQoS overrides for this endpoint.
max_transportrequirementClient (since v0.2.5): the request leg’s worst-case transport, overriding the service’s max_transport; charged on a reaction route’s success branch through the call. Subscriber: the worst-case transport into THIS subscriber, overriding the topic’s (one topic does not have one cost: in-process, another process, another machine). Charged in path and chain latencies, and in a hazard’s reaction route on the GUARD EDGE (the hop into the subscriber that detects the fault), but not after a dwell’s deadline, which the dwelling level’s owner reads on its own clock. A declaration on no guard edge changes no hazard’s numbers (declared-not-charged).
linkfactsince v0.3.4Subscriber only: the link this subscriber’s hop crosses, a name under links:. The link’s max_transport is this subscriber’s, charged wherever a written one is; writing both is refused. A written max_transport stays legal and is reported as transport-inline.
max_transport_msremovedRemoved — write max_transport: <n>ms (or ns/us/s). The unit in a NAME is what lets a value be 1000x wrong and still parse.
on_violationrequirementThe reaction this subscriber owes when its assumption is violated.
ingressremovedRenamed arrival_curve: in v0.3.7: a token bucket bounding what arrives is network calculus’s arrival curve. play_launch migrate <contract> --write rewrites it.
arrival_curverequirementsince v0.3.7Subscriber: what this endpoint is made to ABSORB, an arrival curve in token-bucket form (network calculus: rate ρ, burst σ) { rate_hz, burst }. Not a QoS policy, and not the rate it needs (min_rate_hz): a consumer bounds the device’s read path and the router’s pacing by it. Both keys required, so an unstated burst never reads as unbounded. Refused under pub:/cli:.
min_interarrivalrequirementsince v0.1.68Subscriber: the least time between two arrivals. Its callback is then a sporadic task (T_min). An event input with no rate bound, no min_interarrival and no budget is unanalysable: a consumer that supervises a deadline refuses it. Refused under pub:/cli:, and above 1 / min_rate_hz.
budgetrequirementsince v0.1.68Subscriber: the execution time its callback may use per budget_period. Its callback is then served (a server of budget Q per period P, analysed as a periodic task). Requires budget_period, and may not exceed it. Refused under pub:/cli:.
budget_periodrequirementsince v0.1.68Subscriber: the server period P of budget. Only beside budget.
callfactsince v0.1.69Client: how the code waits for the response. blocking: the callback that sends the request waits for it, so under a preemptive executor the server must run at a more urgent level (a less urgent one is a priority inversion, its own level a deadlock). async: the request is sent and a later callback takes the response. Absent means not stated: a consumer checks a stated call and reports an unstated one. Refused under pub:/sub:.
timeoutfactsince v0.2.5Client: how long the code waits for the response before it gives up (a duration, $(param …)-capable): spin_until_future_complete with a timeout, a pending-request prune, a tick-counting poll. A fact about the code, not a requirement. Absent means the client may wait forever (rclcpp’s default), so a reaction route through the call is unbounded unless the degradation level is supervised (call-unbounded). Refused under pub:/sub:.
on_timeoutfactsince v0.2.5Client: what the code does when timeout passes, { reaction: <mode | event chain> } or { retry: { attempts, backoff }, then: { reaction } }. A route through the call is charged the worse of the success branch and timeout x attempts + backoff x (attempts - 1) + this reaction’s route. Refused under pub:/sub:.
on_rejectedfactsince v0.2.5Client: what the code does when the server answers and refuses (success: false), { reaction: <mode | event chain> }. Needed when the route continues at the client after a blocking call (call-rejected-unhandled). Refused under pub:/sub:.
bufferfactBuffering discriminator for a state subscriber: latest
on_demandremovedRenamed aperiodic: in v0.3.7: an activation with no period and no minimum separation is an aperiodic task. play_launch migrate <contract> --write rewrites it.
aperiodicfactsince v0.3.7Publisher: aperiodic – publishes only when asked (a service call, an operator) and promises no rate. Unlike an omitted min_rate_hz, which says nothing, this is acted on: no rate is derived for the topic, no runtime rate monitor is generated for the endpoint, and a subscriber’s min_rate_hz or a topic rate_hz against it is a rate-hierarchy error. Refused beside min_rate_hz, and under sub:/cli:.
jitterremovedRemoved — jitter is a property of a route, not one publisher. Use max_jitter on a path.
jitter_msremovedRemoved — see jitter.

srv.<endpoint>

keykindstatusmeaning
max_responserequirementDeadline for answering a request on this service.
min_interarrivalrequirementsince v0.1.68The least time between two requests. The server’s callback is then a sporadic task (T_min). See min_interarrival on a subscriber.
budgetrequirementsince v0.1.68The execution time the server’s callback may use per budget_period (a served callback). Requires budget_period, and may not exceed it.
budget_periodrequirementsince v0.1.68The server period P of budget. Only beside budget.
idempotentfactsince v0.2.5A repeated request has the effect of one. Licenses a client’s on_timeout.retry (call-retry-not-idempotent): a retry after a lost response runs the operation twice.
stale_afterfactsince v0.2.5The server refuses a request older than this, by the request’s source timestamp. Without it a request the client timed out on may still act after the client’s fallback (call-late-effect).
max_response_msremovedRemoved — write max_response: <n>ms (or ns/us/s). The unit in a NAME is what lets a value be 1000x wrong and still parse.

topics.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
ifmetaDeclare this topic only when the condition holds.
unlessmetaDeclare this topic unless the condition holds.
typefactROS message type. Required.
pubmetaPublishing endpoints, as node/endpoint.
submetaSubscribing endpoints, as node/endpoint.
qosfactTopic-level QoS, overridable per endpoint.
rate_hzconsequencePublication rate. Derivable from the timers that drive it — see derivable-rate.
max_transportdeprecated — use nodes.<n>.sub.<ep>.max_transportDeprecated in v0.1.60: a transport is the hop into ONE subscriber, stated on that subscriber’s endpoint. Still read for one release as the max_transport of every subscriber of this topic that states none of its own (charged as the subscriber’s is: path and chain latencies, and a reaction route’s guard edge). play_launch migrate copies the value onto each such subscriber declared in the same file and deletes this key. Removed in the next grammar release.
max_transport_msremovedRemoved — write max_transport: <n>ms (or ns/us/s). The unit in a NAME is what lets a value be 1000x wrong and still parse.
droprequirementPermitted message loss on this topic.
externalmetaMark one side of this topic as provided by an external system.

external_topics.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
sidemetaWhich side is external: pub
externaldeprecated — use sideDeprecated spelling.
typefactROS message type, when known.
qosfactQoS the external side uses, when known.

services.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
ifmetaDeclare this service only when the condition holds.
unlessmetaDeclare this service unless the condition holds.
typefactROS service type.
servermetaServer endpoints, as node/endpoint.
clientmetaClient endpoints, as node/endpoint.
externalmetaMark one side of this service as provided by an external system: server
max_transportrequirementsince v0.2.5The request leg’s worst-case transport for every client of this service that states none of its own (cli.<e>.max_transport). Charged on a reaction route’s success branch through the call.

actions.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
ifmetaDeclare this action only when the condition holds.
unlessmetaDeclare this action unless the condition holds.
typefactROS action type.
servermetaServer endpoints, as node/endpoint.
clientmetaClient endpoints, as node/endpoint.
externalmetaMark one side of this action as provided by an external system: server
callfactsince v0.1.69How every client in client waits for its result: blocking (the callback that sends the goal waits for the result) or async (a later callback takes it). Absent means not stated. See call on a cli: endpoint.

includes.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
manifestremovedRemoved in v0.1.59 – nothing ever loaded the named file, so the include declared nothing. Write the child contract inline as includes.<name>: { nodes: ..., ... } (its if/unless at that inline manifest’s root), or delete the entry; a launch include’s own contract is found next to its launch file.

args.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
typemetaArgument type: bool, or omitted for a free string.
choicesmetaPermitted values. Consulted only when type is absent.

paths.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
ifmetaDeclare this path only when the condition holds.
unlessmetaDeclare this path unless the condition holds.
inputdeprecated — use trigger: { input: [...] }Deprecated in v0.1.59: the legacy spelling of trigger: { input: [...] }, read as that trigger when no trigger: is written; play_launch migrate rewrites it. An empty or missing input: does NOT make a timer: a timer is trigger: { timer: ... }, and a path with neither is unclassified. Removed in the next grammar release.
outputfactEndpoints (node path) or topics (event chain) this path produces.
max_latencyrequirementLatency budget for this path. On a NODE path: take -> publish of one callback, and the cost a reaction route charges for the hop; an embedded realizer may ALSO turn it into a derived node deadline and a runtime latency monitor in the image, so a cost that must not be a deadline (a queueing wait, a link) belongs in its own key (max_transport, a timer’s jitter), not here. On a EVENT CHAIN: the NOMINAL end-to-end traversal of the subtree, checked by chain-latency; a hazard’s fault route is derived separately by walking the reactions, and does not read it.
max_latency_msremovedRemoved — write max_latency: <n>ms (or ns/us/s). The unit in a NAME is what lets a value be 1000x wrong and still parse.
correlationremovedRemoved — nothing ever read it. State fan-in policy with sync:.
tolerancefactMax header.stamp spread between a fan-in path’s inputs still treated as one set.
tolerance_msremovedRemoved — write tolerance: <n>ms (or ns/us/s). The unit in a NAME is what lets a value be 1000x wrong and still parse.
droprequirementEvent chain only: the end-to-end loss budget, max_count: N / W and max_consecutive: K (or the bare N / W). No topic on the path’s route may permit more loss than the whole (drop-tightness). On a node path it is refused since v0.1.60: nothing read it there; the loss belongs on the topic the path outputs (topics.<t>.drop), where play_launch migrate moves it.
triggerfactWhat causes this path’s output: timer
syncfactFan-in synchronization policy for an input trigger with two or more endpoints.
max_jitterrequirementPermitted variation in this path’s latency.
min_latencyfactBest-case latency. Exists so that max_jitter is falsifiable.
safe_statefactWhat this path produces when it is a reaction: the endpoint it commands, and the plant’s settle time.
missrequirementWhat a missed deadline costs and what to do about it.
segmentsremovedRemoved with chains: — a written route is a second copy of the graph.

trigger

keykindstatusmeaning
timerfactPeriodic self-clocked callback.
inputfactOutput caused by these input endpoints or topics.

trigger.timer

keykindstatusmeaning
