rate_hzfactTimer rate, Hz. Required, and must be greater than zero. A bare number, or the map form { value, source } (since v0.1.61) to say where the rate comes from: source: allocated lets the consumer refuse a period outside the range it derives.
jitterfactsince v0.1.49Release jitter: how late a tick may be released after its nominal instant, measured (a duration, less than one period). A reaction that waits for this timer is charged period + jitter (the reaction walk’s sampling hop and dwell-expiry’s notice) instead of a bare period. Absent: ticks are on time. A budget: the map form { duration, source } applies.
paramfactsince v0.1.58The parameter of this path’s node that holds the timer’s RATE, Hz (update_rate). Its resolved launch value must equal rate_hz (timer-param). At most one of param and period_param.
period_paramfactsince v0.1.58The parameter of this path’s node that holds the timer’s PERIOD, seconds. Its resolved launch value must equal 1 / rate_hz (timer-param).

sync

keykindstatusmeaning
policyfactFan-in policy. Required.
max_intervalfactWidest permitted spread between matched inputs.
max_interval_msremovedRemoved — write max_interval: <n>ms (or ns/us/s). The unit in a NAME is what lets a value be 1000x wrong and still parse.
timeoutfactHow long to wait for the remaining inputs.
timeout_msremovedRemoved — write timeout: <n>ms (or ns/us/s). The unit in a NAME is what lets a value be 1000x wrong and still parse.

drop

keykindstatusmeaning
max_countrequirementPermitted losses over a window, as N / W.
max_consecutiverequirementPermitted consecutive losses.

qos

keykindstatusmeaning
reliabilityfactreliable
durabilityfactvolatile
depthfactHistory depth.
historyfactkeep_last
lifespanfactHow long a message stays valid after publication.
lifespan_msremovedRemoved — write lifespan: <n>ms (or ns/us/s). The unit in a NAME is what lets a value be 1000x wrong and still parse.
livelinessfactautomatic
deadlinefactQoS deadline between consecutive messages.
lease_durationfactLiveliness lease: how often a publisher must assert it is alive. Checked pub against sub by qos-match.

miss

keykindstatusmeaning
toleraterequirementPermitted misses over a window, as N / W.
consecutiverequirementPermitted consecutive misses.
actionrequirementWhat to do on a miss: continue

concurrency

keykindstatusmeaning
exclusivefactGroups of path names that may not run at the same time.

params.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
typefactROS 2 parameter type: bool
defaultfactsince v0.2.4The value a $(param <name>) reads when no launch source sets the parameter (the code’s compiled-in default, stated). Without it, reading an unset parameter is param-unset.

hazards.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
integrityrequirementsince v0.3.3Integrity level from the HARA (ASIL_D, SIL_3, DAL_A, …): the level the analysis assigns, not ISO 26262’s S0-S3 severity class, which is one of its inputs. Consumed, never computed.
severityremovedRenamed integrity: in v0.3.3: an ASIL, SIL or DAL is an integrity level, and ISO 26262’s severity is the S0-S3 class it is derived from. play_launch migrate <contract> --write rewrites it.
descriptionmetaWhat the hazardous event is.
guardsremovedRenamed monitors: in v0.3.7: the topics watched for a fault are its monitored signals (in formal methods a guard is a transition’s condition). play_launch migrate <contract> --write rewrites it.
monitorsmetasince v0.3.7The monitored signals: topics watched for the fault. A bare name is one guard (a topic, or a function by name: a redundant set is functions.<f>: { all_of: [...] }, guarded as f); a list is a group lost when any member is.
onfactFault classes the monitors report, one or a list: omission
fttirequirementFault-tolerant time interval: fault to hazardous event, absent reaction. Checked by fault-reaction-time.
entersmetasince v0.1.59The mode the hazard enters: the first degradation level of the fallback: sequence it walks to a safe state, each level checked in its own right (degradation-level-time) and the minimal risk condition (the last level) against ftti. Exactly one of enters and reaction; a name that is not a mode of this scope is enters-unknown-mode.
reactionmetaThe event chain whose route reaches the safe state: a one-level reaction. Exactly one of enters and reaction. A mode named here is the pre-0.1.59 spelling of enters (deprecated-spelling; play_launch migrate rewrites it).
whenfactThe value that is the fault, { field: <name>, <op>: <constant> }, on a hazard whose guard is a detector’s output. Requires reported among the on: classes (when-requires-reported).
detectionfactFault to detection when that is physics, not a detector’s timeout (an occlusion building pressure), a duration or { duration, source }. Charged before the detection the consumer derives from the detectors, so stating it never buys slack. Usually derived by an extension (source: { derived: ... }).
deadline_byrequirement<extension>/<check>: the check that is this hazard’s requirement when it is not a time (a safety distance). A hazard states ftti, deadline_by, or both.
reaction_totalremovedRead-only: the consumer computes it (detection + route + settle) and hands it to extension checks. A contract never writes it.

modes.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
descriptionmetaWhat this mode is.
requiresfactFunctions (or bare topics) this mode needs; it is available while every one holds.
fallbackrequirementModes to fall to, in order, when this one is lost: the fallback sequence of degradation levels. The last is the minimal risk condition (MRC) and must require nothing losable.
reactionmetaThe event chain that reaches this mode’s safe state.
overridesrequirementRequirement values that apply IN THIS MODE, pinned over the scalar declared elsewhere.
min_dwellrequirementsince v0.3.3A transitional degradation level’s dwell time (window: before v0.3.3): while the level stays available the system stays AT LEAST this long (the time the level promises whoever it waits for, a driver’s takeover time), then takes the next level. The level below starts no sooner than the deadline and within its own reaction route after it, and that route is where the deadline’s notice is charged (dwell-expiry); its first hop crosses no link (the owner reads its own clock), so a guard edge’s max_transport is not charged there. A duration, or { duration, param } binding it to the parameter that enforces it. Never on the minimal risk condition (dwell-at-mrc); unbound is dwell-unbound.
windowremovedRenamed min_dwell: in v0.3.3: a least time in a mode before the next is the switched-systems dwell time. play_launch migrate <contract> --write rewrites it.
exitrequirement{ holds: <function>, to: <mode> }: while this level is active, the function holding ends the fallback sequence in to. Only on a level with a min_dwell; to is outside every fallback: list.

hazards.<name>.monitors[]

keykindstatusmeaning
all_ofremovedRemoved in v0.1.59 – an inline redundant group is the same group functions.<f>: { all_of: [...] } states by name. Declare the function and monitor it by name: monitors: [<f>]; play_launch migrate does it.

on_violation

keykindstatusmeaning
onfactFault classes that trigger the reaction: omission
reactionmetaA path on this node whose trigger includes the subscription.
withinrequirementThis hop’s share of the fault reaction time.
mechanismfactWhere the runtime observer reads the violation: qos (default)

arrival_curve

keykindstatusmeaning
rate_hzrequirementsince v0.1.64Sustained messages per second the subscriber absorbs. Finite and > 0, and not below the endpoint’s own min_rate_hz.
burstrequirementsince v0.1.64Messages that may arrive back to back before pacing applies. An integer >= 1.

safe_state

keykindstatusmeaning
emitsfactThe endpoint this reaction commands the safe state on.
settlefactHow long the plant takes to reach the safe state once commanded. settle: <d> is shorthand for settle: { duration: <d> }; the map is { duration ; response ; source } plus the keys of a used extension that derives settle.duration (v0.2.0: the braking profile decel, jerk with the hazard’s entry_speed is the bundled vehicle.braking’s; settle-derived prints its trace). response is added to either (omitted: 0). Both a duration and a derivation: the derivation is charged and the two compared (settle-conflict).

functions.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
all_ofmetaMembers of a redundant group, lost only when every member is. At least two.
ofmetaThe topics a value function reads. Requires when:; without one, write the bare list.
whenfactThe predicate that LOSES the function by value. A value function is lost by the value or by silence.

when

keykindstatusmeaning
fieldfactOne scalar field of the message, a dotted path from its root. Checked against the .msg when the ament index resolves it (when-field-unknown).
equalsfactThe field equals the constant: a bool, a number, a message constant name (upper snake case) or a string.
not_equalsfactThe field differs from the constant.
ltfactThe field is below the constant, a number.
lefactThe field is at most the constant, a number.
gtfactThe field is above the constant, a number.
gefactThe field is at least the constant, a number.

modes.<name>.exit

keykindstatusmeaning
holdsfactsince v0.1.59The function whose holding ends the fallback sequence. Some node implementing the level must take its topic on a path trigger (mode-exit-unwired).
ondeprecated — use holdsDeprecated spelling.
tometaThe mode the fallback sequence ends in. Not a member of any fallback: list (mode-exit-target).

safe_state.settle

keykindstatusmeaning
durationfactThe written settle (a measured duration): settle: { duration: 2s } is settle: 2s. Beside an extension’s keys, the fallback when a hazard does not write a key the derivation needs (settle-entry-missing), and compared against the derivation (settle-conflict). Required when no extension derives the settle.
responsefactsince v0.1.58The vehicle’s response: from the braking command to the deceleration the plant then holds (a duration). Added to the settle, a written duration or a derived one alike (an extension that reads settle.response, as vehicle.braking does, adds it in its own formula; settle-derived and --explain print both parts). Omitted: 0, so a written duration that already includes the response omits it. The map form { duration, source } applies.
sourcemetasince v0.1.60Where the written duration comes from, as a budget’s source:. Requires duration: a profile’s settle is derived from its parameters.
superviserequirementsince v0.1.61The runtime supervision of the WHOLE settle (since v0.1.62): from the safe state’s command to standstill, the written duration or the derived profile plus the response. { reaction: <path> | enters: <mode>, mechanism: executor | timer, observes: <node>/<subscriber> }: the platform arms due = command + settle + how late it sees standstill (observes: that input’s period + its max_transport), and a vehicle not at standstill by then starts the reaction. The consumer’s overrun case charges the level up to the settle’s end, that observation, the detection and the reaction’s route and settle. v0.1.61 took it on a written duration only.

<budget> (map form)

keykindstatusmeaning
durationrequirementsince v0.1.58The budget itself, with a unit. Required. max_latency: { duration: 149ms, source: ... } states the same budget as max_latency: 149ms, plus where it comes from. Accepted by max_latency, max_jitter, max_transport, max_age, max_response, within, ftti, a timer’s jitter, a settle’s response and a mode’s min_dwell (where it is the least time the level lasts while it stays available: the level below starts no sooner; positive). See Bounds below.
paramfactsince v0.1.58The parameter whose resolved launch value, in seconds, must equal duration. On max_age: a parameter of this subscriber’s node (max-age-param). On a mode’s min_dwell: <node>.<parameter> (dwell-param). No other bound takes one.
sourcemetasince v0.1.58Where the budget comes from: requirement (chosen: a hazard analysis, a decision, a configured value), measured (an observed maximum plus a margin: NOT a bound), derived (computed from other numbers of the contract or the image’s parameters) or analysed (an upper bound from an analysis). { measured: { max, n, margin } } states the observations, and the consumer checks that max x (1 + margin), rounded up to the next ms, reproduces duration (budget-rule). allocated (since v0.1.61): chosen inside a range the consumer derives.
superviserequirementsince v0.1.61The runtime checks the budget while the system runs and a miss starts a fallback: { reaction: <path> | enters: <mode>, mechanism: executor | timer }. The consumer derives the detection delay and checks that the overrun case (the budget + the detection + the fallback’s route and settle) fits the hazard’s FTTI. A budget’s level is derived from this and source: analysed -> bound; supervised; measured alone -> unsupervised. Not on a min_dwell (a least time).

source.measured

keykindstatusmeaning
maxfactsince v0.1.58Single-term form: the largest value observed (a duration). For a timer tick with period, the largest lateness beyond the period.
nfactsince v0.1.58Single-term form: how many samples the maximum is over.
periodfactsince v0.1.58Single-term form: a timer tick’s period, charged without margin: the term is period + max x (1 + margin).
marginrequirementsince v0.1.58The margin over the observed maximum, a fraction (0.2 = 20 %). Required with max or terms.
runmetasince v0.3.4Where the observations were made (since v0.3.4): a run directory, a date, a method, free text. play_launch measure writes the run it read.
termsfactsince v0.1.58Several terms summed, a map of name -> { max, n, period }: each is rounded up to the next ms on its own, then they are added (tick: { period: 100ms, max: 14.84ms }, work: { max: 25.04ms } -> 118 + 31 = 149 ms). Refused beside max.

source.derived

keykindstatusmeaning
byfactThe extension that derived the value, a dotted name (vehicle.braking). Required.
versionfactThe extension’s version, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Required.
sha256factThe sha256 of the extension’s canonical ASCII form, 64 lowercase hex digits.
inputsfactThe inputs the derivation read, a map of name -> value as written (entry_speed: 8.33 m/s).
tracefactThe derivation’s steps, a list of lines, printed by --explain.

source.measured.terms.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
maxfactsince v0.1.58The largest value observed for this term (a duration). Required.
nfactsince v0.1.58How many samples the maximum is over.
periodfactsince v0.1.58A timer tick’s period, charged without margin.

<budget>.supervise

keykindstatusmeaning
reactionfactsince v0.1.61The path a miss starts: a path of the budget’s own node (as on_violation.reaction), else an event chain of the manifest. Exactly one of reaction and enters.
entersfactsince v0.1.61The mode a miss enters; its reaction: event chain is what runs. Exactly one of reaction and enters.
mechanismfactsince v0.1.61What checks the budget. Required. executor: checked in the spin loop, so the detection waits for the longest callback on that executor, and a stuck callback is not caught (slowness, not a hang). timer: an independent timer and thread, which catches both and adds the platform’s switch (supervision.switch).
observesfactsince v0.1.62A settle’s supervision only: the input the platform sees standstill on, <node>/<subscriber> of this manifest. The consumer derives how late standstill is seen: the input’s period (the slowest of the topic’s rate_hz and the subscriber’s min_rate_hz) + the subscriber’s max_transport, and adds it to the supervised deadline. Refused on any other budget.
earlyrequirementsince v0.3.1A settle’s supervision only: the response check, { within, drop }. The platform arms a second, earlier due, command + within + the observation (observes), and judges the speed against the one it saw when it armed: met when the vehicle has shed at least drop or is at standstill; a miss starts the same reaction as the settle’s. The consumer charges its own overrun row (the level up to the command + within + the observation + the detection + the reaction’s route and settle) and checks drop against the speed the nominal profile sheds by within (supervised-early). Refused on any other budget.
resumefactsince v0.3.2The reaction hands its output back and resumes it, { after }: once the reaction has run, the path that normally publishes the reaction’s output takes it over again when it next runs; if that path then stays silent for after, the reaction resumes the output, once and for good. The consumer charges the gap (after + this supervision’s detection delay) once on every overrun row whose fallback is this reaction (supervised-fit). Absent: the reaction keeps its output, and no gap is charged.

links.<name>

keykindstatusmeaning
max_transportrequirementsince v0.3.4The bound on one message’s transport across the link, from the publish to the subscriber’s take. Required. A best-effort link (serial, TCP, DDS between processes or hosts) has no derivable worst case: state it measured, with source: { measured: { max, n, margin, run } } (link-unsourced otherwise). play_launch check --against <run> holds it: a message in a run over the bound is transport-exceeded.
clockfactsince v0.3.4synced or unsynced (the default): whether the two ends’ clocks are comparable. Synced: a message’s stamp age at the receiver is its transport, so it can be measured per message. Unsynced: only arrivals can be timed, so measure cannot propose the bound.
monitorfactsince v0.3.4Reserved, parsed and not read: a runtime link monitor, { reaction: <path> } or { enters: <mode> }. No consumer builds one and no rule reads it (not adopted): a link’s bound is measured and sourced, and check --against holds it against runs. A best-effort link on an unsynchronised wire could only be monitored by the gap between arrivals, which duplicates the receiver’s own silence detector.

links.<name>.monitor

keykindstatusmeaning
reactionfactsince v0.3.4The path a link fault starts: a path of the subscriber’s node, else an event chain of the manifest. Exactly one of reaction and enters. Reserved: monitor is not read.
entersfactsince v0.3.4The mode a link fault enters; its reaction: event chain is what runs. Exactly one of reaction and enters. Reserved: monitor is not read.

<budget>.supervise.resume

keykindstatusmeaning
afterfactsince v0.3.2How long the handed-back output may stay silent before the reaction resumes it: <n> periods of the path that publishes the reaction’s output in the normal case (the consumer reads its timer’s period), or a duration. Positive. Required.

safe_state.settle.supervise.early

keykindstatusmeaning
withinrequirementsince v0.3.1When the check runs, from the safe state’s command (a duration, positive). Past the settle’s response and before the settle’s end; the observation is added, as on the settle’s own due. Required.
droprequirementsince v0.3.1The least speed the vehicle must have shed by within, against the speed the platform saw when it armed (a speed with m/s or km/h, positive). The consumer refuses a drop above what the nominal profile sheds by within (an extension’s derive settle.speed_lost, as vehicle.braking 1.1 states), which would call a nominal stop a fault. Required.

acknowledged[]

keykindstatusmeaning
rulemetasince v0.2.3The rule id of the finding, as the diagnostic prints it (reaction-unguarded). Required, non-empty.
atmetasince v0.2.3The dotted path the diagnostic reports (hazards.<h>.reaction; check --format json prints it as path). Required, non-empty. Two entries naming the same rule and path are refused.
reasonmetasince v0.2.3Why the finding is kept, printed beside it. Required, non-empty.

cli.<endpoint>.on_timeout

keykindstatusmeaning
reactionmetasince v0.2.5The mode the hazard falls to, or the event chain that runs, when the wait passes. Without retry:.
retryfactsince v0.2.5The code asks again: { attempts, backoff }. Sound only when every server declares idempotent: true (call-retry-not-idempotent), and bounded only with attempts and then: (call-retry-unbounded).
thenmetasince v0.2.5What the code does after the last attempt, { reaction }. Only beside retry:.

cli.<endpoint>.on_timeout.retry

keykindstatusmeaning
attemptsfactsince v0.2.5The tries in all, the first included (>= 1). Absent: the code retries without a bound.
backofffactsince v0.2.5The wait between two tries (a duration, $(param …)-capable).

on_rejected / on_timeout.then

keykindstatusmeaning
reactionmetasince v0.2.5The mode the hazard falls to, or the event chain that runs. Required.

policy

keykindstatusmeaning
unsupervised_measuredrequirementsince v0.1.61The severity of a measured budget nothing supervises (measured-unsupervised): warn (the default) or error.

supervision

keykindstatusmeaning
tickfactsince v0.1.61The period the monitor’s clock is read at: the executor’s tick, the supervision timer’s resolution (a duration, positive). Part of every supervised budget’s detection delay.
switchfactsince v0.1.61The interrupt plus the thread switch before a timer mechanism’s reaction runs (a duration). Required by a mechanism: timer supervision.

trigger.timer.rate_hz (map form)

keykindstatusmeaning
valuefactsince v0.1.61The rate, Hz. Required; greater than zero.
sourcemetasince v0.1.61Where the rate comes from, as a budget’s source:. allocated: chosen inside the range the consumer derives, which refuses a period outside it.

Bounds

Every key below is a spelling of one bound: a value with a unit, what it limits (its kind), from which side, where the number comes from (source, in the map form) and, for two of them, the parameter of the image that must carry it (param). The keys keep their names; each parses to the bound its row gives. map form says what the key accepts besides its bare value: { duration, source } (the budget map form above), or that plus param.

keywherekindlimitunitmap form
max_latencypaths.<name>latencyat mostduration{ duration, source }
min_latencypaths.<name>latencyat leastduration
max_jitterpaths.<name>jitterat mostduration{ duration, source }
jittertrigger.timerjitterat mostduration{ duration, source }
min_rate_hzpub/sub/cli.<endpoint>rateat leastHz
max_rate_hzpub/sub/cli.<endpoint>rateat mostHz
max_agepub/sub/cli.<endpoint>ageat mostduration{ duration, source, param }; param: a parameter of the subscriber’s node, seconds (max-age-param)
max_transportpub/sub/cli.<endpoint>transportat mostduration{ duration, source }
max_transporttopics.<name>transportat mostduration{ duration, source } deprecated
max_transportlinks.<name>transportat mostduration{ duration, source }
max_transportservices.<name>transportat mostduration{ duration, source }
max_responsesrv.<endpoint>responseat mostduration{ duration, source }
withinon_violationdeadlineat mostduration{ duration, source }
fttihazards.<name>deadlineat mostduration{ duration, source }
detectionhazards.<name>latencyat mostduration{ duration, source }
min_dwellmodes.<name>least timeat leastduration{ duration, source, param }; param: <node>.<parameter>, seconds (dwell-param)
settlesafe_stateresponseat mostduration{ duration ; response ; source } plus a used extension’s keys (settle: <d> is { duration: <d> })
durationsafe_state.settleresponseat mostduration
responsesafe_state.settleresponseat mostduration{ duration, source }
max_countdropcountat mostcount / window
max_consecutivedropcountat mostcount
toleratemisscountat mostcount / window
consecutivemisscountat mostcount

Values read from the launch tree

A quantity may READ a number instead of restating it: a duration, a rate, a count, the duration: or value: of a braces form, a QoS duration, and an extension key typed param. The value is an expression:

value  := term (('+' | '-') term)*
term   := factor (('*' | '/') factor)*
factor := number unit? | ref unit | '$(let' name ')' | '(' value ')'
ref    := '$(param' [node] name ')' | '$(var' name ['@' node] ')'
referencereads
$(param [<node>] <name>)the node’s effective parameter value; one argument: the node the key sits under; a bare node: a node key of this contract; /<fqn>: any node of the launch tree
$(var <name> [@<node>])a launch configuration, at the end of the contract’s launch file (or where <node> was declared)
$(let <name>)an entry of the root let:

A $(param) or $(var) takes a unit, always ($(param watchdog_ms) ms): a parameter carries none, and reading it in SI would make a 100 ms lease a 100 s one. On a count it takes none. A $(let) carries its entry’s unit. Units are rlx’s (extension-reference.md); a value of the wrong dimension for its key is param-dimension. source: beside a reference is a parse error (source-on-reference): the reference is the value’s source. A value with no reference is the literal it always was.

The consumer that holds the launch tree evaluates every reference per scope instance and hands each rule a plain number; a contract read alone leaves the value unknown (the key absent), never zero.

Integrity level to criticality

A node a hazard reaches (it feeds, detects for, or reacts for the hazard) takes a scheduling criticality from the hazard’s integrity, the MAX over every hazard that reaches it. The first entry of integrity_levels is “no safety requirement” and derives nothing; the other n entries split into three buckets by ceil(3 rank / n) (1 low, 2 medium, 3 high). A written criticality on such a node is an error; on a node no hazard reaches it stands. The default scale (no integrity_levels declared):

integritycriticality
QMnone
ASIL_Alow
ASIL_Bmedium
ASIL_Chigh
ASIL_Dhigh

A contract that uses a profile (use: { iec61508: "^1" }) draws integrity levels from the profile’s integrity_scale and takes each level’s criticality from the profile’s criticality map, stated level by level, instead of the split above; it may not also write integrity_levels:. Reference profiles ship with the checker: iso26262, iec61508, iec61511, do178c, iec62304, iso13849, en50129 (iso26262 is the default scale and map above).

nros CLI reference

Reference · Level 2: Building real applications

The help of every user-tier nros command, exactly as the CLI prints it: nros --help, then each verb in the groups nros --help lists, then each subcommand a verb lists. The page is generated from the CLI’s own help, so it reads the same as nros <command> --help on the release it documents. nros help --all adds the build-system tier, which is not part of this page, and the extension commands your workspace’s packages provide.

Where each verb is explained

CommandPage
nros setupInstall
nros setup, pinInstall options, pinning, working offline
nros newRun a talker on an emulated board
nros build, listOrganize a larger workspace
nros configure, configConfigure an image
nros run, flash, monitor, benchDeploy to production
nros interfaceMessage generation
nros doctorTroubleshoot
nros locateBuild inside an existing CMake or vendor tree
nros toolchainMove a ROS 2 project over

nros

nros — command-line tool for nano-ros (a lightweight ROS 2 client for embedded RTOS).

Quick start:
  nros setup <board>   provision a board's toolchains + sources (board-scoped)
  nros new <name>      scaffold a project
  nros configure       generate msg bindings, models and build settings
  nros plan            resolve a launch topology
  nros check           validate a plan or workspace
  nros doctor          check SDK paths / toolchains / env

Run `nros setup --list` to see available packages, and `nros help --all` for the build-system tier as well.

Usage: nros [OPTIONS] [COMMAND]

Start:
  new          Scaffold a new nano-ros package (`--template`: talker, listener, server, client, action-server, action-client), workspace, image or component
  setup        Resolve + fetch a board's toolchain/SDK packages

Build:
  build        Build a nano-ros workspace
  configure    Configure a project: generate message bindings and the cargo patch config, then resolve and generate every image's build inputs
  clean        Remove the generated bindings and the managed patch block from each Rust package. Leaves user-written sections alone
  materialize  Take ownership of a generated entry package

Run on a target:
  run          Run an image on its target: a host process or an emulator. Builds it if stale, starts the router it needs, streams its console and stops everything on exit. `--expect` grades the console; `--dry-run [--why]` prints the resolved plan instead. A hardware image is `nros flash --monitor`
  flash        Flash an image onto a real board: builds it if stale, runs the board's human steps, flashes, and with `--monitor` watches the console on the same port. `--expect` grades it; `--dry-run [--why]` prints the plan instead
  monitor      Attach to a running board's console: `--expect` grades it, `--send` writes to it. In a workspace the image's board states the port and baud; elsewhere `--port` names the device
  bench        This machine's boards: `scan` records which attached USB device is which board in `$NROS_HOME/bench.toml`, `list` prints it with what is attached now. It supplies ports and probes, never test scope
  debug        Debug an image on its target (reserved: not available yet)

Workspace:
  list         List the workspace's packages: kind, name and directory per row
  graph        Print the workspace's packages in dependency order, each with the workspace packages it depends on

Interfaces:
  interface    Generate message bindings, list the interfaces the workspace can reach, or show one interface's definition

Inspect:
  doctor       Health-check the workspace (SDK paths, toolchains, env)
  board        Inspect supported boards
  config       Inspect or validate the current project's resolved configuration
  plan         Resolve launch files, manifests, and metadata into nros-plan.json
  check        Validate a generated nros-plan.json
  explain      Render a generated nros-plan.json in human-readable form

Toolchain:
  toolchain    List, remove and garbage-collect installed toolchains and SDK packages
  pin          Report this project's `nros-toolchain.toml`, or move it
  update       Move one pin, editing the pin set and leaving one diff
  locate       Print where a resource is, and with `--why`, which rung answered

Other:
  version      Print toolchain + library versions
  completions  Generate shell completions (bash | zsh | fish | powershell)
  help         Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
      --codegen-version
          Print the codegen version this binary emits, and exit.
          
          The compatibility token between this binary's emitted code and the nano-ros runtime that compiles it — deliberately not a release version. A codegen-version refusal asks you to compare this number against the runtime's accepted range.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

Start

nros new

Scaffold a new nano-ros package (`--template`: talker, listener, server, client, action-server, action-client), workspace, image or component

Usage: nros new [OPTIONS] [NAME] [SYSTEM_NAME]

Arguments:
  [NAME]
          Project directory to create, or a mode keyword.
          
          The literal keyword `system` enters bringup-scaffold mode: `nros new system <name>_bringup --components <pkg1,pkg2,...>`.

  [SYSTEM_NAME]
          The bringup package directory, or the package name in a package-scaffold mode.
          
          The bringup directory when the first positional is the literal `system`; the <name> when it is the literal `platform` or `board`.

Options:
      --for-platform <FOR_PLATFORM>
          The platform a `nros new board <name>` targets.
          
          A platform directory name, e.g. `zephyr`, `bare-metal`, or one scaffolded via `nros new platform`.

      --components <COMPONENTS>
          Comma-separated component package names for `nros new system <bringup> --components <list>`

      --component-name <COMPONENT_NAME>
          One component package name; repeatable.
          
          An alternative to `--components <a,b,c>` when commas in the shell are awkward. Merged with `--components`.

      --workspace-root <WORKSPACE_ROOT>
          Workspace root holding the cargo `Cargo.toml` to update.
          
          Defaults to the parent of the bringup dir.

      --into <INTO>
          Parent dir under which the bringup package is created.
          
          Defaults to the current working directory.

      --no-config
          Skip the optional `config/` sub-dir

      --no-readme
          Skip the optional `README.md`

      --platform <PLATFORM>
          Target platform. In project mode give this or `--board`.
          
          `--board` alone reads the platform from the board. `linux` is the host board. `esp32` is not offered: ESP32 support is dormant.
          
          [possible values: linux, freertos, nuttx, threadx, zephyr, baremetal]

      --rmw <RMW>
          RMW backend. Defaults per mode: `zenoh` for project/component scaffolds (matches the tracked examples), `cyclonedds` for `--workspace` (needs no router — the quick-start default)
          
          [possible values: zenoh, xrce, cyclonedds]

      --ros-edition <ROS_EDITION>
          ROS edition (drives the `ros-<edition>` cargo feature). Defaults to the sourced ROS 2 (`$ROS_DISTRO`) when it is one of these, else humble
          
          [possible values: humble, iron, jazzy]

      --lang <LANG>
          Source language. Defaults per mode: `rust` for project/component scaffolds, `cpp` for `--workspace` (the quick-start language)
          
          [possible values: rust, c, cpp]

      --template <TEMPLATE>
          The node the package holds: a talker (std_msgs/String on /chatter), a listener, an AddTwoInts `server` / `client`, or a Fibonacci `action-server` / `action-client` — the roles of the ROS demos, under the demos' own interfaces. Default: `talker`
          
          [possible values: talker, listener, server, client, action-server, action-client]

      --node-name <NODE_NAME>
          The node's ROS name (as `ros2 pkg create --node-name`). Default: the package name (`-` spelled `_`); for `--component`, the role's demo node name (`talker`, `add_two_ints_server`, …)

      --dependencies <DEPENDENCIES>...
          Extra `<depend>` packages for package.xml, after the template's own interface package (as `ros2 pkg create --dependencies`). Space- or comma-separated

      --license <LICENSE>
          package.xml `<license>` (as `ros2 pkg create --license`). Default: `Apache-2.0`

      --description <DESCRIPTION>
          package.xml `<description>` (as `ros2 pkg create --description`)

      --maintainer-name <MAINTAINER_NAME>
          package.xml maintainer name (as `ros2 pkg create --maintainer-name`). Default: `git config user.name`

      --maintainer-email <MAINTAINER_EMAIL>
          package.xml maintainer email (as `ros2 pkg create --maintainer-email`). Default: `git config user.email`

      --destination-directory <DESTINATION_DIRECTORY>
          Directory to create the package in (as `ros2 pkg create --destination-directory`). Default: the current directory

      --component
          Scaffold a planned-mode component instead of a direct-mode binary project.
          
          A component is a reusable library node with an `nros::Component` and a folded `[component]` `nros.toml`. It is platform-agnostic (platform and RMW are chosen at deploy time), so `--platform` is not needed.

      --image <IMAGE>
          Scaffold an `[image.<name>]` — a buildable image — into the bringup package's `system.toml` instead of a project

      --host <HOST>
          Scaffold a `[host.<name>]` — a machine nodes run on — into the bringup package's `system.toml`

      --deploy <DEPLOY>
          Deprecated: use `--image` or `--host`.
          
          `[deploy.*]` split into `[image.*]` (what is built) and `[host.*]` (where it runs). Still accepted, and dispatched by `--kind`: `self` scaffolds a host, anything else an image.

      --workspace
          Scaffold a minimal multi-node workspace instead of a standalone project.
          
          The workspace holds node packages, a bringup and an entry: the canonical copy-out template with the RMW choice baked into every file that spells it. Defaults: `--lang cpp --rmw cyclonedds`.

      --from <PACKAGE>
          With `--workspace`: grow this single package into a workspace.
          
          Takes a package made by `nros new <name> --board <board>`. Its node moves to `<name>/src/<package>/` unchanged, and its `system.toml` moves to the bringup `<name>/src/<package>_bringup/`. `nros new node <name>` inside the workspace then adds a second node.

      --kind <KIND>
          `runner` or `command`: scaffold a runner or command package.
          
          The package holds its `package.xml`, its descriptor and a stub on `nros-extension` (`--lang rust`, the default) or a CMake executable that speaks the protocol JSON itself (`--lang cpp`). Inside a workspace it lands in `src/<name>/`.

      --target <TARGET>
          Deprecated: accepted and ignored.
          
          The rustc triple comes from the board descriptor, so an image carries none.

      --board <BOARD>
          The board a package's one `[image.<id>]` names (`nros new <name> --board <board>`, the single-package front door: the platform is the board's), or the board an `--image` is built for. With `--platform` instead, a project defaults to the platform's own board from the board catalog (`freertos` -> `mps2-an385-freertos`) and refuses, naming the candidates, when the platform has several (`threadx`)

      --bringup <BRINGUP>
          Deploy mode: pick the bringup package whose `system.toml` to edit when the workspace exposes more than one

      --to <BRINGUP>
          Inside a workspace: the bringup that runs the new node package.
          
          `nros new <node> --to <bringup>` adds the package under `src/`, a `[[component]]` row for it in the bringup's `system.toml` and an `<exec_depend>` in its `package.xml`. Without `--to` no bringup is touched.

      --from-launch <FROM_LAUNCH>
          Deploy mode: also set the bringup `[system].default_launch` (bootstrap)

      --from-profile <FROM_PROFILE>
          Fork an existing block of the same table (`[image.<name>]` with `--image`, `[host.<name>]` with `--host`)

      --force
          Overwrite an existing directory / `[image.<name>]` or `[host.<name>]` table

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

nros setup

Resolve + fetch a board's toolchain/SDK packages

Usage: nros setup [OPTIONS] [BOARD]
       nros setup <COMMAND>

Commands:
  board    Provision a downstream Zephyr consumer's tree for a nano-ros board
  presets  Write a project `CMakePresets.json` that includes the per-board presets `nros setup <board>` wrote. Then `cmake --preset <board>` works
  help     Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Arguments:
  [BOARD]
          Board to set up (resolves its toolchain/SDK package set from the index `[board.*]` table)

Options:
      --list
          List every package in the index + its version

      --licenses
          Show the license-gated packages + how to install them

      --offline-dirs
          Print the directories an air-gapped copy of this host's setup needs, one per line: the nros store, then the rustup and cargo homes the builds use (nros leaves Rust in rustup's own homes). Feed it to `tar`

      --tool <NAME>
          Install tools by name (instead of a board's whole set), e.g. `--tool qemu`. Repeatable, like `--source`: `--tool ninja --tool make` is ONE plan — one system-package ask for the union, one lock write. The `just <module> setup` recipes call this

      --source <SOURCES>
          Provision a single `[source.*]` package by name from the index.
          
          E.g. `--source freertos-kernel`. Repeatable. The index is the SSOT — `dest`/`ref`/`submodule` come from data, never a hardcoded path. The `just <module> setup` recipes call this instead of inlining `git submodule update <path>`.

      --build-sources
          Provision the whole build-stage source union the repo's tests need.
          
          That is what `just test` / `build-test-fixtures` need (every RMW's `-sys` source + the platform sources the workspace graph path-deps), independent of the per-board `nros setup <board>` slice. The index's top-level `build_sources` is the SSOT. With `--check`, only VERIFY they are present and name `nros setup --source <name>` per missing — the preflight the two recipes run.

      --prefix <PREFIX>
          Install prefix override (only with `--tool`): place the tool here instead of the shared store, e.g. `--prefix build/qemu` so the test harness finds it where it already looks. Layout is identical (`<prefix>/bin/…`)

      --index <INDEX>
          Path to the SDK index
          
          [default: nros-sdk-index.toml]

      --rmw <RMW>
          RMW backend whose host daemon/tool to also provision.
          
          Orthogonal to the board: `zenoh` | `xrce` | `cyclonedds`. Defaults to `zenoh`. Resolves `board.packages ∪ rmw.packages`.

      --dry-run
          Resolve + print the plan without fetching/building anything

      --full
          Provision full git history instead of the per-source shallow default (`--depth 1`). Use when you want `git log` / `blame` / branching in a provisioned source or submodule. Overrides the index `shallow` for this invocation only — no shared-file edit. (An already-shallow checkout is deepened in place with `git -C <path> fetch --unshallow`.)

      --shallow
          Force shallow (`--depth 1`) even for sources that set `shallow = false` in the index. The inverse of `--full`

      --system
          Print the native install command for the `[system.*]` OS packages.
          
          Resolves the `[system.*]` OS-package closure for the detected package manager and prints the one native install command (never runs it without `--sudo`). With `--check`, run each entry's presence probe instead and exit non-zero if anything is missing (the doctor surface).

      --workspace [<PATH>]
          Provision from what this workspace declares.
          
          Reads every `package.xml` under the path and answers three questions the tree already states: what the code depends on (`<depend>`), which builder must exist (`<build_type>` / `<buildtool_depend>`), and where it deploys (the `[image.<id>] board` of the `system.toml` beside a package.xml).
          
          Prints the plan, then installs it: every image's board and RMW in one store plan, then the OS-package closure — installed with `--sudo`, otherwise printed as the command to run. `--check` stops after the plan. Plain `nros setup` inside a workspace means `--workspace .`.

      --role <ROLE>
          Narrow `--system` to keys of these roles (repeatable).
          
          A scope's setup wants the HOST facts — `package` and `workspace` roles — and not `infra`: reporting every cross toolchain and emulator to someone provisioning `native` is noise, and noise is how a real missing package gets scrolled past.

      --check
          Run presence probes and report present/missing/unknown instead of installing/printing; exits 1 when anything is missing. With `--system`, probes only the `[system.*]` class; alone, walks EVERY declared class — `[system.*]`, `[rust.*]`, `[python.*]` — printing a remedy computed from each entry

      --sudo
          Execute the composed native install command instead of printing it.
          
          With `--system`, runs the native install command (which invokes sudo where the manager needs it). With `--tool`, a tool declaring its own `[tool.<name>] system = [..]` build deps installs them instead of printing a line to copy. With `<board>` and `--workspace`, the board plan's one system ask (its tools' and `[source.*]`s' `system = [..]`) is installed before any download. Any other use is refused.

  -j, --jobs <N>
          How many packages to install at once.
          
          Default: this host's CPU count; `NROS_SETUP_JOBS` overrides the default, and this overrides both.
          
          Expect less than N times faster: the link saturates long before the cores do, and a tool built from source already uses the whole machine, so source builds run one at a time and the overlap that pays is one package's build or unpack beside another's download. Output stays per package and in plan order whatever the value.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

nros setup board

Provision a downstream Zephyr consumer's tree for a nano-ros board.

Fetches the board's RMW source, applies the zephyr-line patch set, adds the rust targets, and checks the `zephyr-lang-rust` pin — driven by the board's provisioning contract (`board.cmake` / `[package.metadata.nros.board]`).

Usage: nros setup board [OPTIONS] --zephyr-workspace <ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE> <NAME>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          Board crate suffix (after `nros-board-`), e.g. `fvp-aemv8r-smp`

Options:
      --zephyr-workspace <ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE>
          The downstream consumer's Zephyr workspace dir (the tree containing `zephyr/` + `modules/lang/rust/`). The patch set is applied here

      --workspace <WORKSPACE>
          nano-ros SDK root (where the board crate, `scripts/zephyr/`, and `nros-sdk-index.toml` live). Default: `$NROS_WORKSPACE_ROOT`, a checkout enclosing cwd, then this `nros` binary's own SDK root

      --index <INDEX>
          Path to the SDK index (relative paths resolve against the nano-ros workspace root). The RMW source's `dest` is index-driven
          
          [default: nros-sdk-index.toml]

      --dry-run
          Resolve + print the provisioning plan without fetching/patching

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

Write a project `CMakePresets.json` that includes the per-board presets `nros setup <board>` wrote. Then `cmake --preset <board>` works

Usage: nros setup presets [DIR]

Arguments:
  [DIR]  Project directory to write `CMakePresets.json` into (default: current dir) [default: .]

Build

nros build

Build a nano-ros workspace.

Discovers packages, resolves the image, runs preflight, generates the root, and hands off to the native tool. The final stage is an `exec`, so compiler diagnostics are byte-identical to running cargo/cmake/west directly.

Usage: nros build [OPTIONS] [IMAGES]... [-- <NATIVE_ARGS>...]

Arguments:
  [IMAGES]...
          Image(s) to build — `linux`, or `<bringup>:linux` when two bringups declare the same id. Empty uses `[system] default_images`

  [NATIVE_ARGS]...
          Arguments after `--` go to the native tool verbatim

Options:
      --workspace <WORKSPACE>
          Workspace root. Defaults to the current directory

      --nano-ros-path <NANO_ROS_PATH>
          nano-ros SDK root holding `packages/boards`. Defaults to a walk-up from the workspace, then this `nros` binary's own SDK root

      --zephyr-workspace <DIR>
          The west workspace holding Zephyr — the directory that contains `zephyr/`. Zephyr images only.
          
          The explicit rung of the resolution ladder, above `$ZEPHYR_BASE` and `$NROS_ZEPHYR_WORKSPACE`. An environment variable is ambient state that a user has to remember to set and cannot see in the command they ran; this makes the same fact reviewable in a script and in shell history.
          
          Pointing it at the `zephyr/` directory itself also works — that is the commonest way to get this wrong, and both spellings name one place.

      --all
          Build every declared image

      --board <BOARD>
          Build the image whose `[image.*] board` is this board.
          
          Matches the authored word (any case), any alias of the same board descriptor, or the `nros setup` index key the board provisions through (`nros build --board mps2-an385-baremetal` finds a `baremetal` image). One match builds exactly that image, as if it were named; several or none is refused, listing them — the image id stays the unit. Not with image arguments or `--all`.

      --dry-run
          Print the stages and the command that would run, then stop.
          
          Safe by construction: a `Handoff` performs no I/O until `exec`. It still GENERATES (stage 4 writes each image's generated files), which regenerates an application without building it.

  -v, --verbose
          Also print the explanation behind each configure note.
          
          That is: why a pass re-runs, why a size was not derived. Sets `NROS_VERBOSE=1` for every native command; a correct build without it prints one line per fact.

      --offline
          Do not fetch anything; fail naming what is missing.
          
          Note this is a SCOPED guarantee: stages 1–4 touch no network, and stage 5 gets the native tool's own offline spelling. It cannot promise an arbitrary user `CMakeLists.txt` refrains from fetching.

      --packages-select <PKG>...
          Only these packages — no dependencies, no dependents.
          
          colcon's flag, with two differences: a name matching no package is an error, not a warning, and a selection that leaves out a package a selected one depends on is refused, since there is no install prefix for it to come from. That holds for every selection flag.

      --packages-up-to <PKG>...
          These packages and everything they depend on, transitively.
          
          The selection flags compose as an INTERSECTION, which is colcon's composition too: each deselects independently, so adding one can only ever narrow the set.

      --packages-above <PKG>...
          These packages and everything that depends on them, transitively.
          
          A package here that depends on a workspace package left out is refused, as for every selection flag; add `--packages-up-to` for its dependencies. A cargo member with no `package.xml` is refused here: its dependents name it only in their `Cargo.toml`, which the selection does not read.

      --packages-skip <PKG>...
          Leave these packages out

      --base-paths <PATH>...
          The workspace's source roots, relative to the workspace (default: `.`, plus `nros.toml` `package_paths`).
          
          They replace the workspace and its `package_paths`, and nothing else: the nano-ros packages and `NROS_PACKAGE_PATH` stay on the search path. As in colcon, the roots are peers searched recursively, their order does not matter, a path repeated or inside another counts once, and a package name found in two of them is an error. A path that does not exist is an error; one that holds no package is a warning.

      --continue-on-error
          Keep building the other packages when one fails.
          
          A package that depends on a failed one is skipped, as with colcon, and the command still exits non-zero, with the first failure's status. In a workspace with images, the unit is the image: each image is one merged build, so a failure inside it fails the whole image, and the next image is still attempted.

      --cmake-args <ARG>...
          Arguments passed to every CMake configure: a cmake image's, a west image's (after west's own `--`), and a cmake package's.
          
          A cargo image runs no CMake configure and ignores them, as colcon ignores them for a package that is not a CMake package. Ends at the next `nros build` flag or at `--`, as colcon's does.

  -j, --jobs <N>
          Run at most N jobs at once, in total. Default: the number of CPUs.
          
          Every tool below `nros build` (cargo, make, ninja, west's cmake) shares one GNU make jobserver of N tokens, so packages compiling side by side still run N jobs in total, not N each. A package starts once every package it depends on has finished; images build one at a time, each drawing on the same N. Under a `make -jN` that already provides a jobserver, `nros build` joins it instead. Ninja older than 1.13 does not read a jobserver and runs at its own width; a warning names it.

      --build-base <DIR>
          Where each package's build directory goes: `<DIR>/<package>/`. Default: `build`, under the workspace.
          
          Only for a workspace with no bringup. An image's generated tree has a fixed place under `build/`, which the cmake module and the image's other readers all expect, so moving it for one build would split them; it is refused there.

      --check[=<TOOL>]
          Type-check the image instead of building it: `cargo check`, or `cargo clippy` with `--check=clippy`.
          
          Everything before the cargo command is the same as a build — the generated message crates, the `<pkg>_nros_selection` crate, the image's settings file and its lock — because none of it is optional for a check either: a leaf whose manifest names the selection crate cannot even be LOADED until sync has written it, so a bare `cargo check` in a fresh checkout fails at manifest parse with an error that never says why. Only the final verb changes, so a check here and a build here see one dependency graph.
          
          Cargo images only; a cmake or west image is refused, since neither tool has a check that is not a build.

          Possible values:
          - check:  `cargo check`
          - clippy: `cargo clippy`. Lint flags go after a second `--`: `nros build --check=clippy -- -- -D warnings`

      --allow-overriding <NAME>...
          Let a package replace another provider of this name, for this build only.
          
          colcon's flag. A replacement of the nano-ros provider nobody declared is refused for a runner or a command, and the same name in two source trees (the workspace and a `package_paths` entry) is refused for every kind; with this flag the later root wins. To make a choice permanent, add `<name> = "<package path>"` under `[workspace.overrides]` in `nros.toml` instead.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

nros configure

Configure a project: generate message bindings and the cargo patch config, then resolve and generate every image's build inputs.

The message bindings and patch config, then the stages `nros build` runs before it builds (discover, preflight, census, resolve, generate), under a per-project lock. Runs no target build tool. Records a stamp per image, so a rerun with nothing changed is a no-op. An image this host cannot build is skipped unless named.

Usage: nros configure [OPTIONS] [WORKSPACE]

Arguments:
  [WORKSPACE]
          Workspace root (the dir containing `src/`). Defaults to cwd

Options:
      --generated-base <DIR>
          Output dir for the generated message crates, relative to the workspace. Models and other sync output stay under `build/`
          
          [default: generated]

      --ros-edition <ROS_EDITION>
          ROS 2 edition (`humble` | `iron` | `jazzy`).
          
          When omitted, inherits `[system].ros_edition` from a `system.toml` at the workspace root, else `humble`.

      --image <ID>
          Single-package leaf only: sync for this `[image.<id>]`.
          
          Covers its selection package, its `build/<id>/nros-cargo.toml`, and message codegen for its ROS edition. A leaf may declare one image per RMW and edition; without this flag the leaf's own rule applies (one image, or `[system] default_images`).

      --dry-run
          Don't write — just print what would happen

      --check
          Exit non-zero if any patch block is missing or stale (CI hook; also used by `nros ws status`)

  -v, --verbose
          Verbose codegen output

      --nano-ros-root <DIR>
          nano-ros source tree to scan as the FIRST provider search root.
          
          The same root every provider lookup reads, so the provider index this writes is the one later commands read.

      --base-paths <PATH>...
          The workspace's source roots, relative to the workspace (default: `.`, plus `nros.toml` `package_paths`).
          
          They replace the workspace and its `package_paths`, and nothing else: the nano-ros packages and `NROS_PACKAGE_PATH` stay on the search path. As in colcon, the roots are peers searched recursively, their order does not matter, a path repeated or inside another counts once, and a package name found in two of them is an error. A path that does not exist is an error; one that holds no package is a warning.

      --no-provider-index
          Skip the provider index entirely (`<ws>/build/nros/providers.json`).
          
          The index is a CACHE for later commands, not an input to this sync, so a caller that will not read it can skip the scan outright. Same shape as `--no-metadata` above: name the expensive optional step and let the caller decline it.

      --model-dir <MODEL_DIR>
          Write resolved SystemModels here instead of into each bringup's `config/`.
          
          This makes them build output rather than committed source. Consumers find them through the same search order (`nros_orchestration_ir::model_location`): export `NROS_MODEL_DIR` to the same path for the build.

      --no-metadata
          Skip the source-metadata refresh.
          
          The refresh compiles a host probe per Node pkg, which is the slow part of a cold sync; skipping it leaves any existing sidecars untouched and makes bakes fall back to the SystemModel's entity lower bound.

      --nano-ros-path <NANO_ROS_PATH>
          The nano-ros SDK root the probes and board lookups read.
          
          Defaults to a walk-up from the workspace, then this `nros` binary's own SDK root. It adds nothing to the patch block: the canonical shape carries nros-* runtime crates as path-deps in the user's own `[dependencies]`, so duplicating them there triggers cargo's "patch unused" warnings.

      --offline
          Never touch the network. Passed to the `cargo update --workspace` that prunes a single-package leaf's freshly seeded `Cargo.lock`, the one step of a sync that resolves crates

      --force
          Configure even when every image's stamp is current

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

nros materialize

Take ownership of a generated entry package.

The last resort: `panic` and `profile` are declarations on the image and need no materialising. One way — `nros build` stops regenerating it.

Usage: nros materialize [OPTIONS] <IMAGE>

Arguments:
  <IMAGE>
          Image whose entry to materialise — `linux`, or `<bringup>:linux`

Options:
      --workspace <WORKSPACE>
          Workspace root. Defaults to the current directory

      --nano-ros-path <NANO_ROS_PATH>
          nano-ros checkout holding `packages/boards`

      --force
          Overwrite an entry that was already materialised.
          
          Off by default: the whole point is that the builder stops touching it, and so should this verb. A second `materialize` without `--force` would otherwise silently discard the edits the first one existed to enable.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

Run on a target

nros run

Run an image on its target: a host process or an emulator. Builds it if stale, starts the router it needs, streams its console and stops everything on exit. `--expect` grades the console; `--dry-run [--why]` prints the resolved plan instead. A hardware image is `nros flash --monitor`

Usage: nros run [OPTIONS] [IMAGE] [-- <PASSTHROUGH>...]

Arguments:
  [IMAGE]
          The image to run (`<image>` or `<bringup>:<image>`), as `nros build` names it. Omitted: the workspace's one image

  [PASSTHROUGH]...
          Arguments for the target, after `--`

Options:
      --workspace <WORKSPACE>
          Workspace root (auto-detected from cwd if omitted)

      --nano-ros-path <NANO_ROS_PATH>
          nano-ros checkout (auto-detected if omitted)

      --dry-run
          Print the resolved plan and run nothing

      --why
          Add the ladder rung that supplied each field

      --port <PORT>
          The console device

      --json
          Print the plan as the JSON a runner is handed (`--plan`), not TOML

      --expect <TEXT>
          Stop with exit 0 as soon as a console line contains TEXT; exit 1 if the target ends, or `--timeout` passes, first

      --expect-regex <REGEX>
          As `--expect`, with a regular expression over one console line

      --timeout <SECONDS>
          Stop the target after SECONDS

      --router <auto|none|LOCATOR>
          What serves the image's link on this host: `auto` starts the zenoh router or the XRCE agent when the link needs one here, `none` starts nothing, a locator names a router that is already running
          
          [default: auto]

      --prefix <CMD>
          Run a host image under this command (`--prefix 'valgrind -q'`)

      --plan <FILE>
          Execute this plan file as written: resolve nothing, build nothing

      --allow-overriding <NAME>...
          Let a workspace package replace the nano-ros runner of this name, for this run only. A replacement nobody declared is refused; to make it permanent, add `[overrides] <name> = "<package path>"` to `system.toml` instead

      --base-paths <PATH>...
          The workspace's source roots, relative to the workspace (default: `.`, plus `nros.toml` `package_paths`).
          
          They replace the workspace and its `package_paths`, and nothing else: the nano-ros packages and `NROS_PACKAGE_PATH` stay on the search path. As in colcon, the roots are peers searched recursively, their order does not matter, a path repeated or inside another counts once, and a package name found in two of them is an error. A path that does not exist is an error; one that holds no package is a warning.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

nros list

List the workspace's packages: kind, name and directory per row

Usage: nros list [OPTIONS] [WORKSPACE]

Arguments:

Options:

      --packages-select <PKG>...
          Only these packages — no dependencies, no dependents.
          
          colcon's flag, with two differences: a name matching no package is an error, not a warning, and a selection that leaves out a package a selected one depends on is refused, since there is no install prefix for it to come from. That holds for every selection flag.

      --packages-up-to <PKG>...
          These packages and everything they depend on, transitively.
          
          The selection flags compose as an INTERSECTION, which is colcon's composition too: each deselects independently, so adding one can only ever narrow the set.

      --packages-above <PKG>...
          These packages and everything that depends on them, transitively.
          
          A package here that depends on a workspace package left out is refused, as for every selection flag; add `--packages-up-to` for its dependencies. A cargo member with no `package.xml` is refused here: its dependents name it only in their `Cargo.toml`, which the selection does not read.

      --packages-skip <PKG>...
          Leave these packages out

      --base-paths <PATH>...
          The workspace's source roots, relative to the workspace (default: `.`, plus `nros.toml` `package_paths`).
          
          They replace the workspace and its `package_paths`, and nothing else: the nano-ros packages and `NROS_PACKAGE_PATH` stay on the search path. As in colcon, the roots are peers searched recursively, their order does not matter, a path repeated or inside another counts once, and a package name found in two of them is an error. A path that does not exist is an error; one that holds no package is a warning.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

nros update

Move one pin, editing the pin set and leaving one diff.

A pin is a registry crate (`--crate`), a vendored source (`--source`), a host tool (`--tool`) or a west project (`--west`).

Usage: nros update [OPTIONS] <--pins|--crate <NAME>|--source <NAME>|--tool <NAME>|--west <MODULE>>

Options:
      --pins
          Regenerate the registry pin set from the locked roots as they stand — after a `cargo update` or a manifest edit in one root. Disagreements between roots are settled upward first

      --prune
          With `--pins`: also DROP every pinned range no locked root resolves and `locks/leaf-only-pins.toml` does not keep. Regeneration alone never drops a range, so a bump leaves the old one pinned

      --crate <NAME>
          Move a Rust registry crate's pin: every locked root that uses it is re-resolved with `cargo update`, the roots are brought into agreement, and the pin set is regenerated from them

      --precise <VERSION>
          The exact version to move to. Without it, cargo picks the newest semver-compatible one. A different MAJOR is a manifest edit first

      --source <NAME>
          Move a vendored source (`[source.<name>]`) to a commit: its submodule is checked out there and the index `ref` rewritten, forward only

      --ref <SHA>
          The commit for `--source`

      --allow-rewind
          Let `--source` move a pin BACKWARDS (the submodule-pin rule forbids it otherwise; say why in the commit)

      --tool <NAME>
          Move a host tool (`[tool.<name>]`) to a version: the row's version strings are rewritten and every dist artifact is downloaded to recompute its sha256

      --to-version <VERSION>
          The version for `--tool`

      --west <MODULE>
          Move a Zephyr west project's revision in every manifest that lists it

      --revision <REV>
          The revision for `--west`

      --nano-ros-path <NANO_ROS_PATH>
          The nano-ros checkout whose pin set to edit (else the usual ladder)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

          Print version

Configuration surface

One fact can be spelled several ways. Only one of them is a place to make a decision; the rest carry that decision across a layer boundary. This page separates the two, because a list that does not is a list of nine ways to set a locator.

Every symbol on this page is one a user may set. Kconfig says so itself: each carries a PROMPT, which is what a prompt means. An earlier draft split these into public and carrier by asking who read them, and got the layer wrong — cmake reading ${CONFIG_X} to emit ZPICO_X=<value> is cmake CARRYING the choice, not owning it.

The real carriers are one layer down and are NOT Kconfig symbols: the ZPICO_* / NROS_* environment variables, the -D cache variables and the compile definitions this page’s symbols feed. Setting one of those by hand bypasses the question Kconfig asked.

The evidence column is where each value is consumed, so a symbol with no reader stands out: a prompt asking a question whose answer is discarded is worse than no prompt.

142 Kconfig symbols — 69 settable, 1 provided for application code, 72 derived, 0 dead.

Facts with more than one spelling

Where a decision has an authority OUTSIDE Kconfig, that authority is the place to set it and these symbols carry it.

RMW backend

Set it here: [system].rmw in the bringup’s system.toml

symboldefaultclassevidence
CONFIG_NROS_RMW_ZENOH—publiccmake, rust-source, kconfig select/depends
CONFIG_NROS_RMW_XRCE—publiccmake, rust-source, kconfig select/depends
CONFIG_NROS_RMW_CYCLONEDDS—publiccmake, rust-source, kconfig select/depends

nano_ros_workspace(BACKEND …) and -DNROS_RMW are the cmake carriers. cmake already warns that BACKEND silently beats the cache var; nothing yet compares either against [system].rmw.

ROS domain id

Set it here: [system].domain_id in system.toml

symboldefaultclassevidence
CONFIG_NROS_DOMAIN_ID0publicforwarded-to-cargo, c-source, cmake, rust-source, kconfig select/depends
CONFIG_NROS_CYCLONE_DOMAIN_IDNROS_DOMAIN_IDpublicc-define, c-source, cmake, rust-source

CONFIG_NROS_CYCLONE_DOMAIN_ID defaults FROM NROS_DOMAIN_ID — the one derivation edge in this cluster. Do not pin it to a literal: a Cyclone DDS image would then run on that domain whatever domain_id says.

Router / agent endpoint

Set it here: [system].locator in system.toml

symboldefaultclassevidence
CONFIG_NROS_ZENOH_LOCATORtcp/127.0.0.1:7447publicc-source, cmake, rust-source
CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_AGENT_ADDR127.0.0.1publiccmake, rust-source
CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_AGENT_PORT2018publiccmake, rust-source

Zephyr is exempt from the cmake precedence chain by design (see the exemption comments in NanoRosEntry.cmake — no line ref, they move), so the Kconfig spelling is the carrier there rather than an override.

Set it here: environment knobs at build time (see the pool inventory)

symboldefaultclassevidence

CONFIG_NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_SC-1derivedforwarded-to-cargo, cmake, rust-source
CONFIG_NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_NODES-1derivedforwarded-to-cargo, cmake, rust-source
CONFIG_NROS_EXECUTOR_ARENA_SIZE0derivedforwarded-to-cargo, cmake, rust-source
CONFIG_NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_MONITORS-1derivedforwarded-to-cargo, cmake, rust-source
