system.toml keys

Reference · Level 3: Production and tuning

The keys a bringup’s system.toml takes for an image, the files beside it, and a bridge binary’s nros-bridge.toml. The page is hand-kept; a gate holds the [image.<id>] table’s key set to the CLI’s own schema, both ways, so a key the CLI accepts cannot be missing here and a key it refuses cannot be listed. The Kconfig symbols an image can also set are in Configuration surface.

Where each setting lives

FileOwnsPer
system.tomlThe deployment: [system] (RMW, domain, capability features, [safety], sched tasks), [[component]] (what runs), and one [image.<id>] per target with its .run, .flash, .console and .knobs tables. One schema for Rust, C and C++bringup package
Cargo.tomlRust toolchain facts only: the crate, its language dependencies, the RMW feature menu. No board, no target tripleRust node package
CMakeLists.txtC and C++ toolchain facts only: targets and language dependencies. No platform, board or RMW set()C or C++ node package
package.xmlPackage identity and message <depend>severy package
build/<coord>/<image>_entry/nros-cargo.tomlGenerated, never edited: target, runner, rustflags, cross compiler, derived pool sizes as [env], the nros-* profiles, the [patch.crates-io] rowsimage
config.tomlHand-written no_std apps with their own main() only: [node], [<interface>], [network.<name>]application

A system.toml beside a Cargo.toml or CMakeLists.txt is refused. Precedence, highest first: a command-line or build flag, [image.<id>], [system], the board descriptor’s [knobs], the built-in default. nros config show prints the resolved values with where each came from.

[image.<id>]

KeyMeaning
boardnano-ros board id, resolved through the board catalog. Never a framework’s own board string
launchLaunch file, relative to the bringup. Absent: [system] default_launch
argsLaunch arguments bound at resolve time, such as { host = "robot1" }
rmwBackend for this image. Absent: [system] rmw
domain_id, locatorOverride [system]’s. locator is what the image dials
os_configLayer-1 files, in order: a board network file (.toml), Zephyr prj-*.conf or .overlay fragments. conf is read as its alias
rmw_configThe middleware’s own file for this image, or { <domain> = "<file>" } per [[domain]]
panicPanic policy: platform, halt or own
before_boot"<pkg>::<fn>" the generated entry calls before the board boots. Rust only
profilecargo or CMake build profile name
variantFramework build variant (Zephyr prj_<buildtype>.conf)
featuresCapability axes for this image, added to [system]’s
serdes, ros_editionSerialization provider and ROS edition. Absent: the [system] value
env{ NAME = "value" } for an application’s own build variable. A registry knob here is an error naming its knobs spelling
entryThe workspace package that is this image’s application, when it cannot be derived
producersfalse builds without the host board’s census recorder and profiler
params_files, ros_argsParameters and ROS arguments baked into the image for rclcpp::init

Retired and refused by name: ip, gateway, netmask, transport, [image.<id>.net.<if>], and the old [deploy.<id>] table.

Folding over [image_defaults]

Kind of keyHow a specific block folds over the defaults
scalars (board, rmw, profile, …)replaced
argsmerged
os_config, featuresconcatenated, defaults first

[system] default_images = ["<id>", …] is what a bare nros build builds. Without it, a workspace with more than one image lists them and stops.

Board network file

Named by os_config, beside system.toml. One table per interface, and any network other than the built-in qemu:

KeyTableMeaning
network[<if>]The network the interface is on. Default: the board’s (qemu on QEMU boards)
host[<if>]Last octet within the network’s subnet
address[<if>]Full IPv4, or "dhcp" on a network with dhcp = true
mac[<if>]Optional. Derived from the board’s mac_prefix and the image’s names when absent
subnet, gateway[network.<name>]The network’s addressing. An interface never states them
dhcp[network.<name>]The network leases addresses

The built-in qemu network is QEMU user-mode networking, 10.0.2.0/24, with gateway and router host 10.0.2.2. An interface on qemu with no address takes 10.0.2.15. The resolved answer is written to build/nros/net/<image>.toml.

Refused, naming the image: an address outside its subnet or equal to the gateway; a network no file defines; two images with one static address or MAC on a network other than qemu; two files defining one network differently; a board network file on a board whose network belongs to the host OS (linux, freertos-posix, threadx-linux) or that declares no interfaces (Zephyr boards take their address from Kconfig).

[image.<id>.run], .flash and .console

TableKeyMeaning
.runnic"slirp" (default on qemu), { bridge = "<dev>" } or { tap = "<dev>" }, for the first interface under QEMU
.flashcommandReplaces the board’s flash method; {hex} and other placeholders are checked
.flashprepareHuman steps before flashing: { say = "…", wait_for = "<event>" }
.consolebaud, …Overrides a key of the board’s [board.console]

An image on a network other than qemu with no nic is physical only, and launching it under QEMU is refused.

The middleware’s own file

BackendDefault file, beside system.tomlSame document ROS 2 reads as
zenohrmw/zenoh.json5ZENOH_SESSION_CONFIG_URI
Cyclone DDSrmw/cyclonedds.xmlCYCLONEDDS_URI
XRCE-DDSnone: the endpoint is the image’s locator—

[system] rmw_config names another default file; [image.<id>] rmw_config names one image’s. A named file that does not exist is refused. An image with a zenoh file that also states a locator is refused. The flat rmw/zenoh.conf is retired.

[image.<id>.knobs.<group>]

The same shape as a board descriptor’s [knobs.<group>]. The key is the knob registry row’s board key where it has one (executor.max_cbs); otherwise the NROS_* name without NROS_, split at the first _ (NROS_ZEPHYR_HEAP_SIZE is zephyr.heap_size). An unknown key, a wrong type or an out-of-range value stops nros build, naming the key. The image rung sits above the board and below an exported variable.

Standalone config.toml

TableKeys
[node]domain_id, locator
[<interface>]as the board network file, plus a board’s own facts ([uart0] baud, [eth0] device on ThreadX Linux)
[network.<name>]subnet, gateway
[node.rt.<rtos>]raw task priorities, such as app_priority, zenoh_read_priority on FreeRTOS

Read with Config::from_toml(include_str!("../config.toml")). A file in the retired [[transport]] shape panics at boot, naming the new spelling.

Cargo features of the nros crate

FeatureSelects
rmw-cffithe C-vtable RMW registry the backend registers into
platform-bare-metal, platform-freertos, platform-nuttx, platform-threadx, platform-zephyr, platform-posixthe platform
ros-humble, ros-ironthe ROS edition
std, allocoptional, by target

The generated entry selects these from the image. rmw in system.toml picks which linked backend is active.

nros-bridge.toml

A bridge binary’s own file, beside system.toml’s keys because it configures the same thing, a running image, but read at run time by the program, not by the build.

Consumed by nros::run_from_config (Rust) and the future C/C++ mirror (nros::run_from_config in nros-cpp).

Not the orchestration nros.toml. This is the bridge runtime config (multi-RMW byte forwarding). It is named nros-bridge.toml to avoid colliding with the orchestration nros.toml (component/system build config) — different lifecycle, different schema.

The file lives next to the binary (or anywhere the program can read it) and selects:

  1. Which RMW backends to open, under what locator / domain.
  2. How those backends are wired into bridge entries that forward traffic between them.

The binary’s Cargo.toml (or target_link_libraries) still selects which backends are linked — the TOML file selects which of the linked backends are used in this run. Backend names in the file that don’t match a linked backend surface as ConfigError::OpenSession.

Top-level structure

# nros-bridge.toml — sibling of the binary
[[node]]
name    = "field"
rmw     = "zenoh"
locator = "tcp/10.0.0.1:7447"

[[node]]
name    = "control"
rmw     = "cyclonedds"
locator = "domain=0"

[[bridge]]
type      = "std_msgs/Int32"
type_hash = "RIHS01_..."
from      = { node = "field",   topic = "/sensor/raw" }
to        = { node = "control", topic = "/sensor/raw" }

Run via:

fn main() -> Result<(), nros_bridge::ConfigError> {
    nros_bridge::run_from_config("nros-bridge.toml")
    // or, via the umbrella feature: nros::run_from_config("nros-bridge.toml")
}

[[node]]

One block per backend session. The first [[node]] becomes the primary session (extra_sessions[0] in Executor::open_multi); the rest open as extras keyed by rmw.

KeyTypeDefaultNotes
namestringrequiredLogical name. Bridge entries reference this.
rmwstringrequiredCanonical backend name: "zenoh", "xrce", "cyclonedds". Must match a backend the binary linked in.
locatorstring""Backend-specific locator. Zenoh uses tcp/..., udp4/..., serial/...; DDS uses domain=<n>; XRCE uses udp4://...:port.
domain_idu320ROS domain id passed to the backend.
namespacestring"/"Default namespace applied to handles created on this node.

Locator scheme grammar (zenoh)

SchemeExampleMeaning
tcp/<host>:<p>tcp/10.0.0.1:7447TCP unicast
udp/<host>:<p>udp/10.0.0.1:7447UDP unicast
serial/<dev>serial//dev/ttyUSB0UART (host-side) or board UART (bare-metal)
tls/<host>:<p>tls/router.example.org:7447TLS over TCP (requires link-tls on backend)

DDS / XRCE follow their native locator conventions; consult each backend’s docs for the exact form.

[[bridge]]

One block per topic forwarded between two [[node]]s. Each bridge creates a RawSubscription on the source side and an EmbeddedRawPublisher on the destination side and pumps bytes once per executor tick.

KeyTypeDefaultNotes
typestringrequiredROS type name ("std_msgs/Int32"). Backends use it for liveliness / discovery.
type_hashstring""ROS 2 RIHS type hash for the typed binding. May be left empty if both sides ignore it.
fromendpointrequired{ node = "<name>", topic = "<topic>" }. The source node + topic.
toendpointrequired{ node = "<name>", topic = "<topic>" }. The destination node + topic.

Bidirectional bridges are two [[bridge]] entries — one in each direction. The runtime stamps a bridge_origin attachment field on forwarded frames and drops on receive when the origin matches the local backend, so an echo pair does not loop.

Error semantics

run_from_config returns ConfigError:

VariantCause
IoFile read failed (missing / unreadable).
ParseTOML malformed or a required field missing.
UnknownNodeA [[bridge]] references a node name no [[node]] declared.
OpenSessionExecutor::open_multi rejected a spec — usually a backend name no RMW_INIT_ENTRIES entry registered under.
BuildNodecreate_node_on failed (registry exhausted, name too long, …).
BuildEntityCreating the source subscription or destination publisher failed (typically backend rejection of the topic name / type / QoS).

Any error short-circuits the runtime; bridges that opened cleanly before the failure are not pumped.

Linked-backend matrix

Backend nameCargo dep that contributes the RMW_INIT_ENTRIES entry
zenohnros-rmw-zenoh = { ... }
xrcenros-rmw-xrce-cffi = { ... }
cycloneddsnros-rmw-cyclonedds static lib (CMake side, --whole-archive)

Add a backend to your Cargo.toml (or target_link_libraries) to make its name available in the TOML; remove it to fence off use even when the TOML file lists it (yields OpenSession at startup).

Environment Variables Reference

Reference · Level 3: Production and tuning

Set a runtime variable in the shell that starts the program. Set a build-time knob in the shell before nros build, or per image in system.toml (an [image.<id>] env row, or the knob-registry table where the section below says so).

The checkout’s .env file for in-tree builds: see Internals → Build Commands.

Runtime Configuration

Examples use ExecutorConfig::from_env() for configuration:

VariableDescriptionDefault
ROS_DOMAIN_IDROS 2 domain ID0
NROS_LOCATORRMW locator (tcp/…, udp/…, serial/…, or tls/…)tcp/127.0.0.1:7447
NROS_SESSION_MODESession mode: client or peerclient
ZENOH_TLS_ROOT_CA_CERTIFICATEPath to CA certificate (PEM) for TLS(none)
ZENOH_TLS_ROOT_CA_CERTIFICATE_BASE64Base64-encoded CA certificate for TLS(none)
ZENOH_TLS_VERIFY_NAME_ON_CONNECTVerify server hostname in TLS (true/false)(none)

Retired legacy names: ZENOH_LOCATOR and ZENOH_MODE are no longer read. Setting either is a startup ERROR naming its replacement (NROS_LOCATOR / NROS_SESSION_MODE) — Rust panics in resolve_hosted / returns InitError::RetiredEnvVar from nros::init, C / C++ init returns RCL_RET_INVALID_ARGUMENT / NROS_CPP_RET_INVALID_ARGUMENT and logs the reason. Refused rather than ignored: an ignored locator would dial the default router and read as “no delivery”. ZENOH_TLS_* names are kept because TLS is currently zenoh-specific.

TLS Notes

  • POSIX: requires libmbedtls-dev (install it with your host’s package manager). File-path and base64 cert loading are both supported.
  • Bare-metal: only ZENOH_TLS_ROOT_CA_CERTIFICATE_BASE64 is supported (no filesystem). The certificate is embedded at build time.
  • The link-tls Cargo feature must be enabled on both the example and the nros crate.

Build-Time Configuration

VariableDescriptionRequired
ZENOH_PICO_DIRCMake install prefix for pre-built zenoh-pico (use with system-zenohpico feature on zpico-sys)Only with system-zenohpico
NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATHExtra board-search roots (PATH-style : separated). Each entry is a directory shaped like packages/boards/ — subdirs carrying nros-board.toml crates or */boards/<name>/board.cmake bundles. Read by the nros CLI’s board catalog AND nano_ros_use_board() (also settable as a CMake cache var there). Board keys stay global: a name found under two roots is an error, never shadowed.(unset)

ARM FVP (FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R)

Not license-gated: nros setup --tool arm-fvp fetches the model from a pinned Arm CDN permalink ([tool.arm-fvp] in nros-sdk-index.toml, digest-checked) into the SDK store. Arm publishes it for x86_64 Linux only. You need none of the variables below unless you installed a model yourself. See the ARM FVP getting-started chapter for the end-to-end build+run walk-through.

VariableDescriptionDefault
ARMFVP_BIN_PATHDirectory containing FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R (Zephyr-canonical, highest priority).(unset)
ARM_FVP_DIRInstall root; resolver scans models/Linux64_GCC-*/ underneath.(unset)

The model is found in this order: ARMFVP_BIN_PATH, ARM_FVP_DIR, FVP_BaseR_AEMv8R on PATH, then the store copy that nros setup --tool arm-fvp installs. Set ARMFVP_BIN_PATH at BUILD time as well as run time, because Zephyr’s armfvp.cmake caches the location at configure. For a model you downloaded by hand, set ARM_FVP_DIR to the extraction root. nros doctor --board fvp-aemv8r-smp reports whether the model resolves.

Changing how the FVP is resolved or run in the tree: see Internals → Zephyr in-tree examples.

Vendored source trees

You normally set none of these. nros setup puts each tree in the shared store, and every build locates it through one ladder: this variable, then the project’s [sources] row in system.toml, then a checkout submodule you are editing, then the store, then the checkout’s own copy. nros locate <name> --why prints which rung answered. Set a variable only to build against a tree of your own.

VariableTree
FREERTOS_DIRFreeRTOS kernel source
LWIP_DIRlwIP source
NUTTX_DIRNuttX RTOS source
NUTTX_APPS_DIRNuttX apps source
THREADX_DIRThreadX kernel source
NETX_DIRNetX Duo source
CYCLONEDDS_SOURCE_DIRCyclone DDS source

FREERTOS_PORT, FREERTOS_CONFIG_DIR, THREADX_CONFIG_DIR and NETX_CONFIG_DIR are board facts: each board’s nros-board.toml states them, and the build carries them from there. They are not user inputs.

Buffer Tuning

All optional – platform-appropriate defaults apply if unset. See Configuration for deployment-scenario guidance and platform guides for target-specific sizing.

XRCE-DDS (NROS_XRCE_*)

These are read by nros-rmw-xrce-cffi’s build script, either from the environment or — on Zephyr — from CONFIG_<name> in .config. They set C #defines of the same name without the NROS_ prefix; the define is not itself an environment variable, so exporting XRCE_BUFFER_SIZE has no effect and reports no error.

VariableDescriptionDefaultMinCrate

NROS_XRCE_MAX_SERVICE_SERVERSMax concurrent service servers. On Zephyr, DERIVED — see below.40nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_MAX_SERVICE_CLIENTSMax concurrent service clients. DERIVED from the sizing descriptor — see below.40nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_STREAM_HISTORYReliable stream history depth; sizes the per-session output buffer164nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_CUSTOM_TRANSPORT_MTUCustom transport MTU; stream buffers are MTU x STREAM_HISTORY4096128nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_TRANSPORT_MTUUDP/TCP transport MTU, and the Zephyr default of CUSTOM_TRANSPORT_MTU4096 (Zephyr 512)128nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_SUBSCRIBER_BUFFER_SIZESubscriber ring entry size; derived from the declared subscriptions when unstated (Zephyr: -1)BUFFER_SIZE1nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_SERVICE_REQUEST_BUFFER_SIZEApplication service-server request entry size. DERIVED from the declared servers’ requests beside the builtin splitBUFFER_SIZE1nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_SERVICE_REPLY_BUFFER_SIZEService-client reply slot size. DERIVED from the declared clients’ repliesBUFFER_SIZE1nros-rmw-xrce
NROS_XRCE_BUILTIN_SERVICE_SERVERSHow many service-server slots are the parameter / lifecycle services’. DERIVED beside the total0 (no split)0nros-rmw-xrce

Dropping MAX_SUBSCRIBERS, MAX_SERVICE_* and SUBSCRIBER_RING_DEPTH to 1, BUFFER_SIZE to 256, STREAM_HISTORY to 4 and CUSTOM_TRANSPORT_MTU to 512 takes the session struct from ~390 KB to ~10-20 KB.

Every variable in this table is a knob-registry row, so a project states it per image as [image.<id>.knobs.xrce] buffer_size = 256 — the name without NROS_XRCE_, lowercased (max_subscribers, max_service_servers, max_service_clients, subscriber_ring_depth, subscriber_buffer_size, service_request_buffer_size, service_reply_buffer_size, stream_history, transport_mtu, custom_transport_mtu) — rather than as an env row.

On Zephyr the three entity caps DERIVE, and the minimum is 0

CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_MAX_SUBSCRIBERS and CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_MAX_SERVICE_SERVERS default to -1, which means take the number from the entities this image declares (the contract sidecar beside the bringup’s launch file, or beside the bringup’s system.toml when it has no launch/). A listener that declares one subscription and no service is built with one subscriber slot and zero service-server slots, which is what took the session struct from 427,968 bytes to 59,088 on the zephyr cpp listener. Stating a number in Kconfig or the environment still wins over the derivation, in both directions.

CONFIG_NROS_XRCE_MAX_SERVICE_CLIENTS also defaults to -1, and its number comes from the image’s sizing descriptor on every road that writes one: the declared service clients plus three per action client (send_goal, cancel_goal, get_result). With no descriptor, or one that does not state both counts, the crate default of 4 stands.

Zero is a legal, honoured value for all three caps — it is not rounded up to 1. So creating an entity the image never declared does not truncate silently: the create fails with InvalidConfig and the backend logs which cap it hit, which knob moves it, and that the count came from the declaration.

NROS_XRCE_SUBSCRIBER_RING_DEPTH is deliberately NOT derivable — no inventory knows how deep a burst a subscriber must survive — but it does have a Kconfig symbol, and on Zephyr that is the way to set it: a Zephyr cargo build sees only the knobs nros_cargo_build.cmake forwards, and shell exports do not survive that.

NROS_XRCE_BUFFER_SIZE is the XRCE receive ceiling

A subscriber’s receive ring entry is a fixed uint8_t data[XRCE_BUFFER_SIZE], so a subscription’s own buffer size cannot raise it: asking for create_subscription_sized::<M, 16384> still stops at 1024, because the 16384 buffer is the destination of a copy that never happens. A sample that does not fit is refused on take with MessageTooLarge.

The static cost is XRCE_SUBSCRIBER_RING_DEPTH x XRCE_BUFFER_SIZE per subscriber, which is why the default is small — raise it deliberately, and consider lowering the ring depth at the same time.

A payload at or above the transport MTU (4096) arrives fragmented; the receive path reads the fragment chain and delivers it whole.

Design background

  • RFC-0103: one owner per fact — the one source-location ladder, the NROS_<ID> knob spelling, and knob-registry rows

Rust API

Reference · Level 2: Building real applications

The nano-ros Rust API is the nros crate. It re-exports every type a user application needs: Executor, Node, Publisher<M>, Subscription<M>, Service<S>, Client<S>, ActionServer<A>, ActionClient<A>, Timer and GuardCondition, with nros::prelude as the glob import. It is no_std, and its heap use is behind the alloc feature, so the same node code builds for a host and for a board. Message types are generated crates, one per interface package your node depends on (Message Generation).

API reference

nros rustdoc — start here.

The published rustdoc is built from the current main branch with the alloc, log, env, rmw-cffi and ros-humble features on.

Where to start

  • New to nano-ros? → nros::prelude
  • Executor-driven app? → nros::Executor
  • Polling or callbacks? → Two ways to receive, the two layers of the API and when to use each.

How to read the rustdoc

The published pages show the crate with the features listed above turned on. A board build turns on only the features its image asks for, so an item behind a feature your image does not enable is absent from that build even though the published page shows it; the item’s source, linked from its page, shows the #[cfg(feature = ...)] that gates it. Your own package documents nros at the version and features it builds with: run cargo doc --open in that package. That is also where your message crates are documented: they are generated for your workspace, so the published site does not have them.

Porting only

These crates are not part of the user API. They surface only when you write a custom RMW backend or port nano-ros to a new platform; see Custom RMW Backend and Custom Platform.

  • nros_rmw: the RMW trait surface.
  • nros_platform_api: the platform abstraction traits.
  • nros-rmw-zenoh: the zenoh-pico backend, in the source tree.

C API

Reference · Level 2: Building real applications

The nano-ros C API is rclc’s: the rclc_*, rcl_* and rcl_action_* calls a micro-ROS or rclc application makes, over nano-ros’s executor and RMW. Its headers sit at upstream’s paths (rclc/, rcl/, rcl_action/, rclc_parameter/, rclc_lifecycle/) under the SDK’s C include directory, so an #include you know from rclc names the same file here. rclc/detail/ is internal. Message types are generated by the build from the packages your node depends on (Message Generation).

API reference

C API Doxygen — start here.

The Doxygen site is generated from the current main branch. The umbrella header rclc/rclc.h pulls in every public surface a user application needs.

Where to start

  • rclc/rclc.h — convenience umbrella include
  • rclc/init.h — rclc_support_init, rclc_support_fini
  • rclc/node.h — rclc_node_init_default, rcl_node_fini
  • rclc/executor.h — spin loop, executor lifecycle
  • rclc/publisher.h / subscription.h — pub/sub
  • rclc/service.h / client.h — services
  • rclc/action.h — actions
  • rclc_parameter/rclc_parameter.h — parameter services
  • rclc_lifecycle/rclc_lifecycle.h — REP-2002 lifecycle states

Two-layer API. Every entity exposes two parallel C entry-point sets: rclc_*_init_default (Layer 1, caller polls) and rclc_executor_add_* (Layer 2, executor callback). Layer 1 grew an _init_polling + take_*_raw / send_*_raw family for inline-storage callers (no executor arena). Layer 2 pairs the same rclc_*_init_default with the executor-add call, which is where the callback is supplied (rclc’s binding site). See Two ways to receive for the verb discipline and per-layer trade-offs.

Event-driven wake callbacks. Each L1 polling entity supports nros_*_set_wake_callback(entity, &state, cb, ctx) for event- driven RTOS / embassy callers. State is a caller-owned rclc_wake_state_t POD; the backend fires cb(ctx) on rx / reply / request arrival. Per-channel for actions (set_{goal,cancel,get_result}_wake_callback on the server, set_{goal_response,cancel_response,result,feedback}_wake_callback on the client). See the Doxygen for signatures.

How to read the Doxygen site

Each header has a page named after its path (rclc/executor.h is executor_8h.html), listing its functions with their return codes. A call that can fail returns an rcl_ret_t; the codes, with the RCLC_RET_* ones nano-ros adds (RCLC_RET_FULL for a full static pool, RCLC_RET_REENTRANT for a blocking call made from inside a callback), are on the error codes page.

Where it differs from rclc

Behaviourrclcnano-ros
A goal arriving with every goal handle in usequeuedrejected
An accepted goalwaits for the client to ask for its resultexecutes at once, so a result may be sent before the client asks for it
Taking an entity off a running executorrclc_executor_remove_*the same calls; each frees its slot and arena bytes, and fini without one leaves the entity dispatched into

Linking from CMake

A CMake project links the NanoRos::NanoRos target and generates C bindings with nano_ros_generate_interfaces(<pkg> LANGUAGE C). The function defaults to LANGUAGE CPP; Message Generation has the table of spellings.

Porting only

The rmw-cffi and platform-cffi Doxygen sites are not part of the user API. They document the C vtables for porters writing a custom RMW backend or platform port. See RMW API and Platform API.

Design background

  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. The paired examples as image rows of behaviour bringups in the language workspaces.

C++ API

Reference · Level 2: Building real applications

The nano-ros C++ API is a freestanding C++14 interface for ROS 2 nodes on embedded and host targets. It needs no standard library, no exceptions and no RTTI, so the same code builds for Zephyr, FreeRTOS, NuttX, ThreadX, bare metal and Linux.

  • Upstream’s names, in upstream’s namespaces. rclcpp::Node, Publisher<M>, Subscription<M>, Service<S>, Client<S>, Timer, GuardCondition, Executor, and rclcpp_action::Server<A> / Client<A>. Every user-facing name is in rclcpp::, rclcpp_action:: or rclcpp_lifecycle::; there is no nros:: namespace. The extensions with no upstream counterpart (the Poll* types, the *Storage types, FixedString, …) are in rclcpp:: too.
  • Errors are values. Every fallible call returns rclcpp::Result, and RCLCPP_TRY returns early on failure. Nothing throws.
  • Generated message types. std_msgs::msg::Int32, example_interfaces::srv::AddTwoInts and so on, generated by the build from the packages your node depends on (see Message Generation).
  • An opt-in std surface for ported code. Defining NROS_CPP_STD adds the std::string / std::function / std::chrono overloads and the std::shared_ptr-returning rclcpp::Node factories. The build requests it; it is never detected from the toolchain. See Two surfaces.

The headers live in the SDK’s C++ include directory at upstream’s paths: rclcpp/, rclcpp_action/ and rclcpp_lifecycle/. rclcpp/detail/ is internal.

To build and run a first C++ node, start with First Node — C++; to grow it into a workspace, see C++ in a workspace. To bring an existing ROS 2 node across, see Porting a ROS 2 C++ node. This page is the API itself.

API reference

C++ API Doxygen — start here.

The Doxygen site is generated from the current main branch. The umbrella header rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp pulls in every public surface a user application needs.

Where to start

  • rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp — convenience umbrella include
  • rclcpp::init_in / rclcpp::shutdown — session lifetime
  • rclcpp::Node — node + create_publisher/subscription/service/client/action_*
  • rclcpp::Publisher<M> / Subscription<M>. Hosted, a subscription callback may also take upstream’s const rclcpp::MessageInfo& as its second argument (see rclcpp compatibility)
  • rclcpp::Service<S> / Client<S> — the DISPATCH service server and client. A handler is registered into the executor arena, which owns the entity. Service<S>::SharedPtr is rclcpp::ServiceHandle<S>, a two-word keep-alive with nothing to dereference; Client<S>::SharedPtr is rclcpp::ClientHandle<S>, the same two words with one verb, async_send_request. Neither has an operator->.
  • rclcpp::PollService<S> — L1 polling service server. The caller owns the server and drains it with take_request / send_response from its own spin loop. node.create_service<S>(name) with no handler hands one back.
  • rclcpp::PollClient<S> — L1 future-style service client, the client half of the same split. The caller owns the client and drains the reply itself: send_request returns a rclcpp::Future<T> (on a hosted build async_send_request(shared_ptr) returns upstream’s FutureAndRequestId — .future, .request_id, share()), call blocks while driving the executor, call_polling blocks without driving it, and wait_for_service / service_is_ready probe the server. node.create_client<S>(name) with no handler hands one back.
  • rclcpp_action::Server<A> / Client<A> — L2 callback model (executor-arena registered). rclcpp::ActionServer<A> / rclcpp::ActionClient<A> are the same two types. Hosted, upstream’s goal handles too (see rclcpp compatibility).
  • rclcpp::PollingActionServer<A> / PollingActionClient<A> — L1 polling model. Caller drives take_* / accept_goal / complete_goal from a spin loop.
  • rclcpp::Future<T> — async result handle
  • rclcpp::Executor, Timer, GuardCondition
  • Parameters are methods ON the node — declare_parameter<T> / get_parameter<T> / set_parameter<T> / has_parameter, upstream’s names, forwarding to the one store the rcl_interfaces services read. rclcpp::Seq<T, N> is the array VALUE a freestanding node declares with (std::vector<T> under NROS_CPP_STD). There is no standalone rclcpp::ParameterServer: a second store would be invisible to ros2 param get. See How nano-ros differs from ROS 2 for what is intentionally smaller than rclcpp, and Parameters and /parameter_events.

Two-layer API. The rclcpp::ActionServer<A> / ActionClient<A> templates are L2 callback handles, dispatched by the executor. The rclcpp::PollingActionServer<A> / PollingActionClient<A> are L1 polling templates with the same typed serialization glue but caller-driven control flow. Subscriptions, services and service clients have both shapes too (Subscription / PollSubscription, and so on). See Two ways to receive for the per-layer rationale.

Event-driven wake callbacks. PollingActionServer<A> and PollingActionClient<A> expose a nested WakeState POD and typed set_{goal,cancel,get_result,goal_response, cancel_response,result,feedback}_wake_callback(state, cb, ctx) methods. Pair an nros_cpp_wake_state_t with each entity / channel to wake on rx instead of polling.

Errors

Every fallible call returns an rclcpp::Result; RCLCPP_TRY returns early when one fails, and ret.raw() is the rclcpp::ErrorCode. The codes, with their meanings, are on the rclcpp/result.hpp page of the Doxygen site. A Full from a create_* usually means a build-time pool is too small; Static Pool Inventory names the knob that sizes it.

How to read the Doxygen site

The site lists every header under its upstream path, so a page you know from rclcpp’s documentation is at the same name: rclcpp/node.hpp, rclcpp_action/client.hpp, rclcpp_lifecycle/lifecycle_node.hpp. Each class page documents the freestanding surface first; members that exist only on a hosted build say NROS_CPP_STD. The pages under rclcpp/detail/ are internal and may change without notice.

See also

  • rclcpp compatibility: what a ported rclcpp node gets, by the upstream spelling it uses, and the measured ROS 2 examples.
  • Add a second node: a first C++ node, built and run.
  • Zephyr: a C++ application under the nano-ros Zephyr module.

Design background

  • RFC-0018: C++ API design — freestanding C++14, no exceptions, the Result channel
  • RFC-0089: ROS 2 API adoption, and the compile-or-conform rule — upstream’s namespaces and names, the _in rule, the hosted surface
  • RFC-0021: blocking API rules — why blocking calls drive the executor and refuse re-entry

rclcpp compatibility

Reference · Level 3: Production and tuning

What a ported rclcpp node gets, by the upstream spelling it uses. “Hosted builds” means a target built with NROS_CPP_STD, which the ament verbs set for a ported package. The porting steps are in Port a C++ node.

rclcpp surfacenano-rosNotes
class MyNode : public rclcpp::Noderclcpp::Node — ours, and the same name.Ctor takes (name), (name, options) or (name, ns, options).
std::make_shared<MyNode>()worksauto node = std::make_shared<MyNode>() and rclcpp::spin(std::make_shared<MyNode>()) are unchanged. rclcpp::Node::SharedPtr node = std::make_shared<…>(…) does not compile — write auto; see “Node::SharedPtr observes, it does not own” below. shared_from_this() works too, with the same caveat.
rclcpp::Node::make_shared("name")std::make_shared<rclcpp::Node>(…), the owning std::shared_ptrHosted builds. auto node = rclcpp::Node::make_shared("x"); is unchanged; assigning the temporary straight to a global rclcpp::Node::SharedPtr is not — keep it in a local first (auto node = …; g_node = node;).
create_publisher<M>(topic, qos)shared_ptr-returning wrapperqos can be rclcpp::QoS(10) or an int.
create_subscription<M>(topic, qos, callback)registered on the executor arena; dispatched by any spin verbCapturing lambdas + std::function + std::bind all work. The callback may take const M& (no allocation, every target) or, on hosted builds, upstream’s M::UniquePtr / M::SharedPtr / M::ConstSharedPtr / std::shared_ptr<const M>: each delivery is then copied into a fresh heap object the callback owns and may keep. A freestanding build refuses the pointer shapes at compile time, naming const M&.
create_wall_timer(period, callback)registered on the executor arena; dispatched by any spin verbstd::chrono::duration arg, capturing-lambda callback. Returns rclcpp::TimerBase::SharedPtr, which is rclcpp::Timer::SharedPtr — one flat type, two names. See below.
rclcpp::create_timer(node, clock, period, cb)the clock-taking verb; a RCL_ROS_TIME clock follows /clockHumble’s only form. create_wall_timer stays on the steady clock.
create_service<S>(name, handler) with upstream’s std::shared_ptr<Request> / std::shared_ptr<Response> handler (optionally with std::shared_ptr<rmw_request_id_t> first)lent from the dispatch: the handler gets pointers to the request and response the dispatch decodedHosted builds; a plain function, a lambda with or without captures, or std::bind(&Node::on_request, this, _1, _2) (a handler’s state is copied into the service’s executor entry, and whatever it returns, such as Autoware’s bool, is ignored). The handler must not KEEP a pointer past its call: that aborts, naming why. The request header is zero-filled.
rclcpp::executors::SingleThreadedExecutor + add_node + spinthe process executor every node already lives onadd_node checks rather than attaches. MultiThreadedExecutor is a compile error naming the alternative: an executor dispatches on one task, and parallelism is a tier, not a callback group.
executor.spin_some() / rclcpp::spin_some(node)drain what is ready, without waitingThe bound is milliseconds (spin_some(5)), not a std::chrono duration.
client->wait_for_service(1s) / wait_for_action_server(10s)the millisecond wait, convertedHosted builds. The budget is still required; a negative duration is refused at the call.
rclcpp::spin_until_future_complete(node, client->send_request(req))spins until the reply arrivesThe timeout is milliseconds.
auto fut = client->async_send_request(std::make_shared<S::Request>(…)) / fut.get() / fut.wait_for(1s) / client->remove_pending_request(fut)the poll client’s rclcpp::Future, under upstream’s verbsHosted builds, except remove_pending_request. get() returns the reply as an owning std::shared_ptr<Response> but never blocks: call it after spin_until_future_complete returned SUCCESS (before the reply it logs a refusal and returns nullptr). wait_for returns std::future_status and spins the executor while it waits. Each future is keyed by its request’s sequence number, as upstream’s is: several may be in flight on one client, each gets its own reply, and a reply that arrives after remove_pending_request (or prune_pending_requests) is dropped. How many is capped by the transport’s own outstanding-request limit (NROS_ZENOH_MAX_PENDING_GETS on zenoh); a send past it returns an empty future (valid() false). What it returns is upstream’s FutureAndRequestId: the future as .future, the request’s sequence id as .request_id (auto [future, id] = … works), and share() hands back a SharedFutureAndRequestId whose future is a std::shared_future<SharedResponse> every copy of which gets the same response; remove_pending_request takes the id too. .future is an rclcpp::Future, not a std::future. A freestanding build has send_request(req) + fut.try_take(resp); get() and share() there are compile errors naming them.
#include "rclcpp_action/rclcpp_action.hpp"an umbrella over Server<A> / Client<A> and the two free factoriesSee Actions with upstream’s goal handles.
rclcpp::init(argc, argv) / shutdown() / ok() / spin(n) / spin_some(n)wraps rclcpp::init_in/shutdown_in/ok/spin_once--ros-args -r from:=to is honoured, beneath any remap the launch file sets for the same name. -p [node:]name:=value and --params-file <file> are honoured in an image with a parameter store: the value replaces the default when the node declares the parameter (scalars only from a file; a value of the wrong type is logged and the default kept). Any other ROS argument (__node, log flags) aborts, naming it.
RCLCPP_INFO / WARN / ERROR / DEBUG / FATALdispatched through the NROS_LOG_* family into nros_logCarries the logger, so get_logger("x") selects a real per-logger level, and FATAL is a distinct severity. Reaches LOG_ERR/printk on embedded, where the legacy NROS_* sink is a no-op. _THROTTLE variants are REFUSE-LOUD.
get_logger().get_child("sub")a real child logger, <parent>.subIts level, when unset, follows the nearest ancestor’s, so set_level on the node logger reaches it. A full name over 48 bytes or a full runtime-logger arena emits through the PARENT and set_level on it is refused — never a silent move of the parent’s threshold. Iron/Jazzy images publish children on /rosout; Humble ones, as upstream, do not.
executor.spin_once() / client->wait_for_service() / action_client->wait_for_action_server()the budget is requiredUpstream defaults all three to “block forever”, which nano-ros has no form of; the no-argument call is a compile error naming the alternative rather than a silently substituted 10 ms / 5 s budget. Write spin_once(10), wait_for_service(10000).
rclcpp::QoS / KeepLast(n) / SystemDefaultsQoS()one class with upstream’s implicit (depth) ctorChainable setters inherited.
diagnostic_updater::Updater + DiagnosticStatusWrappernano-ros’s own diagnostic_updaterPublishes /diagnostics.
rclcpp_action::Server<A> / Client<A>ours, under upstream’s namesHosted builds take upstream’s goal-handle shapes as written; freestanding builds key goals by id. See Actions with upstream’s goal handles.
class MyNode : public rclcpp_lifecycle::LifecycleNodeours, under upstream’s name (<rclcpp_lifecycle/lifecycle_node.hpp>)It IS an rclcpp::Node. The on_configure(const State&) … on_shutdown overrides, CallbackReturn::SUCCESS, configure() / activate() / … and get_current_state() keep upstream’s signatures; the REP-2002 services are registered by the constructor. create_publisher<M>(topic, qos) returns a managed LifecyclePublisher<M>::SharedPtr that sends only while Active. One managed node per executor.
RCLCPP_COMPONENTS_REGISTER_NODE(class) + rclcpp_components_register_node(lib PLUGIN "ns::Class" EXECUTABLE exe)the macro defines the component’s factory in its own source file; the cmake verb emits a thin int main() per registration that declares the class and calls that factorySingle binary, no class_loader. The PLUGIN’s qualifiers must be namespaces (a class nested in a class cannot be forward-declared). A component library built SHARED is built static.
plain CMake components: add_library(<c> SHARED …), ament_target_dependencies(<c> rclcpp …), rclcpp_components_register_nodes(<c> "ns::Class"), a hand-written main (add_executable + target_link_libraries)each SHARED or MODULE library builds static, and the configure prints a line saying so; the plural verb and ament_environment_hooks are accepted and do nothingOne image is one binary with one runtime. ament_target_dependencies works beside a target_link_libraries in either signature (plain or PRIVATE). A hand-written main gets the link pass the ament verbs give theirs. IMPORTED libraries keep their type. A project that overrides add_library itself replaces this.
find_package(ament_cmake_auto / rclcpp / rclcpp_components / diagnostic_updater / std_msgs / …)find modules in the SDK root’s cmake/find/~28 of the most-cited ROS 2 packages; a message package not among them is found by the resolver from NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH / AMENT_PREFIX_PATH.
ament_auto_find_build_dependencies() + ament_auto_add_library / ament_auto_add_executablereads package.xml; each target gets the package’s include/ and every dependency nano-ros has a module forA dependency nano-ros does not provide (a project helper such as autoware_utils) is listed at configure and not looked up; a source that includes it fails on the include.
a project’s own message packages (autoware_vehicle_msgs, tier4_control_msgs, …) installed under AMENT_PREFIX_PATHgenerated by nano-ros codegen from the installed .msg / .srvNever the installed package’s upstream C++. Source the project’s install first (below).
create_callback_group(rclcpp::CallbackGroupType::MutuallyExclusive), SubscriptionOptions::callback_group, create_subscription<M>(topic, qos, cb, options)accepted; an unnamed group runs on the node’s default contextOne executor task already keeps every callback mutually exclusive, so Reentrant runs them one at a time too. A NAMED group (create_callback_group("name")) is the tier-mapped one.
create_service<S>(name, cb, rmw_qos_profile_services_default, group)upstream’s trailing QoS and grouprmw_qos_profile_t has upstream’s fields and enum values. A profile converts to rclcpp::QoS, QoS(QoSInitialization::from_rmw(p), p) builds one, and qos.get_rmw_qos_profile() reads it back. rmw_qos_profile_system_default is absent, because every field of it is a placeholder for the RMW to fill in, and the RMWs fill it in differently. A file that also includes <nros/rmw_entity.h> is refused, because that header defines the RMW backend’s own struct of the same name.
pub_->publish(msg); as a statementallowed on a ported (ament-built) target, even under -Wall -Werror; a failure is loggedCode written for nano-ros keeps the [[nodiscard]] Result.
several packages in one workspace (a library package such as Nav2’s nav2_util, a cmake-only one such as nav2_common, and the node that finds them)find_package(<sibling>) resolves to the sibling configured earlier in the same run: <pkg>::<pkg> over what it exported with ament_export_libraries / _targets / _dependencies, its include/, and its ament_package(CONFIG_EXTRAS …) files runAdd each package before the packages that find it; the configure refuses an out-of-order find by name. Every package configures in ONE CMake run, so ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR} is the workspace root, not the package: write ${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR} (rare: 0 of 417 Autoware CMakeLists name it).
find_package(<pkg>) for an upstream C++ library nano-ros does not ship (bondcpp, tf2_ros, …)refused at configure, naming the package and the installed file CMake fell back toRemove the dependency, or port the library into your workspace as a package of its own.
rclcpp::Time(msg->header.stamp)implicit, from any {sec, nanosec} message, on the ROS clock
msg.header.stamp = now();, stamp + rclcpp::Duration::from_seconds(0.1)a {sec, nanosec} message converts from rclcpp::Time, and + / - a Duration
last_cmd_.twist == geometry_msgs::msg::Twist()a generated message has field-wise operator== / operator!=Messages only; a service’s or action’s own Request / Goal structs have none.
rclcpp::Node::WeakPtr parent + parent.lock()the same non-owning handle; lock() hands it backlock() cannot tell a destroyed node from a live one, because the handle owns nothing; it answers null only for an unset handle.
rclcpp::Clock::SharedPtr clock_ = get_clock();a pointer to the node’s clockstd::make_shared<rclcpp::Clock>(...) does not convert; hold a rclcpp::Clock by value.
timer_->cancel(); / timer_->reset(); as a statementallowed on a ported target under -WerrorAs publish(): the result is still readable.
descriptor.floating_point_range.resize(1)a bounded sequence resizes within its boundPast the bound it is refused and returns false, where rosidl throws.
rclcpp::spin(node->get_node_base_interface())spins the node
get_node_base_interface()->get_context()->add_pre_shutdown_callback(f)rclcpp::Context views the executor’s shutdown hooks; f runs on rclcpp::shutdown()The hooks share the executor’s table (NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_SHUTDOWN_CBS, default 2). A full table returns an invalid handle.
a package that depends on rclcpp_lifecycleits runtime carries lifecycle (with param_services on a host), and ros2 lifecycle get /<node> finds itOn a board the cmake road gives it lifecycle alone. A Zephyr application states it in system.toml: [system] features = ["lifecycle"].
std::static_pointer_cast<Derived>(shared_from_this()) (Nav2’s nav2_util::LifecycleNode)does not compileThe handle owns nothing, so there is no std::shared_ptr to cast. Drop the override; rclcpp_lifecycle::LifecycleNode::shared_from_this() returns its own type.
pub_->get_subscription_count()takes the executor and an out-parameterSee Publisher::get_subscription_count. Nav2 calls it only in its tests.
declare_parameter(name, rclcpp::ParameterValue(...)[, descriptor]), get_parameter(name) as an rclcpp::Parameter, set_parameter(rclcpp::Parameter(...))the same store the typed declare_parameter<T> uses; the descriptor may be an rcl_interfaces::msg::ParameterDescriptorHosted builds. A byte or string array can be built but not declared. A wrong-type as_double() answers 0.0, not an exception.
add_on_set_parameters_callback(std::bind(&C::cb, this, _1)) with cb(std::vector<rclcpp::Parameter>) returning SetParametersResultruns on every write, local or ros2 param set; successful = false refuses it; the returned handle unregisters on destructionOne parameter per call, because writes are validated one at a time. The reason does not reach the remote caller. Keep the handle as a member of your node class, so it goes before the node does.
node->get_node_parameters_interface()has_parameter, declare_parameter, get_parameter and get_parameter_overrides() through ->get_parameter_overrides() lists this node’s -p / --params-file values as a std::map<std::string, rclcpp::ParameterValue>, one copy per node, so Nav2’s declare_or_get_parameter compiles.
pub_->publish(std::move(msg)) with a std::unique_ptr<M>publishes *msg; the message is freed when the call returnsHosted builds. Every publish serializes, so there is no intra-process hand-over to save a copy. A null pointer is refused and logged.
rclcpp::Client<S>::SharedPtr client_ = create_client<S>(name); + client_->async_send_request(req, callback) with a void(Client<S>::SharedFuture) callbackthe handle holds the poll client; the callback runs from the executor when the reply arrives, with a SharedFuture whose get() returns itHosted builds with std::promise. The client registers one 1 ms timer for its callbacks, cancelled while none is waiting. A removed request’s callback never runs. wait_for_service(1s) inside a callback waits without spinning, so on a polled backend it runs out its budget. On an RTOS toolchain (no std::promise) store the client as rclcpp::Owned<rclcpp::PollClient<S>>, keep the FutureAndRequestId that async_send_request(req) returns, and read it on a later callback with future.is_ready() and get().
diagnostic_updater::Updater updater_{this};publishes /diagnostics on its own timer, every period (setPeriod), as upstream’s doesupdate() still works and is no longer required.
DiagnosticTask, FrequencyStatus, TimeStampStatus, Heartbeat, HeaderlessTopicDiagnostic, TopicDiagnosticupstream’s classes, levels and messages; updater.add(task)A clock argument is a const rclcpp::Clock*, so node->get_clock() still passes. The tasks take no lock, so a node that calls tick() from its own thread must keep that call from overlapping an update. DiagnosedPublisher is absent, because a nano-ros publisher handle can be moved but not copied. Keep the publisher and a TopicDiagnostic, and call tick(stamp) next to each publish.
the six parameter services (ros2 param get/set/list)on for an ament package built on a host: every node serves them, as upstream’s doesComes from the package’s package.xml naming ament_cmake; set NROS_FEATURES to declare the capabilities yourself. Values come from --ros-args --params-file <yaml> or -p. On a board they are off unless declared (param_services in NROS_FEATURES, or [system] features on Zephyr): they cost six queryables and their RAM.

The port runs execute(goal_handle) in the accepted callback and drops rclcpp::Rate::sleep, which would re-enter the executor from that callback
rclcpp/actions/minimal_action_client/member_functions.cpp2generated sequences are FixedSequence/HeapSequence, not std::vector: .back() is spelled [length() - 1] (adding back() would move the codegen version surface, for one line)
rclcpp/executors/multithreaded_executor/multithreaded_executor.cpp18MultiThreadedExecutor is refused (one task per executor, no hidden threads) — renamed to SingleThreadedExecutor; callback groups: create_callback_group(CallbackGroupType) / SubscriptionOptions::callback_group / CallbackGroup::SharedPtr have no counterpart (every group is mutually exclusive on one task); the group plumbing is deleted

Two surfaces: freestanding, and NROS_CPP_STD

One set of headers ships two API shapes, and a build picks one.

The freestanding surface is the default and it is not a fallback. It is plain C++14 with no standard library, no exceptions and no RTTI: rclcpp::Node, create_* writing through an out-reference and returning an rclcpp::Result, const char* for names, uint64_t period_ms for durations. It is the surface for every node written for nano-ros, native host builds included.

The std surface is an opt-in and it is reached only by defining NROS_CPP_STD. Defining it turns on the six NROS_CPP_HAS_* capability macros in rclcpp/detail/std_detect.hpp, and with them: the std::string / std::function / std::chrono / std::vector convenience overloads in nros/std_compat.hpp, the RCLCPP_*_STREAM logging macros, and — the piece that actually motivates the flag — rclcpp::Node’s upstream-shaped factories, which return std::shared_ptr and take const std::string& names.

Do I need this flag?

The split is ported rclcpp code versus code written for nano-ros. It is not host versus embedded. A native Linux build does not want the flag any more than a Cortex-M3 build does; a ported node wants it on both.

You are…FlagWhy
writing a new node against rclcpp::Node / rclcpp::Publisher<M> / rclcpp::ExecutornoThe freestanding surface is the whole API you are using. This is the common case on every platform, native included.
compiling an upstream ROS 2 .cpp unmodified — it says class MyNode : public rclcpp::Node, std::make_shared<MyNode>(), create_publisher<M>(...) returning a SharedPtryesThose signatures are spelled in std::shared_ptr and std::string. Without the flag they do not exist and you get a compile error naming a missing overload.
passing a std::string topic name or a std::chrono period into an otherwise nano-ros-native fileyesThose are the std_compat.hpp overloads.
building for Zephyr, FreeRTOS, NuttX, ThreadX, or any -ffreestanding toolchainnoAnd here it is not merely unnecessary: asking for the std surface asks the headers to #include <string>, which on those toolchains is either absent or a hard #error.

If you are unsure, build without it. The failure direction is loud: a missing overload at compile time, never a silent behaviour change.

Turning it on

Define it on the target, not per file:

target_compile_definitions(my_ported_node PRIVATE NROS_CPP_STD=1)

Per target rather than per #define-before-include, because the macro changes the layout of rclcpp::Node (it carries hosted-only members and an enable_shared_from_this base), so two translation units of one image that disagree about it are an ODR/layout break rather than a missing function. An image may set the flag on one module and not another, so keep the definition at target granularity and give every translation unit of a target the same answer.

A ported package usually needs none of this. nano-ros’s ament surface sets NROS_CPP_STD=1 on every target its ament_* verbs create, and find_package(rclcpp) sets it on whatever links rclcpp::rclcpp, so a ported package already has the surface it needs; see Porting a ROS 2 C++ node.

The ported shape

With the flag set, an upstream node’s own spelling compiles: std::make_shared, SharedPtr returns, a std::string topic, a QoS depth, a capturing lambda and a std::chrono period.

#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>
#include "std_msgs/std_msgs.hpp"

using namespace std::chrono_literals;

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    rclcpp::init(argc, argv);
    auto node = std::make_shared<rclcpp::Node>("talker");
    auto pub = node->create_publisher<std_msgs::msg::Int32>("chatter", 10);
    int count = 0;
    auto timer = node->create_wall_timer(1s, [&]() {
        std_msgs::msg::Int32 msg;
        msg.data = ++count;
        pub->publish(msg);
    });
    rclcpp::spin(node);
    rclcpp::shutdown();
}

A failed create_* here ABORTS, naming the call, because upstream throws and nano-ros has no exceptions. To handle the failure instead, use the Result-returning forms above.

Why it is not detected for you

Earlier releases discovered the capability macros from the include path with __has_include, so a hosted compiler handed you the std-flavoured API whether you asked for it or not. That was removed because no probe answers the question correctly on both embedded toolchains:

__STDC_HOSTED____has_include(<string>)#include <string>
arm-none-eabi 13.2, -ffreestanding (FreeRTOS)0TRUEhard #error
Zephyr -nostdinc++, minimal libcpp1FALSEabsent
hosted g++ 12.31TRUEworks

Each probe is right on exactly one embedded toolchain and wrong on the other: libstdc++ 13 added bits/requires_hosted.h, so header presence stopped implying usability. Only the request is right on both, because it is not a probe — it is you saying which surface you want. The full measurement is in the comments of rclcpp/detail/std_detect.hpp.

Hosted-only shapes

Subscriptions with MessageInfo (hosted)

On a hosted build (NROS_CPP_STD) a dispatch subscription’s callback may take upstream’s const rclcpp::MessageInfo& as a second argument, after the message in any of its four forms (const M&, std::shared_ptr<const M>, std::shared_ptr<M>, std::unique_ptr<M>):

auto sub = node->create_subscription<std_msgs::msg::Int32>(
    "/chatter", 10, [](const std_msgs::msg::Int32& msg, const rclcpp::MessageInfo& info) {
        const auto& r = info.get_rmw_message_info();
        printf("%d from seq %llu at %lld ns\n", msg.data,
               (unsigned long long)r.publication_sequence_number, (long long)r.source_timestamp);
    });

get_rmw_message_info() carries source_timestamp, received_timestamp, publication_sequence_number, reception_sequence_number and the 24-byte publisher_gid, as the backend reported them. A backend that reports none (XRCE, uORB) leaves every field zero. from_intra_process is always false. A freestanding build refuses the shape at compile time: the metadata path keeps the callable on the heap. SubscriptionOptions::message_info = true with a callback that takes no MessageInfo aborts the create, because it would otherwise configure nothing.

Actions with upstream’s goal handles (hosted)

On a hosted build (NROS_CPP_STD) the stock rclcpp_action spellings are drop-ins over the two classes above:

using Fibonacci = example_interfaces::action::Fibonacci;
using GoalHandle = rclcpp_action::ServerGoalHandle<Fibonacci>;
using namespace std::placeholders;

// Server: free factory over the node interfaces, std::bind-ed members.
rclcpp_action::Server<Fibonacci>::SharedPtr server = rclcpp_action::create_server<Fibonacci>(
    get_node_base_interface(), get_node_clock_interface(), get_node_logging_interface(),
    get_node_waitables_interface(), "fibonacci",
    std::bind(&MyNode::handle_goal, this, _1, _2),    // (const GoalUUID&, shared_ptr<const Goal>)
    std::bind(&MyNode::handle_cancel, this, _1),      // (shared_ptr<GoalHandle>)
    std::bind(&MyNode::handle_accepted, this, _1));   // (shared_ptr<GoalHandle>)
// in handle_accepted: goal_handle->get_goal(), ->publish_feedback(fb),
// ->is_canceling(), ->succeed(result) / ->abort(result) / ->canceled(result)

// Client: SendGoalOptions' upstream fields, bound per goal by async_send_goal.
auto client = rclcpp_action::create_client<Fibonacci>(this, "fibonacci");
auto opts = rclcpp_action::Client<Fibonacci>::SendGoalOptions();
opts.goal_response_callback = [](rclcpp_action::ClientGoalHandle<Fibonacci>::SharedPtr h) {};
opts.feedback_callback = [](auto h, const std::shared_ptr<const Fibonacci::Feedback> fb) {};
opts.result_callback = [](const rclcpp_action::Client<Fibonacci>::WrappedResult& r) {
    // r.code: rclcpp_action::ResultCode::SUCCEEDED / ABORTED / CANCELED; r.result
};
auto fut = client->async_send_goal(goal, opts);   // rclcpp::Future<GoalAccept>

// The handle-taking calls return upstream's std::shared_future.
auto result = client->async_get_result(goal_handle);   // shared_future<WrappedResult>
auto cancel = client->async_cancel_goal(goal_handle);  // shared_future<CancelResponse::SharedPtr>
if (rclcpp::spin_until_future_complete(node, result) == rclcpp::FutureReturnCode::SUCCESS) {
    const auto& wrapped = result.get();
}
// server, after handle_goal returned ACCEPT_AND_DEFER:
goal_handle->execute();   // ACCEPTED -> EXECUTING, status array published

X<A>::SharedPtr is rclcpp::Owned<X<A>> (the entity by value), and the get_node_*_interface() handles name the node and do nothing else. A goal handle is a heap token over the goal id: every call forwards to the server or client keyed by it, and the goal’s state stays in the arena. Drive it from the executor’s task only — not from a thread you started — and do not move the server while a handle is in use. The callbacks run from the executor’s dispatch, beside the client-wide set_callbacks ones. async_send_goal returns the goal-keyed rclcpp::Future<GoalAccept>, not a std::shared_future; get_goal_stamp is absent.

async_get_result / async_cancel_goal / async_cancel_all_goals / async_cancel_goals_before return a rclcpp_action::detail::DrivenSharedFuture<T>, which IS-A std::shared_future<T>: its is_ready() (what spin_until_future_complete polls), wait_for and get drive the client’s dispatch and executor while they wait, since no other thread fulfils it. Converted to a bare std::shared_future it still completes, but only when something else drives the client. Every async_get_result for one goal returns the handle’s own future; a result-aware goal’s handle is kept by the client until its result arrives, as upstream’s pending request keeps it. Cancel replies are taken by the executor’s spin, as upstream’s executor delivers them: the spin settles the waiting async_cancel_* future and runs its cancel_callback, so a caller that keeps only the callback needs no poll(). A nano-ros server acts on the zero-id cancel-all / cancel-before forms as an rclcpp server does. A reply no future claims is kept for try_recv_cancel_response, oldest first, up to rclcpp_action::CANCEL_STASH_CAP (4) per client. These need std::promise, so they are hosted-only twice over: a libstdc++ built without threads (arm-none-eabi) refuses them as a freestanding build does.

ServerGoalHandle::execute() and Server<A>::execute(goal_id) move an ACCEPTED goal to EXECUTING and publish the status array; the latter reports NotFound / NotAllowed where upstream raises. create_server executes an ACCEPT_AND_EXECUTE goal before handle_accepted; the goal-id API leaves it ACCEPTED.

Goal slots. Each action sub-client holds at most MAX_CONCURRENT_GOALS (4) requests in flight. A future dropped (or cancel()ed) before its reply frees its request’s slot, unless something else still waits on that reply — a client-wide set_callbacks hook, or an upstream goal (async_send_goal with callbacks, async_get_result). A late reply for a freed slot is dropped. On a freestanding build each of these shapes is a compile error (NROS_RCLCPP_REFUSE_ACTION_GOAL_HANDLE) naming the goal-id-keyed form above; create_client alone works there.

Action client futures

Future-based async. send_goal_future() / get_result_future() return a Future<T> keyed by its goal: each future receives only its own goal’s acceptance or result, whether the executor dispatched it during spin_once or the future’s own poll took it, and a result for a goal nobody waits on is dropped. At most MAX_CONCURRENT_GOALS of each may be pending per client; past that the send is refused and the future is empty (valid() false):

auto fut = client.send_goal_future(goal);
typename decltype(client)::GoalAccept accept;
RCLCPP_TRY(fut.wait(executor.handle(), 5000, accept));
if (accept.accepted) {
    auto rfut = client.get_result_future(accept.goal_id);
    Fibonacci::Result result;
    RCLCPP_TRY(rfut.wait(executor.handle(), 10000, result));
}

GoalAccept is a nested type on rclcpp_action::Client<A> (16-byte UUID + bool accepted).

Parameters and /parameter_events

Parameters are methods on the node (declare_parameter<T>, get_parameter<T>, set_parameter<T>, undeclare_parameter), over the executor’s one store. node.start_parameter_services() serves them on the six rcl_interfaces services, so ros2 param reaches them, and publishes /parameter_events (rcl_interfaces/msg/ParameterEvent, rmw_qos_profile_parameter_events) as rclcpp’s node does:

rclcpp::Node node;
RCLCPP_TRY(executor.create_node(node, "ctrl"));
node.declare_parameter<int64_t>("gain", 3);   // before or after: both reported
RCLCPP_TRY(node.start_parameter_services());  // start-up event: new_parameters = [gain]
node.set_parameter<int64_t>("gain", 4);       // changed_parameters = [gain]
node.undeclare_parameter("gain");             // deleted_parameters = [gain]

Each event names the node’s fully qualified name in node; the events are published on the next spin. The image needs the param_services capability. One publisher per executor serves every node. It is on for every served node unless the node was built with rclcpp::NodeOptions().start_parameter_event_publisher(false), which opts that one node out; the other nodes keep publishing.

To react to OTHER nodes’ changes, a hosted build has rclcpp::ParameterEventHandler. It subscribes to /parameter_events once, on the node you give it:

auto handler = std::make_shared<rclcpp::ParameterEventHandler>(node);
auto h = handler->add_parameter_callback(
    "gain", [](const rclcpp::Parameter& p) { use(p.as_int()); }, "/controller");
auto e = handler->add_parameter_event_callback(
    [](const rcl_interfaces::msg::ParameterEvent& ev) { /* every event */ });

Keep the handles: dropping one unregisters it, as upstream’s do. An empty node name means this node, and a relative one resolves against this node’s namespace. A parameter callback sees new and changed values, never deletions. An event callback receives the type it takes, so rcl_interfaces must be generated for the image. The per-parameter handle is rclcpp::ParameterCallbackHandle, as upstream (the handler’s nested ParameterEventHandler::ParameterCallbackHandle names the same type). A freestanding build refuses the handler at compile time; there, subscribe to /parameter_events with create_subscription yourself.

Design background

  • RFC-0089: ROS 2 API adoption, and the compile-or-conform rule — upstream’s namespaces and names, the _in rule, the hosted surface
  • RFC-0018: C++ API design — freestanding C++14, no exceptions, the Result channel

Platform API and C ABI

Reference · Level 4: Extending nano-ros

The platform API is the porting boundary between nano-ros and a concrete OS / RTOS / bare-metal target. Each platform provides a clock, optionally a heap, optionally threading, optionally networking. Platform is internal — user applications use the Rust / C / C++ APIs, not the platform vtable directly.

nano-ros separates the platform layer (clock, sleep, allocator, threading, critical section, network, timer, …) from the rest of the code via a single canonical C ABI of free extern "C" symbols. Every supported port — POSIX, FreeRTOS, NuttX, ThreadX, Zephyr, bare-metal Cortex-M, bare-metal RISC-V — implements the same symbols against its host kernel. RMW backends, codegen output, and the nros-node runtime all link against the ABI; nobody links against a specific port’s Rust crate.

Canonical reference

The SSoT C headers in packages/platform/nros-platform-api/include/nros/ (platform.h + platform_net.h, platform_timer.h, platform_zephyr.h; Rust consumes committed bindgen output from them) are the source of truth. Every symbol’s brief, parameter docs, ownership rules, blocking / non-blocking classification, and ISR-safe contract live in the Doxygen compiled from those headers.

SurfaceLink
platform ABI Doxygen (canonical)HTML · headers

Regenerating the Doxygen in the tree: see Internals → Build Commands.

This page does not duplicate the interface specification — read the Doxygen for that.

Surface

Three hand-written headers under packages/platform/nros-platform-cffi/include/nros/:

HeaderPurpose
platform.hCore kernel surface: clock, sleep, alloc + heap stats, threading, scheduler, time, yield, random, critical section, opaque wake primitive.
platform_net.hNetwork surface: TCP/UDP/multicast socket helpers, endpoint resolution, IVC.
platform_timer.hPeriodic timer surface (nros_platform_timer_*).

Every symbol has the prefix nros_platform_. A drift gate (scripts/check-platform-abi-mirror.sh) walks each header and asserts that the unsafe extern "C" {} mirror block in packages/platform/nros-platform-cffi/src/lib.rs declares the same set — no symbol can land in C without its Rust mirror, no Rust mirror can declare a symbol without a C header decl. CI runs the gate on every build.

Capability groups

Within platform.h, the symbols are grouped by trait. Each group is exported by one Rust trait + one C-port section + one drift-gate match. Adding a capability means adding a row to every column.

CapabilityRust traitC sectionSymbols
ClockPlatformClockclock_nsnros_platform_clock_ns
SleepPlatformSleepsleep_msnros_platform_sleep_ms
AllocPlatformAllocmalloc/realloc/freenros_platform_alloc{,_realloc,_free}
ThreadingPlatformThreadingmutex/condvar/tasknros_platform_{mutex,condvar,task}_*
Critical sectionPlatformCriticalSectionper-CPU interrupt masknros_platform_critical_section_{acquire,release}
SchedulerPlatformSchedulertask hintsnros_platform_scheduler_*
TimePlatformTimewall-clocknros_platform_time_now_ns
YieldPlatformYieldcooperative yieldnros_platform_yield_now
RandomPlatformRandombest-effort RNGnros_platform_random_*
WakePlatformThreading (wake methods)opaque binary-semaphorenros_platform_wake_{init,drop,wait_ms,signal,signal_from_isr,storage_size,storage_align}

platform_net.h covers TCP/UDP/multicast/IVC, and platform_timer.h covers periodic timers. The shapes follow the same pattern: trait → macro → header → drift gate.

How a port is built

A port can be written in either of two ways. The choice is per-port and not visible to consumers — both shapes resolve to the same symbols.

Path A — Rust trait + macro export

The Rust crate implements PlatformClock, PlatformAlloc, PlatformThreading, … on a marker type, then invokes one of the export macros:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use nros_platform_api::{
    PlatformClock, PlatformSleep, PlatformAlloc, PlatformThreading,
    PlatformCriticalSection,
    nros_platform_export, nros_platform_export_net, nros_platform_export_timer,
};

pub struct PosixPlatform;
impl PlatformClock for PosixPlatform { /* … */ }
impl PlatformSleep for PosixPlatform { /* … */ }
// … etc.

nros_platform_export!(PosixPlatform);
nros_platform_export_net!(PosixPlatform);
nros_platform_export_timer!(PosixPlatform);
}

The macros expand to the full set of #[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn nros_platform_* bodies forwarding to the trait calls. This is what nros-platform-posix does today. It is also what the bare-metal board crates (nros-platform-mps2-an385, nros-platform-stm32f4) use: there is no host kernel to write idiomatic C against, so the single-task stub impls are written in Rust and exported via the macro.

Path B — pure C port

The kernel-side ports (FreeRTOS, NuttX, ThreadX, Zephyr) write the bodies directly in src/platform.c, src/net.c, src/timer.c inside each packages/platform/nros-platform-<rtos>/ directory. The Rust side has no implementation file — the build script (or parent build system: NuttX make, Zephyr west module) compiles the C sources against the kernel’s headers.

Pure-C bodies are the more natural fit when the kernel already speaks C and ships C headers (xSemaphoreCreate*, k_sem_*, tx_thread_*): the impl is one-to-one with the kernel call, no FFI dance through Rust’s calling convention. The shared crate nros-platform-critical-section is the canonical example for a single-symbol shim: the Rust side just calls the externs and registers the result with critical_section::set_impl!.

Adding a new port — checklist

  1. Decide A vs B. Greenfield host build with a Rust crate available? Path A. Vendor RTOS with a C SDK and no Rust toolchain on the build machine? Path B.
  2. Mirror, don’t extend. Implement every symbol in the three headers. The drift gate fails the build otherwise. If the kernel genuinely cannot provide a primitive, return the documented sentinel value (-1 for task_init on single-task RTOS, 0 for mutex_* on single-core no-preempt hardware) rather than skipping the symbol.
  3. Write the smoke test. Land a tests/<port>-c-smoke/ mini-app that links the new C port against the canonical headers and calls a representative symbol from each capability group. Wire it into just <port> test-c-port. The smoke tests are the runtime parity layer that the drift gate cannot enforce.
  4. For platforms that emit critical_section::Impl (i.e. anything that consumes a critical-section-using crate), make sure the binary pulls nros-platform-critical-section once — it does the critical_section::set_impl!(PlatformCs) registration against the canonical externs. Binaries that don’t need the global registration don’t pay for it.
  5. Update the drift gate’s smoke list (the HEADERS_REQUIRE_MACRO array in scripts/check-platform-abi-mirror.sh) if you add a new header. Adding a symbol to an existing header needs no script change — the grep is generic.

The scalar / opaque-struct boundary

Not every kernel service unifies the same way. The ABI splits into two classes, and the split is a design boundary, not tech debt:

  • Scalar services — fully unified. Alloc, sleep, clock, time, yield, random. Their ABI is plain scalars (sizes, millisecond counts, byte buffers) with no host-type in the signature, so a single canonical nros_platform_* symbol works for every RTOS and every consumer (core, RMW, vendored zenoh-pico/XRCE) funnels through it. The allocation gate (check-no-direct-kernel-alloc.sh) enforces this for allocation; the same pattern extends to the other scalars (the vendored z_*/uxr_* funnel is checked by a CI relink lane).

  • Opaque-struct services — stay per-RTOS-vendored. Threading (mutex/condvar/task), the wake primitive, and network sockets carry RTOS-defined structs (SemaphoreHandle_t, TX_MUTEX, struct k_mutex, socket/NX_* control blocks) whose layout the vendor owns. A single C ABI cannot name those types portably, so each port vendors its own body and nano-ros exposes only opaque storage (*_storage_size/*_storage_align + an init/drop pair). This is why the ThreadX board’s tx_byte_allocate thread-stack / NetX-pool sites are not allocation-gate violations — they are the task and net opaque services, allowed on a documented symbol-scoped lint allowlist.

Escape hatch (if an opaque service must move later). The way out is NOT to widen the C ABI with host types; it is to pin a canonical fixed-layout struct in platform.h, give each port a compile-time size_probe / _Static_assert that the canonical layout is ≥ the vendor struct (so opaque storage stays sound), and let the port memcpy/place the vendor object inside the canonical slot. Net is the first candidate — platform_net.h already exposes 29 symbols over an opaque socket handle — but it is deferred (out of scope for the platform split) until there is a consumer that needs portable socket structs. Threads and sync are the least likely to move (deepest struct coupling).

Why free symbols (not a vtable struct)

The RMW layer uses a NrosRmwVtable fn-ptr struct because a single binary registers multiple backends at runtime (bridge nodes). Platforms are different: one platform per binary, resolved at link time. A vtable would add an indirection on every clock read, every mutex lock, every socket send — overhead with no upside, because there is nobody to swap. Free symbols let the linker resolve calls direct, let LTO inline across the boundary, and let static analysis treat them like any other extern.

The full rationale is in docs/design/0006-portable-rmw-platform-interface.md under “Platform ABI: free symbols (no vtable)”.

RMW API

Reference · Level 4: Extending nano-ros

The RMW (ROS middleware) vtable is the porting boundary between nano-ros and a concrete pub/sub transport (zenoh-pico, XRCE-DDS, Cyclone DDS, uORB, …). RMW is internal — user applications use the Rust / C / C++ APIs, not the vtable directly.

Canonical reference

The C vtable nros_rmw_vtable_t is the source of truth. Every function pointer’s brief, parameter docs, ownership rules (buffer-borrowed vs caller-owned), blocking / non-blocking classification, return-code conventions, and lifetime contract for loaned slots live in the Doxygen output.
