Message Binding Generation

Reference · Level 2: Building real applications

nros uses generated Rust bindings for ROS 2 message types. nros build generates no_std compatible bindings from each package’s package.xml dependencies before it builds (nros configure does that step alone, and nros interface generate rust the codegen alone).

Overview

The binding generator is part of the nros CLI and provides:

  • Pure Rust, no_std compatible output using heapless types
  • Automatic dependency resolution through your ROS 2 install’s ament index
  • the [patch.crates-io] rows that point the nano-ros runtime crates at the SDK root, written into the image’s generated build settings

Prerequisites

  1. package.xml in each node package - Declares ROS interface dependencies

    <?xml version="1.0"?>
<package format="3">
  <name>my_package</name>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
  <description>My nros package</description>
  <maintainer email="dev@example.com">Developer</maintainer>
  <license>Apache-2.0</license>
  <depend>std_msgs</depend>
  <depend>geometry_msgs</depend>
  <export>
    <build_type>ament_cargo</build_type>
  </export>
</package>

  2. nros tool built + on PATH

    Install a release; install.sh puts nros in ~/.nros/bin:

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.nros/bin:$PATH"

    See Installation for the full walkthrough.

  3. A ROS 2 install, sourced for the first build

    The bindings are generated from the message definitions of your ROS 2 install, std_msgs included, so the generated layouts and type hashes match the ROS 2 nodes you talk to. Source it before the first nros build, nros run or nros configure of a project:

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash

    That configure records the prefix (AMENT_PREFIX_PATH) in the project, and later configures reuse it, so later shells need not source ROS. With neither, configure refuses and names this step. A project whose packages depend on no message package at all needs no ROS 2.

Workflow

Step 1: Create package.xml

Declare your ROS interface dependencies in <depend> tags:

<depend>std_msgs</depend>      <!-- For std_msgs::msg::Int32, String, etc. -->
<depend>example_interfaces</depend>  <!-- For service types -->

Step 2: Build

cd my_ws
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash   # the first build of the workspace only
nros build

Before it builds, this will:

  1. Parse package.xml to find dependencies
  2. Resolve transitive dependencies through the ament index
  3. Filter to interface packages (those with msg/srv/action)
  4. Generate bindings into the workspace’s generated/ directory
  5. Resolve the bringup’s launch file into the system model
  6. Write each image’s build settings under build/, carrying the board’s triple and flags, the resolved pool budgets, and the [patch.crates-io] rows for the nano-ros runtime crates

Each step is redone only when its inputs changed. To run them without building (before opening the workspace in an IDE, for instance), use nros configure. nros interface generate rust is the codegen-only step underneath — steps 1–4 and nothing else — and is useful when you want bindings without a workspace.

Step 3: there is no step 3 — package.xml is the dependency list

A generated message crate is a path dependency on its own directory, and nros build writes that row for you, before it plans: one per <depend> / <build_depend> / <exec_depend> that names a message package, tagged # nros-managed:

[dependencies]
std_msgs = { path = "../../generated/std_msgs", default-features = false }  # nros-managed
example_interfaces = { path = "../../generated/example_interfaces", default-features = false }  # nros-managed

So adding a message package is one edit — the <depend> — exactly as on the C/C++ road, and deleting the <depend> deletes the row on the next build. A row without the tag is yours: the build never edits or removes it, so deleting the tag is how you take a row over. The nros row is not managed — it carries a feature choice that is yours to make.

Never name a message crate by registry version (std_msgs = "*"): those crates are generated per host from your ament install, they are not published, and a bare name resolves against the public crates.io instead.

The nano-ros runtime crates are the other case — nros, nros-board-<board>, the backends — and they are registry-named with version = "*", because the build writes the [patch.crates-io] rows that redirect them into the nano-ros SDK root.

Why msg crates are RMW-agnostic

Generated msg crates carry only the wire-format data type — no backend-specific code, no per-RMW Cargo feature. A user manifest is the plain pair:

[dependencies]
std_msgs = { path = "../../generated/std_msgs", default-features = false }  # nros-managed
nros     = { version = "*" }

Transport choice and message schema are orthogonal concerns and the manifest reflects that. (Which backend you actually get is [system] rmw in the bringup’s system.toml, not a feature you pick here — see Switch the RMW per image.) This matches upstream rclcpp + rclrs, which both ship msg packages RMW-agnostic and let the RMW pick which descriptor representation it wants at runtime.

For DDS-based backends that need a per-type descriptor on the wire (Cyclone DDS today), the nros-rmw-cyclonedds shim builds those descriptors lazily on first pub/sub for a given message type, walks the static field schema exposed by nros-serdes (the Message trait with const TYPE_NAME + const FIELDS), and caches the result in a bounded no_std registry. No per-msg-pkg backend code is required.

The registry is bounded by the NROS_CYCLONEDDS_MAX_TYPES sizing knob.

Where the nano-ros sources come from

A project uses the SDK root the nros binary belongs to — a release’s own share/nano-ros — so a plain nros build works anywhere. To name a different SDK root, pass it:

nros build --nano-ros-path <sdk-root>

The build then writes the [patch.crates-io] rows into each image’s generated settings, pointing each nros* requirement at a directory in the SDK root. Nothing about the location is baked into a tracked file, so moving the workspace, or installing another release, needs no edit: the next build re-points it.

Use in code

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std_msgs::msg::Int32;
use example_interfaces::srv::{AddTwoInts, AddTwoIntsRequest, AddTwoIntsResponse};

let msg = Int32 { data: 42 };
}

Command Options

nros interface generate rust is the codegen step alone — it writes bindings and nothing else:

nros interface generate rust [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --manifest <PATH>         Path to package.xml [default: package.xml]
  -o, --output <DIR>            Output directory [default: generated]
      --ros-edition <EDITION>   humble | iron | jazzy [default: humble]
      --codegen-config <PATH>   Explicit per-field capacity config (nros-codegen.toml)
      --rename <OLD=NEW>        Rename a generated package
      --force                   Overwrite existing bindings
  -v, --verbose                 Enable verbose output

It also still accepts --generate-config / --nano-ros-path / --nano-ros-git, which write a .cargo/config.toml beside a package by hand. Those are the old shape and are not the path to use: nros build writes the patches into the generated settings instead, where they are regenerated rather than committed.

Generated Output Structure

my_ws/
├── src/
│   ├── my_node/
│   │   ├── package.xml      # Your dependency declarations
│   │   ├── Cargo.toml       # Your package manifest (a library)
│   │   └── src/lib.rs       # Your code using generated types
│   └── my_node_bringup/
│       ├── package.xml
│       └── system.toml      # Board, RMW, components
├── generated/               # Generated bindings (do not edit)
│   ├── std_msgs/
│   │   ├── Cargo.toml
│   │   └── src/
│   │       ├── lib.rs       # #![no_std]
│   │       └── msg/
│   │           ├── mod.rs
│   │           └── int32.rs
│   └── builtin_interfaces/  # Transitive dependency
│       └── ...
└── build/                   # Build output (do not commit)
    └── …/<image>_entry/     # each image's generated entry and its cargo settings, incl. the patches

Generated Code Features

no_std by default:

#![allow(unused)]
#![no_std]

fn main() {
pub mod msg;
}

std feature for optional std support:

[features]
default = []
std = ["nros-core/std", "nros-serdes/std"]

heapless types for embedded:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct String {
    pub data: heapless::String<256>,
}

pub struct Arrays {
    pub data: heapless::Vec<i32, 64>,
}
}

Service types with Request/Response:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct AddTwoInts;
pub struct AddTwoIntsRequest { pub a: i64, pub b: i64 }
pub struct AddTwoIntsResponse { pub sum: i64 }

impl RosService for AddTwoInts {
    type Request = AddTwoIntsRequest;
    type Reply = AddTwoIntsResponse;
}
}

A timestamp message gets SecNanosecMsg, so Time::to_ros_msg() can return it:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl nros_core::SecNanosecMsg for Time {
    fn from_sec_nanosec(sec: i32, nanosec: u32) -> Self { Self { sec, nanosec } }
}
}

Emitted for every message whose field set is exactly { int32 sec, uint32 nanosec } — builtin_interfaces/msg/Time, its Duration twin, and any message of yours with that shape. It is what makes the call a publisher writes work:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
msg.header.stamp = node.now().to_ros_msg();
}

nros-core cannot name a message type — every generated crate depends on it, and your message crates are generated from your packages — so the conversion is implemented on the generated side and the trait is the seam. The C++ side spells the same thing as a template (node.now().to_msg(msg.header.stamp)); Rust has no structural bound, so it needs the named trait. There is no Result: nros’s Time already is { sec, nanosec }, so nothing can fail. (rclrs returns Result<_, TryFromIntError> because its Time is i64 nanoseconds; a ported t.to_ros_msg()? will not compile here, and deleting the ? is the fix.)

Examples

Each example on GitHub is a workspace that carries its own bringup and resolves on its own, so it builds wherever it lives. Build each from its own root:

cd my_talker_ws && nros build
cd my_service_client_ws && nros build

Regenerating Bindings

To regenerate after ROS package updates or dependency changes:

nros interface generate rust --force

Where the definitions come from

nros build reads message definitions from the ROS 2 install you sourced (or the one the project’s first configure recorded), through AMENT_PREFIX_PATH. The release carries copies of a few standard packages, but they only fill gaps under a ROS 2 install, never stand in for one: with no prefix set and none recorded, configure refuses rather than build from them, because they would silently fix a ROS 2 distro and the types would stop matching a peer on another one. A message package in your own workspace shadows the installed one of the same name.

Troubleshooting

“AMENT_PREFIX_PATH is unset and no configure of … has recorded one to reuse”

  • This shell has not sourced ROS 2, and this project has never been configured from one that had. Run source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash (or your overlay’s install/setup.bash), then build again.

“Package ‘X’ not found in ament index or bundled interfaces”

  • Source the ROS 2 environment: source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
  • Check package is installed: ros2 pkg list | grep X
  • Install if missing: sudo apt install ros-humble-X

Build errors with generated code

  • Regenerate with --force flag
  • Check nros crate compatibility

Which CMake spelling (one table)

Five codegen entry points exist in the CMake surface. They are NOT interchangeable spellings of one thing — each serves one audience, and two are back-compat only. Pick by what you are doing:

You are…UseNotes
Consuming an existing msg package from an app/node pkgfind_package(<pkg> REQUIRED)The recommended default. The smart Find-stub resolves the package through the 3-layer search (workspace → ament → bundled) and generates bindings on the fly. Zero codegen calls in your file.
Defining msgs in a message packagerosidl_generate_interfaces(${PROJECT_NAME} msg/… DEPENDENCIES …)Recommended — the stock ROS shape, intercepted by nano-ros. Your msg pkg carries zero nano-ros-specific lines and cross-builds under colcon unchanged.
Defining msgs and you want the nano-ros verb explicitly (or C bindings)nano_ros_generate_interfaces(<name> <files…> [LANGUAGE C|CPP] [DEPENDENCIES …])The ament-shape alias. Defaults to LANGUAGE CPP like rosidl — pass LANGUAGE C for C.
Building a workspace root with several msg pkgsnros_workspace_interfaces() after set(NROS_INTERFACE_SEARCH_PATH …/src)Bulk-builds every workspace msg pkg in topological order; one line, no per-pkg add_subdirectory.
Generating this pkg’s package.xml dependencies (no find_package flow)nros_find_interfaces([LANGUAGE C|CPP] [SKIP_INSTALL])Consume-by-manifest: resolves the transitive interface closure of your own package.xml. Used by the workspace node pkgs. Defaults LANGUAGE CPP.
—nros_generate_interfaces(<target> <files…>)Deprecated for new code. The low-level generator everything above routes through; direct calls are back-compat only.

C Code Generation (CMake)

nano_ros_generate_interfaces(… LANGUAGE C) generates C bindings for .msg, .srv, and .action files (the function defaults to C++ — the LANGUAGE C argument is what makes it the C generator). It uses a bundled codegen library — no external nros binary needed.

Prerequisites

nano_ros_generate_interfaces() becomes available automatically once the consumer’s CMakeLists.txt invokes add_subdirectory(nano-ros). The codegen tool ships inside the in-tree nros CLI binary (packages/cli/target/release/nros; the old nros-codegen submodule is retired); cmake auto-resolves it from PATH / packages/cli/target/release/ / the transitional ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/bin/. No separate build step.

Usage

For a complete example, see the features workspace, examples/workspaces/features: its custom_msgs package defines a message, and c_reading_talker_pkg and c_reading_listener_pkg use the generated C bindings. The custom-message feature demo is a node package there, with its own image row.

Design background

  • RFC-0067: environment-invariant message dependency identity
  • RFC-0048: CMake ament consumption
  • RFC-0122: behaviour bringups, single-node witnesses, and cadence-backed CI. Feature demos as node packages of the features workspace.

What nros build Produces

Reference · Level 3: Production and tuning

nros build ends at an artifact and stops. It discovers your packages, resolves the image, checks the toolchain, generates the root build file and the entry, and then hands off to the native tool — cargo, cmake or west. The last stage is an exec, so the artifact is exactly the one that tool would have produced had you run it yourself.

This page answers the question the build does not: what are you holding, and where is it?

Running it: nros run and nros flash

nros run starts an image whose board is a host process or an emulator: it builds the image if it is stale, starts the router the image’s link needs, streams the console and stops everything when it ends (--expect <text> grades the console, --dry-run --why prints the plan it would execute). How a board is launched is stated once, in its descriptor’s [board.run], so the command nros build prints as its next step is the one nros run executes.

Real silicon is flashed, not run: nros run refuses a hardware image and names nros flash --monitor. nros flash builds the image if stale, runs the board’s human steps ([board.flash] prepare), flashes through the method its descriptor’s [board.flash] names (west, or a command template), and with --monitor watches the console on the same port; --expect <text> grades it as nros run does. nros monitor opens the console of a board that is already running. The port comes from --port, NROS_PORT, the bench file (nros bench scan) or the one attached device that matches the board.

The commands quoted below are the board tooling’s, reproduced here as a reference for a board no flash method covers yet.

There is also no install step: nros build never runs cmake --install, writes no install/ prefix and stages nothing. Whatever the native tool wrote in its own build tree is the deliverable.

Where it lands

Which tool builds an image is decided by its platform and by whether the workspace crosses languages:

platform / shapedriverthe artifact
Rust-only workspace, any non-Zephyr boardcargo<ws>/build/<coordinate>/<image>_entry/target/[<triple>/]<profile>/<image>_entry
any workspace containing C or C++cmake<ws>/build/<coordinate>/cmake/<image>_entry
a zephyr boardwest<ws>/build/<coordinate>/<bringup>__<image>_west/zephyr/zephyr.{elf,bin,exe}

The coordinate is the platform and the RMW — posix-zenoh, freertos-cyclonedds — plus, for CMake, the board, because CMake pins one compiler per configure and two boards on one platform would otherwise share a cache: posix-zenoh-linux, freertos-zenoh-mps2-an385-freertos.

Everything above is under build/, and that is the rule rather than a coincidence: a workspace has no root Cargo.toml and no root CMakeLists.txt. It is a directory of packages, like a colcon workspace, and every generated thing — the entry, the root build file, the cargo settings, the compiled output — lives in build/.

After a successful build nros build prints the artifact itself, and the board’s own command that runs or flashes it — never running either:

nros build: next for `c_talker_node_bringup:linux`:
  artifact: /home/you/c_talker_ws/build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry
  run:
    /home/you/c_talker_ws/build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry

What the run: (or flash) line is depends on the board: the binary for a host board, the board’s QEMU runner with the provisioned qemu-system-* for an emulated one, west build -d <dir> -t run / west flash -d <dir> for Zephyr. --dry-run and --check build nothing, so they print no such block.

One path the build also prints is easy to mistake for the binary:

nros build:   entry → …/build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry

That is the generated entry package — source that nano-ros wrote for you, under build/ because it is build output. The compiled program is elsewhere; see below.

cargo

Every image gets its own cargo settings file, build/<coordinate>/<entry>/nros-cargo.toml, and nros build points cargo at it:

cargo build --manifest-path build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/Cargo.toml \
            --config build/posix-zenoh/linux_entry/nros-cargo.toml

That file states the image’s target-dir, so each image compiles into its own tree rather than sharing one target/. It also carries the board’s triple, linker flags and cross compiler, the resolved pool budgets as [env], the in-repo [patch.crates-io] rows, and the nros-* build profiles. It is generated on every build — read it, never edit it.

The artifact is the generated entry’s binary, inside that entry’s own target dir:

<ws>/build/<coordinate>/<image>_entry/target/[<triple>/]<profile-dir>/<image>_entry

The triple level appears whenever the board pins one — which it does in the generated [build] target, not on your command line.

A Linux image on Cyclone DDS, for instance, is build/posix-cyclonedds/linux_entry/target/debug/linux_entry.

<profile-dir> is debug unless the image declares [image.<id>] profile = …, in which case it is that profile’s directory (cargo’s rule: a profile builds into the directory of its own name, and dev into debug).

Next step: on a host board, run it. It is an ordinary executable.

./build/linux/target/debug/talker

For a QEMU board, the generated settings file also carries that board’s runner, so cargo run through the same --config boots the image — see Build Profiles for driving cargo yourself.

A multi-process zenoh example also needs a router; that is ROS’s rmw_zenohd, not something nano-ros ships — see Deployment Workflow and ROS 2 and the Zenoh router.

C, C++ and mixed workspaces (cmake)

CMake is chosen whenever the package graph contains anything that is not Rust, on the host and when cross-compiling alike. The generated root is <ws>/build/<coordinate>/CMakeLists.txt, it is configured into <ws>/build/<coordinate>/cmake/, and each image’s executable lands at the top of that directory:

<ws>/build/<coordinate>/cmake/<image>_entry

For example, examples/workspaces/c builds [image.linux] to build/posix-zenoh-linux/cmake/linux_entry and its FreeRTOS image to build/freertos-zenoh-mps2-an385-freertos/cmake/freertos_entry. (Node packages also build their own executables, under cmake/pkg/<pkg>/<pkg>; the image is the one at the top level.)

The file has no extension in either case. On the host it is a host executable; for a cross board it is a statically linked ELF for that architecture — the FreeRTOS one above is ELF 32-bit LSB executable, ARM, EABI5, statically linked.

Next step:

  • host — run it directly.
  • QEMU — the ELF is what -kernel takes, with the machine and CPU your board’s guide names.
  • hardware — hand the ELF to your flasher (probe-rs, OpenOCD, a vendor tool). nano-ros has no opinion about which.

Zephyr (west)

nros build resolves your application and its overlays and runs west build from the workspace root with each image’s OWN build directory, <ws>/build/<coordinate>/<bringup>__<image>_west (west’s default, build/ under the cwd, would put every image of a workspace in one tree and refuse the second). Pass -- -d <dir> to choose another. Zephyr writes its image under zephyr/ inside it; for demo_bringup:zephyr on zenoh:

<ws>/build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.elf   # always
<ws>/build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.exe   # native_sim — a host executable
<ws>/build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.bin   # cross targets — the raw image
<ws>/build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.map   # the link map

Which of .exe and .bin appears is Zephyr’s choice, not nano-ros’s: a native_sim build produces zephyr.exe, a Cortex-M build produces zephyr.bin.

Next step — Zephyr’s own verbs, against the image’s build directory (nros build prints whichever the board supports):

west build -d build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west -t run   # native_sim and emulated boards
west flash -d build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west          # hardware: the board's flash runner
./build/zephyr-zenoh/demo_bringup__zephyr_west/zephyr/zephyr.exe    # native_sim: the same as -t run

The -d is not optional here: without it west uses build/ under the current directory, which is not where nros build put the image. west flash picks its runner from the board’s own board.cmake; nano-ros adds nothing to it.

Finding it yourself

When in doubt, ask the build what it is about to do. --dry-run prints the stages and the exact command, and performs no I/O:

nros build <image> --dry-run

The tool named in that command owns the output location, and its own documentation is the authority — which is the whole point of handing off rather than wrapping.

For the generation side of this — which root file is written, why the entry is derived rather than hand-written, and what the coordinate directory holds — see What nros build generates.

The generated entry

Part of the entryDerived from
the no_std / no_main shellthe board’s entry_kind
board boilerplate (use panic_semihosting as _;, esp_app_desc!())the board descriptor’s entry.crate_root_extra
nros::main!(launch = …, args = …)the image
nros::main! formMeaning
nros::main!(launch = "demo_bringup")the bringup’s default launch file
nros::main!(launch = "demo_bringup:sim.launch.xml")a named launch file
nros::main!(launch = "…:multihost.launch.xml", args = [("host", "robot1")])one host’s slice, by launch argument
nros::main!(model = "demo_bringup")deprecated: names the resolved model instead of its input
nros::main!(board = X)retired: a compile error

On the CMake driver, the generated root holds one nano_ros_add_executable(<name> BOARD … BRINGUP … LAUNCH … LANG … TYPED DEPLOY …) per image, with no SOURCES: the verb generates the translation unit that carries main. nano_ros_entry(NAME … LANG … BRINGUP … LAUNCH …) is the hand-written spelling, in an entry taken over with nros materialize.

To add a board, as a package of your own or contributed to nano-ros, see Adding a Board to the Registry.

Caveats by chip family

  • Cortex-M0+ (RP2040, STM32F0, nRF51): only 4 NVIC priority levels. Per-callback OS-priority dispatch (a research scheduler shape originally proposed by Choi et al. as PiCAS, RTAS ’21) is disqualified on this class; nano-ros’s user-space EDF / FIFO scheduler is the only option. Pub/sub works fine.
  • Xtensa (ESP32, ESP32-S2, ESP32-S3): not supported. nano-ros has no Xtensa board, and the RISC-V ESP32 boards are retired (ESP32 — retired).
  • Cortex-A9 / A53: hosted-RTOS only (NuttX, Zephyr). Heap + libc required; bare-metal Cortex-A is not in the coverage matrix.
  • PX4 boards: NuttX is the underlying kernel; the PX4 module template is the canonical entry path — see PX4 Autopilot.

What you get, at which version, tested how hard — the analogue of Rust’s platform-support page. Version strings on this page are parsed from nros-sdk-index.toml and rust-toolchain.toml (the pinning SSoTs), so they cannot drift from what nros setup actually installs.

ROS 2 editions

EditionFeature / flagStatusNotes
Humbleros-humble (default)SupportedTypeHashNotSupported key expressions, XCDR1. No rmw_zenoh_cpp apt package — zenoh interop on Humble needs a source overlay, or use Cyclone DDS.
Ironros-ironSupportedRIHS01 type hashes. Same zenoh-apt caveat as Humble.
Jazzyros-jazzySupportedRIHS01; ships ros-jazzy-rmw-zenoh-cpp — the zenoh-interop reference edition. A default Jazzy peer encodes XCDR1/FINAL, which nano-ros speaks; per-type XCDR2 (@appendable) is not enabled.

Pick the edition of the ROS system you interop with — mismatched editions discover nothing (different key expressions).

Supported means WIRE interop, not API parity. nano-ros’s API is compared against Humble and Jazzy — Jazzy from pinned upstream sources, since it cannot be installed beside Humble (how the comparison runs). Iron is not compared on its own; what it added and Jazzy kept is covered there. Jazzy’s additions over Humble are each RULED, not each implemented: matched/incompatible-type events, timer call info, the small rclcpp accessors, count_clients/count_services, the client GID and event_type_is_supported are implemented; BEST_AVAILABLE QoS is implemented, resolved at creation against the discovered graph; dynamic typesupport, service introspection and the ~/get_type_description service are declined on RAM/flash grounds; rmw_discovery_options_t is answered by the session locator and localhost_only. Type hashes (RIHS01) are on the wire today.

Static pool inventory

Every build-time sizing knob nano-ros reads, with the default it uses when you do not set it. Set them as environment variables at BUILD time.

This page exists because knowing a knob exists is the hard part. An audit of a 256 KB image found it already tuned nine of these and still carried ~145 KB of defaults it did not know to change — every knob it needed was already there. Four separate features had each added a static pool with a knob, silently.

Pools with a computed size

Bytes are at the DEFAULTS below, computed from the pool’s own declared arithmetic (// nros-pool: in the source). Change a knob and the figure moves with it.

Pools sized by a knob, measured per image

These statics move with the knobs beside them, but their element is a struct (or the region is a heap), so no formula over defaults can state their size exactly — and a guessed multiplier is the defect this page exists to avoid. The memory report (Static memory) gives each one’s exact bytes in the image you built, beside the knobs listed here.

Every sizing knob

Every knob says what it costs: a byte figure where a formula prices it, otherwise WHERE its bytes go and why no static figure exists. Nothing in this column is blank, and nothing here is free unless it says so.

knobdefaultread bycost
NROS_ACTION_INBOX_BYTEScomputed — see packages/rmw/zenoh/nros-rmw-zenoh/build.rs:165packages/rmw/zenoh/nros-rmw-zenohpool nros_rmw_zenoh::shim::service::ACTION_INBOX: slot bytes of each action-family inbox ring; the element is an InboxStorage struct (ring header + slots), so only the compiler knows the product
NROS_ACTION_INBOX_DEPTHcomputed — see packages/rmw/zenoh/nros-rmw-zenoh/build.rs:171packages/rmw/zenoh/nros-rmw-zenohpool nros_rmw_zenoh::shim::service::ACTION_INBOX: ring depth of each action-family inbox; same InboxStorage element
NROS_BOOT_REPORTcomputed — see packages/core/nros-node/build.rs:397packages/core/nros-nodepool nros_node::boot_report::NROS_BOOT_REPORT: a switch, not a count: on (the native_sim default, and wherever CONFIG_NROS_BOOT_REPORT=y) it links the one boot-record static, measured per image by mem-report; off, it links nothing
NROS_CAPABILITY_PARAM_SERVICEScomputed — see packages/core/nros-params/build.rs:276packages/core/nros-paramsexecutor: a switch: the bringup declares param_services (Zephyr Kconfig); like NROS_PARAM_STORE it makes the executor’s storage carve the parameter store; whether the six services’ sets and request/reply pair are carved too is the param-services cargo feature
NROS_EXECUTOR_ACTION_CLIENTScomputed — see packages/tooling/nros-zephyr-build/knobs.toml:77packages/tooling/nros-zephyr-buildexecutor: action-client entries the executor arena is sized for
NROS_EXECUTOR_ARENA_SIZEcomputed — see packages/core/nros-node/build.rs:1207packages/core/nros-nodeexecutor: the executor arena itself; the backing is EXECUTOR_BACKING (Rust) or the entry’s __nros_executor_storage / sched_task table (C/C++)
NROS_EXECUTOR_BACKING_U64Scomputed — see packages/tooling/nros-zephyr-build/knobs.toml:143packages/tooling/nros-zephyr-buildexecutor: STATES the boot executor’s backing size in words; EXECUTOR_BACKING is exactly 8x this
NROS_EXECUTOR_EXTRA_SESSIONScomputed — see packages/core/nros-node/build.rs:677packages/core/nros-nodeexecutor: extra-session slots (a session plus its id, 696 B each on thumbv7em with zenoh) carved from the executor backing, at most one per node: backend_count - 1 from the sizing descriptor, else one per node

Conflicting defaults

These knobs are read in more than one place with DIFFERENT defaults, so setting one moves only part of the tree: one setting, two values in the same image.

  • NROS_SUBSCRIBER_BUFFER_SIZE

Troubleshooting — First 10 Minutes

Reference · Level 1: First contact

Every first build of a project needs ROS 2 sourced, because the messages are generated from it (A10). The First Project runs a talker in QEMU over Zenoh, so it also needs ROS 2 for the router; its Linux section runs on Cyclone DDS, where no router exists, so “no output” there is never a router problem. The First Node pages run on Linux over Zenoh and assume nros setup linux --rmw zenoh has run and the ROS 2 router (ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd) is reachable. When something goes wrong in the first ten minutes, the error you see usually points at one of the predictable misses below.

Each branch quotes the real stderr you can grep against — not a paraphrase. If your error text matches, the fix on the right is the one to try.

A. Build failures (cargo / cmake)

A1. Cargo cannot find nros

error: no matching package named `nros` found

A node package’s Cargo.toml declares nano-ros crates registry-style (nros = { version = "*" } — they are not published to crates.io); the [patch.crates-io] block that resolves them into the nano-ros SDK is GENERATED, under build/, and nros build hands it to cargo with --config. nros build and nros run write it themselves, so this error means cargo ran without it: a plain cargo build in a package, or an IDE that opened the workspace before anything was generated. Fix:

cd <the workspace root>
nros build        # or, to prepare without building: nros configure

nros configure writes the generated settings without building; nros build --dry-run prints the cargo line that uses them. Either is also what ties a copied-out workspace to an SDK (the nros binary’s own, or the one --nano-ros-path names), and runs again by itself on the next build after you move the directory.

This is not an nros setup issue — nros setup only fetches the SDK / source-package payload (zenoh-pico, mbedtls, cyclonedds, …); it does not synthesise missing Cargo dependencies.

A2. nros CLI not found

nros (codegen tool) not found on PATH or in packages/cli/target/release/
or ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/bin. …

(The rest of the message names how a contributor builds the CLI from a checkout; as a user you install it instead.)

The nros binary is not installed, or not on PATH. Install a release and put ~/.nros/bin on PATH:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.nros/bin:$PATH"

If ~/.nros/bin/nros exists but PATH doesn’t see it — that’s the [PATH] doctor status (D2 below), not this branch.

The nros binary ships the codegen — there is no separate nros-codegen build step. CMake projects auto-resolve nros from PATH / ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/bin/; -D_NANO_ROS_CODEGEN_TOOL=<path> is an override, not a requirement.

A3. Rust target not installed

error: could not compile … due to previous error
the target `thumbv7m-none-eabi` is not installed

Add it:

rustup target add thumbv7m-none-eabi

The triple is the board’s, not the example’s — you will not find it in any file you wrote. Read it back from the [build] target line of the generated nros-cargo.toml under build/, which nros build writes from the board your bringup’s system.toml names.

A4. Cross linker not found

error: linker `arm-none-eabi-gcc` not found

The cross toolchain wasn’t provisioned. Run nros setup for your board (it ships a prebuilt arm-none-eabi-gcc):

nros setup mps2-an385-freertos       # or qemu-armv7a-nuttx / mps2-an385-baremetal / …

A5. Cyclone DDS runtime missing

ld: cannot find -lddsc
ld: cannot find -lcyclonedds-ddsc

The Cyclone DDS runtime wasn’t provisioned:

nros setup linux --rmw cyclonedds

A6. cargo build --features rmw-cyclonedds can’t link

undefined reference to `nros_rmw_cyclonedds_register`
undefined reference to `dds_create_participant`

rmw-cyclonedds cannot link from cargo alone — the Cyclone backend is C++ + CMake, registered via nros_rmw_cffi_register_named from a CMake-built target — wired through CMakeLists.txt + Corrosion. Use the cmake build path instead, and choose the backend where backends are chosen: [system] rmw in the bringup’s system.toml.

[system]
rmw = "cyclonedds"

cd my_ws                          # a workspace with C or C++ node packages
nros build

There is no -DNROS_RMW= to pass: a backend selected on the command line disagrees with the one the rest of the build resolves from system.toml.

A Rust node package does not take --features rmw-cyclonedds at all: its RMW is its image’s. A bringup that declares a linux_cyclonedds image (as examples/linux/rust/talker does) builds it with nros build linux_cyclonedds — the board crate’s rmw-cyclonedds builds Cyclone through nros-rmw-cyclonedds-sys.

A7. The board name is a typo

…/system.toml: board `mps2-an358` is claimed by no board descriptor under /…/nano-ros

[image.<id>] board is where a bringup names its board, and a typo there is refused by name rather than guessed at. The legal spellings are the names = [...] arrays of the board descriptors, one per board crate at packages/boards/*/nros-board.toml; several are aliases for the same board (mps2-an385-baremetal, baremetal and bare-metal all name one descriptor).

The neighbouring refusals, when the image is missing rather than misspelt:

this workspace declares no `[image.*]`. An image is the buildable unit: add `[image.<id>] board = "<board>"` to system.toml.
…/system.toml: names no board; add `[image.<id>] board = "<board>"`

The first means no bringup in the workspace has a system.toml with an image, so there is nothing for nros build to plan. The second means the file is there and its [image.<id>] table has no board key.

A8. system.toml next to code

nros build refuses a system.toml in a directory that also holds a Cargo.toml or a CMakeLists.txt. A system.toml belongs to a bringup package, never to the package with the code, because it says where that code runs and the code itself must not.

To fix it, give the configuration its own package:

  1. Make src/<pkg>_bringup/ beside your node package, with a package.xml.
  2. Move system.toml into it.
  3. Delete any main that only starts the node; the entry is generated.

nros new <ws> --board <board> --template talker writes this shape, so a scaffolded project never hits it.

A9. direnv allow reminder

NROS_PLATFORM_CFFI_INCLUDE not set (direnv allow, or build via just)
FREERTOS_PORT not set

(The quoted message is emitted by the build script; “direnv allow” and “build via just” in it refer to a contributor checkout.) nros build passes these to cargo from the board’s settings, so a build driven by nros build — or by cargo with the generated --config file — does not hit it. If a cargo command you drive yourself does, you skipped the --config build/<image>/nros-cargo.toml argument.

A10. AMENT_PREFIX_PATH is unset

nros build, nros run or nros configure stops before building anything:

Error: configure: `AMENT_PREFIX_PATH` is unset and no configure of `/home/you/sensor_ws` has recorded one to reuse. Run the setup step once from a shell that has ROS 2: `source /opt/ros/<distro>/setup.bash` (or your overlay's `install/setup.bash`), then `nros configure`; later runs without a sourced shell reuse what it records.

The project has messages to generate (every talker uses std_msgs), and nano-ros generates them from the message definitions of your ROS 2 install, so the types and their hashes match your ROS 2 peers. This shell has not sourced ROS 2, and no earlier configure of the project ran in one that had. It happens on every board and every RMW, Linux and Cyclone DDS included.

Source ROS 2 once, in this shell, and run the same command again:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash   # or your overlay's install/setup.bash
nros build

That configure records the prefix in the project. Later builds and runs of the same project reuse it, from any shell, an IDE or a CI step. A new project records its own, so its first build needs a sourced shell again.

B. Binary runs but no output

B1. Rust: RMW session open failed — Transport(ConnectionFailed)

[ERROR nros] RMW session open failed — Transport(ConnectionFailed)

The zenoh router isn’t running, or isn’t reachable on the locator the talker is pointed at. The router comes from ROS 2 (nano-ros no longer ships one) — start it in another terminal:

ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/127.0.0.1:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd

Default ports: tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 on POSIX, tcp/10.0.2.2:7451 on QEMU FreeRTOS (Slirp forwards to host), 7452 NuttX, 7453 ThreadX-RV, 7454 ESP32, 7455 ThreadX-Linux, 7447 Zephyr.

B2. C: RCLC_CHECK failed: rclc_support_init(...) -> -4

RCLC_CHECK failed at src/main.c:92: rclc_support_init(&app.support, argc, argv, &allocator) -> -4

Process exits 1 (the retval passed to RCLC_CHECK_RET). -4 = RCLC_RET_NOT_FOUND — the locator was unreachable (zenohd not running, or wrong port). Same fix as B1 above.

The C API entry point is rclc_support_init (rclc’s (&support, argc, argv, &allocator)) or, with an explicit locator, rclc_support_init_with_locator — not nros_init or nros::init, which don’t exist in the C API.

B3. C++: process exits 156 after a rclcpp::init_in failure

nros::init returned NROS_CPP_RET_TRANSPORT_ERROR (-100)

Same root cause as B1/B2 — zenohd not reachable. NROS_CPP_RET_TRANSPORT_ERROR = -100 is the C++ result code that RCLCPP_TRY_RET propagates from main(); on POSIX this becomes (unsigned char)-100 = 156 as the process exit code. Treat “exited 156 after starting” as the C++ equivalent of B1.

B4. Override the locator at runtime

When a native talker can’t reach the daemon, override the locator with the canonical env var:

NROS_LOCATOR=tcp/192.168.1.50:7447 ./build/c_talker
ROS_DOMAIN_ID=7 ./build/c_talker         # also overridable

The native Rust / C / C++ talkers all read NROS_LOCATOR, then fall back to the build-time default. The retired ZENOH_LOCATOR / ZENOH_MODE are REFUSED at startup with an error naming NROS_LOCATOR / NROS_SESSION_MODE — unset them. Embedded targets have no runtime env — their locator is compile-baked from system.toml ([image.<id>] locator, or [system] locator for an image that does not state one), so editing that file and rebuilding is the override.

B5. Binary exits immediately, no error printed

Buffering: setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IOLBF, 0) if you piped the run. POSIX terminals flush on newline; piped stdout full-buffers and may eat short outputs. Add a RUST_LOG=info (Rust) or unbuffer the C / C++ output (stdbuf -oL).

C. ROS 2 side sees nothing

C1. RMW mismatch

# On the ROS 2 side, default rmw_fastrtps_cpp will NOT see nano-ros:
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp     # for Zenoh
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp # for Cyclone

C2. QoS mismatch — echo silent, list sees the topic

ros2 topic list           # /chatter shown
ros2 topic echo /chatter  # … nothing

nano-ros publishers default to BEST_EFFORT; stock ros2 topic echo defaults to RELIABLE. The QoS-mismatched subscriber is created but receives no data. Force best-effort on the echo:

ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

D. Doctor + last-resort

D1. Run the doctor first

nros doctor

It prints fixit hints for the toolchain you actually need. (A just-free platform-scoped doctor spelling does not exist today; contributors with an in-tree checkout can scope via the platform recipes.)

D2. [PATH] nros built but not on PATH

The doctor reports this distinct from [MISSING] when the binary is installed at ${NROS_HOME:-~/.nros}/bin/nros but PATH doesn’t see it. Put the directory on PATH (and in your shell’s startup file):

export PATH="$HOME/.nros/bin:$PATH"

D3. Full sweep (slow)

nros doctor
nros setup --check

Only run this when you’re standing up every supported platform in one go. It walks the provisioning checks and can take a few minutes.

D4. File an issue

When all else fails, include:

  • the exact command you ran,
  • the full stderr,
  • rustc --version, cmake --version, qemu-system-arm --version,
  • nros --version.

E. zenoh-pico error codes

CodeNameMeaning
-102_Z_ERR_TRANSPORT_OPEN_FAILEDcould not connect to the router
-73_Z_ERR_SESSION_CLOSEDthe session closed after an earlier failure
-78_Z_ERR_SYSTEM_OUT_OF_MEMORYan allocation did not fit
-100_Z_ERR_TRANSPORT_TX_FAILEDa transmission failed
-128_Z_ERR_GENERICa generic error

The full list is zenoh-pico’s include/zenoh-pico/utils/result.h. Fixes by symptom are in Troubleshoot.

What success looks like

A correctly-running Rust Linux talker (examples/linux/rust/talker) prints something like this on stderr (with RUST_LOG=info):

[INFO  talker] Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
[INFO  talker] Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
[INFO  talker] Publishing: 'Hello World: 3'

(That is the full expected output — the talker logs one line per publish, nothing else.)

A correctly-running C talker (examples/linux/c/talker) prints on stdout:

Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 3'

A correctly-running C++ talker prints the same Publishing: 'Hello World: N' line once per second.

The ROS 2 side (ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort with RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp) should see:

data: 'Hello World: 1'
---
data: 'Hello World: 2'
---
data: 'Hello World: 3'
---

If you see all three of these — talker logging, ROS 2 echo output, and matching counter values — interop is verified end-to-end.

Glossary

Reference · Level 3: Production and tuning

The nano-ros terms this book uses, each in a sentence or two taken from the page that explains it, with a link to that page. A term ROS 2 uses the same way (node, topic, QoS, launch file) is not listed; see the ROS 2 documentation.

TermMeaningExplained in
board descriptorThe board package’s nros-board.toml: the facts true of every copy of a board, such as its name, platform, target triple and how it boots, and its [knobs].How a build becomes an image
board packageThe layer that joins a platform to real hardware: it brings up the clock, the network interface and its drivers, and provides the entry point that starts the scheduler or the main loop.How a build becomes an image
board registryThe one place a board’s facts and support evidence are recorded. The board pages, the support levels and their status words are generated from it.Board Support Levels
bringup packageSays what runs and where. It holds a package.xml and a system.toml, and optionally launch/ and config/; it has no Cargo.toml, no CMakeLists.txt and no code.Organize a larger workspace
censusThe host image generated from a launch file, run once in census mode: it constructs every component against a recording backend and writes what they created. The configure compares it with the contract row by row.Contracts for a C or C++ workspace
command packageAn ordinary package in your workspace, with a package.xml and a small descriptor, that adds a verb to nros. nros help --all lists each extension verb with the package that provides it.Extending overview
componentA [[component]] row in system.toml: which node package runs in the bringup.Add a second node
contractThe <stem>.contract.yaml beside a launch file (or system.contract.yaml in a bringup with no launch/) that states what the image creates, ahead of the build. The build sizes the image’s pools from it.Contract format reference
generated entryThe program’s entry (its main()), which nros build and nros run generate under build/ for each [image.*] block, so there is no package to write for it.Grow your workspace
hostA [host.<name>] block in system.toml: which machine a node runs on, with launch and nodes keys. An image needs no host, and a host needs no image.Organize a larger workspace
imageOne program: the bringup’s nodes, built for one board with one RMW. It is an [image.<id>] block in system.toml, not a package.Grow your workspace
knobA build-time setting, such as a pool size, set on the image ([image.<id>.knobs.<group>]), by the board descriptor’s [knobs], or by an exported variable. nros config explain prints each knob’s value and which rung set it.Configure an image
levelA rank the build derives from the contract: each node’s rank comes from its trigger rate, and each distinct rank is one level, up to a cap that depends on the platform.The execution model
linkHow an image’s middleware reaches the rest of the system. nros reads it, with the launcher or flasher and the console, from the board’s descriptor.Deploy to production
locatorThe address an image dials. On zenoh it is the only thing a board needs to find the router.Configure zenoh
materializenros materialize copies an image’s generated entry into src/<image>_entry/; from then on nros build uses your copy and does not regenerate it. The last resort.Grow your workspace
node packageA library that says what a node does: its publishers, subscriptions, timers and callbacks. It has no main(), no board and no deployment settings, so one node package runs on every board.Organize a larger workspace
runner packageAn ordinary package in your workspace that teaches nros run, nros flash and nros monitor to drive a launcher, flasher or console nano-ros does not ship a runner for.Extending overview
sched taskOne executor on one RTOS thread, with its own priority and spin period. All of an image’s sched tasks share one middleware session; parallelism is a sched task, not a callback group.Pick a scheduling model
static poolAn array of slots, carved at build time, that holds the runtime’s entities with no allocator. Every slot costs its bytes whether an entity uses it or not, so each pool is sized from what the image declares.Static memory and pools
status wordA board’s support level, derived from evidence and never typed: where the board’s image runs, how often that run happens, and which board’s test matrix stands for its breadth. The words and what each means are listed on the generated support-levels page.Board Support Levels
twinAn emulated model of a real board. A board with a hardware twin runs the same firmware in an emulator first and then on the board.Welcome
witnessA board that runs its platform family’s test matrix. A board that inherits shares the witness’s code path and adds its own smoke evidence.Board Support Levels

Per-RMW Feature Matrix

One table per question the capability pages used to answer in contradictory prose. Derived from the backend sources — the C vtables (vtable.c (XRCE-DDS), vtable.cpp (Cyclone DDS), vtable.cpp (uORB)) and the zenoh shim’s trait overrides — so a backend gaining or losing a slot moves this page in the same commit or fails the gate.

wired = the backend implements it. — = not wired: the runtime surfaces UNSUPPORTED or falls back where a fallback exists (the vtable comments name which). A slot filled with a function that only returns UNSUPPORTED (uORB’s service stubs) is —, not wired. Status events count as wired whether the backend calls back (*_event_init) or the runtime polls it (*_take_event). The rows below the parity marker are slots declared in the ABI whose backend wiring is still landing; all-dash rows there mean declared, not yet wired anywhere, and they flip automatically as backends land implementations.

Node-layer features

These live in nros-node on top of pub/sub + services — they are not backend slots, so a backend has them exactly when it has those. tested = at least one Runtime cell for that backend and workload in matrix::CELLS or interop::CELLS (packages/testing/nros-tests/src/); untested = available, but no runtime cell runs it; — = the backend lacks pub/sub or services, so the feature cannot exist there.

QoS policies

A backend advertises the policies it can enforce via supported_qos_policies(); requesting an unadvertised policy fails entity creation loudly (INCOMPATIBLE_QOS) — no silent downgrade. Each column is that backend’s OWN answer: the zenoh shim’s Session::supported_qos_policies, and for a C backend the function its vtable puts in the supported_qos_policies slot. Scheduling Wiring Matrix

Which scheduling capabilities nano-ros delivers per platform, and which portable executor classes are live in dispatch — derived from the two artifacts the runtime executes, not from prose. The per-platform rows are parsed from sched_caps_for() (nros-orchestration-ir), the exact function the workload realizer calls to decide Native-vs-Degrade for a deployment; its rule, quoted from the source: caps describe what nano-ros DELIVERS, not what the OS could do.

Kernel capabilities per platform

PlatformKernel EDFReservation / sporadic serverPreemption thresholdSMP affinityPriority levelsLow number = high priority
Linux host———✓99—
Zephyr✓——✓32✓
FreeRTOS———✓16—
ThreadX——✓✓32✓
NuttX—✓—✓255—
Bare-metal (NVIC)————8—

Notes carried from the source arms: the Linux row is deliberately conservative — no SCHED_DEADLINE consumer exists, so edf is false even though Linux could; its affinity is sched_setaffinity, which is Linux and not POSIX (absent from libc’s apple module), so the row’s reach is linux while the platform layer beneath it stays posix; Zephyr’s EDF is CONFIG_SCHED_DEADLINE; NuttX’s reservation is POSIX SCHED_SPORADIC; ThreadX’s preemption threshold is native; the bare-metal row is NVIC hardware priorities, single core. These are PLATFORM DEFAULTS and there is no per-image override today. ([deploy.<board>] edf / cores, documented in older releases, never took effect and is retired.)

Portable executor classes (SchedClass)

These run inside the executor on every platform — they need no kernel support, which is what makes them portable; where the kernel HAS the native capability (table above), the realizer places the workload natively instead. “Dispatch sites” counts SchedClass::<X> references in the executor’s spin path — a class with zero sites is a type, not a behavior.

ClassDispatch sites in spin.rsStatus
Fifo3Live — the default class; bucketed FIFO ready-set.
Edf2Live — earliest-deadline-first ready-set ordering.
Sporadic6Live — budget/period enforcement in dispatch.

Canonical interface contract. What “Yes” / “—” / specific functions mean — buffer ownership, blocking allowance, valid value ranges — is in the platform-cffi Doxygen reference. This page is a comparison table, not a spec.

Behaviour notes by trait group

Time (PlatformClock)

All ports surface a monotonic clock. Resolution varies:

  • POSIX / NuttX: nanosecond-resolution clock_gettime, exposed at ms + µs.
  • FreeRTOS: xTaskGetTickCount ticks (typically 1 ms). clock_us = clock_ms × 1000 — the resolution lie is documented.
  • Zephyr: k_uptime_get ms + k_cyc_to_us_floor64(k_cycle_get_64()) µs.
  • ThreadX: tx_time_get ticks (default 100 Hz; bump via TX_TIMER_TICKS_PER_SECOND for finer resolution).
  • Bare-metal (Cortex-M): hardware timer counter (CMSDK Timer0, DWT cycle counter). µs is the native resolution; ms is µs / 1000.

The clock is monotonic and wraparound-free from init to shutdown. Platforms with 32-bit timers run a software extender on overflow.

Memory (PlatformAlloc)

Only zenoh-pico calls PlatformAlloc::{alloc, realloc, free}. XRCE-DDS does not allocate. Recommended heap budget: 64 KB minimum for zenoh-pico’s working set; bare-metal ports typically allocate 128 KB+ via a bump allocator (linked-list-allocator or embedded-alloc).

The RTOS allocators (pvPortMalloc, tx_byte_allocate, k_malloc, libc malloc) honour their respective heap-region configurations. On bare-metal the heap region is defined in the linker script and consumed at startup by the bump allocator.

Threading (PlatformThreading)

Multi-threaded ports (POSIX, NuttX, FreeRTOS, Zephyr, ThreadX) expose real tasks, mutexes, and condition variables. zenoh-pico’s lease task and read task spawn into these. Single-threaded bare-metal ports stub task_init to return -1 so the spawn fails gracefully; the application drives spin_once from a single context.

Recursive mutexes are required by zenoh-pico. FreeRTOS uses xSemaphoreCreateRecursiveMutex; ThreadX uses tx_mutex_create(..., TX_INHERIT, ...); POSIX uses PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE.

Sleep / Random / Wall-time (PlatformSleep, PlatformRandom, PlatformTime)

PlatformSleep on RTOS ports uses the kernel’s tickless sleep (vTaskDelay, tx_thread_sleep, k_msleep, libc usleep). On bare-metal with smoltcp, the sleep helper also runs network_poll() in a busy loop — packets must keep flowing during otherwise-idle waits or the zenoh lease times out.

PlatformRandom is a 32-bit xorshift PRNG seeded with hardware entropy (getrandom, RNG peripheral) or a build-time constant on platforms without entropy. Used for session IDs and protocol nonces; not cryptographic.

PlatformTime returns wall-clock for log timestamps. Bare-metal platforms with no RTC fall back to the monotonic clock — log timestamps then count from boot, not Unix epoch.

Networking (PlatformTcp, PlatformUdp, PlatformSocketHelpers, PlatformUdpMulticast, PlatformNetworkPoll)

The split into four traits maps directly onto zenoh-pico’s unix/network.c interface. Each port wires the four traits independently:

  • C-backed networking (NuttX, ThreadX): the platform shim forwards into zenoh-pico’s bundled unix/network.c (NuttX) or a NetX-Duo equivalent (ThreadX) — the C code talks to BSD-shape sockets directly.
  • Rust-backed networking (POSIX, FreeRTOS, Zephyr, bare-metal): the platform crate implements TCP / UDP in Rust. POSIX wraps libc, FreeRTOS wraps lwIP via freertos-lwip-sys, Zephyr wraps the POSIX layer, bare-metal goes through nros-smoltcp.

PlatformUdpMulticast (RTPS SPDP, zenoh scouting) ships fully wired on POSIX, NuttX, Zephyr, and bare-metal (smoltcp 0.12 IGMP group join). FreeRTOS and ThreadX have no multicast yet — gated by lwIP’s IGMP=1 (untested) and NetX Duo’s nx_igmp_* (untested).

PlatformNetworkPoll is bare-metal only. The implementation advances the smoltcp state machine; without it, smoltcp would only receive when the application explicitly asked. PlatformSleep and the wait_event helper both run network_poll() while waiting so packets continue flowing.

Libc (PlatformLibc)

zenoh-pico uses strlen, memcpy, errno, etc. directly. Bare-metal targets that link picolibc or newlib-nano satisfy these for free; the trait exists for no_std targets without a C runtime, which forward to Rust implementations.

Logging (nros-log)

Where a log record goes, by the platform linked into the image:

TargetDelivery
POSIXfprintf(stderr, "[<LEVEL>] <name>: <msg>\n")
ZephyrLOG_INF, LOG_WRN and so on, in module nros (printk if CONFIG_LOG=n)
NuttXsyslog(priority, "%s", buf)
FreeRTOS, ThreadXa UART writer the board registers with nros_platform_register_log_writer at run()
Bare metal (MPS2-AN385)QEMU semihosting, hstderr
Bare metal (STM32F4)defmt::info!("{=str}", msg)

Severities, as the nros_platform_log_write ABI numbers them. They are not rcutils_log_severity_t’s numbers, and there is no Unset level in Rust (Logger::unset_level() is the “no level of its own” state). The C surface’s rcl_log_severity_t uses rcutils’s numbers, UNSET included.

SeverityValueUse
Trace0per-instruction detail; compiled out unless the ceiling allows it
Debug1diagnostics while developing
Info2normal events worth one line; the process default
Warn3unexpected but recoverable
Error4errors the caller surfaces; the system continues
Fatal5unrecoverable; the system is about to stop

The log crate bridge (nros-log/log-compat) maps Trace, Debug, Info, Warn and Error both ways, and Fatal to log’s Error one way.

What nano-ros can show for each board it knows about. Each level is derived from evidence, never typed: where the board’s image runs (on a host, in an emulator, on hardware, or nowhere yet), how often that run happens (every merge, daily, weekly, or by hand on a date) and which board’s test matrix stands for its breadth.

StatusWhat it means
Verified on host / in emulator / on hardware (cadence)an automated lane boots it and asserts a message, at that cadence
Boots, manual (date)a maintainer booted it by hand on that date; after 120 days it reads Builds until booted again
Buildsa lane builds it; nothing boots it
Not supportednothing builds or boots it

A witness board runs its platform family’s test matrix; a board that inherits shares the witness’s code path and adds its own smoke evidence. Each board links to its evidence page.

Porting Overview

Explanation · Level 4: Extending nano-ros

nano-ros is designed for customization at three independent levels: RMW (transport protocol), Platform (OS or RTOS), and Board (hardware). The core crates define stable interfaces through Rust traits; your implementation lives in your own crates. Be aware of the honest boundary: a board of yours can live in your own tree (NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATH), but registering a new platform still touches a handful of files inside nano-ros itself (the registration steps below) — that is a fork, built the way Contributing describes.

Which chapter do I need?

I want to…Chapter
Add a new transport protocol (MQTT, DDS, custom)Custom RMW Backend
Port to a new RTOS or bare-metal targetCustom Platform
Bring up nano-ros on a new MCU boardCustom Board Package

Most porting work falls into the second or third category. Adding a new RMW backend is rare and substantially more involved.

Quickstart — 2 crates + 2 tomls

Scaffold the two packages, fill in the TODOs:

nros new platform myrtos                       # nros-platform-myrtos/ + nros-platform.toml
nros new board myboard --for-platform myrtos   # nros-board-myboard/  + nros-board.toml
  • nros-platform.toml (platform package) — software-stack facts ([capabilities]), knob defaults ([knobs.*], only flip what you measured), and what any vendored C build on the platform needs (top-level arch_profiles, compile, required_env). How zenoh-pico builds there is a [port.<platform>] row in the zenoh backend’s own nros-rmw.toml, not part of the platform file. An empty file is valid: built-in defaults always produce a working build.
  • nros-board.toml (board package) — the hardware descriptor plus per-board [capabilities]/[knobs] deltas.
  • Values resolve through a fixed ladder — builtin < platform < board < env/Kconfig/-D — and an explicit build-time setting (including an explicit 0/n) always wins. Debug any knob with:
nros config explain --platform myrtos [--board-toml path/to/nros-board.toml]
# knob                     value      set by
# zenoh.tx.batch           false      builtin

Kconfig appears only where the host framework is Kconfig-native (the Zephyr and NuttX packagings) — a hand-wired fragment whose defaults mirror the platform toml (drift-tested). A port to a non-Kconfig RTOS never touches it.

What stays untouched

The following core packages define the interfaces you implement. They compile and work without modification for any new target.

PackageRole
nrosFacade crate: re-exports and feature-axis enforcement
nros-coreMessage, service, and action type traits
nros-serdesCDR serialization
nros-nodeExecutor, Node, pub/sub/service/action handles
nros-rmwRMW trait definitions (Session, Publisher, Subscriber, etc.)
nros-platformPlatform trait definitions and ConcretePlatform type alias
zpico-sys alias TUMaps zenoh-pico z_* C symbols to nros_platform_* (default-on platform-aliases)
nros-rmw-xrce alias TUMaps XRCE-DDS uxr_* C symbols to nros_platform_*
nros-c, nros-cppC and C++ API wrappers

These define the interfaces. You implement them; you do not modify them.

The customization boundary

Everything in nano-ros sits on one side of a trait boundary defined in nros-platform/src/traits.rs.

Above the boundary (yours to write): board crates, platform crates, peripheral drivers, and application code.

Below the boundary (fixed): RMW backends, shim crates, core library, executor, and serialization.

Your platform crate implements traits as inherent methods on a zero-sized type. The shim crates automatically forward RMW-layer C symbols to your implementation through the ConcretePlatform type alias – no dynamic dispatch, no generics propagation.

Platform trait requirements by RMW backend

Not every trait is required. The set depends on which RMW backend the application uses.

Traitzenoh-picoXRCE-DDS
PlatformClockRequiredRequired
PlatformAllocRequired (~64 KB heap)Not needed
PlatformSleepRequiredNot needed
PlatformRandomRequiredNot needed
PlatformTimeRequiredNot needed
PlatformThreadingRequired (multi-threaded platforms)Not needed
PlatformTcpRequiredNot needed
PlatformUdpRequiredNot needed
PlatformSocketHelpersRequiredNot needed
PlatformNetworkPollBare-metal onlyNot needed
PlatformUdpMulticastDesktop platforms onlyNot needed
PlatformLibcBare-metal onlyNot needed

XRCE-DDS is significantly simpler to port: it is single-threaded, allocates only when a session or entity is created (nothing per message), and uses user-provided transport callbacks rather than a full socket API. A minimal XRCE-DDS port requires only PlatformClock and four C function pointers (open, close, read, write).

zenoh-pico requires a complete platform implementation but provides richer functionality (peer-to-peer, scouting, zero-copy receive, actions).

Registration

After implementing the required traits, you register your platform with two changes:

  1. Add a platform-<name> feature to nros-platform/Cargo.toml that pulls in your crate as an optional dependency.
  2. Add a ConcretePlatform type alias in nros-platform/src/resolve.rs gated by that feature.

The shim crates pick up the new platform automatically. No changes to RMW backends or core crates are needed.

Existing platform implementations

These serve as reference when writing a new port.

Platform crateTargetThreadingNetworking
nros-platform-posixLinux, *BSDpthreadslibc BSD sockets
nros-platform-freertosFreeRTOSFreeRTOS taskslwIP
nros-platform-nuttxNuttXpthreadsPOSIX sockets
nros-platform-threadxThreadXThreadX threadsNetX Duo
nros-platform-zephyrZephyrZephyr POSIXZephyr sockets
nros-platform-mps2-an385Cortex-M3 bare-metalSingle-threadedsmoltcp
nros-platform-stm32f4STM32F4 bare-metalSingle-threadedsmoltcp

Runner packages

A runner package teaches nros run, nros flash and nros monitor to drive a launcher, flasher or console that nano-ros does not ship a runner for. It is an ordinary package in your workspace, with a package.xml and a small descriptor, built for the host by nros build.

Command packages

A command package adds a verb to nros. It is an ordinary package in your workspace, with a package.xml and a small descriptor, built for the host by nros build. nros help --all lists each extension verb with the package that provides it.

A verb nros does not know is looked up as an announced command package (<nano_ros_provides kind="command" name="<verb>"/>). The command runs with NROS_WS_ROOT, NROS_TOOLCHAIN and NROS_CLI set, and its exit status is nros’s. A package announcing a built-in verb is refused.
